question_text: Northgate Savings Bank is a federally chartered savings association that converted to a state-chartered savings bank three years ago and is now organized as a bank holding company with its primary regulator being the Federal Reserve Board. The holding company has total consolidated assets of $38 billion and operates exclusively within the United States. It does not file form FR Y-9C or form FR Q-1. The holding company's legal counsel is advising the board of directors on whether the Federal Reserve's capital adequacy rules apply to this entity and, if so, what specific capital calculations the holding company must perform. Identify whether this holding company is subject to the Federal Reserve's minimum capital requirements, and enumerate each category of capital calculation it must perform under those requirements.
required_facts: Northgate qualifies as a Board-regulated institution because it is a bank holding company domiciled in the United States not subject to 12 CFR part 225, appendix C
As a Board-regulated institution, Northgate must calculate minimum capital requirements and meet overall capital adequacy standards under subpart B
Northgate must calculate its regulatory capital in accordance with subpart C
Northgate must calculate standardized total risk-weighted assets using subpart D methodologies
Northgate is not required to make the subpart D public disclosures because its total consolidated assets of $38 billion are below the $50 billion threshold
The advanced approaches risk-weighted asset calculation under subpart E does not apply because Northgate is not identified as an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Determine applicability under §217.1(c)(1), then enumerate required calculations under §217.1(c)(2)–(5)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Applicability: §217.1(c)(1)(i) lists three categories of Board-regulated institutions. Northgate converted from a savings association to a state-chartered savings bank and is now organized as a bank holding company. A bank holding company domiciled in the United States that is not subject to 12 CFR part 225, appendix C qualifies under §217.1(c)(1)(i)(B). Nothing in the facts indicates it is subject to appendix C, so it is a Board-regulated institution. Step 2 — Minimum capital requirements: §217.1(c)(2) requires each Board-regulated institution to calculate minimum capital requirements and meet overall capital adequacy standards in subpart B. Step 3 — Regulatory capital: §217.1(c)(3) requires calculation of regulatory capital per subpart C. Step 4 — Risk-weighted assets: §217.1(c)(4)(i) requires use of subpart D methodologies to calculate standardized total risk-weighted assets. Because the institution is not identified as an advanced approaches institution, §217.1(c)(4)(ii) does not apply. Step 5 — Disclosures: §217.1(c)(5)(i) requires public disclosures under subpart D only for Board-regulated institutions with total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more. At $38 billion, Northgate falls below this threshold and is not required to make those disclosures. The instruction note in §217.1(c)(1)(i)(C) regarding FR Y-9C/FR Q-1 filers applies to savings and loan holding companies, not bank holding companies, so it is inapplicable here.

scenario_parameters.institution_type: bank holding company (converted from savings association)

question_text: Midwest Community Bancshares is a state member bank supervised by the Federal Reserve. At the end of its most recent quarter, the bank reported total assets of $18.4 billion on its Call Report. Its trading assets stood at $1.6 billion and trading liabilities at $0.3 billion, for a combined trading book of $1.9 billion. The bank's chief risk officer is evaluating whether the institution must comply with the market risk capital framework applicable to Board-regulated institutions with significant trading activity. Separately, the Board has informally indicated that it is considering whether to apply the market risk framework to a peer institution, Lakefront Savings Bank, which has trading assets and liabilities totaling only $420 million and representing 4.2 percent of its quarter-end total assets, but whose derivatives portfolio has recently drawn supervisory concern. Determine: (1) whether Midwest Community Bancshares is subject to the market risk capital requirements based on its reported figures, identifying which threshold(s) it meets or exceeds; and (2) whether the Board has any authority to subject Lakefront Savings Bank to the same market risk capital framework despite Lakefront not meeting either standard numeric threshold, and if so, under what circumstances.
required_facts: Midwest's aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities total $1.9 billion ($1.6B + $0.3B)
Midwest meets the dollar threshold: $1.9 billion is equal to or greater than $1 billion
Midwest meets the percentage threshold: $1.9B / $18.4B ≈ 10.33%, which equals or exceeds 10% of quarter-end total assets
Midwest is subject to the market risk capital framework because it satisfies both numeric prongs independently
Lakefront fails both numeric thresholds: $420M is below $1B and 4.2% is below 10%

The Board retains discretionary authority to apply the market risk framework to Lakefront if it deems it necessary or appropriate due to the institution's level of market risk or to ensure safe and sound banking practices
No numeric threshold must be met for the Board to exercise its discretionary authority to extend applicability

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the two-prong applicability threshold in §217.201(b)(1) to Midwest's figures, then assess the Board's discretionary authority under §217.201(b)(2) for Lakefront.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Midwest Community Bancshares threshold check under §217.201(b)(1): Aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities = $1.6B + $0.3B = $1.9B. Prong (i): $1.9B / $18.4B = 10.33%, which equals or exceeds the 10% of quarter-end total assets threshold. Prong (ii): $1.9B ≥ $1 billion threshold. Midwest meets BOTH prongs independently; either one alone would trigger applicability. Therefore Midwest is subject to the market risk capital subpart. Step 2 — Lakefront Savings Bank discretionary authority under §217.201(b)(2): Lakefront's trading book is $420M (below $1B) and represents 4.2% of total assets (below 10%), so it fails both numeric prongs of §217.201(b)(1) and is not automatically subject to the subpart. However, §217.201(b)(2) grants the Board discretionary authority to apply the subpart to any Board-regulated institution if the Board deems it necessary or appropriate because of the level of market risk of that institution or to ensure safe and sound banking practices. The Board's supervisory concern about Lakefront's derivatives portfolio could constitute a basis for exercising this authority. No numeric threshold needs to be met for the Board to invoke §217.201(b)(2).

question_text: Heartland Mutual Holdings is a top-tier depository institution holding company that is part of a supervised insurance organization. At the close of the prior calendar year, the company's building block available capital (BBAC) stood at $4.80 billion, and its minimum required BBAC under the applicable capital framework was $4.20 billion, producing a BBA ratio of 114.3 percent against the minimum requirement. During the current calendar year, Heartland's BBAC as of December 31 of the current year is $4.95 billion, while its BBAC as of December 31 of the prior year was $4.80 billion. The company issued $60 million of new qualifying capital instruments during the current year (none of which replaced retired instruments), and paid $30 million in dividends on tier 1 capital instruments during the year. No capital instruments were issued in the immediately preceding calendar year. Management is now evaluating whether the company may declare an additional $50 million discretionary bonus payment to senior executives before year-end. Determine whether Heartland may make this additional discretionary bonus payment, and if so, whether any cap applies to the aggregate distributions and discretionary bonus payments for the current calendar year.
required_facts: Capital conservation buffer = max(114.3% - 250%, 0) = 0%; this still falls in the 'less than or equal to 38 percent' Table 1 tier.
Eligible retained income = annual change in BBAC ($150M) minus distributions ($30M) minus new capital instrument issuances in current year ($60M) = $60 million (positive)
Maximum payout amount = eligible retained income ($60M) × maximum payout ratio (0%) = $0
The outright prohibition on distributions does not apply because eligible retained income is positive ($60M > $0)
Heartland may not make the additional $50M discretionary bonus payment under the standard rules; only a Board-approved exception under the safety-and-soundness waiver provision could permit it

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Compute capital conservation buffer from BBA ratio vs. minimum under §217.604(a)(3); look up maximum payout ratio from Table 1; compute eligible retained income under §217.604(a)(2)(ii); compute maximum payout amount under §217.604(a)(2)(iii); apply limit under §217.604(a)(4)(i) and check exemption under §217.604(a)(4)(ii)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Capital conservation buffer [§217.604(a)(3)]: Buffer = BBA ratio minus minimum capital requirement = 114.3% − 100% = 14.3 percentage points. The regulation states the buffer is the greater of (BBA ratio − minimum requirement) and zero, so buffer = 14.3%. Expressed as a percentage of the minimum, this is 114.3% − 100% = 14.3 percentage points above the floor. However, Table 1 uses the buffer itself (not the ratio) as the comparator. The minimum capital requirement under §217.603(c) is 100% of the required BBAC. The BBA ratio is 114.3%, so the capital conservation buffer = 114.3% − 100% = 14.3%. Wait — Table 1 thresholds are expressed as percentages (e.g., 'greater than 150 percent'). The buffer here is 14.3 percent (i.e., 14.3 percentage points above the minimum), which is less than or equal to 38 percent. Therefore the maximum payout ratio = 0 percent per Table 1. Step 2 — Eligible retained income [§217.604(a)(2)(ii)]: Annual change in BBAC = $4.95B − $4.80B = $150 million. Net of distributions: subtract $30M dividends paid. Net of accretion from new capital instruments issued in current or preceding year (excluding retirements): subtract $60M new issuances. Eligible retained income = $150M − $30M − $60M = $60 million (positive). Step 3 — Maximum payout amount [§217.604(a)(2)(iii)]: Maximum payout amount = eligible retained income × maximum payout ratio = $60M × 0% = $0. Step 4 — Check exemption [§217.604(a)(4)(ii)]: The exemption from the maximum payout cap applies only if the capital conservation buffer is greater than 150 percent. Heartland's buffer is 14.3%, which is not greater than 150%. Exemption does not apply. Step 5 — Check prohibition [§217.604(a)(4)(iii)]: Eligible retained income is positive ($60M), so the outright prohibition under (a)(4)(iii) (which requires both negative eligible retained income AND buffer < 150%) does not apply. Step 6 — Conclusion: Heartland is subject to a maximum payout amount of $0 for the current calendar year. The $30M in dividends already paid exceeds $0, meaning the company has already exceeded its maximum payout amount. The additional $50M discretionary bonus payment is not permitted under the standard limit. Heartland could only make such a payment if the Board grants an exception under §217.604(a)(4)(iv).

scenario_parameters.institution_type: top-tier depository institution holding company in a supervised insurance organization
scenario_parameters.table1_tier: less than or equal to 38 percent

question_text: A Board-regulated institution entered into a delivery-versus-payment securities transaction with a normal settlement period. The contractual settlement date was a Monday. The counterparty failed to deliver the securities on the settlement date. As of the close of business on the 18th business day after the contractual settlement date, the counterparty has still not made delivery. At that point, the current market price of the securities is $4,200,000, and the agreed settlement price was $3,900,000 (i.e., the institution was to pay $3,900,000 and receive securities now worth $4,200,000). Determine whether the institution must hold risk-based capital against this transaction, and if so, calculate the risk-weighted asset amount the institution must assign to this exposure.
required_facts: The transaction is a DvP transaction with a normal settlement period and falls within the scope of § 217.38; it is not excluded by any of the four carve-outs.
Capital must be held because the counterparty has not made delivery within five business days after the contractual settlement date (18 business days have elapsed, exceeding the 5-day threshold).
Positive current exposure = $4,200,000 (current market price) − $3,900,000 (agreed settlement price) = $300,000, representing a credit exposure of the institution to the counterparty.
18 business days after the contractual settlement date falls in the 'From 16 to 30' band in Table 1, which carries a risk weight of 625.0%.
Risk-weighted asset amount = $300,000 × 625.0% = $1,875,000.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the DvP unsettled transaction rule: confirm the transaction qualifies (DvP, normal settlement period), confirm the 5-business-day threshold after settlement date has been exceeded, compute positive current exposure, then look up the applicable risk weight from Table 1 based on the number of business days elapsed since the contractual settlement date.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Transaction type: The transaction is a DvP transaction (buyer pays only if seller delivers, seller delivers only if buyer pays), with a normal settlement period (contractual settlement period ≤ market standard and ≤ 5 business days). It is not a cleared/marked-to-market transaction, not a repo-style transaction, not a one-way OTC cash payment, and not a long-settlement transaction, so it falls within the scope of § 217.38.

Step 2 — Threshold check: Under § 217.38(d), a Board-regulated institution must hold risk-based capital against a DvP transaction with a normal settlement period if the counterparty has not made delivery within five business days after the settlement date. Here, 18 business days have elapsed since the contractual settlement date, which exceeds the 5-business-day threshold. Capital must be held.

Step 3 — Positive current exposure: Positive current exposure is the difference between the transaction value at the agreed settlement price and the current market price, if that difference results in a credit exposure to the institution. The institution agreed to pay $3,900,000 and receive securities now worth $4,200,000. The institution has a credit exposure because the securities it is owed are worth more than what it agreed to pay: $4,200,000 − $3,900,000 = $300,000. Positive current exposure = $300,000.

Step 4 — Risk weight from Table 1: The number of business days after the contractual settlement date is 18, which falls in the range 'From 16 to 30.' The applicable risk weight is 625.0%.

Step 5 — Risk-weighted asset amount: RWA = $300,000 × 625.0% = $1,875,000.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution acts as an originating bank for a synthetic securitization it sponsors. The securitization satisfies all operational criteria required for such structures. To hedge its retained exposure in the synthetic securitization, the institution has purchased an eligible credit derivative from a highly rated protection seller. The credit derivative covers three reference tranches within the same synthetic securitization structure. The three hedged tranches have residual maturities of 2 years, 4 years, and 7 years, respectively. The notional protection amount of the credit derivative is $150 million, and the maturity of the credit derivative itself is 5 years. Determine how the institution must treat the residual maturity of the hedged exposures when applying the required maturity mismatch adjustments to the protection amount, and identify the effective residual maturity figure the institution must use across all three hedged tranches for purposes of computing any maturity mismatch adjustment.
required_facts: The institution must apply the maturity mismatch adjustment rules of § 217.36(d), (e), and (f) to the hedged securitization exposure.

Because a single eligible credit derivative covers multiple hedged exposures with different residual maturities within a synthetic securitization, the institution must use the longest residual maturity of any hedged exposure as the residual maturity for all hedged exposures.
The longest residual maturity among the three tranches is 7 years (the tranche with the 7-year maturity).
The effective residual maturity the institution must use for all three hedged tranches is 7 years.

A maturity mismatch exists, but under §217.36(d)(5) the 7-year hedged exposure and 5-year credit derivative produce T=5 and t=5, so the maturity-mismatch formula does not reduce the $150 million protection amount.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.45(b) governs maturity mismatch treatment for synthetic securitizations where a single eligible credit derivative covers multiple hedged exposures with different residual maturities — the institution must use the longest residual maturity of any hedged exposure as the residual maturity for all hedged exposures.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Confirm the institution is an originating Board-regulated institution that has obtained an eligible credit derivative to hedge a synthetic securitization exposure — this brings the scenario within § 217.45. Step 2: § 217.45(a)(1) confirms that an originating institution may recognize the credit risk mitigant under §§ 217.36 or 217.37, but only as provided in § 217.45. Step 3: § 217.45(b) requires the institution to make any applicable maturity mismatch adjustment to the protection amount as required under § 217.36(d), (e), and (f). Step 4: The second sentence of § 217.45(b) provides the specific rule for synthetic securitizations where a single eligible guarantee or eligible credit derivative covers multiple hedged exposures with different residual maturities: the institution must use the longest residual maturity of any of the hedged exposures as the residual maturity of all hedged exposures. Step 5: The three tranches have residual maturities of 2, 4, and 7 years. The longest is 7 years. Therefore, the institution must treat all three hedged exposures as having a residual maturity of 7 years when computing the maturity mismatch adjustment. Step 6: The credit derivative itself matures in 5 years, which is shorter than the 7-year effective residual maturity of the hedged exposures — this creates a maturity mismatch that will reduce the recognized protection amount under § 217.36(d)–(f).

question_text: Heartland Savings Bank is a Board-regulated institution that uses the standardized approach for calculating risk-weighted assets. The bank's risk management team is preparing its quarterly regulatory capital report. The bank holds a portfolio that includes the following positions: (1) a $200 million portfolio of foreign exchange spot contracts that are not designated as trading positions, (2) $150 million in OTC interest rate swap contracts, (3) $75 million in cleared futures contracts on a qualifying central counterparty, (4) $50 million in equity securities held in the trading account that qualify as covered positions under the market risk framework, and (5) $30 million in unsettled securities purchase transactions. The bank has recently been designated as a market risk institution due to its trading activity exceeding applicable thresholds. Determine which of these five position types must be excluded from the bank's standardized approach risk-weighted asset calculation, and which must be included. Explain the governing principle that determines inclusion versus exclusion for a market risk institution computing its standardized risk-weighted assets.
required_facts: As a market risk Board-regulated institution, Heartland must exclude covered positions (as defined under the market risk framework) from its standardized approach RWA calculation, subject to four enumerated exceptions
Foreign exchange positions that are not trading positions are explicitly excepted from the exclusion and must remain in the standardized RWA calculation — position (1) is INCLUDED
OTC derivative positions are explicitly excepted from the exclusion and must remain in the standardized RWA calculation — position (2) is INCLUDED
Cleared transactions are explicitly excepted from the exclusion and must remain in the standardized RWA calculation — position (3) is INCLUDED
Unsettled transactions are explicitly excepted from the exclusion and must remain in the standardized RWA calculation — position (5) is INCLUDED

The trading account equity securities qualifying as covered positions under Subpart F do not fall within any of the four exceptions and must be EXCLUDED from the Subpart D standardized RWA calculation — position (4) is EXCLUDED

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.30(a) establishes that Subpart D applies to all Board-regulated institutions for standardized RWA; §217.30(b) carves out market risk institutions, requiring them to exclude covered positions from Subpart D RWA — but with four enumerated exceptions that remain in Subpart D
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Confirm Heartland is a Board-regulated institution subject to Subpart D per §217.30(a). Step 2: Confirm Heartland is a market risk Board-regulated institution, triggering §217.30(b). Step 3: Under §217.30(b), a market risk institution must EXCLUDE from its Subpart D RWA calculation the risk-weighted asset amounts of all 'covered positions' as defined in Subpart F — EXCEPT for four carve-outs that remain in Subpart D: (i) foreign exchange positions that are not trading positions, (ii) OTC derivative positions, (iii) cleared transactions, and (iv) unsettled transactions. Step 4: Apply to each position: (1) FX spot contracts not designated as trading positions → carve-out (i), INCLUDED in Subpart D; (2) OTC interest rate swaps → carve-out (ii) OTC derivative positions, INCLUDED in Subpart D; (3) cleared futures on QCCP → carve-out (iii) cleared transactions, INCLUDED in Subpart D; (4) trading account equity securities qualifying as covered positions → no carve-out applies, EXCLUDED from Subpart D (handled under Subpart F market risk framework); (5) unsettled securities transactions → carve-out (iv) unsettled transactions, INCLUDED in Subpart D.

scenario_parameters.position_1: FX spot contracts, not trading positions, $200M

question_text: Apex Financial Group is a global systemically important bank holding company subject to enhanced prudential standards. As of December 31 of the prior calendar year, Apex reported the following balance sheet and activity figures: total exposures of $2,800 billion; intra-financial system assets of $420 billion; intra-financial system liabilities of $390 billion; securities outstanding of $310 billion; notional amount of over-the-counter derivatives of $8,500 billion; trading and available-for-sale securities of $95 billion; Level 3 assets of $18 billion; cross-jurisdictional claims of $640 billion; and cross-jurisdictional liabilities of $580 billion. Calculate Apex's aggregate systemic indicator score (excluding any short-term wholesale funding component) by applying the appropriate coefficient to each of the nine systemic indicators and summing the results. Show your work for each indicator and provide the total.
required_facts: Each systemic indicator score equals the indicator amount in billions of dollars multiplied by its corresponding coefficient from Table 1 of § 217.405
Total exposures score = $2,800B × 4.423% = 123.844
Level 3 assets score = $18B × 161.177% = 29.012 (highest-coefficient indicator)
Notional OTC derivatives score = $8,500B × 0.155% = 13.175 (largest notional but lowest coefficient)
Cross-jurisdictional claims score = $640B × 9.277% = 59.373 and cross-jurisdictional liabilities score = $580B × 9.926% = 57.571
The sum of all nine systemic indicator scores equals approximately 438.850
This aggregate figure excludes the short-term wholesale funding score, which is a separate additive component of the full Method 2 score

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply § 217.405(b) to compute each systemic indicator score (dollar amount in billions × coefficient from Table 1), then sum per § 217.405(a)(1)(i). The short-term wholesale funding score under § 217.406 is explicitly excluded from this sub-question.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Per § 217.405(b)(1), express each indicator in billions of dollars as reported as of December 31 of the prior calendar year. Step 2 — Per § 217.405(b)(2), multiply each indicator by its Table 1 coefficient: (1) Total exposures: $2,800B × 4.423% = 123.844; (2) Intra-financial system assets: $420B × 12.007% = 50.429; (3) Intra-financial system liabilities: $390B × 12.490% = 48.711; (4) Securities outstanding: $310B × 9.056% = 28.074; (5) Notional OTC derivatives: $8,500B × 0.155% = 13.175; (6) Trading and AFS securities: $95B × 30.169% = 28.661; (7) Level 3 assets: $18B × 161.177% = 29.012; (8) Cross-jurisdictional claims: $640B × 9.277% = 59.373; (9) Cross-jurisdictional liabilities: $580B × 9.926% = 57.571. Step 3 — Per § 217.405(a)(1)(i), sum all nine scores: 123.844 + 50.429 + 48.711 + 28.074 + 13.175 + 28.661 + 29.012 + 59.373 + 57.571 = 438.850.

question_text: Heartland Bancorp is a Board-regulated institution that qualifies as an advanced approaches institution. It completed its parallel run process eighteen months ago and received the required notification from its primary federal regulator confirming it may use the advanced approaches framework. Heartland is organized as a direct subsidiary of a U.S. bank holding company that is itself subject to the same public disclosure requirements applicable to advanced approaches institutions. Heartland's compliance team is preparing its quarterly regulatory reporting package and is debating two questions: (1) Must Heartland publicly disclose its total and tier 1 risk-based capital ratios and their components — including common equity tier 1 capital, additional tier 1 capital, tier 2 capital, total qualifying capital, and total risk-weighted assets as computed under the advanced approaches framework — on a quarterly basis? (2) Must Heartland separately comply with the detailed quarterly public disclosure obligations (formal disclosure policy approved by the board of directors, senior officer attestation, internal controls over disclosures, and publication of the full set of required disclosure tables) given its corporate structure as a consolidated subsidiary of a holding company that already meets those same disclosure requirements? Analyze both questions and explain the applicable obligations and any exemptions that may apply.
required_facts: Heartland must publicly disclose each quarter its total and tier 1 risk-based capital ratios and their components (CET1 capital, AT1 capital, tier 2 capital, total qualifying capital, and total risk-weighted assets) as calculated under the advanced approaches framework, because it has completed the parallel run and received the required Board notification.

The quarterly capital ratio disclosure obligation under the first paragraph of §217.172 applies to all qualifying advanced approaches institutions and contains no exemption for consolidated subsidiaries.

The detailed quarterly disclosure requirements — including a formal disclosure policy approved by the board of directors, senior officer attestation, internal controls, and publication of the full required disclosure tables — apply under the second paragraph of §217.172 only if no exemption is triggered.

An institution that is a consolidated subsidiary of a bank holding company that is itself subject to the same disclosure requirements is explicitly exempt from the detailed disclosure obligations described in the third paragraph of §217.172.

Because Heartland is a consolidated subsidiary of a U.S. bank holding company that is subject to the same advanced approaches disclosure requirements, Heartland qualifies for the subsidiary exemption and is not required to separately comply with the detailed disclosure regime.

The subsidiary exemption applies only to the detailed disclosure obligations (board policy, attestation, internal controls, full tables) and does NOT relieve Heartland of the basic quarterly capital ratio disclosure obligation.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.172(a) imposes the quarterly capital ratio disclosure obligation on all qualifying advanced approaches institutions; §217.172(b) then carves out the detailed disclosure requirements of §217.172(c) for consolidated subsidiaries of holding companies already subject to those same requirements.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — §217.172(a): Heartland is a Board-regulated institution that is an advanced approaches institution, has completed the parallel run, and has received the Board notification under §217.121(d). Therefore §217.172(a) applies and Heartland MUST publicly disclose each quarter its total and tier 1 risk-based capital ratios and their components (CET1 capital, AT1 capital, tier 2 capital, total qualifying capital, total risk-weighted assets) as calculated under the advanced approaches subpart. No subsidiary exemption exists for this paragraph — it applies unconditionally to all qualifying institutions. Step 2 — §217.172(b): This paragraph imposes the additional detailed disclosure obligations of §217.172(c) (formal policy, board approval, senior officer attestation, internal controls, full disclosure tables) on the same class of institutions described in §217.172(a), BUT it contains an explicit carve-out: an institution is NOT required to comply with §217.172(c) if it is a consolidated subsidiary of a bank holding company that is itself subject to these disclosure requirements. Heartland is a direct consolidated subsidiary of a U.S. bank holding company that is subject to the same advanced approaches disclosure requirements. Therefore Heartland qualifies for the §217.172(b) exemption and is NOT required to separately comply with the detailed §217.172(c) obligations. Conclusion: Heartland must satisfy the quarterly capital ratio disclosure under §217.172(a) but is exempt from the standalone detailed disclosure regime of §217.172(c) by virtue of §217.172(b).

scenario_parameters.corporate_structure: consolidated subsidiary of a U.S. bank holding company
scenario_parameters.question_2_topic: detailed disclosure regime exemption for consolidated subsidiaries (§217.172(b))

question_text: Heartland Mutual Holdings, Inc. is a top-tier depository institution holding company. As of June 30 of the prior calendar year, Heartland's total consolidated assets (calculated under GAAP) were $18.4 billion, of which $4.3 billion were held in insurance underwriting subsidiaries engaged solely in underwriting credit risk. Heartland itself does not write insurance policies directly. Heartland is not part of any supervised insurance organization and has not been separately designated by its federal regulator as subject to any special insurance capital framework. Determine whether this subpart's insurance-focused capital framework applies to Heartland, and explain your reasoning.
required_facts: Heartland is not itself an insurance underwriting company, so the first applicability prong is not satisfied
The $4.3 billion in insurance underwriting subsidiaries must be excluded from the 25% threshold calculation because those assets are associated with insurance underwriting for credit risk
After excluding the credit-risk underwriting assets, qualifying insurance underwriting assets are $0, yielding a 0% ratio against $18.4 billion in total consolidated assets
0% is below the 25% threshold required by the second applicability prong, so that prong is not satisfied
Heartland is not part of a supervised insurance organization, so the third applicability prong is not satisfied
Heartland has not been designated by the Board under the catch-all fourth prong
The insurance-focused capital framework does not apply to Heartland

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the three applicability prongs in §217.601(b): (1) is Heartland itself an insurance underwriting company? (2) does it hold ≥25% of total consolidated assets in insurance underwriting companies (excluding credit-risk underwriting assets)? (3) is it in a supervised insurance organization? Then check §217.601(b)(4) catch-all.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — §217.601(b)(1): Heartland is a top-tier depository institution holding company, but it is not itself an insurance underwriting company. Prong (1) is not satisfied.

Step 2 — §217.601(b)(2): The prong requires that, as of June 30 of the previous calendar year, the institution held 25% or more of its total consolidated assets in insurance underwriting companies, OTHER THAN assets associated with insurance underwriting for credit risk. Heartland's total consolidated assets = $18.4 billion. The $4.3 billion in insurance underwriting subsidiaries is explicitly carved out because those subsidiaries underwrite only credit risk. After the carve-out, qualifying insurance underwriting assets = $0. The ratio is $0 / $18.4 billion = 0%, which is below the 25% threshold. Prong (2) is not satisfied.

Step 3 — §217.601(b)(3): Heartland is not part of a supervised insurance organization. Prong (3) is not satisfied.

Step 4 — §217.601(b)(4): Heartland has not been otherwise made subject to this subpart by the Board. Prong (4) is not satisfied.

Conclusion: None of the four applicability prongs in §217.601(b) are met. The insurance-focused capital framework in this subpart does NOT apply to Heartland Mutual Holdings, Inc.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has received prior written approval to use the Internal Models Approach (IMA) for equity exposures, but only for its publicly traded equity holdings — it does not model non-publicly traded equity exposures under the IMA. The institution's internal equity exposure model generates an estimate of potential losses on the relevant modeled equity exposures of $480 million. The institution also holds the following equity exposures (all adjusted carrying values): (1) publicly traded equity exposures that do not belong to a hedge pair and do not qualify for a 0%, 20%, or 100% risk weight, and are not exposures to an investment fund: $900 million aggregate; (2) the aggregate ineffective portion of all hedge pairs: $150 million; (3) non-publicly traded equity exposures that do not qualify for a 0%, 20%, or 100% risk weight and are not exposures to an investment fund: $200 million; (4) equity exposures qualifying for a 400% risk weight: $50 million adjusted carrying value (risk-weighted asset amount already determined as $200 million); (5) equity exposures qualifying for a 600% risk weight: $30 million adjusted carrying value (risk-weighted asset amount already determined as $180 million); (6) equity exposures to investment funds with a risk-weighted asset amount already determined as $120 million; (7) equity exposures qualifying for a 0%, 20%, or 100% risk weight with a combined risk-weighted asset amount already determined as $75 million. Determine the institution's aggregate risk-weighted asset amount for all equity exposures.
required_facts: Because the institution models only publicly traded equity exposures, § 217.153(d) applies rather than § 217.153(c)
The (d)(1) fixed-weight component equals $575 million ($75M + $200M + $180M + $120M)
The model-based amount under (d)(2)(i) equals $480M × 12.5 = $6,000 million
The formula floor under (d)(2)(ii) equals 200% × $900M + 200% × $150M = $2,100 million; there is no (C) sub-clause for non-publicly traded exposures under paragraph (d)
The greater of $6,000M and $2,100M is $6,000 million
The aggregate risk-weighted asset amount for all equity exposures is $575M + $6,000M = $6,575 million

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Because the institution models only publicly traded equity exposures, paragraph (d) applies. The aggregate RWA equals the sum of: (d)(1) fixed risk-weight exposures (0%/20%/100%, 400%, 600%, and investment funds) plus (d)(2) the greater of the model output × 12.5 or the floor formula under (d)(2)(ii).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify applicable paragraph: The institution models only publicly traded equity exposures, so § 217.153(d) governs (not (c)).

Step 2 — Compute (d)(1) fixed-weight component: Sum of risk-weighted asset amounts for exposures that qualify for 0%/20%/100% risk weights, 400% risk weight, 600% risk weight, and investment funds = $75M + $200M + $180M + $120M = $575 million.

Step 3 — Compute (d)(2)(i) model-based floor: $480M × 12.5 = $6,000 million.

Step 4 — Compute (d)(2)(ii) formula floor:
  (A) 200% × $900M (publicly traded, no hedge pair, not 0/20/100%, not investment fund) = $1,800M
  (B) 200% × $150M (ineffective portion of hedge pairs) = $300M
  Note: Non-publicly traded exposures ($200M) are NOT included in (d)(2)(ii) because paragraph (d) only covers publicly traded equity exposures in the model; the formula floor under (d)(2)(ii) has no (C) component (unlike (c)(2)(ii)(C)).
  (d)(2)(ii) total = $1,800M + $300M = $2,100 million.

Step 5 — Take the greater of (d)(2)(i) and (d)(2)(ii): greater of $6,000M and $2,100M = $6,000 million.

Step 6 — Aggregate RWA = (d)(1) + (d)(2) = $575M + $6,000M = $6,575 million.

Key insight tested: Under (d), non-publicly traded equity exposures that are not in the fixed-weight bucket are excluded from the (d)(2)(ii) formula floor (there is no sub-clause (C) analogous to (c)(2)(ii)(C)), and the model output × 12.5 dominates here.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds an equity exposure to a diversified investment fund with an adjusted carrying value of $50 million. The fund's prospectus permits investments in the following asset classes with stated investment limits: up to 60% in investment-grade corporate bonds (risk weight 100%), up to 30% in residential mortgage-backed securities (risk weight 20%), up to 40% in equity securities of publicly traded companies (risk weight 300%), and up to 20% in U.S. Treasury securities (risk weight 0%). The institution does not have sufficient information to calculate risk-weighted asset amounts for each individual exposure held by the fund on a proportional ownership basis, so it cannot use the most granular approach. The institution's compliance team is evaluating whether to use the approach that assigns the full adjusted carrying value at the single highest permissible risk weight, versus the approach that allocates the adjusted carrying value proportionally across risk weight categories based on the fund's investment limits. Under the proportional allocation approach, what is the risk-weighted asset amount for this equity exposure, and what is the minimum risk weight that may be applied to any portion of the exposure regardless of the asset class?
required_facts: The investment limits sum to 150%, which exceeds 100%, triggering the over-limit allocation rule under the alternative modified look-through approach
The institution must allocate first to the highest risk-weight category: 40% to equity securities at 300% risk weight, then 60% to corporate bonds at 100% risk weight
RWA from equity securities portion: 0.40 × $50M × 300% = $60 million
RWA from corporate bonds portion: 0.60 × $50M × 100% = $30 million
Total risk-weighted asset amount under the alternative modified look-through approach = $90 million
The minimum risk weight that may be applied to any equity exposure to an investment fund under this section is 20 percent, regardless of the underlying asset class

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.53(a)(1) establishes the 20% minimum risk weight floor and the three available approaches; §217.53(d) governs the alternative modified look-through approach including the pro rata allocation mechanic and the over-100% investment limit rule
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — §217.53(a)(1): Confirm the institution must use one of three approaches (full look-through, simple modified look-through, or alternative modified look-through) and that the minimum risk weight is 20% regardless of approach. Step 2 — §217.53(d): Under the alternative modified look-through approach, assign the $50M adjusted carrying value on a pro rata basis to each exposure type based on investment limits. Step 3 — Check whether investment limits sum to more than 100%: 60% + 30% + 40% + 20% = 150%, which exceeds 100%. Therefore, per §217.53(d), the institution must assume the fund invests to the maximum extent in the highest risk-weight category first, then the next highest, and so on until 100% is reached. Step 4 — Rank by risk weight descending: equity securities 300% (limit 40%), corporate bonds 100% (limit 60%), RMBS 20% (limit 30%), Treasuries 0% (limit 20%). Step 5 — Allocate: 40% to equity (300%), then remaining 60% to corporate bonds (100%); RMBS and Treasuries are not reached. Step 6 — Compute RWA: (0.40 × $50M × 300%) + (0.60 × $50M × 100%) = $60M + $30M = $90M. Step 7 — Apply floor: §217.53(a)(1) states the minimum risk weight is 20%; the 300% and 100% weights already exceed this floor, so no adjustment needed. Final RWA = $90 million; minimum risk weight floor = 20%.

question_text: A state member bank holds the following equity exposures on its balance sheet (adjusted carrying values shown): (1) an equity stake in a publicly traded domestic corporation, $18 million; (2) an equity stake in a non-publicly traded domestic operating company, $9 million; (3) an equity exposure to a public-sector entity (PSE), $5 million; (4) a community development investment qualifying under 12 U.S.C. 24 (Eleventh), $4 million; and (5) an equity exposure to a foreign sovereign whose credit exposures receive a zero percent risk weight, $3 million. The bank's total capital is $350 million. The bank does not hold any equity exposures to investment funds, and none of the exposures are part of a hedge pair. Determine the applicable risk weight for each of the five equity exposures under the Simple Risk-Weight Approach, and identify whether any of the exposures qualify for the 100 percent risk weight bucket as non-significant equity exposures given the bank's total capital.
required_facts: The sovereign equity exposure receives a 0 percent risk weight because the sovereign's credit exposures receive a zero percent risk weight under the standardized approach
The PSE equity exposure receives a 20 percent risk weight
The community development investment qualifying under 12 U.S.C. 24 (Eleventh) receives a 100 percent risk weight
The non-significant equity exposure threshold equals 10 percent of total capital, which is $35 million (10% × $350M)

The aggregate adjusted carrying value of the two remaining exposures ($18M + $9M = $27M) does not exceed the $35M threshold, so both qualify as non-significant equity exposures at 100 percent risk weight
Under the ordering rule, publicly traded exposures are included before non-publicly traded exposures when determining which exposures fit within the non-significant bucket
Both the publicly traded ($18M) and non-publicly traded ($9M) exposures receive a 100 percent risk weight as non-significant equity exposures

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply SRWA risk-weight tiers in §217.52(b)(1)-(5) to each exposure, then test the non-significant equity exposure threshold in §217.52(b)(3)(iii) using the 10% of total capital limit, applying the ordering rule in §217.52(b)(3)(iii)(B)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Assign preliminary risk weights by category:
• Exposure (5) sovereign at 0% risk weight → §217.52(b)(1)
• Exposure (3) PSE at 20% risk weight → §217.52(b)(2)
• Exposure (4) community development investment (12 U.S.C. 24 Eleventh) at 100% risk weight → §217.52(b)(3)(i)(A)
• Exposures (1) and (2) do not fit (b)(1), (b)(2), or (b)(3)(i)-(ii); they are candidates for (b)(3)(iii) non-significant, (b)(4) significant investment in unconsolidated FI common stock, (b)(5) publicly traded, or (b)(6) non-publicly traded.

Step 2 — Check whether exposures (1) and (2) are significant investments in unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock (§217.52(b)(4), 250% risk weight). The scenario does not identify either as a financial institution investment, so they are not assigned 250%.

Step 3 — Absent the significant-investment designation, exposure (1) (publicly traded, $18M) would be assigned 300% under §217.52(b)(5), and exposure (2) (non-publicly traded, $9M) would be assigned 400% under §217.52(b)(6).

Step 4 — Test non-significant equity exposure threshold under §217.52(b)(3)(iii):
• Compute aggregate adjusted carrying value eligible for the non-significant bucket. Exclude exposures covered by (b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3)(i), and (b)(3)(ii): exclude (5) $3M, (3) $5M, (4) $4M. Remaining exposures: (1) $18M + (2) $9M = $27M.
• 10% of total capital = 10% × $350M = $35M.
• $27M < $35M, so the entire $27M aggregate qualifies as non-significant equity exposures.

Step 5 — Apply ordering rule in §217.52(b)(3)(iii)(B): first include SBIC exposures (none here), then publicly traded exposures, then non-publicly traded. Publicly traded (1) $18M is included first; remaining capacity = $35M − $18M = $17M. Non-publicly traded (2) $9M is included next; $9M < $17M remaining, so it also qualifies.

Step 6 — Final risk weights:
• Exposure (5): 0%
• Exposure (3): 20%
• Exposure (4): 100% (community development)
• Exposure (1): 100% (non-significant, publicly traded, within 10% total capital threshold)
• Exposure (2): 100% (non-significant, non-publicly traded, within 10% total capital threshold)

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a securitization exposure with an original exposure amount (SE) of $50 million, calculated under the applicable exposure amount rules. To hedge this exposure, the institution has posted eligible financial collateral with a current fair value (C) of $30 million. The collateral is denominated in euros while the securitization exposure is denominated in US dollars. The institution does not have prior written approval to use its own internal estimates for haircuts, so it must rely on standard supervisory haircuts. The applicable collateral type haircut (Hs) from the standard supervisory table is 4 percent, and the institution has confirmed that the holding period for this exposure is 65 business days. After applying all required haircut adjustments, compute the adjusted exposure amount (SE*) and determine the ratio SE*/SE that would be applied to scale the risk-weighted asset amount for this collateralized securitization exposure.
required_facts: The standard supervisory haircuts must be multiplied by the square root of 6.5 (≈ 2.549510), yielding an adjusted Hs of approximately 10.198% and an adjusted Hfx of approximately 20.396%
A currency mismatch haircut (Hfx) of 8 percent applies because the collateral (EUR) and the exposure (USD) are denominated in different currencies
No upward holding-period adjustment is required because the holding period is exactly 65 business days, which equals the minimum threshold
The scaling ratio SE*/SE ≈ 29,178,230 / 50,000,000 ≈ 0.5836 (approximately 58.36%)
The institution cannot use own-estimates haircuts because it lacks prior written approval from the Board, so standard supervisory haircuts are mandatory

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the SE* formula under §217.145(b)(1), then use standard supervisory haircuts from §217.145(b)(3) including the currency mismatch haircut and the square-root-of-6.5 multiplier, to compute SE* and the scaling ratio.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the formula: SE* = max{0, [SE − C × (1 − Hs − Hfx)]} per §217.145(b)(1)(i). Step 2 — Determine haircuts under §217.145(b)(3): since the institution does not qualify for own-estimates haircuts, it must use standard supervisory haircuts. The collateral type haircut Hs = 4% = 0.04 (from Table 1 to §217.132). The exposure and collateral are in different currencies (USD vs. EUR), so the currency mismatch haircut Hfx = 8% = 0.08 per §217.145(b)(3)(ii). Step 3 — Apply the square-root-of-6.5 multiplier per §217.145(b)(3)(iii): adjusted Hs = 0.04 × 2.549510 = 0.101980; adjusted Hfx = 0.08 × 2.549510 = 0.203961. Step 4 — No upward adjustment for holding period is required because the holding period is exactly 65 business days (the minimum), not longer, per §217.145(b)(3)(iv). Step 5 — Compute SE*: SE* = max{0, [50,000,000 − 30,000,000 × (1 − 0.101980 − 0.203961)]} = max{0, [50,000,000 − 30,000,000 × (1 − 0.305941)]} = max{0, [50,000,000 − 30,000,000 × 0.694059]} = max{0, [50,000,000 − 20,821,770]} = max{0, 29,178,230} = $29,178,230. Step 6 — Compute the scaling ratio: SE*/SE = 29,178,230 / 50,000,000 ≈ 0.5836 (58.36%). This ratio is then multiplied by the risk-weighted asset amount calculated under SSFA or SFA to obtain the collateral-adjusted RWA.

question_text: A compliance officer at a mid-sized Board-regulated institution is reviewing the bank's capital adequacy framework under the US Basel III rules. During an internal audit, the officer notes that the institution's total assets fall below the thresholds that would trigger advanced approaches requirements, and the institution has never opted into the advanced approaches framework. The officer is preparing a memo for the board explaining which specific capital calculation sections of the US Basel III capital rules apply to the institution's standardized approach calculations for the current reporting period. The officer specifically wants to confirm whether any reserved or placeholder regulatory sections in the subpart governing standardized risk-weighted asset calculations for on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet exposures impose any affirmative compliance obligations on the institution. Identify what compliance obligations, if any, arise from the sections numbered 217.23 through 217.29 of the applicable capital rules, and explain what this means for the institution's capital calculation methodology.
required_facts: Sections 217.23 through 217.29 are all designated [Reserved] and contain no substantive regulatory text.
A [Reserved] designation means the regulatory agency has not promulgated any rules in those sections, so no compliance obligations arise from them.
The institution's standardized approach capital calculations are unaffected by the absence of text in §§ 217.23–217.29.
The compliance officer's memo should note that these sections impose zero affirmative requirements on the institution for the current reporting period.
The institution must look to other substantive sections of the capital rules, including Subpart D for standardized risk-weighted asset methodologies, rather than to reserved §§ 217.23-217.29.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Direct lookup of §§ 217.23–217.29, which are all marked [Reserved] — no substantive rules exist in this range
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Locate §§ 217.23–217.29 within Subpart C of 12 CFR Part 217. Step 2: Observe that every section in this range (217.23, 217.24, 217.25, 217.26, 217.27, 217.28, 217.29) is marked '[Reserved]', meaning the OCC/Federal Reserve has not promulgated any substantive rule text in these sections. Step 3: Conclude that no affirmative compliance obligations arise from these sections. Step 4: Advise the institution that its standardized approach capital calculations are governed by the sections that do contain substantive text (e.g., §§ 217.20–217.22 and §§ 217.30 onward), and that the reserved sections impose no requirements.

question_text: Heartland Mutual Insurance Holding Company is a savings and loan holding company whose primary business is underwriting insurance. As of January 1, 2023, Heartland was not subject to the Board's regulatory capital requirements. It is now February 15, 2025. Heartland's board of directors is considering declaring a discretionary cash bonus for senior executives and a common stock dividend to shareholders. A compliance officer raises the question of whether the capital conservation buffer rules impose any restrictions on these payments given Heartland's capital position. Determine whether Heartland is subject to any restrictions on distributions or discretionary bonus payments under the capital conservation buffer framework, and identify the date on which any applicable exemption or transitional relief expires.
required_facts: Heartland qualifies as an insurance savings and loan holding company that was not subject to Part 217 capital requirements on January 1, 2023
As of February 15, 2025, Heartland is not subject to any restrictions on distributions or discretionary bonus payments under the capital conservation buffer framework
The transitional exemption from capital conservation buffer distribution restrictions applies notwithstanding any other provision of the capital rules
The transitional relief expires after March 31, 2026, at which point Heartland would become subject to standard capital conservation buffer distribution restriction rules

Both the proposed common stock dividend and the discretionary executive bonus payments are covered by the exemption and may proceed without capital conservation buffer-based restriction as of the question date

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.306(a) grants a blanket exemption from capital conservation buffer distribution restrictions for qualifying insurance holding companies that were not subject to Part 217 on January 1, 2023; §217.306(b) sets the sunset date of March 31, 2026.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the entity type — Heartland is an insurance savings and loan holding company. Step 2: Check the qualifying condition under §217.306(a): was the institution 'not subject to this part' on January 1, 2023? Yes, the facts state it was not subject to the Board's capital requirements as of that date. Step 3: Apply §217.306(a): notwithstanding any other provision of Part 217, such an institution is not subject to any restrictions on distributions or discretionary bonus payments under §§217.11 and 217.604. Therefore, as of February 15, 2025, Heartland faces no capital conservation buffer-based restrictions on the proposed dividend or bonus payments. Step 4: Apply §217.306(b): this transitional relief ceases to be effective after March 31, 2026. Any distributions or bonus payments after that date would be subject to the standard capital conservation buffer restriction rules.

scenario_parameters.entity_type: insurance savings and loan holding company

question_text: Heartland Savings Bank is a state member bank that is not an advanced approaches institution. As of its most recent year-end Call Report, Heartland reported total consolidated assets of $48.7 billion. However, when averaged across the four most recent quarters of Call Report filings, Heartland's total consolidated assets come to $51.3 billion. Heartland is a standalone institution — it is not a consolidated subsidiary of any bank holding company, savings and loan holding company, or depository institution, and it is not a subsidiary of a non-U.S. banking organization. Determine whether Heartland is subject to the public disclosure requirements related to capital adequacy, and explain the basis for your conclusion.
required_facts: Total consolidated assets for threshold purposes are determined using the four-quarter average from Call Report filings, not the most recent year-end figure alone.
Heartland's four-quarter average total consolidated assets of $51.3 billion exceeds the $50 billion threshold.
The most recent year-end figure of $48.7 billion is below $50 billion but is not the operative measure under the applicable rule.
Heartland is a state member bank, so the relevant report is the Call Report (not the FR Y-9C).
Heartland is not an advanced approaches institution making disclosures under the advanced approaches framework, so that carve-out does not apply.
Heartland does not qualify for the consolidated-subsidiary or non-U.S. banking organization exclusions.
Heartland is subject to the public capital disclosure requirements.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.61 establishes the $50 billion asset threshold for public disclosure applicability, and specifies that total consolidated assets are determined using the four-quarter average from Call Report filings, not the most recent year-end figure alone.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the applicable threshold. §217.61 states that the disclosure requirements apply to a Board-regulated institution with total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more as reported on the institution's most recent year-end Call Report (for a state member bank). Step 2: Determine how 'total consolidated assets' is measured. §217.61 further specifies that for purposes of this section, total consolidated assets are determined based on the average of the institution's total consolidated assets in the four most recent quarters as reported on the Call Report (for a state member bank), not solely the most recent year-end figure. Step 3: Apply the definition. The four-quarter average is $51.3 billion, which exceeds $50 billion. The most recent year-end figure of $48.7 billion is not the operative measure. Step 4: Check exclusions. Heartland is not an advanced approaches institution making disclosures under §217.172, is not a consolidated subsidiary of a BHC/SLHC/depository institution subject to §217.62, and is not a subsidiary of a non-U.S. banking organization subject to comparable home-jurisdiction disclosure requirements. Step 5: Conclude. Heartland meets the $50 billion threshold (using the four-quarter average) and none of the exclusions apply, so it is subject to the public disclosure requirements of §217.62.

question_text: A large U.S. insurance holding company that is also a depository institution holding company is preparing its Building Block Analysis (BBA) ratio calculation. The holding company's indicated capital framework is NAIC Risk-Based Capital (RBC). One of its downstream subsidiaries is a federally regulated bank whose indicated capital framework is the U.S. Federal banking capital rules. The bank subsidiary has a recalculated building block capital requirement of $800 million. When the holding company consolidates this bank subsidiary into its BBA ratio calculation, what available capital scaling modifier must it apply to the bank subsidiary's figures, and what is the resulting scaled available capital contribution from that subsidiary?
required_facts: The upstream building block parent's indicated capital framework is NAIC RBC
The downstream building block parent's indicated capital framework is U.S. Federal banking capital rules
The available capital scaling modifier from Table 2 for this upstream/downstream combination is: recalculated building block capital requirement multiplied by 0.063
Scaled available capital = $800 million × 0.063 = $50.4 million

A holding company whose indicated capital framework is NAIC RBC does not scale its own building block available capital or capital requirement for BBA ratio purposes, but does apply the Table 2 modifier when consolidating a downstream entity under U.S. Federal banking capital rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply Table 2 in § 217.606(a)(1)(ii): upstream (holding company) indicated framework is NAIC RBC, downstream (bank subsidiary) indicated framework is U.S. Federal banking capital rules → available capital scaling modifier = Recalculated building block capital requirement × 0.063
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the upstream building block parent's indicated capital framework — the holding company uses NAIC RBC. Step 2: Identify the downstream building block parent's indicated capital framework — the bank subsidiary uses U.S. Federal banking capital rules. Step 3: Look up the available capital scaling modifier in Table 2 to § 217.606(a)(1)(ii). The cell at [Upstream = NAIC RBC, Downstream = U.S. Federal banking capital rules] reads: 'Recalculated building block capital requirement × 0.063'. Step 4: Apply the modifier: $800 million × 0.063 = $50.4 million. This is the scaled available capital contribution from the bank subsidiary.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a credit exposure to an asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) program. The exposure is structured as a program-level credit enhancement that sits in a second loss position; the first loss position is a cash collateral account funded by the program sponsor equal to 8% of the total pool, which the institution's credit analysts have determined provides substantial credit protection to the second loss position. The institution does not hold or provide any support to that first loss position. The exposure carries an external rating equivalent to BBB+ (investment grade). The underlying assets in the ABCP program consist entirely of trade receivables, each individually risk-weighted at 75%. The institution has not applied the Simplified Supervisory Formula Approach or the gross-up approach to this exposure. The notional exposure amount is $50 million. What risk-weighted asset amount must the institution assign to this exposure, and what is the applicable risk weight?
required_facts: The default risk weight for a securitization exposure where neither the SSFA nor the gross-up approach is applied is 1,250%.

The second-loss-position exception requires four conditions: (1) not an eligible ABCP liquidity facility, (2) economically in second loss or better with significant first-loss credit protection, (3) investment-grade rating, and (4) the institution does not hold or protect the first loss position — all four are satisfied here.
The applicable risk weight under the second-loss exception is the higher of 100% and the highest individual underlying exposure risk weight (75%), which equals 100%.
The risk-weighted asset amount is $50 million × 100% = $50 million.
The 1,250% default risk weight does not apply because the exposure qualifies for the second-loss-position exception.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.44(a) general 1,250% default rule, then check whether the §217.44(c) second-loss-position exception applies by verifying all four conditions in §217.44(c)(2), then apply the §217.44(c)(1) risk-weight formula.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Default rule (§217.44(a)): Because the institution has not applied the SSFA or gross-up approach, the default risk weight is 1,250%. Step 2 — Check §217.44(b) eligible ABCP liquidity facility exception: The exposure is a program-level credit enhancement, not a liquidity facility, so §217.44(b) does not apply. Step 3 — Check §217.44(c) second-loss exception. Four conditions under §217.44(c)(2) must all be satisfied: (i) The exposure is not an eligible ABCP liquidity facility — confirmed, it is a credit enhancement. (ii) The exposure must be economically in a second loss position or better, and the first loss position must provide significant credit protection — confirmed, the 8% cash collateral account is in first loss and provides substantial protection. (iii) The exposure qualifies as investment grade — confirmed, BBB+ is investment grade. (iv) The institution must not retain or provide protection to the first loss position — confirmed, the sponsor holds the first loss position. All four conditions are met. Step 4 — Apply §217.44(c)(1) risk weight: The risk-weighted asset amount equals the exposure amount multiplied by the higher of (i) 100% or (ii) the highest risk weight applicable to any individual underlying exposure. The underlying trade receivables are each risk-weighted at 75%. The higher of 100% and 75% is 100%. Step 5 — Compute RWA: $50 million × 100% = $50 million.

question_text: A bank holding company that was established solely to hold employer securities on behalf of employees through a qualified retirement arrangement has been notified by its primary federal regulator that it may be subject to consolidated regulatory capital requirements. The holding company has no banking subsidiaries other than its sponsoring depository institution, and it has never filed a capital adequacy report. The holding company's legal counsel argues that the entity is categorically exempt from consolidated capital requirements and that no minimum capital ratios, buffer requirements, or deduction rules apply to it at this time. Is legal counsel's position correct, and if so, what is the basis and scope of that exemption?
required_facts: The holding company qualifies as an employee stock ownership plan that is a bank holding company.
A bank holding company that is an employee stock ownership plan is exempt from the entirety of Part 217 (the Board's regulatory capital framework).
The exemption applies notwithstanding the general applicability provision that would otherwise subject bank holding companies to Part 217.
The exemption remains in effect until the Board adopts regulations that directly relate to the application of capital regulations to employee stock ownership plans.
Because no such Board regulations have been adopted, the exemption is currently operative and legal counsel's position is correct.
The exemption covers all requirements under Part 217, including minimum capital ratios, buffer requirements, and deduction rules — no partial compliance is required.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-paragraph applicability determination: §217.502(a) grants a categorical exemption from the entire Part 217 capital framework to bank holding companies that are employee stock ownership plans, pending Board rulemaking specifically addressing ESOPs.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the entity type — a bank holding company organized as an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP). Step 2: Locate §217.502(a), which states that notwithstanding §217.1(c) (the general applicability provision), a bank holding company or covered savings and loan holding company that is an employee stock ownership plan is exempt from the entirety of Part 217 until the Board adopts regulations that directly relate to the application of capital regulations to employee stock ownership plans. Step 3: Confirm that no such Board regulations have been adopted. Step 4: Conclude that legal counsel's position is correct — the ESOP holding company is fully exempt from Part 217, meaning no minimum CET1, Tier 1, or total capital ratios apply, no capital conservation buffer or countercyclical buffer requirements apply, and no threshold deduction rules apply, for as long as the Board has not issued ESOP-specific capital regulations.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution operates a trading book that includes a portfolio of investment-grade corporate bond positions. The institution's value-at-risk (VaR) model has been validated and captures all material aspects of specific risk for this corporate bond portfolio, including event risk, idiosyncratic risk, and sensitivity to changes in portfolio composition and concentrations. The institution also maintains a separate portfolio of securitization positions (non-correlation-trading) that are not captured by any internal model approved for specific risk measurement. For the corporate bond portfolio, the institution's risk managers argue that no additional specific-risk capital charge is needed beyond what the VaR model already produces. For the securitization portfolio, the institution proposes to also rely on the VaR model to avoid a separate add-on charge. Assess whether each of these two positions is correct under applicable capital rules, and identify what specific-risk measurement obligation, if any, applies to each portfolio.
required_facts: For the corporate bond portfolio, because the VaR-based measure captures all material aspects of specific risk (including event risk, idiosyncratic risk, and concentration sensitivity), no specific-risk add-on is required for that portfolio.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution uses an internal models approach to measure specific risk for its trading book portfolio of corporate bond positions and CDS contracts referencing investment-grade and high-yield issuers. The institution's incremental risk model produces the following weekly incremental risk measures (in millions) over the most recent 12-week period: 410, 395, 420, 430, 415, 440, 425, 410, 450, 435, 420, 460. The most recent week's measure is 460. The institution also holds a portfolio of synthetic CDO tranches referencing a mix of corporate names, as well as a set of equity positions in the same issuers whose debt is already captured in the incremental risk model. The institution's risk managers propose (1) including the equity positions in the incremental risk model, and (2) including the synthetic CDO tranche positions in the same model to achieve netting benefits. Determine the institution's incremental risk capital requirement in dollars, and assess the permissibility of each of the two proposed model inclusions.

Most recent incremental risk measure = 460 million
Incremental risk capital requirement = 460 million (the greater of the two values)

Equity positions may only be included in the incremental risk model with prior Board approval and must be included consistently with how the institution internally measures and manages incremental risk at the portfolio level; if included, default is deemed to occur upon default of any debt of the equity issuer
Synthetic CDO tranche positions are securitization positions (and/or correlation trading positions) and are explicitly prohibited from inclusion in the incremental risk measure

The most recent measure is 460. The incremental risk capital requirement is the greater of the two: max(425.83, 460) = 460 million. Step 2 — Equity position inclusion under §217.208(a): The regulation permits a Board-regulated institution to include equity positions in its incremental risk model only with the prior approval of the Board, provided the institution consistently includes such equity positions in a manner consistent with how it internally measures and manages incremental risk of those positions at the portfolio level. Additionally, for modeling purposes, default is considered to have occurred upon the default of any debt of the issuer of the equity position. The proposal is conditionally permissible subject to prior Board approval and the consistency requirement. Synthetic CDO tranches are securitization positions (and likely correlation trading positions). Their inclusion is impermissible.

question_text: Heartland Community Bank, a Board-regulated institution with a calendar fiscal year, adopted the current expected credit loss methodology effective January 1, 2023. Upon adoption, the bank recorded a reduction in retained earnings of $18 million. Specifically, as of January 1, 2023 (the first day of the new fiscal year), retained earnings stood at $142 million, compared to $160 million at December 31, 2022 (the close of the prior fiscal year). The bank's deferred tax assets arising from temporary differences were $9 million as of January 1, 2023, versus $5 million as of December 31, 2022. The bank's allowance for credit losses under the new standard was $31 million as of January 1, 2023, compared to an allowance for loan and lease losses of $13 million as of December 31, 2022. The bank timely elected the transition provision in its first regulatory report filed after adoption. It is now the second year of the transition period. Determine: (1) the CECL transitional amount, (2) the DTA transitional amount, and (3) the percentage adjustments the bank must apply to retained earnings and to its deferred tax assets arising from temporary differences when calculating its regulatory capital ratios during the current (second) year of the transition period.
