DTA transitional amount = $4 million (increase in DTAs from temporary differences: $9M − $5M)
In the second year of the transition period, retained earnings must be increased by 50% of the CECL transitional amount = $9 million
In the second year of the transition period, DTAs arising from temporary differences must be decreased by 50% of the DTA transitional amount = $2 million
The election was valid because the bank recorded a reduction in retained earnings upon CECL adoption and elected in its first post-adoption regulatory report

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply definitions in §217.301(b) to compute CECL transitional amount and DTA transitional amount, then apply the second-year adjustment percentages from §217.301(c)(1)(i) and (c)(1)(ii)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — CECL transitional amount (§217.301(b)(2)): The CECL transitional amount is the difference, net of any DTAs, in retained earnings at the beginning of the adoption fiscal year versus the close of the prior fiscal year. Retained earnings dropped from $160M to $142M, a reduction of $18M. This $18M reduction (net of DTAs) is the CECL transitional amount. Note: the regulation defines this as the difference net of DTAs already embedded in the retained earnings change; the $18M figure as stated represents that net amount. Step 2 — DTA transitional amount (§217.301(b)(3)): The DTA transitional amount is the difference in DTAs arising from temporary differences at the beginning of the adoption year versus the close of the prior year. DTAs went from $5M (Dec 31, 2022) to $9M (Jan 1, 2023), an increase of $4M. DTA transitional amount = $4M. Step 3 — Second-year adjustments (§217.301(c)(1)(i) and (c)(1)(ii)): During the second year of the transition period, the bank must increase retained earnings by 50% of its CECL transitional amount = 50% × $18M = $9M. During the second year, the bank must decrease DTAs arising from temporary differences by 50% of its DTA transitional amount = 50% × $4M = $2M.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution subject to market risk capital requirements maintains an internal models-based framework for its covered positions. The institution's compliance team is preparing its quarterly public disclosures and annual qualitative disclosures. The institution holds a material portfolio of covered positions that includes correlation trading positions and securitization exposures. During the current quarter, the institution experienced several VaR backtesting outliers that it believes are material. The institution's management has determined that certain details about its proprietary correlation trading valuation methodology would, if disclosed publicly, seriously prejudice its competitive position. The institution is a wholly-owned consolidated subsidiary of a large U.S. bank holding company that is itself subject to the same market risk disclosure requirements under the applicable federal capital rules. Determine: (1) whether this institution is required to independently comply with the public market risk disclosure requirements, and (2) if it were required to comply, which specific quantitative items must be disclosed at least quarterly versus which qualitative items may be disclosed annually, and (3) what obligations, if any, apply when the institution believes that disclosing specific proprietary information would seriously prejudice its competitive position.
required_facts: The institution is exempt from independently complying with the market risk disclosure requirements because it is a consolidated subsidiary of a U.S. bank holding company that is itself subject to those same requirements.

If compliance were required, quantitative disclosures under §217.212(c) — including VaR measures, stressed VaR measures, incremental risk capital requirements, comprehensive risk capital requirements, risk-category-specific VaR components, VaR back-testing comparisons, securitization position aggregates, and correlation trading position aggregates — must be made at least quarterly.

Qualitative disclosures under §217.212(d) — including portfolio composition, valuation policies, internal model characteristics, validation approaches, stress test descriptions, back-testing sample results, soundness standard descriptions, securitization monitoring processes, and credit risk mitigation policies — may be disclosed annually (after the fourth calendar quarter), with more frequent disclosure required only if material changes occur.
The VaR backtesting outliers that management considers material must be analyzed and disclosed as part of the quarterly quantitative comparison of VaR-based estimates with actual gains or losses.

For proprietary or confidential information whose disclosure would seriously prejudice the institution's competitive position, the institution may withhold the specific items but must disclose more general information about the subject matter and must explicitly state that specific items have not been disclosed and explain why.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.212(a) scope exemption for consolidated subsidiaries → §217.212(c) quarterly quantitative disclosure requirements → §217.212(d) annual qualitative disclosure requirements → §217.212(a) proprietary/confidential information carve-out
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (§217.212(a) scope): The institution is a consolidated subsidiary of a U.S. bank holding company that is itself subject to these same disclosure requirements. §217.212(a) explicitly exempts a Board-regulated institution from compliance if it is 'a consolidated subsidiary of a bank holding company or a depository institution that is subject to these requirements.' Because the parent BHC is subject to the same requirements, the subsidiary institution is NOT independently required to comply. Step 2 (hypothetical §217.212(c) quarterly quantitative): If the institution were required to comply, §217.212(c)(1) mandates at least quarterly disclosure for each material portfolio of covered positions: (i) high/low/mean and period-end VaR-based measures; (ii) high/low/mean and period-end stressed VaR-based measures; (iii) high/low/mean and period-end incremental risk capital requirements; (iv) high/low/mean and period-end comprehensive risk capital requirements broken down by risk classification; (v) separate measures for interest rate, credit spread, equity price, foreign exchange, and commodity price risk; (vi) comparison of VaR-based estimates with actual gains/losses including analysis of important outliers. §217.212(c)(2) additionally requires at least quarterly: aggregate on- and off-balance sheet securitization positions by exposure type, and aggregate correlation trading positions. Step 3 (§217.212(d) annual qualitative): Qualitative disclosures for each material portfolio are required at least annually after the end of the fourth calendar quarter, or more frequently if material changes occur. These include portfolio composition, valuation policies, internal model characteristics, validation approaches, stress test descriptions, back-testing results, soundness standard descriptions, securitization risk monitoring processes, and credit risk mitigation policies. Step 4 (§217.212(a) proprietary carve-out): Where disclosure of specific commercial or financial information would seriously prejudice the institution's position because it is proprietary or confidential, the institution is not required to disclose those specific items, but must disclose more general information about the subject matter and must state that, and explain why, the specific items have not been disclosed.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a $50 million commercial loan to a corporate borrower. The institution has purchased an eligible credit derivative from a highly rated guarantor to hedge this exposure. The credit derivative has a protection amount of $35 million and is denominated in euros, while the hedged loan is denominated in US dollars. The institution does not qualify for the use of its own internal estimates of foreign exchange volatility. The institution revalues the credit derivative once every 10 business days. The credit derivative does not include restructuring of the hedged exposure as a credit event. The residual maturity of the hedged loan is 4 years; the credit derivative matures in 3 years and contains no embedded options. The risk weight applicable to the corporate borrower is 100%, and the risk weight applicable to the guarantor is 20%. Determine how the institution should treat this hedged exposure for risk-weighting purposes, including the adjusted effective notional amount of the credit derivative after all applicable adjustments, and the risk-weighted asset amounts for each resulting exposure.
required_facts: Protection amount ($35M) is less than the exposure amount ($50M), so partial coverage treatment applies and the exposure must be split into protected and unprotected portions
Maturity mismatch exists (credit derivative maturity 3 years < hedged exposure maturity 4 years); adjusted notional Pm = $35M × (3 − 0.25)/(4 − 0.25) ≈ $25.667M
Restructuring event adjustment applies because the credit derivative excludes restructuring as a credit event; Pr = $25.667M × 0.60 ≈ $15.40M
Currency mismatch haircut HFX = 8% (institution does not qualify for own internal FX volatility estimates); no upward adjustment needed since revaluation frequency is every 10 business days
Final adjusted effective notional amount Pc = $15.40M × (1 − 0.08) ≈ $14.168M
RWA for protected exposure = $14.168M × 20% ≈ $2.834M; RWA for unprotected exposure = ($50M − $14.168M) × 100% ≈ $35.832M
Total RWA for the hedged exposure ≈ $38.666M

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.36(c) partial coverage split, then apply maturity mismatch adjustment under §217.36(d), then restructuring event adjustment under §217.36(e), then currency mismatch adjustment under §217.36(f), yielding final Pc used to determine protected vs. unprotected RWA
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Determine coverage type (§217.36(c)(2)): Protection amount P = $35M < exposure amount $50M, so this is partial coverage. The institution must split the hedged exposure into a protected portion and an unprotected portion.

Step 2 — Maturity mismatch adjustment (§217.36(d)): Residual maturity of hedged exposure = 4 years; residual maturity of credit derivative = 3 years (no embedded options, so longest possible maturity applies to the exposure and the stated maturity applies to the mitigant). A maturity mismatch exists because 3 < 4. Apply formula: Pm = P × (t − 0.25) / (T − 0.25), where t = residual maturity of credit risk mitigant = 3, T = residual maturity of hedged exposure = 4. Pm = $35M × (3 − 0.25) / (4 − 0.25) = $35M × 2.75 / 3.75 = $35M × 0.7333 = $25.667M (rounded).

Step 3 — Restructuring event adjustment (§217.36(e)): The credit derivative does not include restructuring as a credit event. Apply: Pr = Pm × 0.60 = $25.667M × 0.60 = $15.40M.

Step 4 — Currency mismatch adjustment (§217.36(f)): The credit derivative is denominated in euros; the hedged exposure is in USD. The institution does not qualify for own internal estimates of FX volatility, so HFX = 8% (0.08). The institution revalues every 10 business days, so no upward adjustment to HFX is required. Apply: Pc = Pr × (1 − HFX) = $15.40M × (1 − 0.08) = $15.40M × 0.92 = $14.168M.

Step 5 — Split into protected and unprotected exposures (§217.36(c)(2)): Protected exposure = Pc = $14.168M, risk-weighted at the guarantor's risk weight of 20%. Unprotected exposure = $50M − $14.168M = $35.832M, risk-weighted at the borrower's risk weight of 100%.

Step 6 — Compute RWA: RWA (protected) = $14.168M × 20% = $2.834M. RWA (unprotected) = $35.832M × 100% = $35.832M. Total RWA = $38.666M.

question_text: Apex Financial Group is a bank holding company that has been identified as a global systemically important institution by its primary federal regulator. As part of its year-end capital planning process, Apex's treasury team has computed the following scores under the two prescribed systemic risk measurement methodologies: a score of 485 under the first methodology and a score of 610 under the second methodology. Based solely on these scores, determine Apex's applicable systemic risk capital surcharge for the upcoming compliance period, and identify which methodology drives the final surcharge determination.
required_facts: Method 1 score of 485 falls in the 430–529 band under Table 1, producing a method 1 surcharge of 2.5%
Method 2 score of 610 falls in the 530–629 band under Table 2, producing a method 2 surcharge of 3.0%
The applicable GSIB surcharge is the greater of the two surcharges
3.0% (method 2) exceeds 2.5% (method 1), so the binding surcharge is 3.0%
The method 2 calculation drives the final surcharge determination

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply § 217.403(a) general rule (greater of method 1 and method 2 surcharges), then look up method 1 score of 485 in Table 1 to § 217.403(b)(1) and method 2 score of 610 in Table 2 to § 217.403(c)(1), compare the two results to determine the binding surcharge.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.403(a): The GSIB surcharge equals the greater of the method 1 surcharge and the method 2 surcharge. Step 2 — § 217.403(b)(1), Table 1: A method 1 score of 485 falls in the 430–529 band, yielding a method 1 surcharge of 2.5%. Step 3 — § 217.403(c)(1), Table 2: A method 2 score of 610 falls in the 530–629 band, yielding a method 2 surcharge of 3.0%. Step 4 — § 217.403(a) comparison: 3.0% > 2.5%, so the binding GSIB surcharge is 3.0%, driven by the method 2 calculation.

question_text: Ridgeline Community Bank is a Board-regulated institution that is NOT an advanced approaches institution. It has a consolidated subsidiary, Ridgeline Mortgage Corp., which has issued regulatory capital that is not wholly owned by Ridgeline Community Bank — third-party investors hold a minority stake. After applying all required regulatory adjustments and deductions, Ridgeline Community Bank's own common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital elements (excluding any minority interest) total $180 million, and its CET1 regulatory adjustments and deductions under the applicable rules amount to $12 million. The CET1 minority interest attributable to Ridgeline Mortgage Corp. is $22 million. Determine the maximum amount of CET1 minority interest that Ridgeline Community Bank may include in its consolidated CET1 capital, and state whether the full $22 million qualifies.
required_facts: Ridgeline Community Bank is subject to the paragraph (a) minority interest limitations because it is not an advanced approaches institution and its consolidated subsidiary has issued regulatory capital not wholly owned by the bank
The applicable cap formula is 10% of the sum of all CET1 capital elements (excluding minority interest itself) less CET1 regulatory adjustments and deductions
Net CET1 base = $180M − $12M = $168 million
CET1 minority interest cap = 10% × $168M = $16.8 million
Actual CET1 minority interest of $22 million exceeds the $16.8 million cap by $5.2 million
Maximum includable CET1 minority interest is $16.8 million; the full $22 million does not qualify

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Applicability check under §217.21(a)(1) confirms the non-advanced-approaches institution is subject to paragraph (a) limitations; §217.21(a)(2) provides the 10% cap formula applied to the institution's own CET1 elements net of adjustments/deductions.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Applicability: Ridgeline Community Bank is a Board-regulated institution that is not an advanced approaches institution, and its consolidated subsidiary has issued regulatory capital not wholly owned by the bank. Therefore §217.21(a)(1) applies and the paragraph (a) minority interest limitations govern.

Step 2 — Identify the cap formula under §217.21(a)(2): The includable CET1 minority interest must be no greater than 10% of the sum of all CET1 capital elements of the Board-regulated institution (excluding the minority interest itself), less any CET1 regulatory adjustments and deductions.

Step 3 — Compute the cap: CET1 elements (ex-minority interest) = $180 million; CET1 adjustments and deductions = $12 million. Net base = $180M − $12M = $168 million. Cap = 10% × $168M = $16.8 million.

Step 4 — Compare to actual minority interest: Actual CET1 minority interest = $22 million. Since $22M > $16.8M, only $16.8 million may be included; the remaining $5.2 million must be excluded.

Conclusion: The maximum includable CET1 minority interest is $16.8 million; the full $22 million does NOT qualify.

scenario_parameters.subsidiary: Ridgeline Mortgage Corp. (consolidated, minority-owned regulatory capital)

question_text: A large Board-regulated institution has a formal disclosure policy that was approved by its risk committee rather than its full board of directors. The policy addresses the institution's approach for determining public disclosures, including internal controls and disclosure controls and procedures. Two senior vice presidents have jointly attested that the quarterly disclosures meet all applicable requirements. The institution publishes its quarterly capital adequacy disclosures across three separate documents: its quarterly earnings release, its 10-Q filing, and a standalone regulatory capital report on its website. It does not publish any document that consolidates or cross-references the locations of all three disclosure sources. For qualitative disclosures that do not change quarter-to-quarter — such as its risk management objectives and definitions — the institution discloses these only in its annual report filed after the fourth calendar quarter. During the third calendar quarter, the institution completed a significant acquisition that materially altered its risk profile, but it did not update any public disclosures until its next scheduled quarterly filing six weeks later. Identify all the ways in which this institution's disclosure practices are non-compliant with the applicable requirements, and explain what corrective actions are needed for each deficiency.
required_facts: The disclosure policy must be approved by the board of directors, not a sub-committee such as the risk committee; risk committee approval alone is non-compliant.

When disclosures are spread across multiple public reports, the institution must publish a summary table specifically indicating the location of each disclosure; the absence of such a table is a deficiency.
A significant change — such as a material acquisition that alters the institution's risk profile — must be disclosed as soon as practicable, not deferred to the next scheduled quarterly filing.

Qualitative disclosures may be made annually only if no significant changes occur in the interim; a significant mid-year acquisition triggers an obligation to disclose the change and its likely impact promptly.
Attestation by one or more senior officers is required and is satisfied by the two SVPs jointly attesting; this element is compliant.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: All deficiencies are resolved by reading §217.62(a) and §217.62(b) directly: (a) requires a summary table indicating locations of all disclosures when spread across multiple reports, requires 'as soon as practicable' disclosure of significant changes, and permits annual qualitative disclosures only if no significant changes occur in the interim; (b) requires board of directors (not a sub-committee) approval of the disclosure policy, and requires attestation by one or more senior officers.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — §217.62(b): The disclosure policy must be 'approved by the board of directors.' Approval by the risk committee alone does not satisfy this requirement. Corrective action: obtain full board approval.

Step 2 — §217.62(b): Attestation by 'one or more senior officers' is required. Two SVPs attesting jointly satisfies the 'one or more senior officers' requirement, so this is NOT a deficiency (SVPs are senior officers). No corrective action needed here.

Step 3 — §217.62(a): When disclosures are spread across more than one public financial report or regulatory report, the institution 'must publicly provide a summary table specifically indicating the location(s) of all such disclosures.' Publishing across three documents without a summary table is non-compliant. Corrective action: publish a summary table cross-referencing all three disclosure locations.

Step 4 — §217.62(a): Qualitative disclosures that do not change each quarter may be disclosed annually after the fourth calendar quarter, 'provided that any significant changes are disclosed in the interim.' The significant acquisition in Q3 materially altered the risk profile, constituting a significant change. The institution was required to disclose the change and its likely impact 'as soon as practicable' — not six weeks later at the next scheduled filing. Corrective action: issue an interim disclosure as soon as practicable after the acquisition.

Step 5 — §217.62(a): The annual treatment of qualitative disclosures is permissible in general, but because a significant change occurred mid-year, the institution was also required to update those qualitative disclosures in the interim. Delaying until the next quarterly filing may not satisfy 'as soon as practicable.'

Step 4: Advise that the institution has zero compliance obligations arising from §§ 217.102-217.120 because there are no rules to comply with. Step 5: Note that the institution should monitor future Federal Register publications in case the agency promulgates rules in these reserved sections, but as of the current regulatory text, no action is required.

question_text: A global systemically important bank holding company is calculating its short-term wholesale funding score for the current reporting period. The firm's average risk-weighted assets over the prior calendar year were $850 billion. During that year, the firm maintained the following daily average positions: (1) $40 billion in secured funding transactions collateralized by Level 2A liquid assets with a remaining maturity of 31 to 90 days; (2) $25 billion in unsecured wholesale funding to non-financial-sector counterparties with a remaining maturity of 30 days or less; (3) $10 billion in covered asset exchanges involving the future exchange of a Level 1 liquid asset for a Level 2A liquid asset, with a remaining maturity of 91 to 180 days; (4) $15 billion in secured funding transactions collateralized by Level 2B liquid assets with a remaining maturity of 181 to 365 days; and (5) $8 billion in brokered deposits provided by retail customers with no stated maturity. Calculate the firm's short-term wholesale funding score, showing the weighted short-term wholesale funding amount and the final score.
required_facts: Secured funding collateralized by Level 2A liquid assets with 31–90 day maturity falls under Category 2 at a 25% weight, contributing $10.0 billion to the weighted STWF amount
Unsecured wholesale funding to non-financial-sector counterparties with ≤30 day maturity falls under Category 1 at a 25% weight, contributing $6.25 billion
Covered asset exchanges involving a Level 1 for Level 2A exchange with 91–180 day maturity fall under Category 2 at a 10% weight, contributing $1.0 billion
Secured funding collateralized by Level 2B liquid assets with 181–365 day maturity falls under Category 3 at a 10% weight, contributing $1.5 billion

Brokered deposits provided by retail customers with no stated maturity are treated as having a remaining maturity of 30 days or less, falling under Category 1 at a 25% weight, contributing $2.0 billion
Total weighted short-term wholesale funding amount = $20.75 billion
Short-term wholesale funding score = ($20.75B ÷ $850B) × 350 ≈ 8.54

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the short-term wholesale funding score formula under §217.406(a): average weighted STWF amount divided by average RWA, multiplied by 350. Each funding component must be classified into the correct category from Table 1 and weighted by the applicable maturity bucket.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Classify and weight each component using Table 1:

(1) $40B secured funding / Level 2A collateral / 31–90 day maturity → Category 2, 25% weight → $40B × 0.25 = $10.0B

(2) $25B unsecured wholesale / non-financial-sector counterparty / ≤30 day maturity → Category 1, 25% weight → $25B × 0.25 = $6.25B

(3) $10B covered asset exchange (Level 1 for Level 2A) / 91–180 day maturity → Category 2, 10% weight → $10B × 0.10 = $1.0B

(4) $15B secured funding / Level 2B collateral / 181–365 day maturity → Category 3, 10% weight → $15B × 0.10 = $1.5B

(5) $8B brokered deposits / retail / no maturity (treated as ≤30 days per no-maturity rule) → Category 1, 25% weight → $8B × 0.25 = $2.0B

Step 2 — Sum weighted amounts:
$10.0B + $6.25B + $1.0B + $1.5B + $2.0B = $20.75B

Step 3 — Apply score formula per §217.406(a):
Score = ($20.75B ÷ $850B) × 350
Score = 0.024412 × 350
Score ≈ 8.54

question_text: A Board-regulated institution (the acquirer) that calculates its risk-based capital requirements using advanced systems completed the acquisition of a regional bank on March 15, 2023. The acquired regional bank did not use advanced systems to calculate its risk-based capital requirements prior to the acquisition. As of the acquisition date, the acquired company's exposures carried an allowance for loan and lease losses (ALLL) of $180 million, and the acquired company's risk-weighted assets (calculated under the standardized approach) total $12 billion. The acquirer is now in the 18th month following the calendar quarter in which the acquisition closed and is still applying the standardized approach to the acquired company's exposures under the applicable transitional arrangement. The acquirer has not yet received any extension from the Board beyond the standard transition window. How much of the acquired company's ALLL may the acquiring Board-regulated institution include in its tier 2 capital, and what is the maximum dollar amount permitted under the applicable cap?
required_facts: The acquired company did not use advanced systems, so the transitional arrangement for companies without advanced systems applies.
The standard transition period is up to 24 months after the calendar quarter in which the acquisition consummates; at month 18, the acquirer is still within this window.
During the transition period, the acquired company's ALLL may be included in the acquiring institution's tier 2 capital up to 1.25% of the acquired company's risk-weighted assets.
The cap equals 1.25% × $12,000 million = $150 million.
The actual ALLL of $180 million exceeds the $150 million cap, so only $150 million may be included in tier 2 capital.

The acquiring institution must also disclose publicly the risk-weighted assets and qualifying capital calculated under the advanced approaches for itself and under the standardized approach for the acquired company.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single paragraph: §217.124(a) governs mergers/acquisitions of companies without advanced systems, specifying the 24-month transition window and the 1.25% of acquired company's risk-weighted assets cap on ALLL inclusion in tier 2 capital.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the applicable transitional arrangement: The acquired company did not use advanced systems, so §217.124(a) applies (not §217.124(b)). Step 2 — Confirm the transition period is still active: The acquisition closed in Q1 2023 (calendar quarter ending March 31, 2023). The 24-month window runs from the end of that calendar quarter, i.e., through Q1 2025. At month 18, the acquirer is still within the 24-month window and no Board extension is needed yet. Step 3 — Apply the ALLL cap: During the period in which the standardized approach (subpart D) applies to the acquired company, any ALLL associated with the acquired company's exposures may be included in the acquiring institution's tier 2 capital up to 1.25% of the acquired company's risk-weighted assets. Step 4 — Compute the cap: 1.25% × $12,000 million = $150 million. Step 5 — Compare to actual ALLL: The ALLL is $180 million, which exceeds the $150 million cap. Therefore, only $150 million may be included in tier 2 capital.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a non-resecuritization position in a securitization backed by residential mortgage loans that make monthly payments. The institution's risk analysts have assembled the following data for the position: the weighted-average total capital requirement of the underlying exposures (using unpaid principal as weights, calculated under the standardized approach) is 6.4%, and 8% of the underlying exposure balance (by dollar amount) consists of loans that are 90 days or more past due. The position has an attachment point of 4% and a detachment point of 9% of the current dollar amount of underlying exposures. The data used to assign these parameters was last refreshed 95 calendar days ago. Determine the specific risk-weighting factor the institution must assign to this securitization position.
required_facts: The underlying exposures require monthly payments, so the data used to assign SSFA parameters must be no more than 91 calendar days old.
The institution's parameter data is 95 calendar days old, which exceeds the 91-calendar-day limit.
Because the data does not satisfy the freshness requirement, the institution does not have 'appropriate data' to assign the SSFA parameters.
The institution must therefore assign a specific risk-weighting factor of 100 percent to the position.
The SSFA formula inputs (KG = 6.4%, W = 8%, A = 4%, D = 9%) are irrelevant because the data-freshness condition is not met and the fallback rule applies.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.211(a) requires that for securitizations with monthly or quarterly payment contracts, parameter data must be no more than 91 calendar days old; data that is 95 days old fails this threshold, triggering the 100% specific risk-weighting factor fallback in the same paragraph.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the data-freshness requirement: § 217.211(a) states that if the contracts governing the underlying exposures require payments on a monthly or quarterly basis, the data used to assign the SSFA parameters must be no more than 91 calendar days old. Step 2 — Apply to the scenario: the underlying residential mortgage loans make monthly payments, so the 91-day cap applies. The institution's data is 95 calendar days old, which exceeds 91 days. Step 3 — Apply the fallback rule: § 217.211(a) further states that a Board-regulated institution that does not have the appropriate data to assign the parameters must assign a specific risk-weighting factor of 100 percent to the position. Because the data is stale (95 > 91 days), the institution cannot validly use the SSFA parameters it has assembled. Step 4 — Conclusion: the institution must assign a specific risk-weighting factor of 100% to the position, regardless of what the SSFA formula would otherwise produce using the stated KG, W, A, and D values.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution's trading desk has completed its quarterly backtesting review. Over the preceding 250 business days, the desk recorded actual daily net trading losses (excluding fees, commissions, reserves, net interest income, and intraday trading) that exceeded the corresponding daily VaR-based measure on 7 separate occasions. The institution's internal risk models produce the following figures for the current period: yesterday's VaR-based measure was $18.2 million, and the average of the daily VaR-based measures over the preceding 60 business days was $14.5 million. Additionally, the most recent stressed VaR-based measure was $41.0 million, and the average of the stressed VaR-based measures over the preceding 12 weeks was $16.8 million. The institution has no specific risk add-ons, no incremental risk capital requirement, no comprehensive risk capital requirement, and no de minimis exposures. Determine the institution's VaR-based capital requirement and stressed VaR-based capital requirement, and compute the total standardized measure for market risk.
required_facts: 7 exceptions maps to a multiplication factor of 3.65 per the backtesting table
VaR-based capital requirement = greater of $18.2M and ($14.5M × 3.65 = $52.925M) = $52.925M
Stressed VaR-based capital requirement = greater of $41.0M and ($16.8M × 3.65 = $61.32M) = $61.32M
All other components (specific risk add-ons, incremental risk, comprehensive risk, de minimis) equal $0
Total standardized measure for market risk = $52.925M + $61.32M = $114.245M

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Determine multiplication factor from backtesting exceptions table, apply to 60-day average VaR and 12-week average stressed VaR, compare each against the non-multiplied current measure, take the greater for each component, then sum all components for the standardized measure.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Backtesting exception count: 7 exceptions over 250 business days. Per Table 1 to §217.204, 7 exceptions maps to a multiplication factor of 3.65. Step 2 — VaR-based capital requirement (§217.204(a)(2)(i)): Compare (A) previous day's VaR-based measure = $18.2M vs. (B) 60-day average × multiplication factor = $14.5M × 3.65 = $52.925M. The greater is $52.925M, so VaR-based capital requirement = $52.925M. Step 3 — Stressed VaR-based capital requirement (§217.204(a)(2)(ii)): Compare (A) most recent stressed VaR-based measure = $41.0M vs. (B) 12-week average × multiplication factor = $16.8M × 3.65 = $61.32M. The greater is $61.32M, so stressed VaR-based capital requirement = $61.32M. Step 4 — All other components (specific risk add-ons, incremental risk, comprehensive risk, de minimis) = $0. Step 5 — Total standardized measure for market risk = $52.925M + $61.32M + $0 + $0 + $0 + $0 = $114.245M.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution is in the process of computing its total wholesale and retail risk-weighted assets under the advanced approaches. During Phase 3 of the calculation, the institution's credit risk modeling team is assigning risk parameters to its loan portfolios. The institution has a large book of residential mortgage exposures that it has segmented into three groups: (1) conventional conforming mortgages with no government backing, (2) mortgages where the full principal of each loan is directly and unconditionally guaranteed by the full faith and credit of a sovereign entity, and (3) mortgages insured under a federal agency program where the guarantee is contingent on the servicer meeting ongoing servicing requirements. The modeling team proposes the following LGD estimates for the three segments: Segment 1 at 8%, Segment 2 at 6%, and Segment 3 at 7%. Additionally, the institution has a portfolio of corporate wholesale exposures rated to an internal grade associated with a PD of 0.02%, and a separate portfolio of loans to a multilateral development bank also assigned a PD of 0.02%. Determine which, if any, of the proposed LGD and PD estimates are permissible under the applicable regulatory floors, and identify the minimum permissible values for any that are not.
required_facts: The LGD floor for residential mortgage segments is 10% under the Phase 3 risk parameter rules
Segment 1 (conventional mortgages, no government backing) at 8% LGD violates the 10% floor and must be raised to at least 10%
Segment 2 (full principal directly and unconditionally guaranteed by a sovereign's full faith and credit) is exempt from the 10% LGD floor, so 6% is permissible
Segment 3 (contingent U.S. government agency guarantee dependent on meeting servicing requirements) is exempt from the 10% LGD floor under the contingent-guarantee exception, so 7% is permissible
The PD floor for wholesale obligors is 0.03%, so the corporate wholesale portfolio's proposed PD of 0.02% is not permissible and must be raised to 0.03%
Exposures to a multilateral development bank are explicitly exempt from the 0.03% PD floor, so the MDB portfolio's proposed PD of 0.02% is permissible

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Phase 3 risk parameter assignment under §217.131(d); PD floor at 0.03% per §217.131(d)(2) with sovereign/MDB exception; LGD floor at 10% for residential mortgage segments per §217.131(d)(3) with exceptions for sovereign-guaranteed and contingent-government-guaranteed exposures
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — LGD floor for residential mortgages: §217.131(d)(3) establishes that the LGD for each segment of residential mortgage exposures may not be less than 10%, subject to two exceptions. Segment 1 (conventional, no government backing): no exception applies, so the 10% floor applies. The proposed 8% LGD is below the floor and is NOT permissible; the minimum permissible LGD is 10%. Segment 2 (full principal directly and unconditionally guaranteed by the full faith and credit of a sovereign entity): this falls under §217.131(d)(3)(i), so the 10% floor does not apply. The proposed 6% LGD is permissible. Segment 3 (contingent federal agency guarantee dependent on servicer meeting servicing requirements): this falls under §217.131(d)(3)(ii), which covers guarantees by a contingent obligation of the U.S. government or its agencies where enforceability depends on some affirmative action by the beneficiary or a third party (e.g., meeting servicing requirements). The 10% floor does not apply. The proposed 7% LGD is permissible. Step 2 — PD floor for wholesale exposures: §217.131(d)(2) establishes that the PD for each wholesale obligor may not be less than 0.03%, except for exposures to or directly and unconditionally guaranteed by a sovereign entity, the Bank for International Settlements, the IMF, the European Commission, the ECB, the ESM, the EFSF, or a multilateral development bank, to which the institution assigns a rating grade associated with a PD of less than 0.03%. Corporate wholesale portfolio PD of 0.02%: no exception applies; the 0.03% floor applies. The proposed 0.02% PD is NOT permissible; the minimum permissible PD is 0.03%. Multilateral development bank portfolio PD of 0.02%: the MDB exception in §217.131(d)(2) applies. The proposed 0.02% PD is permissible.

scenario_parameters.segment_2_guarantee_type: direct unconditional sovereign full faith and credit
scenario_parameters.segment_3_guarantee_type: contingent US government agency guarantee requiring servicer compliance

question_text: A state member bank is preparing to issue a new class of perpetual equity instruments to raise regulatory capital. The instruments are structured as follows: they are paid-in and issued directly by the bank; they represent the most subordinated claim in any liquidation or insolvency proceeding; holders are entitled to a residual claim proportional to their share of issued capital after all senior claims are satisfied; the instruments have no maturity date and can only be redeemed through discretionary repurchases with prior regulatory approval; the bank made no communication at issuance creating any expectation of buyback or redemption; cash dividends are paid solely from the bank's net income and retained earnings, with no contractual cap on dividend amounts; the bank retains full discretion at all times to skip dividends without triggering any default or payment-in-kind obligation; dividend payments may only occur after all legal and contractual obligations, including payments on more senior claims, are satisfied; holders bear losses equally, proportionately, and simultaneously with all other holders of the same instrument class before any more senior claimholder absorbs losses; the paid-in amount is classified as equity under GAAP; and the instruments are reported separately from other capital instruments on the bank's regulatory financial statements. However, the bank's employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) purchased 8% of the total issuance using a loan provided directly by the bank, and the instruments are not publicly traded. The bank's compliance team argues that the ESOP-held portion qualifies for inclusion in the bank's highest-quality regulatory capital component because a specific carve-out applies. A second tranche of the same instrument class — representing the remaining 92% not held by the ESOP — was purchased entirely by third-party investors with no funding from the bank or any affiliate. Assess whether each tranche qualifies for inclusion in the bank's highest-quality regulatory capital component, identifying any criterion that is satisfied, waived, or violated for each tranche.
required_facts: The highest-quality regulatory capital component is common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital, and the instruments must satisfy all criteria in §217.20(b)(1)(i)–(xiii) to qualify.
The 92% third-party tranche satisfies all 13 CET1 eligibility criteria on the stated facts and qualifies for CET1 inclusion without any carve-out.
The 8% ESOP tranche facially violates criterion (b)(1)(x) because the bank directly funded the ESOP's purchase of the instruments.
A specific carve-out provides that an instrument issued by a Board-regulated institution to its ESOP does not violate criterion (b)(1)(x), regardless of whether the institution is publicly traded.

The carve-outs for criteria (b)(1)(iii), (b)(1)(iv), and (b)(1)(xi) also apply to the ESOP tranche because the instruments are not publicly traded and any repurchase would be required solely by virtue of ERISA.

The 8% ESOP tranche qualifies for CET1 inclusion because the applicable carve-out waives the criterion (x) violation, and the non-publicly-traded condition is met for the remaining ERISA-related carve-outs.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the 13 CET1 common stock eligibility criteria in §217.20(b)(1)(i)–(xiii) to both tranches, then evaluate whether the ESOP carve-out in §217.20(b)(5) waives the criterion in §217.20(b)(1)(x) for the bank-funded ESOP tranche, subject to the non-publicly-traded condition.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify that the highest-quality regulatory capital component is common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital under §217.20(b). Step 2: Apply each of the 13 criteria in §217.20(b)(1)(i)–(xiii) to both tranches. For the 92% third-party tranche, all 13 criteria are satisfied on the facts given — no maturity, most subordinated, residual claim, discretionary dividends, GAAP equity classification, no guarantee, no bank funding, reported separately, etc. Step 3: For the 8% ESOP tranche, criterion (x) — that the Board-regulated institution did not purchase or directly or indirectly fund the purchase of the instrument — is facially violated because the bank provided the loan used by the ESOP to purchase the instruments. Step 4: Evaluate §217.20(b)(5), which provides that an instrument issued by a Board-regulated institution to its ESOP does not violate criterion (b)(1)(x). This carve-out applies here because the instruments were issued to the bank's ESOP. Step 5: Check the condition attached to the §217.20(b)(5) carve-out for criterion (x): the provision states the ESOP carve-out for criterion (x) applies without a publicly-traded restriction — the non-publicly-traded condition applies only to the carve-outs for criteria (iii), (iv), and (xi) (i.e., the repurchase/redemption and seniority-enhancement criteria). Since the instruments are not publicly traded, the carve-outs for (iii), (iv), and (xi) also apply to the ESOP tranche, provided any repurchase is required solely by virtue of ERISA. Step 6: Conclude that the 8% ESOP tranche qualifies for CET1 inclusion because §217.20(b)(5) waives the otherwise-violated criterion (x), and the non-publicly-traded condition is satisfied for the ERISA-related carve-outs. Step 7: Conclude that the 92% third-party tranche independently satisfies all 13 criteria and qualifies for CET1 inclusion without reliance on any carve-out.

question_text: A compliance officer at a mid-sized bank holding company is reviewing the institution's regulatory capital framework documentation. During an internal audit, the officer discovers that the institution's capital policy manual references a set of rules under the Basel III US implementation framework that are described as 'reserved' — meaning no substantive regulatory requirements have been promulgated in those numbered sections. The officer needs to determine whether any binding capital adequacy obligations, calculation methodologies, or reporting requirements exist under those reserved provisions that the institution must comply with or incorporate into its capital planning process. Specifically, the institution wants to know if it must account for any requirements from those reserved sections when preparing its annual capital adequacy assessment and stress testing documentation.
required_facts: Sections 217.213 through 217.299 are entirely reserved with no substantive regulatory text
No binding capital adequacy obligations exist under §§ 217.213-217.299
No calculation methodologies or reporting requirements are promulgated in §§ 217.213-217.299
The institution is not required to incorporate any provisions from these reserved sections into its capital planning or stress testing documentation

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Direct lookup of §§ 217.213-217.299, which are entirely reserved with no substantive content
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Locate §§ 217.213-217.299 in Subpart F of 12 CFR Part 217. Step 2: Observe that all sections in this range are marked '[Reserved]', meaning no regulatory text has been promulgated. Step 3: Conclude that there are zero binding obligations, calculation methodologies, or compliance requirements arising from these sections. Step 4: The institution's capital adequacy assessment and stress testing documentation need not reference or account for any requirements from §§ 217.213-217.299 because no such requirements exist.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds an equity exposure to a diversified investment fund with an adjusted carrying value of $18 million. The institution has reviewed the fund's prospectus and confirmed it is not a community development equity exposure. The fund's prospectus permits investments in the following asset classes with the stated maximum allocation limits: corporate exposures (up to 60%), sovereign exposures (up to 50%), residential mortgage exposures (up to 40%), and equity exposures to publicly traded companies (up to 30%). The institution does not have sufficient information to calculate risk-weighted asset amounts for each individual exposure held by the fund on a look-through basis, so it cannot use the full look-through approach. The institution's risk and compliance team is evaluating whether to use the simple modified look-through approach or the alternative modified look-through approach. Under the simple modified look-through approach, the applicable risk weight for the highest-risk permitted exposure type is 300%. Under the alternative modified look-through approach, the applicable risk weights by exposure type are: corporate exposures at 100%, sovereign exposures at 0%, residential mortgage exposures at 50%, and equity exposures to publicly traded companies at 300%. Calculate the risk-weighted asset amount under each available approach, and determine which approach produces the lower risk-weighted asset amount. Also identify whether the investment limits in the fund's prospectus create any special calculation requirement under the alternative modified look-through approach.
required_facts: Simple modified look-through RWA = $18 million × 300% = $54 million
The sum of the fund's investment limits (60% + 50% + 40% + 30% = 180%) exceeds 100%, triggering the waterfall allocation rule under the alternative modified look-through approach

Under the waterfall rule, the institution allocates 30% to equity exposures (300% risk weight), then 60% to corporate exposures (100% risk weight), then the remaining 10% to residential mortgage exposures (50% risk weight)
Alternative modified look-through RWA = ($18M × 30% × 300%) + ($18M × 60% × 100%) + ($18M × 10% × 50%) = $16.2M + $10.8M + $0.9M = $27.9 million
The alternative modified look-through approach produces the lower risk-weighted asset amount ($27.9 million vs. $54 million)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply § 217.154(c) simple modified look-through and § 217.154(d) alternative modified look-through; the sum of investment limits exceeds 100%, triggering the waterfall rule in § 217.154(d)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Confirm approach eligibility: The institution cannot use the full look-through approach (§ 217.154(b)) because it lacks the data to calculate RWA for each individual fund exposure. The exposure is not a community development equity exposure (§ 217.154(a)(2) is inapplicable). Therefore the institution may use either the simple modified look-through (§ 217.154(c)) or the alternative modified look-through (§ 217.154(d)).

Step 2 — Simple modified look-through (§ 217.154(c)): RWA = adjusted carrying value × highest risk weight applicable to any permitted exposure type = $18M × 300% = $54 million.

Step 3 — Alternative modified look-through (§ 217.154(d)), check investment limit sum: 60% + 50% + 40% + 30% = 180%, which exceeds 100%. This triggers the special waterfall rule: the institution must assume the fund invests to the maximum extent in the highest-risk-weight exposure first, then the next highest, and so on until 100% is reached.

Step 4 — Apply waterfall under § 217.154(d): Rank by risk weight descending: (1) equity exposures to publicly traded companies at 300% — max 30%; (2) corporate exposures at 100% — max 60%; (3) residential mortgage exposures at 50% — max 40%; (4) sovereign exposures at 0% — max 50%. Allocate: 30% to equity (300%), then 60% to corporate (100%), then 10% to residential mortgage (50%) to reach 100% total. Sovereign (0%) receives 0% allocation.

Step 5 — Calculate RWA under alternative modified look-through: ($18M × 30% × 300%) + ($18M × 60% × 100%) + ($18M × 10% × 50%) = $1.62M × 3 + $10.8M × 1 + $1.8M × 0.5 = wait, recalculate: (0.30 × $18M × 3.00) + (0.60 × $18M × 1.00) + (0.10 × $18M × 0.50) = $16.2M + $10.8M + $0.9M = $27.9 million.

Step 6 — Compare: Simple modified look-through = $54M; Alternative modified look-through = $27.9M. The alternative modified look-through produces the lower RWA. The investment limit sum exceeding 100% triggered the waterfall allocation rule.

question_text: Maple Ridge Mutual Holdings is a supervised insurance organization that is currently conducting its annual building block determination. During the inventory process, the compliance team identifies a special purpose entity called Cedarwood Re Ltd. Cedarwood Re enters into reinsurance transactions exclusively with Maple Ridge's inventory companies that were identified through FR Y-6 and FR Y-10 reporting requirements. The actuarial team estimates that Maple Ridge's inventory companies are expected to absorb approximately 62 percent of Cedarwood Re's expected losses. Cedarwood Re has not previously been classified as an affiliate under NAIC SSAP No. 25 and Schedule Y, and it does not appear on any FR Y-6 or FR Y-10 report. The compliance team must determine whether Cedarwood Re must be included in the inventory of companies for purposes of the building block determination. Separately, Maple Ridge also identifies a small holding company, Birchwood Capital LLC, that engages solely in transferring risk from Maple Ridge affiliates to third-party reinsurers. Birchwood Capital would otherwise qualify as a material financial entity. Maple Ridge's CFO asks whether Birchwood Capital can be excluded from material financial entity treatment, and if so, what procedural step is required to make that election effective. Analyze both questions and state your conclusions.
required_facts: Cedarwood Re must be included as an inventory company because it satisfies all four conditions of the special-entity inclusion test: it transacts with FR Y-6/FR Y-10 inventory companies, the 62% expected-loss absorption exceeds the 50% threshold, and it is not otherwise identified as an inventory company (subject to a materiality confirmation).
The 62% expected-loss absorption figure exceeds the regulatory threshold of more than 50%, satisfying that specific prong of the four-part test.

Birchwood Capital may qualify for the material financial entity election because it engages solely in transactions that transfer risk from affiliates to third parties, which is one of the enumerated permissible transaction types.

The election is also conditioned on Maple Ridge's ability to calculate the adjustment required under the relevant building block adjustment provision; if that calculation cannot be performed, the election is unavailable.

The election must be included with the first financial statements submitted to the Board after Birchwood Capital is included in the supervised insurance organization's inventory; failure to make the election at that time forfeits it.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Cedarwood Re analysis requires applying the four-part conjunctive test in §217.605(b)(1)(ii)(A)–(D); Birchwood Capital analysis requires applying the material financial entity election criteria in §217.605(c)(1)–(2) and the procedural timing rule in §217.605(c)(1).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Cedarwood Re inventory inclusion: Under §217.605(b)(1)(ii), a company must be added to inventory if it satisfies all four conditions: (A) it enters into reinsurance or derivative transactions with inventory companies identified under §217.605(b)(1)(i); (B) it is material; (C) inventory companies identified under §217.605(b)(1)(i) are expected to absorb more than 50 percent of its expected losses; and (D) it is not otherwise identified as an inventory company. Cedarwood Re satisfies (A) because it enters into reinsurance transactions with FR Y-6/FR Y-10 inventory companies. The 62% expected-loss absorption exceeds the 50% threshold, satisfying (C). It is not on FR Y-6, FR Y-10, or classified under SSAP No. 25/Schedule Y, satisfying (D). Materiality under (B) is a factual determination; assuming the compliance team confirms materiality, all four prongs are met and Cedarwood Re must be included as an inventory company. Step 2 — Birchwood Capital material financial entity election: Under §217.605(c)(1), a supervised insurance organization may elect not to treat an inventory company as a material financial entity if the conditions in §217.605(c)(2) are met. Under §217.605(c)(2)(i)(A), the company must engage in transactions consisting solely of transferring risk from affiliates within the supervised insurance organization to third parties — Birchwood Capital meets this criterion. Under §217.605(c)(2)(ii), Maple Ridge must be able to calculate the adjustment required in §217.607(b)(4). If that calculation is feasible, the election is available. Procedurally, §217.605(c)(1) requires that the election be included with the first financial statements submitted to the Board after the company is included in the supervised insurance organization's inventory — missing this filing window forfeits the election.

scenario_parameters.second_entity_activity: risk transfer from affiliates to third-party reinsurers

question_text: A large bank holding company recently crossed the threshold that requires it to adopt the advanced approaches for calculating risk-weighted assets. The institution's board of directors approved a written implementation plan on March 1, 2024. The plan comprehensively addresses qualification requirements for the institution and all consolidated subsidiaries, includes a self-assessment of current practices, identifies gaps, and specifies measurable milestones with delivery dates. The institution proposes to begin its parallel run on June 1, 2024, and submits the implementation plan along with a copy of the board minutes to its primary federal regulator on April 15, 2024. The institution then conducts a parallel run beginning June 1, 2024, during which it reports its risk-based capital ratios on a calendar quarterly basis. After three consecutive calendar quarters of satisfactory compliance with qualification requirements, the institution requests approval to begin calculating risk-based capital requirements under the advanced approaches. Identify (1) whether the implementation plan submission timing satisfies the applicable regulatory requirement, (2) the minimum duration of the parallel run required before the institution may seek approval to use the advanced approaches, and (3) what the institution's minimum risk-based capital ratios are governed by during the parallel run period.
required_facts: The implementation plan must be submitted to the Board at least 60 days before the proposed parallel run start date (unless the Board waives prior notice)
April 15 to June 1, 2024 is approximately 47 days, which is less than the required 60-day advance submission window, so the submission timing does not satisfy the requirement absent a Board waiver
A satisfactory parallel run requires no less than four consecutive calendar quarters of compliance with qualification requirements to the Board's satisfaction
Three consecutive calendar quarters is insufficient to constitute a satisfactory parallel run; the institution must complete a fourth quarter before seeking approval
During the parallel run, the institution's minimum risk-based capital ratios are governed by subpart D of Part 217, not the advanced approaches rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.121(b)(2) governs the 60-day advance submission requirement for the implementation plan before the parallel run begins; § 217.121(c) defines the minimum four consecutive calendar quarters for a satisfactory parallel run and specifies that minimum risk-based capital ratios during the parallel run are governed by subpart D
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Submission timing: Under § 217.121(b)(2), the institution must submit the implementation plan to the Board at least 60 days before the proposed parallel run start date, unless the Board waives prior notice. The institution proposes to begin its parallel run on June 1, 2024, and submits the plan on April 15, 2024. The gap between April 15 and June 1 is 47 days, which is less than the required 60 days. Therefore, the submission timing does NOT satisfy the requirement (absent a Board waiver). Step 2 — Minimum parallel run duration: Under § 217.121(c), a satisfactory parallel run is a period of no less than four consecutive calendar quarters during which the institution complies with qualification requirements to the Board's satisfaction. Three consecutive quarters is insufficient; the institution must complete at least four. Step 3 — Capital ratios during parallel run: Under § 217.121(c), during the parallel run the institution's minimum risk-based capital ratios are determined as set forth in subpart D of Part 217 (the standardized approach minimums), not the advanced approaches.

question_text: A large U.S. bank holding company is subject to the global systemically important bank (GSIB) surcharge framework and must compute its Method 1 score for the current assessment year. The company reported the following systemic indicator amounts as of December 31 of the previous calendar year: total exposures of $2.8 trillion; intra-financial system assets of $420 billion; intra-financial system liabilities of $380 billion; securities outstanding of $310 billion; payments activity of $18 trillion; assets under custody of $22 trillion; underwritten transactions in debt and equity markets of $1.1 trillion; notional amount of OTC derivatives of $9.5 trillion; trading and available-for-sale securities of $480 billion; Level 3 assets of $55 billion; cross-jurisdictional claims of $620 billion; and cross-jurisdictional liabilities of $540 billion. The Board published the following aggregate global indicator amounts for the same year: total exposures $85 trillion; intra-financial system assets $14 trillion; intra-financial system liabilities $13 trillion; securities outstanding $11 trillion; payments activity $900 trillion; assets under custody $150 trillion; underwritten transactions $18 trillion; OTC derivatives notional $500 trillion; trading and AFS securities $16 trillion; Level 3 assets $1.8 trillion; cross-jurisdictional claims $28 trillion; cross-jurisdictional liabilities $26 trillion. Compute the company's Method 1 score in basis points, applying all applicable caps or limits. Show the systemic indicator score for each of the twelve indicators and the final summed score.
required_facts: The systemic indicator score for each indicator equals (indicator amount / aggregate global indicator amount) × 10,000 × indicator weight in basis points
The substitutability category uncapped sum equals approximately 151.93 basis points (payments activity ≈ 13.34 bp + assets under custody ≈ 97.83 bp + underwritten transactions ≈ 40.76 bp)
The substitutability category score is capped at 100 basis points because the uncapped sum exceeds that limit
The total exposures (size category) systemic indicator score is approximately 65.88 basis points
The cross-jurisdictional activity category contributes approximately 42.91 basis points (claims ≈ 22.14 bp + liabilities ≈ 20.77 bp)
The Method 1 score is the sum of all twelve systemic indicator scores after applying the substitutability cap, totaling approximately 320.14 basis points

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply § 217.404(b)(1) formula to each of the twelve systemic indicators using Table 1 weights, then apply the § 217.404(b)(2) substitutability category cap of 100 basis points before summing all scores under § 217.404(a).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Formula per § 217.404(b)(1): score_i = (indicator_amount_i / aggregate_global_i) × 10,000 × weight_i.

Step 2 — Compute each score:
• Total exposures (weight 20%): (2.8T / 85T) × 10,000 × 0.20 = 0.032941 × 10,000 × 0.20 = 329.41 × 0.20 = 65.88 bp
• Intra-financial system assets (weight 6.67%): (420B / 14T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.030000 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 300.00 × 0.0667 = 20.01 bp
• Intra-financial system liabilities (weight 6.67%): (380B / 13T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.029231 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 292.31 × 0.0667 = 19.49 bp
• Securities outstanding (weight 6.67%): (310B / 11T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.028182 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 281.82 × 0.0667 = 18.79 bp
• Payments activity (weight 6.67%): (18T / 900T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.020000 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 200.00 × 0.0667 = 13.34 bp
• Assets under custody (weight 6.67%): (22T / 150T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.146667 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 1,466.67 × 0.0667 = 97.83 bp
• Underwritten transactions (weight 6.67%): (1.1T / 18T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.061111 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 611.11 × 0.0667 = 40.76 bp
• OTC derivatives notional (weight 6.67%): (9.5T / 500T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.019000 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 190.00 × 0.0667 = 12.67 bp
• Trading and AFS securities (weight 6.67%): (480B / 16T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.030000 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 300.00 × 0.0667 = 20.01 bp
• Level 3 assets (weight 6.67%): (55B / 1.8T) × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 0.030556 × 10,000 × 0.0667 = 305.56 × 0.0667 = 20.38 bp
• Cross-jurisdictional claims (weight 10%): (620B / 28T) × 10,000 × 0.10 = 0.022143 × 10,000 × 0.10 = 221.43 × 0.10 = 22.14 bp
• Cross-jurisdictional liabilities (weight 10%): (540B / 26T) × 10,000 × 0.10 = 0.020769 × 10,000 × 0.10 = 207.69 × 0.10 = 20.77 bp

Step 3 — Apply substitutability cap per § 217.404(b)(2): The substitutability category comprises payments activity (13.34 bp), assets under custody (97.83 bp), and underwritten transactions (40.76 bp). Uncapped sum = 13.34 + 97.83 + 40.76 = 151.93 bp. This exceeds 100 bp, so the substitutability category score is capped at 100 bp.

Step 4 — Sum all scores: Size (65.88) + Interconnectedness (20.01 + 19.49 + 18.79 = 58.29) + Substitutability (capped at 100.00) + Complexity (12.67 + 20.01 + 20.38 = 53.06) + Cross-jurisdictional (22.14 + 20.77 = 42.91) = 65.88 + 58.29 + 100.00 + 53.06 + 42.91 = 320.14 bp.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has received supervisory approval to use an internal model for measuring the price risk of its correlation trading portfolio. The institution has been operating under this approved model for 14 months and has documented ongoing model validation results, including robust benchmarking outputs, that demonstrate the model's effectiveness. During the most recent 12-week period, the institution's weekly comprehensive risk measures (in millions) were as follows: Week 1: $42M, Week 2: $38M, Week 3: $45M, Week 4: $41M, Week 5: $39M, Week 6: $44M, Week 7: $47M, Week 8: $43M, Week 9: $40M, Week 10: $46M, Week 11: $48M, Week 12: $50M. The most recent comprehensive risk measure (Week 12) is $50M. Separately, the total specific risk add-on for the institution's modeled correlation trading positions, calculated under the applicable standardized methodology, is $180M. The institution wishes to use the more favorable of the two permissible calculation methods for its comprehensive risk capital requirement. (1) Identify which calculation method the institution is eligible to use and why. (2) Under that method, determine the comprehensive risk capital requirement, showing all intermediate calculations.
required_facts: The institution qualifies for the favorable method (Method ii) because it has operated under the approved model for more than one year (14 months) and has demonstrated model effectiveness through robust benchmarking

Under Method (ii), each weekly comprehensive risk measure equals the greater of the modeled measure or 8.0% × $180M = $14.4M; since all modeled measures exceed $14.4M, each week's measure equals the modeled measure
The most recent (Week 12) comprehensive risk measure = $50M
The comprehensive risk capital requirement = the greater of $43.58M and $50M = $50M
Method (i) would have yielded a higher capital requirement ($64.4M), confirming Method (ii) is more favorable

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Determine eligibility for the favorable method under §217.209(a)(2)(ii) (≥1 year + demonstrated effectiveness), then apply §217.209(d) to compute the capital requirement as the greater of the 12-week average or the most recent measure under that method.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Method eligibility under §217.209(a)(2): Two methods exist. Method (i) under §217.209(a)(2)(i) is always available: capital = modeled measure + surcharge (8% × specific risk add-on). Method (ii) under §217.209(a)(2)(ii) requires Board approval, ≥1 year of compliance, and demonstrated model effectiveness via benchmarking. The institution has 14 months (>1 year) and documented benchmarking results, so it qualifies for Method (ii). Under Method (ii), the comprehensive risk measure = the GREATER of (A) the modeled measure of all price risk, or (B) 8.0% × total specific risk add-on. Step 2 — Compute the Method (ii) weekly measures: The surcharge floor = 8.0% × $180M = $14.4M. Each week's comprehensive risk measure under Method (ii) = max(modeled measure, $14.4M). Since all weekly modeled measures ($38M–$50M) exceed $14.4M, each week's measure equals the modeled measure. Step 3 — Compute the 12-week average under §217.209(d)(1): Sum = 42+38+45+41+39+44+47+43+40+46+48+50 = $523M. Average = $523M / 12 = $43.583M. Step 4 — Most recent measure under §217.209(d)(2): $50M. Step 5 — Comprehensive risk capital requirement under §217.209(d) = greater of $43.583M and $50M = $50M. Step 6 — Compare to Method (i) for context: Under Method (i), each week's measure = modeled measure + $14.4M surcharge. Most recent = $50M + $14.4M = $64.4M; 12-week average = $43.583M + $14.4M = $57.983M; capital requirement under Method (i) = $64.4M. Method (ii) yields $50M < $64.4M, confirming it is the more favorable method.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution uses the Internal Models Approach (IMA) for market risk capital purposes and has entered into a portfolio of equity derivative contracts with a single corporate counterparty. The institution has computed its market risk capital charge for these contracts under its approved internal models. The risk management team is now reviewing whether any additional capital must be held against these same contracts, and if so, how that additional capital requirement should be calculated. Separately, another Board-regulated institution at the same firm uses the Standardized Risk-Weighted Assets (SRWA) approach and holds a mixed book of equity derivative contracts with various counterparties, some of which are covered by a qualified master netting agreement and some of which are not. The SRWA institution's compliance officer proposes to exclude only the contracts under the qualified master netting agreement from the counterparty credit risk exposure measure, while retaining the uncovered contracts in the measure. Is the IMA institution required to hold additional capital beyond its market risk charge for these equity derivative contracts, and what methodology governs that additional requirement? Is the SRWA compliance officer's proposed selective exclusion permissible?
required_facts: Under the IMA, the institution must hold risk-based capital against counterparty credit risk in equity derivative contracts in addition to the market risk capital charge — the market risk charge alone does not satisfy the full capital requirement.

The supplemental counterparty credit risk capital for IMA equity derivatives is computed by treating the contract as a wholesale exposure and calculating a supplemental risk-weighted asset amount under the wholesale exposure framework (§ 217.132).

Under the SRWA, a Board-regulated institution may elect to hold no capital against counterparty credit risk for equity derivative contracts, but only if that election applies to all such contracts — selective exclusion of a subset is not permitted.

For equity derivative contracts subject to a qualified master netting agreement under the SRWA, the institution must either include all or exclude all of those contracts from the counterparty credit risk exposure measure — partial inclusion or exclusion within the netting set is prohibited.
State that the proposal is impermissible because the SRWA opt-out must apply to all equity derivative contracts; do not say the source separately makes this a QMNA all-or-nothing violation.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.155(a) imposes a supplemental counterparty credit risk capital requirement on IMA institutions for equity derivatives, treating them as wholesale exposures under §217.132. §217.155(b) permits SRWA institutions to opt out of counterparty credit risk capital for equity derivatives only if the election applies to all such contracts; for contracts under a qualified master netting agreement, the institution must include all or exclude all — partial exclusion is not permitted.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — IMA institution: §217.155(a) states that under the IMA, in addition to the market risk capital already held, the institution must also hold risk-based capital against the counterparty credit risk in the equity derivative contract by treating it as a wholesale exposure and computing a supplemental risk-weighted asset amount under §217.132. The market risk charge alone is insufficient; a separate wholesale-exposure CCR capital charge is mandatory. Step 2 — SRWA institution, opt-out election: §217.155(b) permits a SRWA institution to choose not to hold capital against counterparty credit risk of equity derivative contracts, but only if it does so for all such contracts — the election is all-or-nothing across the entire equity derivatives book. Step 3 — SRWA institution, qualified master netting agreement subset: §217.155(b) further specifies that where equity derivative contracts are subject to a qualified master netting agreement, the institution must either include all or exclude all of those contracts from any measure used to determine counterparty credit risk exposure. The compliance officer's proposal to exclude only the netting-agreement-covered contracts while retaining the uncovered contracts is impermissible on two grounds: (i) the all-or-nothing opt-out must apply across all equity derivative contracts, not just a subset; and (ii) within the netting-agreement-covered group, partial inclusion/exclusion is also prohibited.

scenario_parameters.proposed_treatment: selective exclusion of netting-covered contracts only

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a securitization exposure in a non-resecuritization transaction. The underlying loan pool has the following characteristics: the weighted-average total capital requirement of the underlying exposures (using unpaid principal as weights) is 6.4%, and 12% of the underlying exposures by dollar balance meet one or more of the following conditions — they are 90 or more days past due, subject to bankruptcy proceedings, in foreclosure, held as real estate owned, have contractually deferred payments for 90 or more days (outside the permitted exceptions), or are in default. The institution's securitization exposure has an attachment point of 3.2% and a detachment point of 7.5% of the current dollar amount of underlying exposures. The data used to assign these parameters is 45 calendar days old, and the underlying loan contracts require monthly payments. Determine the appropriate risk weight for this securitization exposure under the simplified supervisory formula approach, showing all intermediate calculations.
required_facts: Data is 45 calendar days old, which is within the 91-calendar-day limit for monthly-payment contracts, so SSFA may be used
KG = 0.064, W = 0.12, A = 0.032, D = 0.075, p = 0.5 (non-resecuritization)
Because D (0.075) is less than or equal to KA (0.11632), the detachment-point condition is triggered
The risk weight assigned to the securitization exposure is 1,250 percent

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply SSFA: verify data freshness under §217.144(a), assign parameters under §217.144(b), compute KA under §217.144(d), then determine risk weight branch under §217.144(c)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Data freshness check (§217.144(a)): The underlying contracts require monthly payments, so data must be no more than 91 calendar days old. The data is 45 days old, which satisfies this requirement. The institution may proceed with SSFA.

Step 2 — Assign SSFA parameters (§217.144(b)):
  KG = 0.064 (weighted-average capital requirement of 6.4%, expressed as decimal)
  W = 0.12 (12% of underlying exposures meet the distressed criteria listed in §217.144(b)(2)(i)–(vi))
  A = 0.032 (attachment point of 3.2%)
  D = 0.075 (detachment point of 7.5%)
  p = 0.5 (non-resecuritization exposure per §217.144(b)(5))

Step 3 — Compute KA (§217.144(d)):
  KA = (1 − W) × KG + 0.5 × W
  KA = (1 − 0.12) × 0.064 + 0.5 × 0.12
  KA = 0.88 × 0.064 + 0.06
  KA = 0.05632 + 0.06
  KA = 0.11632

Step 4 — Determine risk weight branch (§217.144(c)):
  A = 0.032, D = 0.075, KA = 0.11632
  Check §217.144(c)(1): Is D ≤ KA? → 0.075 ≤ 0.11632? YES.
  Therefore the entire exposure must be assigned a risk weight of 1,250 percent.

Step 5 — Floor check (§217.144(c)): The assigned risk weight is the larger of 1,250%, the formula result, and 20%. 1,250% is already the maximum applicable value.

Final risk weight: 1,250 percent.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution originated a portfolio of revolving home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and transferred them to a newly formed special purpose entity (SPE) as part of a traditional securitization. The HELOCs allow borrowers to draw, repay, and redraw amounts up to an agreed credit limit at any time during the draw period. The SPE issued asset-backed securities to third-party investors, and the transferred exposures are no longer reported on the institution's consolidated balance sheet under GAAP. The institution transferred all credit risk associated with the underlying exposures to the third-party investors, and the only call option retained is a clean-up call that qualifies as an eligible clean-up call. The institution holds no residual interest or other securitization exposure in connection with this transaction. May the institution exclude the transferred HELOC exposures from its risk-weighted asset calculation, and what capital treatment applies to the transferred exposures?
required_facts: The four conditions of §217.141(a) must all be satisfied for the institution to exclude transferred exposures from risk-weighted assets
Condition (4) requires that the securitization not include line-of-credit exposures under (4)(i) and not contain an early amortization provision under (4)(ii).
HELOCs satisfy the revolving-exposure prong of condition (4)(i) because borrowers may vary the drawn amount within an agreed credit limit
Because the securitization includes HELOCs covered by §217.141(a)(4)(i), condition (4) is not satisfied even if there is no early amortization provision.
The institution may not exclude the transferred HELOC exposures from risk-weighted assets and must hold capital against them as if they had not been securitized.
Because the institution retains no securitization exposures in connection with the transaction, it is not required to hold additional risk-based capital against any retained interest

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the four operational conditions in §217.141(a) for traditional securitizations; condition (4) disqualifies the transaction because the underlying HELOCs permit borrowers to vary the drawn amount within an agreed limit under a line of credit, satisfying §217.141(a)(4)(i)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the applicable rule. The institution transferred exposures to an SPE in a traditional securitization, so §217.141(a) governs whether the exposures may be excluded from RWA. Step 2: Check each of the four conditions. Condition (1): Exposures are off-balance-sheet under GAAP — satisfied. Condition (2): Credit risk transferred to third parties — satisfied. Condition (3): Clean-up call is an eligible clean-up call — satisfied. Condition (4): The securitization must NOT include (i) underlying exposures where the borrower is permitted to vary the drawn amount within an agreed limit under a line of credit AND (ii) contain an early amortization provision. Step 3: Analyze condition (4)(i). HELOCs by definition allow borrowers to draw, repay, and redraw up to a credit limit — this is precisely the feature described in §217.141(a)(4)(i). Therefore the securitization includes underlying exposures in which the borrower is permitted to vary the drawn amount within an agreed limit under a line of credit. Step 4: Determine whether both prongs of (4) must be present. The regulation uses 'and' connecting (4)(i) and (4)(ii), meaning the disqualifying condition requires BOTH a revolving feature AND an early amortization provision. The scenario states no early amortization provision exists, so condition (4) is technically satisfied (the disqualifying combination is not present). Step 5: Re-read condition (4) carefully. The condition states the securitization does not include (i) revolving exposures AND (ii) an early amortization provision.
