Since there is no early amortization provision, the conjunction is not fully met, and condition (4) is satisfied. Step 6: All four conditions are satisfied. The institution MAY exclude the transferred exposures from RWA. Step 7: Because the institution holds no retained securitization exposures, it holds no additional risk-based capital against this transaction.

question_text: Apex Financial Group is a large U.S. bank holding company that completed its annual systemic risk scoring exercise on November 15. Its method 1 score, computed using the five equally-weighted indicator categories, came out to 128 basis points. The compliance team is debating whether Apex must be treated as a global systemically important bank holding company for the upcoming capital planning cycle. Determine whether Apex qualifies as a global systemically important BHC based on its score, and identify the deadline by which a bank holding company in Apex's position must complete its annual score calculation.
required_facts: A bank holding company is identified as a GSIB only if its method 1 score equals or exceeds 130 basis points
Apex's method 1 score of 128 basis points is below the 130 basis point threshold
Apex does not qualify as a global systemically important BHC based on its current score
A bank holding company must calculate its method 1 score on an annual basis by December 31 of each year
Apex's November 15 calculation date satisfies the December 31 annual deadline

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-paragraph threshold check: method 1 score must equal or exceed 130 basis points for GSIB identification; annual calculation deadline is December 31.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Locate the identification rule for global systemically important BHCs. The rule states that a bank holding company is a GSIB if its method 1 score equals or exceeds 130 basis points. Step 2: Compare Apex's score of 128 basis points against the 130 basis point threshold. 128 < 130, so Apex does NOT meet the threshold and is not identified as a GSIB. Step 3: Note the annual calculation deadline. The rule requires the method 1 score to be calculated on an annual basis by December 31 of each year (subject to the exception provision). Apex completed its calculation on November 15, which is before the December 31 deadline, so the timing is compliant regardless of the GSIB determination.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution recently acquired a $45 million position in a mezzanine tranche of a residential mortgage-backed securitization. The institution's risk management team conducted a pre-acquisition analysis of the structural features, including the cash flow waterfall, credit enhancement levels, and deal-specific default definitions. However, the team did not document this analysis until 12 business days after the position was acquired, citing internal workflow delays. The underlying pool consists of 1,200 residential mortgage loans with an average LTV ratio of 78%, an average credit score of 695, and 4.2% of loans currently 60 days past due. The institution has not yet performed any subsequent review of the exposure since acquisition four months ago. The position represents approximately 0.8% of the institution's total regulatory capital base of $5.6 billion. Assess whether the institution is in compliance with the due diligence requirements applicable to this securitization exposure, identifying each specific deficiency and the regulatory consequence that would follow from any failure to satisfy those requirements.
required_facts: The institution violated the three-business-day documentation requirement because it documented the pre-acquisition analysis 12 business days after acquiring the exposure
The institution violated the quarterly ongoing review requirement because no subsequent review was performed in the four months since acquisition
Both deficiencies prevent the institution from demonstrating a comprehensive understanding of the securitization exposure to the Board's satisfaction
The regulatory consequence of failing the due diligence requirements is assignment of a 1,250% risk weight to the $45 million securitization exposure
The due diligence analysis must be commensurate with the complexity of the exposure and its materiality relative to capital (here, approximately 0.8% of the $5.6 billion capital base)
The carve-outs for CET1-deducted exposures and exposures subject to the specific alternative treatment do not apply to this position, so the full due diligence regime governs

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.41(c)(1) establishes the general due diligence standard and the 1,250% risk weight penalty; §217.41(c)(2)(i) requires pre-acquisition analysis documented within three business days; §217.41(c)(2)(ii) requires ongoing quarterly review
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify the applicable rule: §217.41(c) governs due diligence requirements for securitization exposures held by a Board-regulated institution. The general standard under §217.41(c)(1) requires the institution to demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of features that would materially affect performance; failure to do so triggers a 1,250% risk weight on the exposure.

Step 2 — Check documentation timing: §217.41(c)(2)(i) requires that the pre-acquisition risk analysis be documented within three business days after acquiring the exposure. The institution documented 12 business days after acquisition — a clear violation of the three-business-day documentation requirement.

Step 3 — Check ongoing review: §217.41(c)(2)(ii) requires evaluation, review, and updating of the analysis on an ongoing basis, no less frequently than quarterly. The institution acquired the position four months ago and has performed no subsequent review — this violates the quarterly minimum review requirement.

Step 4 — Determine consequence: Because the institution has failed to meet the documentation timing requirement and the ongoing quarterly review requirement, it cannot demonstrate to the Board's satisfaction a comprehensive understanding of the securitization exposure. Under §217.41(c)(1), the institution must assign the exposure a risk weight of 1,250% rather than the standard securitization risk weight. The analysis must be commensurate with complexity and materiality (0.8% of capital, $45 million position).

Step 5 — Note the carve-outs: §217.41(c)(1) exempts exposures deducted from CET1 capital and exposures subject to §217.42(h); neither carve-out is indicated here, so the full due diligence regime applies.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution that is not an advanced approaches institution holds a single, uncollateralized OTC interest rate swap with a remaining maturity of three years. The swap has a notional principal amount of $50 million and a current fair value of negative $200,000. The institution has not elected to use the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk and has not entered into any qualifying master netting agreement covering this contract. Calculate the exposure amount for this derivative contract under the current exposure methodology.
required_facts: Current credit exposure = max(−$200,000, 0) = $0 because the fair value is negative
The applicable conversion factor for an interest rate contract with remaining maturity greater than one year and up to five years is 0.005
Total CEM exposure amount = $0 + $250,000 = $250,000
The institution uses CEM because it is not an advanced approaches institution and has not elected SA-CCR

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply CEM to a single OTC derivative not subject to a qualifying master netting agreement: exposure = current credit exposure + PFE. Current credit exposure = max(fair value, 0); PFE = notional × conversion factor from Table 1 based on asset class and remaining maturity.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Confirm methodology: The institution is not an advanced approaches institution and has not elected SA-CCR, so it must use CEM per § 217.34(a)(1)(i). Step 2 — Identify the formula: For a single OTC derivative not subject to a qualifying master netting agreement, exposure amount = current credit exposure + PFE per § 217.34(b)(1). Step 3 — Current credit exposure: Per § 217.34(b)(1)(i), current credit exposure = max(fair value, 0) = max(−$200,000, 0) = $0. Step 4 — PFE: Per § 217.34(b)(1)(ii)(A), PFE = notional × conversion factor from Table 1. The contract is an interest rate derivative with remaining maturity of 3 years (greater than one year and less than or equal to five years). The applicable conversion factor from Table 1 is 0.005. PFE = $50,000,000 × 0.005 = $250,000. Step 5 — Exposure amount = $0 + $250,000 = $250,000.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution uses an internal model to calculate its market risk capital requirements. The institution's risk management team is reviewing its stressed VaR program. As of the current reporting date, the institution's VaR-based measure (99th percentile, 10-business-day holding period) is $85 million. The institution last calculated its stressed VaR-based measure six days ago, producing a result of $78 million. The stressed VaR model uses a 12-month historical window ending in Q2 2008 (covering the lead-up to the financial crisis), calibrated to the institution's portfolio composition from that period rather than its current portfolio. The institution's current portfolio has shifted significantly toward investment-grade corporate credit exposures, which behaved differently during the 2008 stress period than the legacy mixed-asset portfolio used for calibration. The institution's policies and procedures for selecting the stress period were last updated two years ago and have not been reviewed since the portfolio shift. These policies were implemented without prior Board approval. Identify all compliance deficiencies in this institution's stressed VaR program.
required_facts: The stressed VaR-based measure ($78 million) is less than the VaR-based measure ($85 million), violating the requirement that stressed VaR be no less than the VaR-based measure
Model inputs must be calibrated to a stress period appropriate to the institution's current portfolio, not a legacy portfolio composition
The institution must obtain prior Board approval for its policies and procedures governing stress period selection before implementing them
Policies and procedures must address how the stress period is linked to the composition and directional bias of the current portfolio
Policies and procedures must address the process for reviewing, updating, and monitoring the appropriateness of the selected stress period to the current portfolio
The stressed VaR-based measure must be calculated at least weekly

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply § 217.206 requirements: (a) weekly calculation frequency, (b)(2) floor constraint (stressed VaR ≥ VaR), (b)(1) calibration to current portfolio, (b)(3) policies/procedures including Board prior approval and linkage to current portfolio composition
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Frequency check under § 217.206(a) and (b)(2): The stressed VaR-based measure must be calculated at least weekly. Six days since last calculation may or may not breach the weekly requirement depending on calendar interpretation, but the institution should confirm it meets the 'at least weekly' standard. Step 2 — Floor constraint under § 217.206(b)(2): The stressed VaR-based measure ($78 million) is less than the VaR-based measure ($85 million). This directly violates the requirement that the stressed VaR-based measure 'be no less than the Board-regulated institution's VaR-based measure.' Step 3 — Calibration requirement under § 217.206(b)(1): Model inputs must be calibrated to historical data from a continuous 12-month period that reflects a period of significant financial stress 'appropriate to the Board-regulated institution's current portfolio.' Using a stress period calibrated to a legacy portfolio composition rather than the current portfolio violates this requirement. Step 4 — Policies and procedures: Board prior approval under § 217.206(b)(3): The institution must obtain prior Board approval for its policies and procedures describing how it determines the stress period. Implementing these without prior Board approval is a violation. Step 5 — Linkage to current portfolio under § 217.206(b)(3)(i): Policies must address how the institution links the stress period to the composition and directional bias of its current portfolio. The failure to update policies after a significant portfolio shift indicates non-compliance. Step 6 — Review and update process under § 217.206(b)(3)(ii): Policies must address the process for selecting, reviewing, and updating the stress period and monitoring its appropriateness to the current portfolio. The two-year-old, unreviewed policies following a material portfolio shift indicate this process is not functioning.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a reverse repurchase agreement with a corporate counterparty. Under the transaction, the institution has taken as collateral a sovereign bond that qualifies for a zero percent risk weight under the standardized approach. The fair value of the sovereign bond collateral is $10 million, and the institution has discounted that fair value by 20 percent before applying it against the exposure. The gross exposure under the agreement is $9 million. The institution wants to use the simple approach to recognize the credit risk mitigation benefit of this collateral. The collateral agreement covers the full life of the exposure, the collateral is revalued monthly, and both the collateral and the exposure are denominated in US dollars. Determine the risk weight the institution may assign to the collateralized portion of the exposure, and calculate the resulting risk-weighted asset amount for that collateralized portion.
required_facts: The collateral meets all three simple approach eligibility requirements: collateral agreement covers the life of the exposure, revaluation at least every six months (monthly satisfies this), and same-currency denomination

The general 20 percent risk-weight floor under the simple approach does not apply here because the exception for sovereign collateral qualifying for zero percent risk weight with a 20 percent fair-value discount is triggered
Discounted collateral value = $10 million × (1 − 0.20) = $8 million, which sets the collateralized portion of the $9 million exposure
The risk weight assigned to the collateralized portion ($8 million) is zero percent, resulting in RWA of $0 for that portion
The unsecured portion of the exposure is $9 million − $8 million = $1 million, which must be risk-weighted at the counterparty's applicable risk weight under the standardized approach

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.37(b)(1) simple approach eligibility requirements, confirm collateral qualifies, then apply §217.37(b)(2)(i) risk weight substitution rule (20% floor), then check §217.37(b)(3)(iii)(B) exception which allows zero percent risk weight when collateral is a sovereign qualifying for 0% risk weight and fair value has been discounted by 20%.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Confirm simple approach eligibility under §217.37(b)(1): (A) collateral agreement covers at least the life of the exposure ✓; (B) collateral revalued at least every six months (monthly revaluation satisfies this) ✓; (C) collateral and exposure denominated in same currency (both USD) ✓. Step 2 — Identify the collateral type: sovereign bond qualifying for 0% risk weight under §217.32 (referenced in §217.37(b)(3)(iii)(B)). Step 3 — Under §217.37(b)(2)(i), the general rule is that the risk weight for the collateralized portion may not be less than 20%. Step 4 — Check §217.37(b)(3)(iii)(B) exception: the institution may assign a zero percent risk weight to the collateralized portion where the financial collateral is an exposure to a sovereign qualifying for zero percent risk weight AND the institution has discounted the fair value of the collateral by 20%. Both conditions are met: sovereign bond qualifies for 0% risk weight, and the institution has applied the 20% discount. Step 5 — Discounted collateral value = $10M × (1 − 0.20) = $8 million. The collateralized portion of the $9M exposure is capped at the discounted collateral value = $8 million. Step 6 — Risk weight on collateralized portion = 0% (exception applies). RWA for collateralized portion = $8M × 0% = $0. Step 7 — Unsecured portion = $9M − $8M = $1 million, to which the counterparty's applicable risk weight under subpart D applies per §217.37(b)(2)(ii).

scenario_parameters.collateral_type: sovereign bond qualifying for 0% risk weight

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has the following off-balance sheet items outstanding at quarter-end: (1) an unused revolving credit facility of $80 million that the institution may cancel at any time without condition; (2) a trade finance facility of $50 million supporting the movement of goods, with an original maturity of nine months, that the institution cannot unilaterally cancel; (3) a performance standby letter of credit of $30 million issued in connection with a construction contract; (4) a financial standby letter of credit of $25 million guaranteeing payment obligations of a corporate borrower; and (5) a forward agreement to purchase mortgage-backed securities with a notional value of $40 million. None of these exposures are securitization exposures. Calculate the total credit-equivalent exposure amount for each item and the aggregate exposure amount across all five items.
required_facts: The unconditionally cancelable commitment receives a 0% CCF, resulting in a $0 exposure amount
The nine-month trade finance facility receives a 20% CCF (original maturity ≤ one year, self-liquidating trade-related item), resulting in a $10 million exposure amount
The performance standby letter of credit receives a 50% CCF as a transaction-related contingent item, resulting in a $15 million exposure amount
The financial standby letter of credit receives a 100% CCF, resulting in a $25 million exposure amount
The forward agreement receives a 100% CCF, resulting in a $40 million exposure amount
The aggregate credit-equivalent exposure amount across all five items is $90 million

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the correct CCF from § 217.33(b) to each off-balance sheet item based on its type and maturity characteristics, then sum the resulting exposure amounts.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Item 1 ($80M unconditionally cancelable commitment): Under § 217.33(b)(1), a zero percent CCF applies to the unused portion of a commitment that is unconditionally cancelable. Exposure = $80M × 0% = $0.

Step 2 — Item 2 ($50M trade finance, 9-month maturity, not unconditionally cancelable): Under § 217.33(b)(2)(ii), a 20% CCF applies to self-liquidating, trade-related contingent items arising from the movement of goods with an original maturity of one year or less. Nine months is ≤ one year. Exposure = $50M × 20% = $10M.

Step 3 — Item 3 ($30M performance standby letter of credit): Under § 217.33(b)(3)(ii), a 50% CCF applies to transaction-related contingent items, including performance standby letters of credit. Exposure = $30M × 50% = $15M.

Step 4 — Item 4 ($25M financial standby letter of credit): Under § 217.33(b)(4)(vi), a 100% CCF applies to financial standby letters of credit. Exposure = $25M × 100% = $25M.

Step 5 — Item 5 ($40M forward agreement): Under § 217.33(b)(4)(vii), a 100% CCF applies to forward agreements. Exposure = $40M × 100% = $40M.

Step 6 — Aggregate: $0 + $10M + $15M + $25M + $40M = $90M total credit-equivalent exposure.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a wholesale term loan to a mid-size corporate borrower (the obligor). The institution has purchased a single-name credit default swap from a highly rated domestic bank (the protection provider) referencing the same corporate obligor. The CDS is uncollateralized and provides immediate payout upon a credit event. The institution has received prior written Board approval for its process to detect excessive correlation between the obligor's creditworthiness and the protection provider's creditworthiness, and no excessive correlation has been detected. The obligor is not affiliated with the protection provider, and neither party is a sovereign. The protection amount under the CDS is $80 million, while the exposure at default (EAD) of the loan is $100 million. The institution wishes to recognize the credit risk mitigation benefit of the CDS using the most favorable treatment available under the advanced approaches framework. The obligor's probability of default (PDo) is 0.8%, and the protection provider's probability of default (PDg) is 0.3%. The LGD of the underlying loan (unadjusted for the CDS) is 45%, and the LGD of the CDS itself is 40%. The effective maturity of the CDS is 2.5 years. Determine: (1) whether the institution may apply the special double default treatment to this position; (2) how the exposure must be split for capital calculation purposes; and (3) the dollar risk-based capital requirement for the protected portion of the exposure, using the double default formula with the asset value correlation (R) for a non-HVCRE wholesale exposure derived from the standard formula evaluated at PDo, and the maturity adjustment coefficient (b) evaluated at the lesser of PDo and PDg.
required_facts: All six eligibility criteria for double default treatment are satisfied, so the institution may apply double default treatment to this position.

Because the protection amount ($80M) is less than the EAD ($100M), the exposure must be split: a protected portion with EAD = $80M (subject to the double default formula) and an unprotected portion with EAD = $20M (subject to the standard wholesale capital calculation).
LGDg = 40% (the lower of the loan LGD of 45% and the CDS LGD of 40%), because the CDS provides the institution with the option to receive immediate payout upon triggering protection.
The asset value correlation ρos is computed using the standard non-HVCRE wholesale formula evaluated at PDo = 0.8%, yielding approximately 0.2004.

The maturity adjustment coefficient b is computed at the lesser of PDo (0.8%) and PDg (0.3%), i.e., at PD = 0.3%, yielding approximately 0.1907; with M = 2.5 years the maturity adjustment factor equals approximately 1.4007.
KDD ≈ 0.04154, and the dollar risk-based capital requirement for the protected portion is KDD × $80M ≈ $3.32 million.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Check eligibility criteria in §217.135(a), then apply partial coverage split under §217.135(c) because P ($80M) < EAD ($100M), then compute KDD under §217.135(e) using the formula with PDo, PDg, LGDg (lower of loan LGD and CDS LGD since immediate payout applies), ρos from Table 1 in §217.131 at PDo, and b from Table 1 in §217.131 at min(PDo, PDg).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Eligibility (§217.135(a)): (a)(1) the hedged exposure is covered by an eligible credit derivative from an eligible double default guarantor; (a)(2)(i) the CDS is uncollateralized and single-reference-obligor; (a)(3) the exposure is wholesale and non-sovereign; (a)(4) the obligor is not affiliated with the protection provider; (a)(5) no other CRM benefit is recognized; (a)(6) Board-approved excessive-correlation process exists and no excessive correlation detected. All criteria satisfied → double default treatment is available. Step 2 — Coverage test (§217.135(b) vs (c)): P = $80M < EAD = $100M → partial coverage under §217.135(c). Split into: protected exposure EAD = $80M (use §217.135(e)); unprotected exposure EAD = $100M − $80M = $20M (use §217.131). Step 3 — LGDg selection (§217.135(e)(4)(i)): CDS provides immediate payout → use lower of LGD of hedged exposure (45%) and LGD of CDS (40%) → LGDg = 40%. Step 4 — ρos (§217.135(e)(5)): use Table 1 in §217.131 wholesale (non-HVCRE) formula at PDo = 0.008: ρos = 0.12×(1−e^(−50×0.008))/(1−e^(−50)) + 0.24×[1−(1−e^(−50×0.008))/(1−e^(−50))]. e^(−0.4) ≈ 0.6703; numerator factor ≈ (1−0.6703)/(1−e^(−50)) ≈ 0.3297/1 ≈ 0.3297. ρos ≈ 0.12×0.3297 + 0.24×(1−0.3297) = 0.03956 + 0.24×0.6703 = 0.03956 + 0.16087 ≈ 0.2004. Step 5 — b (§217.135(e)(6)): use lesser of PDo (0.008) and PDg (0.003) → PD = 0.003. b = (0.11852 − 0.05478×ln(0.003))^2 = (0.11852 − 0.05478×(−5.8091))^2 = (0.11852 + 0.31822)^2 = (0.43674)^2 ≈ 0.19074. Step 6 — Ko (§217.135(e)(1)): Ko = LGDg × N[(N^{-1}(PDo) + √ρos × N^{-1}(0.999))/√(1−ρos)] − LGDg × PDo, then multiplied by maturity adjustment (1 + (M−2.5)×b)/(1−1.5×b). N^{-1}(0.008) ≈ −2.4089; N^{-1}(0.999) ≈ 3.0902; √0.2004 ≈ 0.4477; √(1−0.2004) ≈ 0.8944. Numerator inside N: (−2.4089 + 0.4477×3.0902)/0.8944 = (−2.4089 + 1.3831)/0.8944 = (−1.0258)/0.8944 ≈ −1.1470. N(−1.1470) ≈ 0.1257. Ko (before maturity adj.) = 0.40×0.1257 − 0.40×0.008 = 0.05028 − 0.0032 = 0.04708. Maturity adj. = (1 + (2.5−2.5)×0.19074)/(1−1.5×0.19074) = 1/(1−0.28611) = 1/0.71389 ≈ 1.4007. Ko = 0.04708 × 1.4007 ≈ 0.06594. Step 7 — KDD (§217.135(e)): KDD = Ko × (0.15 + 160 × PDg) = 0.06594 × (0.15 + 160×0.003) = 0.06594 × (0.15 + 0.48) = 0.06594 × 0.63 ≈ 0.04154. Step 8 — Dollar capital requirement for protected portion: KDD × EAD_protected = 0.04154 × $80M ≈ $3.32M.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has been operating under the advanced approaches framework and completed a satisfactory parallel run. During a routine supervisory review, the Board determines that the institution's advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets are materially understated relative to the institution's actual credit, market, and operational risk profile — specifically, the institution's internal models for wholesale credit exposures have been calibrated using a narrow historical window that excludes a significant stress period, resulting in probability of default estimates that the Board considers inconsistent with the institution's true risk. The institution has not yet notified the Board of any changes to its advanced systems. The Board issues a written notice of non-compliance with the ongoing qualification requirements. Describe the institution's obligations following receipt of that written notice, and explain what additional authority the Board may exercise given its finding about the relationship between the institution's advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets and its actual risk profile.
required_facts: Upon receipt of the Board's written notice of non-compliance, the institution must establish and submit a remediation plan satisfactory to the Board to return to compliance with the qualification requirements
The remediation plan must be submitted to the Board, not merely developed internally

The Board's finding that advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets are not commensurate with the institution's credit, market, operational, or other risks triggers a separate, additional Board authority
Under that additional authority, the Board may require the institution to calculate its advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets using any modifications specified by the Board
The Board's authority to impose modified RWA calculations is discretionary ('may require') and is conditioned on the commensurateness finding, not solely on the non-compliance finding

Both obligations — the remediation plan and the potential modified RWA calculation — apply because the institution has conducted a satisfactory parallel run and is subject to the advanced approaches framework

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.123(b)(1) triggers written notice of non-compliance; (b)(2) requires the institution to establish and submit a remediation plan satisfactory to the Board; (b)(3) grants the Board additional authority to require modified RWA calculations when advanced approaches RWA are not commensurate with actual risk
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The Board has already issued written notice under (b)(1), satisfying that procedural step. Step 2: Under (b)(2), the institution must now establish and submit a plan — satisfactory to the Board — to return to compliance with the qualification requirements. Step 3: Because the Board has separately determined that the institution's advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets are not commensurate with the institution's credit, market, and operational risks (the PD underestimation finding), (b)(3) is independently triggered. Under (b)(3), the Board may require the institution to calculate its advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets with any modifications the Board provides — this is a distinct, additive authority beyond simply requiring a remediation plan.

scenario_parameters.trigger_event: Board determination of non-compliance with qualification requirements
scenario_parameters.secondary_finding: advanced approaches RWA not commensurate with actual credit, market, and operational risk
scenario_parameters.root_cause: PD models calibrated on narrow historical window excluding stress period
scenario_parameters.notification_status: institution has not notified Board of any system changes

question_text: Ridgeline State Bank is a state member bank that is a Board-regulated institution. In early June 2020, Ridgeline's management is evaluating whether to take advantage of a temporary regulatory relief measure that would allow the bank to exclude certain assets from its total leverage exposure calculation. As of the first day of the reporting quarter beginning July 1, 2020, Ridgeline holds $4.2 billion in U.S. Treasury securities and $1.8 billion in funds on deposit at a Federal Reserve Bank. The bank's total leverage exposure before any exclusions is $62 billion. Ridgeline's management wants to apply the exclusions starting with the July 1, 2020 quarter and intends to pay a $50 million dividend to shareholders in August 2020. Ridgeline has not yet taken any action to notify its regulator. Determine: (1) whether Ridgeline is eligible to apply the exclusions, (2) what procedural step must be completed before the exclusions can be applied, (3) the maximum amount that could be excluded from total leverage exposure if eligibility is established, and (4) whether the planned August 2020 dividend distribution is permissible without additional regulatory action.
required_facts: Ridgeline is eligible in category as a state member bank, but the exclusion is permissive (may exclude), not mandatory
Ridgeline must file an opt-in notice with the Board before July 1, 2020 to be eligible for the exclusions
If the opt-in notice is filed before July 1, 2020, relief applies from the beginning of the reporting quarter in which it was filed; for a June 2020 filing, that would be April 1, 2020.
The maximum excludable amount is $6.0 billion ($4.2 billion U.S. Treasury securities + $1.8 billion Federal Reserve deposits), reducing total leverage exposure to $56 billion

The planned August 2020 dividend of $50 million requires prior Board approval because Ridgeline would be an opted-in state member bank making a distribution during the period July 1, 2020 through March 31, 2021
The temporary exclusion relief terminates after the reporting period ending March 31, 2021

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: §217.303(a) establishes that a state member bank MAY (not must) exclude U.S. Treasury securities and Federal Reserve deposits; §217.303(b) gates eligibility on filing an opt-in notice before July 1, 2020; §217.303(c) determines when relief begins; §217.303(g) restricts distributions without Board approval for opted-in state member banks during the relief period
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Applicability under §217.303(a): Ridgeline is a state member bank that is a Board-regulated institution. Under §217.303(a), a state member bank MAY (permissive, not mandatory) exclude U.S. Treasury securities and funds on deposit at a Federal Reserve Bank from on-balance sheet assets when calculating total leverage exposure. Ridgeline is therefore eligible in category, but eligibility is conditioned on paragraphs (b) through (g). Step 2 — Opt-in requirement under §217.303(b): Before applying the relief, a state member bank must first notify the Board before July 1, 2020. Ridgeline has not yet notified the Board and is evaluating in early June 2020. The deadline is July 1, 2020, so Ridgeline still has time to file the opt-in notice, but it must do so before that date. If it fails to notify before July 1, 2020, it cannot apply the exclusions. Step 3 — Calculation of relief under §217.303(c): Relief applies from the beginning of the reporting quarter in which the opt-in notice was filed. If Ridgeline files before July 1, 2020, relief would apply starting July 1, 2020 (the beginning of that reporting quarter). Step 4 — Maximum exclusion amount: If eligible, Ridgeline may exclude $4.2 billion (U.S. Treasury securities) + $1.8 billion (Federal Reserve deposits) = $6.0 billion from total leverage exposure, reducing it from $62 billion to $56 billion. Step 5 — Distribution restriction under §217.303(g): During the calendar quarter beginning July 1, 2020 and until March 31, 2021, no state member bank that has opted in may make a distribution or create an obligation to make a distribution without prior Board approval. Ridgeline's planned $50 million August 2020 dividend falls squarely within this period. Therefore, even if Ridgeline opts in and is eligible for the exclusions, it cannot pay the August 2020 dividend without first obtaining Board approval. Step 6 — Termination under §217.303(d): The entire section ceases to be effective after the reporting period ending March 31, 2021, confirming the temporary nature of the relief.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has a wholesale loan to a mid-market corporate obligor with an exposure at default (EAD) of $80 million. The institution has purchased an eligible credit derivative from a highly rated protection provider to hedge this exposure. The credit derivative's notional amount is $50 million, and the derivative's reference obligation is a subordinated bond issued by the same corporate obligor. The hedged exposure (the loan) is a senior secured obligation of the same obligor. The institution wishes to recognize the credit risk mitigation benefit of this credit derivative under the PD substitution approach. Determine whether the institution may recognize the credit risk mitigation benefit of this credit derivative, and if so, describe how it must calculate the risk-based capital requirement for this exposure, including the treatment of the protected and unprotected portions.
required_facts: The credit derivative may be recognized because the reference obligation (subordinated bond) is junior to the hedged exposure (senior secured loan), satisfying the pari passu or junior ranking condition, provided cross-default or cross-acceleration clauses are legally enforceable
Because the protection amount ($50 million) is less than the EAD ($80 million), this is partial coverage and the institution must split the hedged exposure into two separate exposures
The protected exposure has EAD equal to $50 million (the protection amount P) and uses the protection provider's PD
The unprotected exposure has EAD equal to $30 million ($80M minus $50M) and uses the obligor's own PD and the unadjusted LGD of the hedged exposure
Separate risk-based capital requirements must be calculated for the protected and unprotected portions under the applicable wholesale risk-based capital formula

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.134(b)(2) rules of recognition for credit derivatives where reference exposure differs from hedged exposure, then proceed to §217.134(c)(1)(ii) partial coverage PD substitution treatment
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Rules of recognition (§217.134(b)(2)): The credit derivative's reference obligation (subordinated bond) is different from the hedged exposure (senior secured loan). Under §217.134(b)(2), the institution may only recognize the credit risk mitigation benefit if two conditions are met: (i) the reference exposure ranks pari passu with or is junior to the hedged exposure, and (ii) the reference exposure and hedged exposure are to the same legal entity with legally enforceable cross-default or cross-acceleration clauses. Here, the reference obligation is a subordinated bond, which is junior to the senior secured loan (hedged exposure). Condition (i) is satisfied. Condition (ii) requires the same legal entity (satisfied — same corporate obligor) and legally enforceable cross-default/cross-acceleration clauses. Assuming such clauses are in place, both conditions are met and the institution may recognize the credit risk mitigation benefit. Step 2 — Partial coverage determination (§217.134(c)(1)(ii)): The protection amount P = $50 million is less than the EAD of $80 million, so this is partial coverage, not full coverage. The institution must treat the hedged exposure as two separate exposures. Step 3 — Protected exposure: EAD = P = $50 million; PD = protection provider's PD; LGD determined under §217.134(c)(1)(iii). Step 4 — Unprotected exposure: EAD = $80M − $50M = $30 million; PD = obligor's PD; LGD = hedged exposure's LGD unadjusted for the credit derivative. Step 5 — Separate risk-based capital requirements are calculated under §217.131 for each portion.

question_text: A large depository institution holding company, Meridian Financial Group, is evaluating whether it qualifies as a 'supervised insurance organization' under the Board's insurance capital framework. As of June 30 of the prior calendar year, Meridian reported total consolidated assets of $180 billion calculated under GAAP. Of those assets, $48 billion are held in insurance underwriting subsidiaries — none of which relate to insurance underwriting for credit risk. Meridian is not itself an insurance underwriting company at the top-tier level, but it controls several insurance underwriting companies through intermediate holding companies. A compliance officer argues that Meridian meets the threshold for inclusion in the insurance capital framework based solely on the proportion of assets held in insurance underwriting companies. A second officer contends that Meridian would only qualify if it were itself an insurance underwriting company at the top-tier level. Determine which officer is correct, identify the precise asset percentage that Meridian's insurance underwriting holdings represent, state whether that percentage satisfies the applicable threshold, and explain what additional structural condition Meridian must satisfy to be treated as a supervised insurance organization under this framework.
required_facts: Meridian's insurance underwriting assets as a percentage of total consolidated GAAP assets = $48B / $180B = 26.67%
The applicable threshold for the asset-proportion test is 25% of total consolidated assets held in insurance underwriting companies (excluding credit-risk insurance)
26.67% exceeds 25%, so Meridian satisfies the asset-proportion threshold
The first officer is correct: a top-tier DIHC need not itself be an insurance underwriting company — the 25% asset test is an independent qualifying path
The second officer is incorrect: top-tier DIHC status as an insurance underwriting company is only one of two alternative qualifying conditions

The additional structural condition Meridian must satisfy is that it must be a top-tier depository institution holding company — meaning it is not controlled by another depository institution holding company
Total consolidated assets must be calculated under GAAP (or estimated subject to Board review if GAAP is not used for any regulatory purpose)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the two-prong definition of 'supervised insurance organization' under § 217.602(b): prong (i)(A) covers a top-tier DIHC that is itself an insurance underwriting company; prong (i)(B) covers a top-tier DIHC that holds 25% or more of total consolidated GAAP assets in insurance underwriting companies (excluding credit-risk insurance). Meridian is not itself an insurer (ruling out (i)(A)), so the analysis turns on (i)(B): $48B / $180B = 26.67%, which exceeds the 25% threshold. The structural condition is that Meridian must be a 'top-tier depository institution holding company,' meaning it is not controlled by another depository institution holding company.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify the two alternative paths to qualify as a supervised insurance organization under § 217.602(b)(i): (A) top-tier DIHC that is itself an insurance underwriting company, or (B) top-tier DIHC holding ≥25% of total consolidated assets in insurance underwriting companies (excluding credit-risk insurance). Step 2: Meridian is not itself an insurance underwriting company at the top-tier level, so path (A) does not apply — the second officer's contention is incorrect as a universal rule. Step 3: Evaluate path (B): $48B / $180B = 26.67%, which exceeds the 25% threshold. The first officer is correct that the asset-proportion test can independently qualify Meridian. Step 4: The 25% calculation uses GAAP total consolidated assets (confirmed here). Step 5: The remaining structural condition is that Meridian must be a 'top-tier depository institution holding company' — defined in § 217.602(b) as a depository institution holding company not controlled by another depository institution holding company. Step 6: Conclusion: Meridian satisfies the 25% asset threshold under path (i)(B) and qualifies as a supervised insurance organization provided it is a top-tier DIHC (i.e., not controlled by another DIHC).

question_text: A Board-regulated institution is preparing its quarterly regulatory capital report. Its balance sheet includes the following items that require risk-weighting under the general credit risk framework: (1) a $200 million commercial real estate loan held on-balance sheet; (2) a $50 million unfunded loan commitment with an original maturity of 18 months; (3) a $75 million interest rate swap executed bilaterally with a corporate counterparty (an OTC derivative contract); (4) a $30 million equity investment in an unconsolidated financial institution (not structured as a derivative); (5) a $100 million position in a residential mortgage-backed securities tranche that the institution originated and retains a subordinated interest in; and (6) a $40 million repurchase agreement with a primary dealer. The institution's risk management team is determining which of these six items must be included in the general credit risk risk-weighted asset calculation — that is, which items require the institution to (a) determine an exposure amount and (b) multiply that exposure amount by the applicable risk weight to produce a risk-weighted asset amount. Identify which items are subject to the general credit risk mechanics, which items are explicitly excluded from that calculation, and explain the basis for each determination.
required_facts: The $200 million on-balance sheet CRE loan is subject to the general credit risk mechanics: the institution must determine its exposure amount and multiply by the applicable risk weight.
The $50 million unfunded loan commitment is subject to the general credit risk mechanics as an off-balance sheet commitment; no exclusion applies.

The $75 million bilateral OTC interest rate swap is subject to the general credit risk mechanics as an OTC derivative contract; being bilateral (not centrally cleared) means the cleared-transaction exclusion does not apply.

The $30 million equity investment (not a derivative) is excluded from the general credit risk mechanics because it is an equity exposure other than an equity OTC derivative contract, and is instead subject to the equity exposure rules.
The $100 million retained subordinated RMBS tranche is excluded from the general credit risk mechanics because it is a securitization exposure, subject to the securitization framework.

The $40 million repurchase agreement is subject to the general credit risk mechanics; repo-style transactions are explicitly listed among the transaction types covered, and no exclusion applies on the given facts.

Total risk-weighted assets for general credit risk equals the sum of the risk-weighted asset amounts (exposure amount × risk weight) for the four included items: the CRE loan, the unfunded commitment, the OTC swap, and the repo.

Step 2 — Apply exclusions to each item:

  Item 2 ($50M unfunded commitment, 18-month maturity): An off-balance sheet commitment. No exclusion applies (it is not an unsettled transaction, cleared transaction, default fund contribution, securitization exposure, or equity exposure). → INCLUDED under §217.31(a)(1).

question_text: A Board-regulated institution participated in the Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility announced in March 2020. Under the facility, the institution received a non-recourse loan advance of $500 million and used those funds to purchase eligible assets at a purchase price of $480 million. The institution is now preparing its regulatory capital and leverage calculations. Specifically, it wants to know: (1) whether the $500 million exposure acquired through this facility may be excluded from its total leverage exposure and risk-weighted asset calculations, and (2) how the institution's liability under the facility should be measured for purposes of any such exclusion. Explain the regulatory treatment that applies to these exposures and compute the net liability amount the institution must recognize under the applicable rule.

The exposure may also be excluded from average total consolidated assets, advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets, and standardized total risk-weighted assets
The exclusion applies only because the loan is non-recourse and was provided as part of the MMLF announced March 18, 2020
The institution's liability under the facility must be reduced by the purchase price of the assets acquired with the advanced funds
Net liability = $500 million (advance) minus $480 million (purchase price) = $20 million

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section rule: §217.302 permits exclusion of MMLF non-recourse loan exposures from total leverage exposure, average total consolidated assets, advanced approaches RWA, and standardized RWA, with the liability reduced by the purchase price of assets acquired.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify that the institution is a Board-regulated institution that acquired exposures pursuant to a non-recourse loan provided as part of the Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility announced March 18, 2020. Step 2: Apply §217.302, which states that notwithstanding any other section of Part 217, such exposures may be excluded from total leverage exposure, average total consolidated assets, advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets, and standardized total risk-weighted assets. question_text: Heartland State Bank is a state member bank and a wholly-owned subsidiary of a global systemically important bank holding company. As of the last day of the previous calendar quarter, Heartland reports a supplementary leverage ratio of 3.72 percent. The most recent method 1 surcharge calculated by its parent holding company was 2.0 percent. During the current calendar quarter, Heartland's board of directors is considering paying a discretionary bonus pool of $18 million to senior executives and declaring a common dividend of $7 million. Heartland's eligible retained income for the relevant four-quarter lookback period is $40 million (net of distributions and associated tax effects), and the average net income over the same four quarters is $44 million. Determine whether Heartland may make these payments, and if so, compute the maximum aggregate amount it is permitted to distribute and pay as discretionary bonuses during the current calendar quarter.
required_facts: Leverage buffer requirement = lesser of 1.0% or 50% × 2.0% = 1.0%
Leverage buffer = 3.72% − 3.0% = 0.72%
Leverage buffer (0.72%) is less than leverage buffer requirement (1.0%), so payout restrictions apply
0.72% is greater than 50% and less than or equal to 75% of the 1.0% requirement, so the maximum payout ratio from Table 3 is 40%
Eligible retained income = greater of $40M and $44M = $44M
The source supports only that the leverage-buffer side of the ratio is 40%; the actual maximum payout amount under §217.11(f)(1) also depends on the capital-conservation-buffer payout ratio.
Heartland may not make the full proposed distributions and bonus payments because its leverage buffer is below the leverage buffer requirement under §217.11(f)(2)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Identify Heartland as a state member bank subsidiary of a GSIB → compute leverage buffer requirement under (a)(2)(v)(B) → compute leverage buffer under (f)(3)(ii) → check (f)(2) prohibition threshold → apply Table 3 payout ratio → compute maximum payout amount using eligible retained income
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Leverage buffer requirement: Under (a)(2)(v)(B), the leverage buffer requirement for a state member bank subsidiary of a GSIB is the lesser of 1.0% or 50% of the parent's most recent method 1 surcharge. 50% × 2.0% = 1.0%. min(1.0%, 1.0%) = 1.0%. So the leverage buffer requirement is 1.0%.

Step 2 — Leverage buffer: Under (f)(3)(ii), the leverage buffer = supplementary leverage ratio − 3.0% = 3.72% − 3.0% = 0.72%.

Step 3 — Check (f)(2) prohibition: Heartland's leverage buffer (0.72%) is greater than its leverage buffer requirement (1.0%)? No — 0.72% < 1.0%. So the outright prohibition in (f)(2) does NOT apply (that prohibition applies only when leverage buffer < leverage buffer requirement AND the institution is below the buffer entirely). Wait — re-reading (f)(2): 'a state member bank ... may not make distributions or discretionary bonus payments during the current calendar quarter if the Board regulated institution's leverage buffer, calculated as of the last day of the previous calendar quarter, is less than its leverage buffer requirement.' 0.72% < 1.0%, so the leverage buffer IS less than the leverage buffer requirement. However, (f)(2) says 'Except as provided in paragraph (a)(4)(iv)' — but the key operative rule is that if leverage buffer < leverage buffer requirement, distributions are prohibited UNLESS the payout ratio table applies. Actually, re-reading carefully: (f)(2) states the outright prohibition when leverage buffer < leverage buffer requirement. But (f)(1) says the maximum payout ratio is determined by Table 3. These two provisions must be read together: (f)(2) is the general prohibition, but (f)(1) and Table 3 provide the payout ratio framework. The correct reading is that Table 3 governs the payout ratio when the leverage buffer is less than the requirement — the table has a 0% payout ratio row for leverage buffer ≤ 25% of requirement, which effectively enforces the prohibition in graduated fashion. At 0.72% leverage buffer vs. 1.0% requirement: 0.72/1.0 = 72%, which is greater than 50% but less than or equal to 75% of the requirement. Per Table 3: leverage buffer > 50% of requirement and ≤ 75% of requirement → maximum payout ratio = 40%.

Step 4 — Eligible retained income: Under (a)(2)(i), eligible retained income is the GREATER of (A) net income for four preceding quarters net of distributions = $40M, or (B) average net income for four preceding quarters = $44M. Greater of $40M and $44M = $44M.

Step 5 — Maximum payout amount: Under (a)(2)(ii), maximum payout amount = eligible retained income × maximum payout ratio = $44M × 40% = $17.6M.

Step 6 — Proposed payments total $18M + $7M = $25M, which exceeds $17.6M. Heartland may NOT make the full proposed payments. The maximum aggregate amount permitted is $17.6M.

scenario_parameters.institution_type: state member bank, subsidiary of GSIB

question_text: Westbrook National Bank is a Board-regulated institution acting solely as a clearing member client (not itself a clearing member) for its centrally cleared interest rate swap portfolio. The bank clears all swaps through a central counterparty that has been designated as a qualifying central counterparty (QCCP). The bank posts $50 million of initial margin to the QCCP through its clearing member. The clearing member holds this collateral in a segregated account, but the account structure does NOT prevent the bank from suffering a loss if both the clearing member and another clearing member client of that clearing member default simultaneously. The bank has completed a legal review of the arrangement and maintains written documentation concluding the arrangement is legally enforceable. The bank calculates its exposure-at-default (EAD) for the swap portfolio at $120 million using the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk. None of the posted collateral is held by a custodian in a manner that is bankruptcy remote from the CCP and clearing member. What risk weight must the bank apply to its cleared swap transactions, and what is the resulting risk-weighted asset amount for those cleared transactions?
required_facts: The bank is a clearing member client, so the clearing member client methodology under §217.133(b) applies
The CCP is a QCCP, so the risk weight is determined under the two-tier QCCP rule rather than the non-QCCP subpart D rule

The 2% risk weight requires both (a) a joint-default loss-prevention arrangement and (b) a sufficient legal review with written documentation; the scenario's collateral arrangement fails condition (a)
Because the 2% conditions are not fully met, the applicable risk weight is 4%
Trade exposure amount = EAD ($120M) + fair value of non-bankruptcy-remote collateral ($50M) = $170 million
Risk-weighted asset amount = $170M × 4% = $6.8 million

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Clearing member client rules in §217.133(b)(3)(i) set out two risk weight tiers for QCCP-cleared transactions: 2% if the joint-default loss-prevention arrangement AND legal review conditions are both met; 4% if either condition fails. The scenario satisfies the legal review prong but fails the joint-default loss-prevention prong, triggering the 4% risk weight. RWA = trade exposure amount × risk weight.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify institution type: Westbrook is a clearing member client (not a clearing member), so §217.133(b) governs. Step 2 — Identify CCP type: the CCP is a QCCP, so §217.133(b)(3)(i) applies (not the non-QCCP rule in §217.133(b)(3)(ii)). Step 3 — Check the 2% risk weight conditions under §217.133(b)(3)(i)(A): (a) the collateral arrangement must prevent any loss to the clearing member client due to the joint default or concurrent insolvency of the clearing member and any other clearing member clients, AND (b) the bank must have conducted a sufficient legal review with written documentation. The scenario states the account structure does NOT prevent loss from a joint default of the clearing member and another client — condition (a) fails. Step 4 — Because the requirements of §217.133(b)(3)(i)(A) are not met, §217.133(b)(3)(i)(B) applies: the risk weight is 4%. Step 5 — Trade exposure amount: for a derivative contract, trade exposure amount = EAD + fair value of collateral posted and held in a non-bankruptcy-remote manner. The $50 million initial margin is held by the clearing member in a manner that is NOT bankruptcy remote, so it is added: trade exposure amount = $120M + $50M = $170M. Step 6 — RWA = $170M × 4% = $6.8 million.

The bank must publicly disclose quarterly: total risk-weighted assets ($94 billion), including all regulatory adjustments and deductions needed to calculate total RWA

The bank must publicly disclose quarterly: regulatory capital ratios during any transition periods, including descriptions of all capital elements and adjustments for numerator and denominator of each ratio during any transition period
The bank must publicly disclose quarterly: a reconciliation of regulatory capital elements as they relate to its balance sheet in any audited consolidated financial statements
The CET1 capital of $8.2B, AT1 capital of $1.1B, and tier 2 capital of $2.4B are required disclosure inputs under the first quarterly disclosure item
Total RWA of $94B is a required disclosure input under the second quarterly disclosure item
There are exactly four items enumerated for mandatory quarterly public disclosure under this provision

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.63(b) enumerates the four specific items a Board-regulated institution described in §217.61 must publicly disclose each quarter; each sub-item (b)(1)–(b)(4) specifies a distinct capital data element
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Identify that First National Bancorp is a Board-regulated institution described in §217.61, triggering §217.63 disclosure obligations. Step 2: Locate §217.63(b), which mandates quarterly public disclosure of four specific items. Step 3: Item (b)(1) requires disclosure of CET1 capital ($8.2B), additional tier 1 capital ($1.1B), tier 2 capital ($2.4B), tier 1 and total capital ratios, including all regulatory capital elements and adjustments/deductions used to calculate the numerator of such ratios. question_text: A Board-regulated institution uses an internal model to calculate its daily VaR-based measure for general market risk across all covered positions. The institution's risk team is configuring the quantitative parameters for the model. They have set the confidence level at 99.0 percent (one-tail) and are debating the appropriate holding period and historical observation period. One analyst proposes calculating VaR directly using a 1-business-day holding period and then scaling up to a 10-business-day equivalent using the square-root-of-time rule. A second analyst argues the institution must calculate 10-business-day VaR measures directly and cannot use a scaling approach. Additionally, the institution currently updates its historical data set quarterly and uses a weighting scheme for the observation period. The weighted scheme produces an effective observation period of 14 months, but the average time lag of the observations is only 4 months. The risk team wants to know: (1) Is the first analyst correct that a scaling approach from a shorter holding period to a 10-business-day equivalent is permissible, and if so, what condition must the institution satisfy? (2) Does the institution's current weighting scheme satisfy the regulatory requirements for the historical observation period, and if not, what must change?
required_facts: Scaling a VaR measure from a holding period shorter than 10 business days to a 10-business-day equivalent is explicitly permitted under the regulation.
An institution that uses a scaling approach must be able to justify the reasonableness of that approach to the satisfaction of the Board.

For a weighting scheme, the regulation requires either: (i) an effective observation period of at least one year with an average time lag of at least six months, or (ii) a demonstrated superior weighting scheme with more-than-monthly data updates.
The institution's average time lag of 4 months fails the minimum 6-month average time lag requirement under option (i).
The institution's quarterly data update frequency fails the requirement to update data sets at least monthly.

To rely on option (ii), the institution would need to update data more frequently than monthly and demonstrate superior effectiveness to the Board — neither of which the institution currently satisfies.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.205(b)(1) governs the holding period requirement and explicitly permits scaling from shorter holding periods to 10-business-day equivalent, subject to a justification condition. § 217.205(b)(2) and (b)(2)(i) govern the historical observation period requirement, specifying that a weighting scheme must produce an effective observation period of at least one year AND an average time lag of at least six months.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Holding period (§ 217.205(b)(1)): The regulation requires a holding period equivalent to a 10-business-day movement. It explicitly states the institution 'may calculate 10-business-day measures directly or may convert VaR-based measures using holding periods other than 10 business days to the equivalent of a 10-business-day holding period.' Therefore the first analyst is correct that scaling is permissible. However, the institution 'must be able to justify the reasonableness of its approach to the satisfaction of the Board.' The second analyst is wrong. Step 2 — Historical observation period (§ 217.205(b)(2)): The regulation requires data based on a historical observation period of at least one year, updated at least monthly. For institutions using a weighting scheme, § 217.205(b)(2)(i) requires EITHER (i) an effective observation period of at least one year in which the average time lag is at least six months, OR (ii) demonstrating the scheme is more effective than a six-month average time lag scheme (with more-than-monthly updates). The institution's weighting scheme has an effective observation period of 14 months (satisfies ≥1 year) but an average time lag of only 4 months (fails the ≥6 month requirement under option (i)). To use option (ii) instead, the institution must demonstrate superior effectiveness to the Board AND update data more frequently than monthly — but the institution currently updates only quarterly, which also fails the monthly update baseline requirement of § 217.205(b)(2). Therefore the institution's current setup fails on two counts: average time lag < 6 months under option (i), and quarterly updates fail the at-least-monthly update requirement.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds the following exposures on its balance sheet and must determine the appropriate standardized risk weights for each: (1) A $50 million loan to a foreign bank headquartered in a country with a Country Risk Classification (CRC) of 3. The loan is a standard term loan with a remaining maturity of 18 months. (2) A $30 million self-liquidating, trade-related contingent item arising from the movement of goods, with a maturity of 60 days, extended to a foreign bank whose home country has a CRC of 2. (3) A $20 million exposure to a sovereign government that is not a member of the OECD and has no CRC assigned to it. (4) A $15 million deposit held at a U.S. federally chartered credit union, where $10 million is unconditionally guaranteed by the FDIC and the remaining $5 million is conditionally guaranteed by the FDIC. For each of the four exposures, identify the applicable risk weight (in percent) and compute the resulting risk-weighted asset amount.
required_facts: Exposure 1 (CRC-3 foreign bank, 18-month term loan) receives a 100% risk weight, yielding RWA of $50 million
Exposure 2 (CRC-2 foreign bank, 60-day self-liquidating trade item) qualifies for the short-maturity trade exception and receives a 20% risk weight, yielding RWA of $6 million
Exposure 3 (non-OECD sovereign with no CRC) receives a 100% risk weight, yielding RWA of $20 million
The $10 million unconditionally FDIC-guaranteed portion of the credit union deposit receives a 0% risk weight
The $5 million conditionally FDIC-guaranteed portion of the credit union deposit receives a 20% risk weight, yielding RWA of $1 million
Total risk-weighted assets across all four exposures equal $77 million

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply Table 2 for foreign bank CRC-3 term loan; apply the short-maturity trade-related exception for CRC-2 foreign bank; apply non-OECD/no-CRC sovereign rule; apply unconditional vs. conditional U.S. government guarantee split for FDIC-backed deposit.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Exposure 1: Foreign bank, CRC-3, standard term loan (maturity >3 months). Under Table 2 to §217.32, CRC 3 maps to 100% risk weight. RWA = $50M × 100% = $50M. The short-maturity trade exception under §217.32(d)(2)(iii) does not apply because maturity is 18 months (>3 months). Exposure 2: Foreign bank, CRC-2, self-liquidating trade-related contingent item, maturity 60 days (≤3 months). Under §217.32(d)(2)(iii), a self-liquidating, trade-related contingent item arising from movement of goods with maturity ≤3 months to a foreign bank with CRC 0, 1, 2, or 3 receives a 20% risk weight. RWA = $30M × 20% = $6M. Exposure 3: Sovereign, non-OECD member, no CRC. Under §217.32(a)(4), a Board-regulated institution must assign 100% risk weight to a sovereign exposure if the sovereign is not an OECD member and has no CRC (absent any exception under (a)(3), (a)(5), or (a)(6)). RWA = $20M × 100% = $20M. Exposure 4: U.S. credit union deposit, split guarantee. The $10M unconditionally guaranteed by the FDIC falls under §217.32(a)(1)(i)(B) — zero percent risk weight. The $5M conditionally guaranteed by the FDIC falls under §217.32(a)(1)(ii) — 20% risk weight. RWA = ($10M × 0%) + ($5M × 20%) = $0 + $1M = $1M. Total RWA across all four exposures = $50M + $6M + $20M + $1M = $77M.

question_text: Northgate Financial Group is a bank holding company headquartered in the United States. It is not a subsidiary of any other bank holding company or foreign banking organization. Northgate has total consolidated assets of $310 billion and has been subject to the advanced approaches capital framework for the past three years. Northgate's board of directors has received a letter from its chief compliance officer stating that the company may be subject to a risk-based capital surcharge related to its systemic importance. The CCO's memo notes that Northgate became subject to the advanced approaches framework on January 15 of Year 1. Determine: (1) whether Northgate is subject to the rules governing the global systemically important bank holding company capital surcharge framework, (2) by what date Northgate must first determine whether it qualifies as a global systemically important BHC, and (3) if Northgate is identified as a global systemically important BHC on December 15 of Year 2, by what date must it calculate its surcharge and when does that surcharge first affect its maximum payout ratio?

Northgate became an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution in Year 1
Northgate must determine whether it qualifies as a global systemically important BHC by December 31 of Year 2
If identified as a GSIB on December 15 of Year 2, Northgate must calculate its GSIB surcharge by December 31 of Year 2
The GSIB surcharge first affects Northgate's maximum payout ratio beginning January 1 of Year 4

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the three-part applicability test in §217.400(b)(1), then derive the two sequential deadlines in §217.400(b)(2)(i) and (b)(2)(ii)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — §217.400(b)(1) applicability test: Northgate must satisfy all three prongs. Prong (i): Northgate has been subject to the advanced approaches framework for three years, so it is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution — satisfied. Prong (ii): Northgate is not a consolidated subsidiary of another bank holding company (its parent is a non-bank financial holding company) — satisfied. Prong (iii): Northgate is not a consolidated subsidiary of a foreign banking organization — satisfied. Therefore Northgate is subject to this subpart. Step 2 — §217.400(b)(2)(i) first deadline: A bank holding company identified under (b)(1) must determine whether it qualifies as a global systemically important BHC by December 31 of the year immediately following the year in which it became an advanced approaches institution. Northgate became an advanced approaches institution in Year 1, so the deadline is December 31 of Year 2. Step 3 — §217.400(b)(2)(ii) surcharge calculation and payout ratio deadlines: If Northgate is identified as a GSIB on December 15 of Year 2, it must calculate its GSIB surcharge by December 31 of Year 2 (the year of identification). The surcharge then applies for purposes of the maximum payout ratio beginning January 1 of the year immediately following the full calendar year after identification. The full calendar year after Year 2 identification is Year 3; therefore the surcharge affects the maximum payout ratio beginning January 1 of Year 4.

question_text: A state member bank uses the Simple Risk Weight Approach for its equity exposures. The community development equity investment ($12M) qualifying under 12 U.S.C. 24 (Eleventh) is assigned a 100% risk weight, producing RWA of $12 million
The 10% non-significant threshold equals $40 million (10% of $400 million total capital), and the aggregate of the three remaining exposures ($49 million) exceeds this threshold by $9 million

Only $15 million of non-publicly traded private firm A qualifies for the 100% non-significant risk weight; the remaining $3 million is assigned a 400% risk weight

The aggregate risk-weighted asset amount for all five equity exposures is $89.6 million

annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Federal Home Loan Bank stake ($8M): § 217.152(b)(2) assigns a 20% risk weight to equity exposures to a Federal Home Loan Bank. RWA = $8M × 20% = $1.6M.

Step 2 — Community development investment ($12M): § 217.152(b)(3)(i)(A) assigns a 100% risk weight to a community development equity exposure qualifying under 12 U.S.C. 24 (Eleventh) for state member banks, excluding SBIC-related exposures. This exposure qualifies. RWA = $12M × 100% = $12M.

Step 3 — Non-significant threshold check for remaining exposures: § 217.152(b)(3)(iii) assigns 100% to equity exposures (excluding significant investments in common stock of unconsolidated institutions and certain investment firm exposures) to the extent the aggregate adjusted carrying value does not exceed 10% of total capital. Total capital = $400M; 10% threshold = $40M.

For computing the aggregate adjusted carrying value under § 217.152(b)(3)(iii)(A), the bank may exclude exposures already covered by § 217.152(b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3)(i), and (b)(3)(ii). So the FHLB stake ($8M) and the community development investment ($12M) are excluded from the aggregate calculation. Remaining exposures: publicly traded corporate ($25M) + non-publicly traded private firm A ($18M) + non-publicly traded private firm B ($6M) = $49M aggregate.

Step 4 — Ordering rule under § 217.152(b)(3)(iii)(B): When determining which exposures qualify for 100% under the non-significant bucket, the bank must first include publicly traded equity exposures, then non-publicly traded. So the publicly traded corporate ($25M) is included first, then non-publicly traded exposures in order.

Aggregate cap = $40M. After including the publicly traded corporate ($25M), remaining capacity = $40M − $25M = $15M. Next, include non-publicly traded private firm A ($18M): only $15M fits within the cap. The remaining $3M of private firm A and all $6M of private firm B exceed the 10% threshold.

Step 5 — Risk weights for remaining exposures:
- Publicly traded corporate ($25M): qualifies for 100% non-significant weight (within cap). RWA = $25M × 100% = $25M.
- Non-publicly traded private firm A: $15M qualifies at 100% (non-significant); $3M exceeds the cap and is assigned 400% per § 217.152(b)(6). RWA = ($15M × 100%) + ($3M × 400%) = $15M + $12M = $27M.
- Non-publicly traded private firm B ($6M): entirely above the cap, assigned 400% per § 217.152(b)(6). RWA = $6M × 400% = $24M.

Step 6 — Aggregate RWA = $1.6M + $12M + $25M + $27M + $24M = $89.6M.

question_text: A bank holding company compliance officer is reviewing the firm's systemic risk profile for the current reporting period. The firm reports the following figures on its most recent FR Y-15 submission: total foreign claims on an ultimate risk basis of $180 billion, total cross-jurisdictional liabilities of $95 billion, assets held as a custodian on behalf of customers of $2.1 trillion, total intra-financial system assets of $310 billion, total intra-financial system liabilities of $275 billion, total notional amount of OTC derivatives of $8.4 trillion, total adjusted trading and available-for-sale securities of $420 billion, assets valued using Level 3 measurement inputs of $22 billion, total payments activity of $14 trillion, total underwriting activity of $190 billion, and total securities outstanding of $640 billion. The compliance officer needs to confirm which of these reported figures qualify as systemic indicators under the applicable capital framework, and separately identify the precise regulatory term for the firm's foreign claims figure. Identify all systemic indicators from the list above and state the defined regulatory term that corresponds to the firm's foreign claims on an ultimate risk basis.
required_facts: All 11 reported figures qualify as systemic indicators under the applicable definitions
The defined term for foreign claims on an ultimate risk basis as reported on the FR Y-15 is 'cross-jurisdictional claims'
Systemic indicators are enumerated in the definitions section and include exactly 12 named indicators, of which total exposures is the one not represented in the scenario's reported figures
Assets under custody is defined as assets held as a custodian on behalf of customers as reported on the FR Y-15, and qualifies as a systemic indicator
Level 3 assets are defined as assets valued using Level 3 measurement inputs as reported on the FR Y-15, and qualify as a systemic indicator
Underwritten transactions in debt and equity markets corresponds to total underwriting activity as reported on the FR Y-15, and qualifies as a systemic indicator

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the enumerated definition of 'systemic indicator' in §217.401(y) to classify each reported FR Y-15 figure, then apply §217.401(j) to identify the defined term for foreign claims on an ultimate risk basis as 'cross-jurisdictional claims'

Step 2: Map each reported figure to the enumerated list.
