Cross-jurisdictional liabilities ($95B) → §217.401(k) → systemic indicator (item 12). Assets under custody ($2.1T) → §217.401(b) → systemic indicator (item 6). Intra-financial system assets ($310B) → §217.401(l) → systemic indicator (item 2). Intra-financial system liabilities ($275B) → §217.401(m) → systemic indicator (item 3). OTC derivatives notional ($8.4T) → §217.401(r) → systemic indicator (item 8). Trading and AFS securities ($420B) → §217.401(aa) → systemic indicator (item 9). Level 3 assets ($22B) → §217.401(q) → systemic indicator (item 10). Payments activity ($14T) → §217.401(t) → systemic indicator (item 5). Underwriting activity ($190B) → §217.401(bb) → systemic indicator (item 7). Securities outstanding ($640B) → §217.401(w) → systemic indicator (item 4). Step 3: Note that total exposures (§217.401(z), item 1) is NOT in the reported list — the firm did not report a 'total exposures' figure separately, so that indicator is absent from the scenario. All 11 figures provided do qualify as systemic indicators. Step 4: The defined regulatory term for foreign claims on an ultimate risk basis is 'cross-jurisdictional claims' per §217.401(j).

question_text: A supervised insurance organization is evaluating whether a subordinated debt instrument issued by one of its inventory companies qualifies as a capital instrument eligible for inclusion in building block available capital. The instrument was issued and paid-in on March 15, 2018, with an original principal amount of $50 million and an original maturity of seven years (maturing March 15, 2025). As of the current evaluation date of January 10, 2024, the instrument has not been redeemed or repurchased in any amount. The instrument is unsecured, is not covered by any guarantee from the building block parent or any affiliate, and contains no terms that legally or economically enhance its seniority relative to more senior claims. It is subordinated to depositors and general creditors of the building block parent. The instrument contains no terms requiring or creating significant incentives for early redemption prior to maturity. Determine: (1) whether the instrument currently qualifies as a qualifying capital instrument, (2) the dollar amount of the instrument that is eligible to be included in building block available capital as of January 10, 2024, and (3) whether any portion would be excluded if the evaluation date were instead March 16, 2024.
required_facts: The instrument meets all general qualifying criteria under the applicable rule, including minimum original maturity of at least five years (7 years ≥ 5 years).

The amortization schedule reduces eligible amount by 20% of the original $50 million (i.e., $10 million) at the beginning of each of the last five years of the instrument's life, starting March 15, 2020.
As of January 10, 2024, four amortization steps have occurred (March 15, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023), resulting in a total reduction of $40 million.
The eligible amount as of January 10, 2024 is $50M − $40M = $10 million.
As of March 16, 2024, the remaining maturity is less than one year, so the instrument is fully excluded from building block available capital regardless of any remaining amortized amount.
No redemptions have occurred, so the 20% reduction is applied to the full original $50 million principal at each step.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single paragraph: apply the maturity amortization schedule and exclusion threshold in § 217.608(a)(1)(iv) to the instrument's original amount, issuance date, and current remaining maturity.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Confirm general qualifying criteria are met: The instrument is issued and paid-in (§ 217.608(a)(1)(i) ✓), subordinated to depositors and general creditors (§ 217.608(a)(1)(ii) ✓), unsecured and not guaranteed or seniority-enhanced (§ 217.608(a)(1)(iii) ✓), and contains no early-redemption incentive terms (§ 217.608(a)(1)(iv) last sentence ✓). Original maturity is 7 years ≥ 5 years minimum (§ 217.608(a)(1)(iv) first sentence ✓). Step 2 — Apply the amortization schedule: The rule states that at the beginning of each of the last five years of the instrument's life, the eligible amount is reduced by 20% of the original amount (net of redemptions). The instrument matures March 15, 2025. The last five years begin on March 15, 2020 (year 5 of 7), March 15, 2021 (year 4), March 15, 2022 (year 3), March 15, 2023 (year 2), and March 15, 2024 (year 1, i.e., the final year). Step 3 — Compute eligible amount as of January 10, 2024: As of January 10, 2024, we are in the period beginning March 15, 2023 (the start of the second-to-last year). Four amortization steps have occurred (at March 15, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023), each reducing eligibility by 20% × $50M = $10M. Total reduction = 4 × $10M = $40M. Eligible amount = $50M − $40M = $10M. Step 4 — Exclusion test as of March 16, 2024: On March 15, 2024, the fifth and final amortization step triggers (beginning of the last year of life), reducing eligibility by another $10M, leaving $0M eligible. Moreover, the rule states the instrument is excluded from building block available capital when remaining maturity is less than one year. As of March 16, 2024, remaining maturity is approximately 364 days, which is less than one year. Therefore, the instrument is fully excluded from building block available capital as of March 16, 2024.

question_text: Heartland Bancorp is a large U.S. bank holding company that has completed its parallel run process and received the required notification from its primary federal regulator allowing it to use its internal models for risk-based capital purposes. Heartland is not a subsidiary of another bank holding company, savings and loan holding company, depository institution, or a non-U.S. banking organization. Heartland's total leverage exposure is $1.2 trillion, and its tier 1 capital is $85 billion, resulting in a supplementary leverage ratio of approximately 7.1%. Heartland is required to publicly disclose its supplementary leverage ratio. The bank's compliance team is preparing its public regulatory capital disclosures and is debating two questions: (1) Which disclosure tables must Heartland publish — specifically, must it publish both the general capital structure and adequacy tables as well as the supplementary leverage ratio table? (2) For how many consecutive quarters must each category of disclosure be maintained publicly, and from what starting date does each retention period begin?
required_facts: Heartland must publish Tables 1 through 12 because it is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has completed the parallel run process and received the required notification.

Heartland must also publish Table 13 (supplementary leverage ratio disclosures) because it is required to publicly disclose its supplementary leverage ratio and does not qualify for the subsidiary exception.

The subsidiary exception to Table 13 does not apply because Heartland is not a consolidated subsidiary of another bank holding company, savings and loan holding company, depository institution, or a non-U.S. banking organization subject to comparable home-jurisdiction disclosure requirements.

Tables 1 through 12 must be made publicly available for twelve consecutive quarters beginning January 1, 2014, or a shorter period beginning after Heartland completed its parallel run and received notification.

Table 13 must be made publicly available for twelve consecutive quarters beginning January 1, 2015, or a shorter period beginning after Heartland became subject to the supplementary leverage ratio disclosure requirement.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.173(a)(1) requires advanced approaches institutions described in §217.172(b) to publish Tables 1–12; §217.173(a)(2) requires advanced approaches institutions required to publicly disclose their supplementary leverage ratio under §217.172(d) to also publish Table 13, unless a subsidiary exception applies; §217.173(a)(3) sets the retention periods: 12 consecutive quarters for Tables 1–12 beginning January 1, 2014 (or shorter if parallel run completed later), and 12 consecutive quarters for Table 13 beginning January 1, 2015 (or shorter if SLR disclosure obligation arose later).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Heartland has completed its parallel run and received notification under §217.121(d), making it an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution described in §217.172(b). Therefore §217.173(a)(1) requires it to publish Tables 1 through 12. Step 2: Heartland is also required to publicly disclose its supplementary leverage ratio under §217.172(d). It is not a consolidated subsidiary of another BHC, SLHC, depository institution, or a non-U.S. banking organization subject to comparable home-jurisdiction disclosure requirements. Therefore the subsidiary exception in §217.173(a)(2) does not apply, and Heartland must also publish Table 13. Step 3: Under §217.173(a)(3), Tables 1–12 must be publicly available for 12 consecutive quarters beginning January 1, 2014, or a shorter period beginning after Heartland completed its parallel run and received notification. Table 13 must be publicly available for 12 consecutive quarters beginning January 1, 2015, or a shorter period beginning after Heartland became subject to the SLR disclosure requirement. Because Heartland has already completed its parallel run, the applicable period for Tables 1–12 runs from the quarter after notification; for Table 13, from the quarter it became subject to SLR disclosure.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has been operating under the advanced approaches framework for several years following a satisfactory parallel run. During a routine supervisory review, the Board identifies that the institution's internal ratings-based credit risk models have undergone a significant recalibration of loss-given-default (LGD) assumptions for its wholesale portfolio, resulting in a 12% increase in the institution's advanced approaches total risk-weighted asset amount for wholesale credit exposures. The institution did not proactively notify the Board of this change prior to the supervisory review. Subsequently, the Board determines that the institution's advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets are materially understated relative to the actual credit and operational risks embedded in the portfolio, and that the institution's qualification standards have lapsed. Describe the full sequence of regulatory obligations and supervisory actions that apply to this institution, including what the institution must do and what the Board is authorized to require.
required_facts: The institution was required to notify the Board when it made a significant change to its LGD modeling assumptions and when that change resulted in a material change in advanced approaches total RWA for wholesale exposures, and it failed to do so.

Because the institution has completed a satisfactory parallel run and the Board finds it has failed to comply with qualification requirements, the Board must issue written notice of non-compliance to the institution.

Upon receiving the Board's written notice, the institution must establish and submit a remediation plan satisfactory to the Board describing how it will return to compliance with the qualification requirements.

Because the Board has determined that the institution's advanced approaches total RWA is not commensurate with its actual credit, market, operational, or other risks, the Board is authorized to require the institution to recalculate its advanced approaches total RWA using Board-specified modifications.

The 12% increase in wholesale credit RWA resulting from the LGD recalibration constitutes both a material change in advanced approaches total RWA for an exposure type and a significant change to modeling assumptions, each independently triggering the notification obligation.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Single-section reasoning within § 217.123: (a) triggers notification obligation for material RWA change and significant modeling assumption changes; (b)(1) governs Board's written notice upon finding non-compliance; (b)(2) requires institution to submit a remediation plan; (b)(3) grants Board authority to impose modified RWA calculations when advanced approaches RWA is not commensurate with actual risk.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.123(a): The institution made a significant change to its modeling assumptions (LGD recalibration) that resulted in a material change in advanced approaches total RWA for wholesale exposures. The institution was required to notify the Board of both the material RWA change and the significant modeling assumption change. Failure to do so before the supervisory review constitutes a breach of the ongoing notification obligation. Step 2 — § 217.123(b)(1): Because the Board determines the institution (which has completed a satisfactory parallel run and is using the advanced approaches) has failed to comply with the qualification requirements in § 217.122, the Board must notify the institution in writing of its failure to comply. Step 3 — § 217.123(b)(2): Upon receiving that written notice, the institution must establish and submit to the Board a remediation plan that is satisfactory to the Board, outlining how it will return to compliance with the qualification requirements. Step 4 — § 217.123(b)(3): Because the Board has also determined that the institution's advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets are not commensurate with its credit, market, operational, or other risks, the Board is additionally authorized to require the institution to calculate its advanced approaches total risk-weighted assets using any modifications the Board specifies.

scenario_parameters.rwa_impact: 12% increase in advanced approaches total RWA for wholesale exposures
scenario_parameters.board_finding_1: failure to comply with qualification requirements
scenario_parameters.board_finding_2: advanced approaches RWA not commensurate with actual risk

question_text: A state member bank is evaluating whether a newly designed capital instrument qualifies as a common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital element. The instrument has the following characteristics: (1) it is paid-in and issued directly by the bank; (2) it represents the most subordinated claim in any liquidation or insolvency proceeding; (3) holders are entitled to a residual claim proportional to their share of issued capital after all senior claims are satisfied; (4) the instrument has no stated maturity date; (5) the bank's board retains full discretion to omit dividends at any time without triggering an event of default or payment-in-kind obligation; (6) dividend payments may only be made after all legal and contractual obligations, including payments on more senior claims, have been satisfied; (7) holders bear losses equally, proportionately, and simultaneously with all other common stockholders before any more senior claimants absorb losses; (8) the paid-in amount is classified as equity under GAAP; (9) the instrument was not purchased or funded, directly or indirectly, by the bank or any entity it controls; (10) the instrument is unsecured and not covered by any guarantee from the bank or its affiliates; (11) the instrument has been issued in compliance with all applicable laws and regulations; and (12) the instrument is reported separately from other capital instruments on the bank's regulatory financial statements. However, the instrument's contractual terms specify that cash dividends may only be paid out of current-year net income — not from retained earnings or surplus related to common stock — and the terms impose a cap limiting annual dividends to no more than 60% of current-year net income. Additionally, the instrument includes a provision stating that if the bank's CET1 ratio falls below 6.5%, the bank is contractually obligated to repurchase the instrument within 90 days at par, without requiring prior regulatory approval. Determine whether this instrument qualifies as a CET1 capital element, identifying specifically which eligibility criteria are violated and why.
required_facts: The instrument violates criterion (v) because cash dividends are restricted to current-year net income only, excluding retained earnings and surplus related to common stock, contrary to the requirement that dividends may be paid from any of those three sources
The instrument violates criterion (v) because the 60% cap on annual dividends constitutes a contractual limit on dividend payments, which is expressly prohibited

The instrument violates criterion (iii) because the mandatory repurchase-at-par provision triggered by a capital ratio threshold is a non-discretionary redemption feature that does not require prior Board approval and creates an incentive to redeem
The instrument does NOT qualify as a CET1 capital element because it fails to satisfy all 13 required eligibility criteria — specifically criteria (iii), (v), and (vi)
Criteria (i), (ii), (iv), (vii), (viii), (ix), (x), (xi), (xii), and (xiii) are satisfied based on the stated facts

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply the 13 enumerated CET1 common stock eligibility criteria in § 217.20(b)(1)(i)–(xiii); identify violations in (v) (dividend source restriction and cap), (vi) (mandatory repurchase trigger removes full discretion), and (iii) (mandatory repurchase feature creates incentive/obligation to redeem without prior Board approval)
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1: Identify the governing provision. The instrument is being evaluated as a CET1 common stock instrument under § 217.20(b)(1), which requires satisfaction of all 13 criteria in (i)–(xiii).

Step 2: Check criterion (v) — dividend source and discretion. § 217.20(b)(1)(v) requires that cash dividends be paid out of net income, retained earnings, OR surplus related to common stock, and must NOT be subject to a contractual cap. The instrument restricts dividends to current-year net income only (excluding retained earnings and surplus) AND imposes a 60% cap. Both sub-elements of criterion (v) are violated.

Step 3: Check criterion (vi) — full discretion to omit dividends. § 217.20(b)(1)(vi) requires that the bank have full discretion at all times to refrain from paying dividends without triggering any event of default, payment-in-kind requirement, or other restriction. The mandatory repurchase obligation triggered when CET1 falls below 6.5% effectively removes full discretion and imposes a restriction on the bank — this violates criterion (vi).

Step 4: Check criterion (iii) — no maturity, redemption only via discretionary repurchase with prior Board approval. § 217.20(b)(1)(iii) requires that the instrument can only be redeemed via discretionary repurchases with prior Board approval (to the extent required by law or regulation), and must not contain any term or feature that creates an incentive to redeem. The mandatory repurchase-at-par provision triggered by a CET1 ratio breach is a non-discretionary redemption feature that bypasses prior Board approval and creates a structural incentive to redeem — violating criterion (iii).

Step 5: Confirm all other criteria (i), (ii), (iv), (vii)–(xiii) are satisfied based on the facts given.

Step 6: Conclusion — the instrument fails at minimum criteria (iii), (v), and (vi) and therefore does NOT qualify as a CET1 capital element.

scenario_parameters.dividend_source_restriction: current-year net income only (excludes retained earnings and surplus)
scenario_parameters.repurchase_terms: at par within 90 days, no prior regulatory approval

question_text: A compliance officer at a mid-sized Board-regulated institution is reviewing the bank's capital adequacy documentation for an upcoming examination. The institution's legal counsel notes that certain sections of the federal capital rules that were originally reserved as placeholders have never been populated with substantive requirements. The compliance officer wants to confirm whether any affirmative capital calculation obligations, minimum ratio requirements, deduction rules, or buffer requirements arise from the reserved sections numbered 217.13 through 217.19 of the applicable capital rules. The officer also wants to know whether the absence of substantive content in those sections creates any compliance gap or exemption that the institution could rely upon in its capital planning. Provide a definitive compliance determination.
required_facts: Sections 217.13 through 217.19 are all designated [Reserved] and contain no substantive regulatory text.
No capital calculation obligations, minimum ratio requirements, deduction rules, or buffer requirements arise from §§ 217.13–217.19.
A [Reserved] designation has no operative legal effect — it neither imposes requirements nor grants exemptions.
The institution cannot rely on the reserved status of these sections as a basis for any capital planning exemption or advantage.
There is no compliance gap created by the reserved sections because they were never intended to contain operative rules in their current form.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sections 217.13 through 217.19 are entirely reserved with no substantive regulatory text; no capital obligations, deductions, or buffers arise from them.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Locate §§ 217.13–217.19 in Subpart B of 12 CFR Part 217. Step 2: Observe that every section in this range is marked '[Reserved]', meaning no regulatory text has been promulgated. Step 3: Conclude that no affirmative compliance obligations, capital ratio requirements, deduction rules, or buffer requirements exist within these sections. Step 4: Confirm that a '[Reserved]' designation neither grants an exemption nor imposes a requirement — it is simply a placeholder with no operative legal effect. Step 5: The institution cannot rely on these sections for any capital planning advantage, nor is it burdened by any requirement from them.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution acts as a clearing member client and has entered into a derivatives transaction that it wishes to treat as a cleared transaction for risk-weighting purposes. The transaction is booked through a clearing member, and the institution's collateral is held in an omnibus account established under 17 CFR parts 190 and 300. The institution has conducted a legal review and prepared written documentation concluding that, in the event of the clearing member's insolvency, the collateral arrangement would be found legal, valid, binding, and enforceable by the relevant courts. However, the transaction documents do not contain any provision allowing the offsetting transaction to be transferred to another clearing member if the current clearing member defaults or enters receivership. The institution's compliance team is evaluating whether all operational requirements have been satisfied to recognize this exposure as a cleared transaction. Identify which operational requirements are met and which, if any, are not satisfied, and state whether the institution may recognize the exposure as a cleared transaction for risk-weighting purposes.
required_facts: The omnibus account under 17 CFR parts 190 and 300 satisfies the collateral-segregation requirement of § 217.3(a)(2)
The institution's legal review with written documentation satisfies the enforceability requirement of § 217.3(a)(3)
The absence of a transferability provision in the transaction documents means the requirement of § 217.3(a)(4) is not met
All four sub-requirements of § 217.3(a) must be satisfied to recognize an exposure as a cleared transaction
Because § 217.3(a)(4) is not satisfied, the institution may NOT recognize the exposure as a cleared transaction for risk-weighting purposes

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: All four sub-requirements of § 217.3(a) must be satisfied to recognize an exposure as a cleared transaction; the scenario satisfies (a)(1), (a)(2), and (a)(3) but fails (a)(4) because the transaction is not transferable to another clearing member upon default.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.3(a)(1): The offsetting transaction must be identified by the CCP as a transaction for the clearing member client. The scenario states the transaction is booked through a clearing member on behalf of the client institution — this requirement is met (assumed from the scenario setup). Step 2 — § 217.3(a)(2): Collateral must be held in a manner preventing loss upon default of the clearing member or its other clients. The scenario states collateral is held in an omnibus account under 17 CFR parts 190 and 300, which the regulation explicitly states satisfies this requirement. Met. Step 3 — § 217.3(a)(3): The institution must have conducted sufficient legal review with written documentation concluding the collateral arrangement would be found legal, valid, binding, and enforceable in the event of a legal challenge including insolvency. The scenario states this review and documentation exist. Met. Step 4 — § 217.3(a)(4): The offsetting transaction with the clearing member must be transferable under the transaction documents and applicable laws to another clearing member should the clearing member default, become insolvent, or enter similar proceedings. The scenario explicitly states the transaction documents contain no such transferability provision. NOT met. Conclusion: Because § 217.3(a)(4) is not satisfied, the institution cannot recognize the exposure as a cleared transaction for risk-weighting purposes under subparts D and E.

scenario_parameters.account_type: omnibus account under 17 CFR parts 190 and 300
scenario_parameters.recognition_sought: cleared transaction under subparts D and E

question_text: Ridgeline State Bank, a state member bank supervised by the Federal Reserve, is evaluating whether it can exclude certain assets from its total leverage exposure calculation for the reporting quarter ending March 31, 2021. The bank holds $4.2 billion in U.S. Treasury securities and maintains $1.8 billion in funds on deposit at a Federal Reserve Bank. Ridgeline submitted a written opt-in notice to the Board on June 15, 2020. The bank is also classified as a custodial banking organization and had previously included $1.8 billion in a specific line item within its total leverage exposure calculation related to its custodial deposit liabilities. Ridgeline's compliance team wants to know: (1) whether the bank is eligible to exclude the Treasury securities and Federal Reserve deposits from its on-balance sheet assets for the quarter ending March 31, 2021; (2) what adjustment, if any, must be made to the custodial banking organization line item in the total leverage exposure calculation as a result of excluding the Federal Reserve deposits; and (3) whether the bank may declare a dividend of $50 million during the calendar quarter beginning July 1, 2020 without any regulatory approval, given its opt-in status.
required_facts: Ridgeline is eligible to exclude U.S. Treasury securities and Federal Reserve deposits as a state member bank that opted in before July 1, 2020 (notice filed June 15, 2020 satisfies the deadline)
The exclusion remains effective for the reporting quarter ending March 31, 2021, as that is the final eligible reporting period under the termination provision

As a custodial banking organization excluding $1.8 billion in Federal Reserve deposits, Ridgeline must reduce the relevant custodial line item in its total leverage exposure calculation by $1.8 billion, bringing it to $0 (no less than zero)

Ridgeline may not declare the $50 million dividend during the calendar quarter beginning July 1, 2020 without prior Board approval, because it has opted in to the exclusion relief and the distribution restriction applies through March 31, 2021
The Board's review of any distribution request considers factors including safety and soundness, the nature and extent of the request, and the particular circumstances

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Apply § 217.303(a) eligibility for state member bank exclusions, check opt-in timing under (b), confirm termination date under (d), apply custodial banking organization adjustment under (e), and assess distribution restriction under (g).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Eligibility under § 217.303(a): Ridgeline is a state member bank, so exclusion of U.S. Treasury securities and Federal Reserve deposits is permissive ('may'), not mandatory. It is eligible to exclude both items if it has properly opted in. Step 2 — Opt-in timing under § 217.303(b): The bank must have notified the Board before July 1, 2020. Ridgeline filed on June 15, 2020, which satisfies this requirement. Step 3 — Termination under § 217.303(d): The exclusion ceases to be effective after the reporting period ending March 31, 2021. The quarter in question ends March 31, 2021, which is the final eligible reporting period — so the exclusion still applies for this quarter. Step 4 — Custodial banking organization adjustment under § 217.303(e): Because Ridgeline is a custodial banking organization and is excluding $1.8 billion in Federal Reserve deposits under paragraph (a)(2), it must reduce the amount in § 217.10(c)(2)(x)(A) by $1.8 billion (to no less than zero). Since the line item was $1.8 billion, it is reduced to $0. Step 5 — Distribution restriction under § 217.303(g): During the calendar quarter beginning July 1, 2020 and until March 31, 2021, a state member bank that has opted in may not make a distribution or create an obligation to make one without prior Board approval. Ridgeline has opted in, so the proposed $50 million dividend during this period requires prior Board approval — it cannot be declared unilaterally.

Provide a definitive compliance determination.

Reserved sections impose no affirmative capital calculation requirements on the institution
Reserved sections impose no minimum ratio thresholds
