question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a wholesale corporate loan to Obligor X with an exposure at default (EAD) of $80 million. The institution has purchased an nth-to-default credit derivative referencing a basket of five obligors (Obligor X is one of them) from Protection Provider Y, a highly-rated insurance company that qualifies as an eligible double default guarantor. The protection amount of the credit derivative is $60 million. The institution wishes to apply double default treatment to the protected portion of this exposure. After confirming eligibility, the institution must determine the appropriate risk weight for the unprotected portion of the exposure. The unprotected portion does not qualify for the supervisory formula approach. The institution has elected not to apply the simplified supervisory formula approach to the unprotected portion. Separately, for a different securitization exposure held by the same institution — a mezzanine tranche with an attachment point of 8% and a detachment point of 12%, where the augmented capital requirement (KA) is calculated to be 10% — the institution must determine the correct risk-weighting methodology. The institution does not qualify for the supervisory formula approach for this tranche. Identify: (1) the capital treatment for the $20 million unprotected portion of the wholesale loan, and (2) the risk-weighting approach and resulting risk weight range applicable to the mezzanine securitization tranche, given that KA falls between the attachment and detachment points.
required_facts: The nth-to-default credit derivative is eligible for double default treatment only if it satisfies the conditions of § 217.142(m), as cross-referenced by § 217.135(a)(2)(ii).

Because the protection amount ($60M) is less than the EAD ($80M), the exposure must be split: protected portion EAD = $60M (double default treatment) and unprotected portion EAD = $20M (standard wholesale RWA under § 217.131).
The unprotected $20M portion is risk-weighted under the standard wholesale capital framework, not the securitization hierarchy.

For the mezzanine securitization tranche, because KA (10%) falls between attachment point A (8%) and detachment point D (12%), the applicable SSFA rule requires a weighted-average risk weight blending 1,250% and 1,250% × KSSFA.
The minimum risk weight applicable to any securitization exposure under the SSFA is 20%, and the blended risk weight must be no less than this floor.
If the institution does not apply the SSFA to the securitization tranche and the SFA is unavailable, the fallback is a 1,250% risk weight under the hierarchy of approaches in § 217.142(a)(4).

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.135 permits double default treatment for nth-to-default credit derivatives subject to § 217.142(m); § 217.142 establishes the hierarchy of approaches for securitization exposures and, when SFA and SSFA are unavailable or not applied, mandates 1,250% risk weight; § 217.142(a)(3) directs use of § 217.144 (SSFA) when SFA is unavailable; § 217.144(c)(3) governs the split-tranche weighted-average calculation when KA falls between A and D.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Double default eligibility for nth-to-default derivative: Under § 217.135(a)(2)(ii), an nth-to-default credit derivative qualifies for double default treatment only if it meets the requirements of § 217.142(m). The institution must therefore consult § 217.142(m) to confirm the nth-to-default derivative satisfies those conditions before applying double default treatment.

Step 2 — Partial coverage split: The protection amount ($60M) is less than the EAD ($80M), so under § 217.135(c) the exposure is split: (a) protected portion EAD = $60M, treated under § 217.135(e) double default formula; (b) unprotected portion EAD = $80M − $60M = $20M, treated under § 217.131 (standard wholesale RWA rules).

Step 3 — Unprotected portion capital treatment: § 217.135(c)(2) directs the unprotected $20M to § 217.131 for risk-weighted asset calculation — i.e., standard IRB/advanced approaches wholesale treatment, not securitization hierarchy.

Step 4 — Mezzanine securitization tranche approach hierarchy: Under § 217.142(a), the institution must first check for gain-on-sale/CEIO deduction (not applicable here), then SFA (institution does not qualify), then SSFA under § 217.144 (institution has not applied it), and if none apply, assign 1,250% risk weight per § 217.142(a)(4). However, the question posits the institution is evaluating the SSFA route under § 217.144.

Step 5 — SSFA mechanics for split tranche: Under § 217.144(c), KA = 10%, A = 8%, D = 12%. Since A (8%) < KA (10%) < D (12%), this falls under § 217.144(c)(3): the risk weight is a weighted average of 1,250% (for the portion from A to KA) and 1,250% × KSSFA (for the portion from KA to D). The floor risk weight is 20%. The institution must compute KSSFA per § 217.144(d) to determine the blended risk weight for the tranche.

question_text:
A Board-regulated institution is applying the supervisory formula approach (SFA) to a multi-layer securitization structure. The securitization pool contains three types of underlying exposures: (1) $180 million in wholesale term loans with EAD already calculated under the institution's internal ratings-based framework; (2) $40 million in subordinated notes issued by a separate asset-backed vehicle, which themselves represent interests in a pool of consumer receivables; and (3) $30 million in equity interests in a small-business investment fund held on the institution's balance sheet, with an adjusted carrying value of $30 million. The institution holds a mezzanine tranche of $25 million in the securitization, which represents 10% of the total tranche. The tranche sits above $60 million of subordinated exposures in the capital structure. Total UE for the SFA calculation is $250 million.

For the $40 million subordinated notes described above, the institution's risk officer is uncertain whether those notes qualify as 'securitization exposures' for purposes of computing UE under the SFA, or whether they should instead be treated as wholesale exposures. The institution's credit risk team notes that the subordinated notes were issued by a securitization special purpose entity and represent a beneficial interest in a pool of retail receivables.

Separately, the institution's operations team flags that a $12 million securities transaction — a standard equities trade with a normal contractual settlement period — has gone unsettled for 22 business days past its contractual settlement date. The counterparty has not delivered the securities. The institution delivered cash on settlement date. The operations team asks whether this unsettled trade creates any additional risk-based capital requirement, and if so, how it should be calculated. Note that the institution's repo-style transactions are handled under a separate framework.

For both issues: (1) determine how the $40 million subordinated notes should be classified and included in the UE calculation under the SFA, and (2) determine the risk-based capital treatment for the unsettled $12 million securities transaction, including the applicable risk weight and the resulting risk-weighted asset amount.
required_facts: The $40 million subordinated notes issued by a securitization SPE qualify as 'securitization exposures' as defined in §217.142(e), and must be included in UE under the SFA as securitization exposures, not as wholesale EAD.
UE = $180M (wholesale EAD) + $40M (securitization exposures per §217.142(e) definition) + $30M (equity adjusted carrying value) = $250M, consistent with the given total.
The unsettled $12M equities trade is a DvP transaction subject to §217.136(d) because the institution paid cash but has not received securities delivery.
At 22 business days past the contractual settlement date, the applicable risk weight from Table 1 to §217.136 is 625% (range: 16 to 30 business days after contractual settlement date).
The risk-weighted asset amount for the unsettled DvP transaction = positive current exposure × 625%; if positive current exposure equals $12M, RWA = $75M.
Repo-style transactions are excluded from §217.136 treatment and handled under a separate framework (§§217.131 and 217.132), consistent with the facts as stated.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: SFA UE parameter in §217.143(e)(1) cross-references §217.142(e) for the definition of 'securitization exposure'; §217.142 in turn references §217.131 for the categorization phase that determines what counts as a securitization exposure vs. wholesale exposure; the unsettled transaction question routes through §217.131(b) (Phase 1 categorization, which identifies unsettled transactions subject to §217.136) and then to §217.136(d) for the DvP risk-weight table.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — SFA UE classification of the $40M subordinated notes: Under §217.143(e)(1), UE includes 'the amount of any underlying exposures that are securitization exposures (as defined in §217.142(e)).' The answerer must navigate to §217.142(e) to find the definition of 'securitization exposure.' §217.142(e) defines a securitization exposure as an on- or off-balance-sheet exposure to a securitization (including asset-backed securities, mortgage-backed securities, and other instruments where the credit risk of the underlying exposures is tranched). The $40M subordinated notes issued by a securitization SPE representing a beneficial interest in a pool of retail receivables meet this definition. Therefore, the $40M notes are securitization exposures under §217.142(e) and must be included in UE as securitization exposures (not as wholesale EAD). UE = $180M (wholesale EAD) + $40M (securitization exposures per §217.142(e)) + $30M (equity adjusted carrying value per §217.151(b)) = $250M, consistent with the given total.

Step 2 — Unsettled transaction: The $12M equities trade is a standard securities transaction with a normal settlement period. The institution delivered cash but has not received securities 22 business days after the contractual settlement date. Under §217.131(b) (Phase 1 categorization), the institution must identify unsettled transactions to which §217.136 applies. This routes to §217.136. Under §217.136(b), the section applies to transactions involving securities with risk of delayed settlement; repo-style transactions are excluded (handled separately, consistent with the facts). The transaction is a delivery-versus-payment (DvP) transaction because the buyer (institution) paid cash and the seller was obligated to deliver securities only upon payment. Under §217.136(d), a Board-regulated institution must hold risk-based capital against a DvP transaction if the counterparty has not made delivery within five business days after the settlement date. At 22 business days past the contractual settlement date, Table 1 to §217.136 applies: the range 'From 16 to 30' business days after the contractual settlement date carries a 625% risk weight applied to the positive current exposure. The positive current exposure is the difference between the transaction value at the agreed settlement price and the current market price, if that difference results in a credit exposure to the institution. Assuming the positive current exposure equals the $12M transaction value (i.e., the institution is fully exposed), the risk-weighted asset amount = $12M × 625% = $75M.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation_notes: The chain requires: (1) §217.143(e)(1) → §217.142(e) for securitization exposure definition in UE; (2) §217.143 → §217.142 → §217.131 for categorization framework; (3) §217.131(b) → §217.136(d) for unsettled DvP treatment and risk weight table.

question_text:
A Board-regulated institution that uses the advanced approaches for risk-based capital purposes originated a pool of commercial real estate loans and transferred them to a securitization special purpose entity in a traditional securitization. The institution retained a subordinate tranche with a fair value of $18 million and a notional amount of $20 million. The institution's compliance team has confirmed that the transferred exposures are off-balance sheet under GAAP, that credit risk has been transferred to third parties, that no clean-up calls other than eligible clean-up calls exist, and that the underlying exposures do not include revolving credit facilities with an early amortization provision.

Separately, the institution also holds a purchased credit derivative from a non-SPE counterparty with a notional amount of $50 million, used to hedge a securitization exposure. The institution has elected not to recognize this credit derivative as a credit risk mitigant for the securitization exposure. The derivative has a current mark-to-market value of $3 million in the institution's favor and has a remaining maturity of 2.5 years.

For the retained subordinate tranche, the institution cannot demonstrate to its primary regulator's satisfaction a comprehensive understanding of the structural features and underlying credit performance data that would materially affect the tranche's performance — specifically, it lacks current loan-level delinquency data (30/60/90-day past due percentages) and has not documented its pre-acquisition risk analysis within the required timeframe.

For the purchased credit derivative from the non-SPE counterparty that the institution is not recognizing as a credit risk mitigant: what risk weight must the institution apply to determine the risk-weighted asset amount for that derivative exposure, and what framework governs the calculation of the exposure amount? Additionally, what risk weight must the institution assign to the retained subordinate tranche given the due diligence failure described above?
required_facts: The retained subordinate tranche must be assigned a 1,250 percent risk weight because the institution cannot demonstrate comprehensive understanding of the securitization exposure's material features (missing delinquency data and undocumented pre-acquisition analysis), and the exposure is neither deducted from CET1 nor subject to the § 217.142(k) carve-out.

For the purchased credit derivative from the non-SPE counterparty that the institution elects not to recognize as a credit risk mitigant, the exposure amount must be determined under the OTC derivative exposure calculation framework (§ 217.132(c)).

Because the credit derivative counterparty is not a securitization SPE, the risk weight for that counterparty credit risk exposure is determined under the wholesale risk-weighting mechanics of § 217.131 — not under the securitization exposure hierarchy.

The § 217.141(c) due diligence 1,250% risk weight rule applies only when the exposure is not already deducted from CET1 and is not subject to the § 217.142(k) treatment; both carve-outs must be checked before applying the penalty risk weight.

Section 217.131 Phase 1 categorization requires the institution to identify OTC derivative contracts and unsettled transactions (cross-referencing § 217.136) as part of the wholesale exposure categorization process that governs the risk weight determination for the non-SPE credit derivative counterparty.

The traditional securitization operational criteria are satisfied (off-balance sheet under GAAP, credit risk transferred, only eligible clean-up calls, no revolving/early amortization features), so the institution may exclude the transferred exposures from risk-weighted assets and must hold capital only against retained securitization exposures.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.141(c) establishes the due diligence failure rule (1,250% risk weight for the retained tranche) and carves out exposures subject to § 217.142(k). § 217.142(k) addresses purchased credit derivatives not recognized as credit risk mitigants from non-SPE counterparties, directing the institution to determine the exposure amount under § 217.132(c) and the risk weight under § 217.131. § 217.131(b) Phase 1 categorization identifies the derivative as an OTC derivative contract and directs the institution to § 217.136 for unsettled transaction treatment where applicable, and more broadly governs the wholesale/retail risk-weight mechanics that apply to the counterparty credit risk capital requirement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.141(c): The institution has a retained securitization exposure (the subordinate tranche). Because it cannot demonstrate comprehensive understanding of the exposure's material features (missing delinquency data, undocumented pre-acquisition analysis), and the exposure is not deducted from CET1 and is not subject to § 217.142(k), § 217.141(c)(1) requires the institution to assign a 1,250 percent risk weight to the retained subordinate tranche.

Step 2 — § 217.142(k): The institution holds a purchased credit derivative from a non-SPE counterparty and has elected not to recognize it as a credit risk mitigant. Under § 217.142(k)(ii), the institution must determine the exposure amount of the credit derivative under § 217.132(c). Under § 217.142(k)(ii)(A), because the counterparty is not a securitization SPE, the institution must determine the risk weight for the exposure according to § 217.131.

Step 3 — § 217.131: Section 217.131 governs the mechanics for calculating total wholesale and retail risk-weighted assets. Under Phase 1 categorization (§ 217.131(b)), the institution must identify OTC derivative contracts among its wholesale exposures. The purchased credit derivative is an OTC derivative contract. The institution must also identify unsettled transactions to which § 217.136 applies. The risk weight for the counterparty credit risk on the purchased credit derivative is determined through the wholesale obligor rating grade assignment and risk parameter framework of § 217.131, with the exposure amount calculated per § 217.132(c).

Step 4 — § 217.136: Section 217.136 governs unsettled transactions involving securities, foreign exchange instruments, and commodities. While the purchased credit derivative itself is an OTC derivative (addressed under §§ 217.131 and 132 rather than § 217.136 directly), § 217.131(b) cross-references § 217.136 for unsettled transactions, completing the chain. The risk weight for the non-SPE counterparty on the credit derivative is determined under § 217.131's wholesale framework (not the securitization hierarchy), and the exposure amount is calculated under § 217.132(c).

Conclusion: (1) The retained subordinate tranche receives a 1,250% risk weight due to the due diligence failure under § 217.141(c). (2) The purchased credit derivative from the non-SPE counterparty that is not recognized as a credit risk mitigant has its exposure amount determined under § 217.132(c) and its risk weight determined under the wholesale framework of § 217.131 — not under the securitization hierarchy.

question_text: First National Clearing Bank (FNCB) is a Board-regulated institution that is not an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution. FNCB acts as a clearing member client on a central counterparty (CCP) that qualifies as a QCCP. FNCB has not made any election to change its default methodology for calculating OTC derivative exposure amounts, and it has not received any Board approval to do so. FNCB holds a single cleared interest rate swap with a current mark-to-market value of $2.8 million (in FNCB's favor) and a notional of $100 million. FNCB has posted $3.5 million of initial margin to the clearing member, which holds the collateral in an omnibus account commingled with margin from other clearing member clients — the arrangement does not prevent losses to FNCB in the event of a joint default of the clearing member and another clearing member client. FNCB has also purchased an eligible credit default swap (CDS) from a AA-rated guarantor bank to hedge a separate $10 million corporate loan exposure on its books. The CDS has a notional of $10 million, matures in 18 months, and the hedged loan matures in 36 months. The CDS is denominated in USD, matching the loan currency. No restructuring credit event is included in the CDS contract. Determine: (1) the methodology FNCB must use to calculate the trade exposure amount for the cleared interest rate swap, (2) the applicable risk weight for the cleared transaction, and (3) the effective notional amount of the CDS after all required adjustments, and the resulting risk-weighted asset treatment for the hedged loan.
required_facts: FNCB has not elected SA-CCR under the provision allowing non-advanced-approaches institutions to opt into SA-CCR, so the alternate cleared-transaction treatment does not apply and FNCB uses the standard clearing member client methodology

The trade exposure amount for the cleared interest rate swap equals the CEM-based exposure amount (current credit exposure plus PFE under § 217.34(b)) plus the $3.5 million of posted initial margin, because the omnibus collateral arrangement is not bankruptcy remote

The applicable risk weight for the cleared transaction is 4 percent because the collateral arrangement does not prevent losses to FNCB from a joint default of the clearing member and other clearing member clients
A maturity mismatch exists between the 18-month CDS and the 36-month loan, requiring an adjusted notional of approximately $4.545 million (= $10M × (1.5 − 0.25)/(3.0 − 0.25))
Because the CDS omits restructuring as a credit event, the effective notional must be further reduced: Pr = $4.545M × 0.60 ≈ $2.727 million

The protected portion ($2.727M) is risk-weighted at the AA-rated guarantor bank's risk weight (20%), and the unprotected portion ($7.273M) is risk-weighted at the corporate obligor's risk weight (100%)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.35(a)(3) gates whether the alternate SA-CCR path applies (it does not here because FNCB has not elected SA-CCR under § 217.34(a)(1)); therefore § 217.35(b) governs, and the trade exposure amount for the cleared derivative is calculated using the methodology under § 217.34 (CEM, since no SA-CCR election). The risk weight is then determined under § 217.35(b)(3). For the CDS hedge, § 217.36 applies with maturity mismatch adjustment under § 217.36(d) and restructuring adjustment under § 217.36(e).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Determine applicable methodology for cleared transaction (§ 217.35(a)(3)): FNCB is not an advanced approaches institution and has not elected SA-CCR under § 217.34(a)(1). Therefore the alternate requirement in § 217.35(a)(3) does NOT apply, and FNCB uses § 217.35(b) as a clearing member client. Step 2 — Trade exposure amount (§ 217.35(b)(2)(i)): For a cleared derivative, trade exposure = exposure amount calculated under § 217.34 (CEM, since no SA-CCR election) PLUS fair value of collateral posted in a non-bankruptcy-remote manner. The $3.5M initial margin is held in an omnibus account that is not bankruptcy remote, so it is included. CEM exposure = current credit exposure ($2.8M, since MTM > 0) plus PFE (for a 5-year IR swap, the add-on factor under CEM is 0.5% × $100M = $500K, but the exact PFE is scenario-dependent; the key point is that both components are summed per § 217.34(b)). Trade exposure amount = CEM exposure amount + $3.5M posted collateral. Step 3 — Risk weight for cleared transaction (§ 217.35(b)(3)): The collateral is held in an omnibus account that does NOT prevent losses from joint default of the clearing member and other clients. Therefore the condition in § 217.35(b)(3)(i)(A) is not met, and FNCB must apply a 4% risk weight (§ 217.35(b)(3)(i)(B)). Step 4 — CDS hedge treatment (§ 217.36): The CDS is an eligible credit derivative covering the full $10M loan, so § 217.36(c)(1) (full coverage substitution) would normally apply. Step 5 — Maturity mismatch adjustment (§ 217.36(d)): CDS residual maturity = 18 months; hedged loan residual maturity = 36 months. A maturity mismatch exists. Adjusted notional Pm = P × (t − 0.25)/(T − 0.25) where t = 1.5 years, T = 3.0 years: Pm = $10M × (1.5 − 0.25)/(3.0 − 0.25) = $10M × 1.25/2.75 = $10M × 0.4545 = $4.545M. Step 6 — Restructuring adjustment (§ 217.36(e)): CDS does not include restructuring as a credit event. Therefore Pr = Pm × 0.60 = $4.545M × 0.60 = $2.727M. Step 7 — No currency mismatch (§ 217.36(f)): Both denominated in USD, so no further adjustment. Step 8 — Risk-weighted asset treatment: Protected portion = $2.727M, risk-weighted at the AA-rated guarantor's risk weight (20% for a AA-rated bank under the standardized approach). Unprotected portion = $10M − $2.727M = $7.273M, risk-weighted at the corporate obligor's applicable risk weight (100% for a standard corporate). RWA for protected portion = $2.727M × 20% = $545K. RWA for unprotected portion = $7.273M × 100% = $7.273M.

question_text: First National Bancorp, a Board-regulated institution, has purchased an over-the-counter credit derivative from a counterparty that is not a securitization special purpose entity. The credit derivative provides protection on a pool of commercial mortgage loans that were securitized by a third party. First National cannot satisfy the conditions required to recognize the purchased credit derivative as a credit risk mitigant under the applicable credit risk mitigation rules, and therefore does not treat it as such. The notional amount of the credit derivative is $50 million, and the exposure at default (EAD) calculated under the applicable OTC derivative counterparty credit risk rules is $4.2 million. First National's internal ratings-based system assigns the counterparty an obligor rating grade corresponding to a probability of default (PD) of 0.45% and a loss given default (LGD) of 40%. The institution uses the advanced internal ratings-based approach for wholesale exposures. Determine the risk weight that First National must apply to this purchased credit derivative exposure for purposes of computing its risk-weighted asset amount, and describe the four-phase process the institution must follow to arrive at that risk weight.
required_facts: Because the purchased credit derivative cannot be recognized as a credit risk mitigant under the credit risk mitigation rules, First National must determine the exposure amount using the OTC derivative counterparty credit risk EAD rules, yielding an exposure amount of $4.2 million (not the $50 million notional).

Because the counterparty is not a securitization SPE, the risk weight for the exposure is determined according to the wholesale and retail risk-weighted asset mechanics section (§ 217.131), not the securitization hierarchy.
The exposure is categorized as a wholesale exposure (specifically an OTC derivative contract) in Phase 1 of the four-phase process under § 217.131.
In Phase 2, the counterparty obligor is assigned to a rating grade with PD = 0.45% and the exposure is assigned to a loss severity rating grade with LGD = 40%.
In Phase 3, risk parameters PD = 0.45%, LGD = 40%, and EAD = $4.2 million are assigned to the wholesale exposure, and effective maturity M must also be determined.
In Phase 4, the risk-weighted asset amount is computed using the IRB wholesale exposure formula (Table 1 of § 217.131) applied to the assigned risk parameters.

The risk weight is derived from the advanced IRB wholesale formula and is not 1,250% — the 1,250% treatment applies only under the securitization hierarchy (§ 217.142(a)), which is displaced here by the cross-reference to § 217.131 for non-SPE counterparties.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.142(m)(2)(ii)(A) directs that when a Board-regulated institution purchases a credit derivative it cannot recognize as a credit risk mitigant and the counterparty is not a securitization SPE, the risk weight for the exposure must be determined according to § 217.131 (the wholesale/retail risk-weighted asset mechanics section). The answerer must navigate from the securitization exposure rules in § 217.142 to the wholesale exposure rating and risk-weighting framework in § 217.131.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the applicable rule in § 217.142(m)(2): Because First National purchased an OTC credit derivative that it cannot (or chooses not to) recognize as a credit risk mitigant under § 217.145, it must determine the exposure amount under § 217.132(c). Step 2 — Identify the counterparty type: The counterparty is not a securitization SPE, so § 217.142(m)(2)(ii)(A) applies, directing the institution to determine the risk weight 'according to § 217.131.' Step 3 — Apply § 217.131 wholesale mechanics: The exposure is a wholesale exposure (OTC derivative with a non-SPE counterparty). Under § 217.131(a), the institution must follow four phases: (1) Phase 1 — categorize the exposure as a wholesale exposure (OTC derivative contract); (2) Phase 2 — assign the counterparty obligor to a rating grade (PD = 0.45%) and assign the exposure to a loss severity rating grade (LGD = 40%); (3) Phase 3 — assign risk parameters: PD = 0.45%, LGD = 40%, EAD = $4.2 million, and compute effective maturity M; (4) Phase 4 — apply the wholesale exposure formula (Table 1 of § 217.131) to compute the risk-weighted asset amount. The risk weight is derived from the IRB wholesale formula using PD = 0.45% and LGD = 40%, which yields a risk weight materially above the standardized floor but well below 1,250%. The exposure amount used is the EAD of $4.2 million (not the $50 million notional), consistent with § 217.142(e)(3) and § 217.132(c).

scenario_parameters.exposure_type: purchased OTC credit derivative, not recognized as credit risk mitigant

question_text: A Board-regulated institution that uses the advanced approaches for risk-based capital purposes enters into two categories of transactions on the same trading day. First, it executes a classic repo-style transaction in which it sells U.S. Treasury securities subject to an agreement to repurchase them, receiving $50 million in cash from the counterparty; the repo matures in 14 days and is not subject to daily variation margin. Second, it executes a spot foreign exchange trade (a payment-versus-payment structure) in which it agrees to deliver €40 million and receive $43.5 million from the same counterparty, with a contractual settlement period of two business days, which equals the market standard for such instruments. Both transactions remain open. Seven business days after the contractual settlement date of the foreign exchange trade, the counterparty has still not delivered the $43.5 million, even though the institution has already delivered the euros. The current market value of the $43.5 million receivable is $43.2 million. The institution's compliance team must determine: (1) which regulatory framework governs each of the two transactions for capital purposes, and (2) what risk weight the institution must apply to compute risk-weighted assets for the unsettled foreign exchange trade as of the seventh business day past its settlement date.
required_facts: The repo-style transaction is excluded from § 217.136 and is instead governed by the counterparty credit risk rules in §§ 217.131 and 217.132.
The FX trade qualifies as a payment-versus-payment (PvP) transaction with a normal settlement period and therefore remains within the unsettled-transactions framework.
Because the counterparty has not delivered payment within five business days after the contractual settlement date, the institution must hold risk-based capital against the FX trade.
Seven business days after the contractual settlement date falls in the '5 to 15 business days' band in Table 1, which prescribes a 100 percent risk weight applied to positive current exposure.
The RWA should use positive current exposure as defined in § 217.136(a)(4), i.e. the difference between the agreed settlement value and the current market price, then apply the 100% Table 1 weight.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.136(b)(2) explicitly excludes repo-style transactions from its scope and redirects them to §§ 217.131 and 217.132. The FX trade is a PvP transaction with a normal settlement period that has gone unsettled beyond five business days, so it remains within § 217.136(d), which requires the institution to apply the risk weight from Table 1 to § 217.136 based on the number of business days elapsed after the contractual settlement date.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Classify the repo-style transaction: § 217.136(b)(2) states that repo-style transactions, including unsettled repo-style transactions, are excluded from § 217.136 and are instead addressed in §§ 217.131 and 217.132. Therefore the repo falls under the counterparty credit risk framework in § 217.132, with Phase 1 categorization mechanics governed by § 217.131(b). Step 2 — Classify the FX trade: The FX trade is a payment-versus-payment (PvP) transaction as defined in § 217.136(a)(2) (each counterparty obligated to make a final transfer of currency only if the other has done so). Its contractual settlement period of two business days equals the market standard and is ≤ five business days, so it has a 'normal settlement period' under § 217.136(a)(3). It is not a repo-style transaction, not a cleared transaction subject to daily margining, not a one-way cash payment on an OTC derivative, and its settlement period is not longer than normal — so none of the § 217.136(b) exclusions apply. Step 3 — Determine when capital must be held: Under § 217.136(d), the institution must hold risk-based capital against a PvP transaction with a normal settlement period if the counterparty has not made payment within five business days after the settlement date. Here, seven business days have elapsed past the settlement date, which exceeds five, so capital is required. Step 4 — Apply Table 1 to § 217.136: Seven business days after the contractual settlement date falls in the 'From 5 to 15' band, which carries a 100 percent risk weight. Step 5 — Compute RWA: The positive current exposure is $43.2 million (current market value of the deliverables owed). RWA = $43.2 million × 100% = $43.2 million.

question_text: A large Board-regulated institution operating as an advanced approaches institution holds a portfolio of OTC interest rate derivative contracts with a single corporate counterparty. The institution has entered into a qualifying master netting agreement covering these contracts and has elected to use the internal models methodology to calculate exposure at default (EAD) for this netting set. The resulting EAD under the internal models methodology is $480 million. The institution also holds a securitization exposure in the form of an off-balance-sheet liquidity facility extended to an asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) program sponsored by a third party. The notional amount of the liquidity facility is $200 million, but given the ABCP program's current underlying assets, the maximum potential funding obligation is $140 million. The institution has purchased an OTC credit derivative from a non-securitization-SPE counterparty to hedge a portion of its exposure to the ABCP program's underlying assets. The credit derivative has a notional of $60 million and does not qualify for recognition as a credit risk mitigant under the applicable credit risk mitigation rules. The institution's risk management team must determine: (1) how the $480 million EAD from the internal models methodology feeds into the institution's total wholesale and retail risk-weighted assets calculation; (2) what exposure amount to assign to the ABCP liquidity facility for risk-weighting purposes; and (3) how to treat the purchased OTC credit derivative that cannot be recognized as a credit risk mitigant, including which risk-weighting framework applies given the counterparty is not a securitization SPE. Provide a complete analysis of each of the three determinations.
required_facts: The definition of 'total wholesale and retail risk-weighted assets' in § 217.101 item (5) directs that risk-weighted assets for IMM exposures are determined under § 217.132(d), so the $480 million EAD from the internal models methodology feeds into total wholesale and retail RWA via that cross-reference.

The exposure amount of the ABCP liquidity facility may be reduced from the $200 million notional to $140 million, which is the maximum potential amount the institution could be required to fund given the program's current underlying assets.

State that § 217.142(m)(2)(ii) sends the exposure amount to § 217.132(c), and under § 217.132(c)(1) the institution uses its elected derivative methodology; given the scenario's IMM election, a mandatory SA-CCR conclusion is not supported.

Because the credit protection was purchased from a counterparty that is not a securitization SPE, the risk weight for the resulting exposure is determined under the wholesale counterparty credit risk framework (§ 217.131), not the securitization hierarchy.

The institution's election of the internal models methodology under § 217.132(d) is permissible for OTC derivative netting sets subject to a qualifying master netting agreement, and requires prior written Board approval for cross-product master netting agreements.
The ABCP liquidity facility reduction to maximum potential funding is calculated without regard to the current credit quality of the underlying assets.

annotator_grounding.start_clause: § 217.101 (definition of 'Total wholesale and retail risk-weighted assets', item (5))

annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Total wholesale and retail RWA, IMM component (§ 217.101 → § 217.132(d)): The definition of 'total wholesale and retail risk-weighted assets' in § 217.101 explicitly lists, as item (5), 'risk-weighted assets for IMM exposures (as determined in § 217.132(d)).' The institution has elected the internal models methodology under § 217.132(d) for its qualifying master netting set of OTC interest rate derivatives. Therefore the $480 million EAD produced by the internal models methodology feeds directly into the total wholesale and retail RWA calculation as the IMM exposure component. The institution applies the appropriate risk weight to this EAD under § 217.131 to arrive at risk-weighted assets for that netting set.

Step 2 — Exposure amount of the ABCP liquidity facility (§ 217.142(e)(2)): The ABCP liquidity facility is an off-balance-sheet securitization exposure that is not an OTC derivative contract, repo-style transaction, eligible margin loan, or cleared transaction. Under § 217.142(e)(2), the exposure amount is the notional amount of the exposure. However, for an off-balance-sheet securitization exposure to an ABCP program such as an eligible ABCP liquidity facility, the notional amount may be reduced to the maximum potential amount that the institution could be required to fund given the ABCP program's current underlying assets (calculated without regard to current credit quality). The maximum potential funding obligation is $140 million, so the institution may use $140 million as the exposure amount rather than the full $200 million notional.

Step 3 — Purchased OTC credit derivative not recognized as credit risk mitigant (§ 217.142(m)(2)(ii) → § 217.132(c) → § 217.131): Under § 217.142(m)(2)(ii), if a Board-regulated institution cannot, or chooses not to, recognize a purchased credit derivative as a credit risk mitigant under § 217.145, the institution must determine the exposure amount of the credit derivative under § 217.132(c) (the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk). Then, under § 217.142(m)(2)(ii)(A), because the institution purchased the credit protection from a counterparty that is NOT a securitization SPE, the institution must determine the risk weight for the resulting exposure according to § 217.131 (the wholesale/retail risk-weighting framework), not the securitization hierarchy. The EAD is calculated per § 217.132(c) on the $60 million notional credit derivative, and the resulting exposure is risk-weighted as a wholesale counterparty credit risk exposure under § 217.131.

The § 217.135 link: § 217.135(a)(2)(ii) references § 217.142(m) in the context of nth-to-default credit derivatives eligible for double default treatment, confirming that § 217.142(m) is the governing provision for credit derivative treatment in the securitization subpart and that the chain through § 217.135 is structurally consistent with the analysis above.

question_text: Northgate Financial Holdings, a large Board-regulated institution that crossed the advanced approaches threshold 30 months ago, is preparing to exit its parallel run and begin calculating risk-weighted assets under the advanced approaches framework. The institution has submitted its implementation plan and completed three consecutive calendar quarters of parallel run reporting. During the parallel run, Northgate's internal audit function conducted its annual review of the advanced systems six months ago but did not separately assess the effectiveness of controls supporting those systems — it only reviewed the operations of the credit function and documented PD, LGD, and EAD estimation processes. The institution's board of directors approved the implementation plan, and the plan was submitted to the Board 45 days before the proposed parallel run start date (the Board did not waive prior notice). Northgate also holds a securitization exposure of $80 million in a traditional securitization it originated. To hedge this exposure, it obtained an eligible credit derivative from an eligible guarantor with a protection amount of $50 million. The credit derivative and the securitization exposure are denominated in different currencies. Northgate intends to use standard supervisory haircuts for the currency mismatch and has not sought Board approval for own-estimates haircuts. The residual maturity of the hedged securitization exposure is 3 years; the credit derivative's stated term is 2 years. Northgate proposes to set the risk-weighted asset amount for the covered portion of the securitization exposure using the wholesale risk weight function, applying its PD for the guarantor, its LGD for the credit derivative, and an EAD equal to the protection amount. For the uncovered portion, it proposes to apply the relevant securitization exposure framework. Identify all compliance deficiencies in Northgate's parallel run qualification and its proposed credit risk mitigation treatment for the securitization exposure, and determine the correct risk-weighted asset calculation approach for both the covered and uncovered portions.
required_facts: The implementation plan submission 45 days before the parallel run start date (without Board waiver) violates the 60-day advance submission requirement, constituting a procedural deficiency.
Three consecutive calendar quarters of parallel run is insufficient; a satisfactory parallel run requires no fewer than four consecutive calendar quarters.

The internal audit's failure to assess the effectiveness of controls supporting the advanced systems (performing only the operations review and documentation steps) is a qualification deficiency under the annual internal audit requirements.

Use the adjusted protection amount (after the required §217.134(d) maturity-mismatch and §217.134(f) currency-mismatch adjustments) for the covered EAD and the uncovered-portion ratio, not raw $50 million / $80 million.

A maturity mismatch adjustment is required because the credit derivative's term (2 years) is shorter than the residual maturity of the hedged securitization exposure (3 years), and the protection amount must be adjusted accordingly before applying the partial coverage formula.

A currency mismatch haircut (HFX) of 8 percent must be applied to the protection amount because the credit derivative and the securitization exposure are denominated in different currencies and Northgate uses standard supervisory haircuts.
Northgate's proposed RWA calculation is deficient because it omits the required maturity mismatch and currency mismatch adjustments to the protection amount.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.121 (qualification process) requires compliance with § 217.122 (qualification requirements) for parallel run approval; § 217.122(i)(5) specifies internal audit must assess effectiveness of controls; § 217.121(b)(2) requires plan submission 60 days before parallel run; § 217.121(c) requires four consecutive quarters; § 217.145 governs credit risk mitigants for securitization exposures, cross-referencing § 217.134(c)(1) for the wholesale risk weight function and § 217.134(d)-(f) for mismatch adjustments including the 8% currency haircut.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.121(a)(1): Institution crossed threshold 30 months ago; implementation plan must have been adopted within 6 months (satisfied, assumed) and start date must be no later than 36 months after threshold crossing — 30 months elapsed, so the timeline is still within the 36-month window, no deficiency here. Step 2 — § 217.121(b)(2): The implementation plan must be submitted at least 60 days before the proposed parallel run start date unless the Board waives prior notice. Northgate submitted 45 days before — this is a deficiency (15 days short of the 60-day requirement) and the Board did not waive prior notice. Step 3 — § 217.121(c): A satisfactory parallel run requires no less than four consecutive calendar quarters. Northgate has completed only three — this is a deficiency; it cannot yet exit the parallel run. Step 4 — § 217.121(d)(1) and (3): Board approval requires full compliance with § 217.122 qualification requirements and an adequate ongoing compliance process. Step 5 — § 217.122(i)(5): The internal audit function must at least annually (i) review advanced systems and associated operations including credit function and PD/LGD/EAD estimations, (ii) assess the effectiveness of controls supporting the advanced systems, and (iii) document and report findings to the board. Northgate's audit only performed items (i) and (iii) — it did not assess the effectiveness of controls (item ii). This is a qualification deficiency under § 217.122 that would prevent Board approval under § 217.121(d)(1). Step 6 — § 217.145(a): Northgate is an originating Board-regulated institution that obtained a credit risk mitigant to hedge a securitization exposure in a traditional securitization satisfying § 217.141 operational criteria — § 217.145 applies. Step 7 — § 217.145(c)(1): Only eligible guarantees or eligible credit derivatives from eligible guarantors may be recognized — satisfied here. Step 8 — § 217.145(c)(3)(ii) (partial coverage): Protection amount ($50M) < securitization exposure ($80M), so partial coverage rules apply. Covered portion RWA = wholesale risk weight function per § 217.131 using guarantor PD, LGD for the credit derivative, EAD = $50M protection amount. Uncovered portion RWA = (1 − 50/80) × RWA for the securitization exposure without the mitigant under §§ 217.142–217.146. Northgate's proposed approach for covered and uncovered portions is correct in structure. Step 9 — § 217.145(c)(4): Mismatch adjustments per § 217.134(d), (e), and (f) must be applied. The credit derivative term (2 years) is shorter than the hedged exposure residual maturity (3 years) — this is a maturity mismatch requiring adjustment under § 217.134(d). Additionally, the currency mismatch requires an HFX haircut. Step 10 — § 217.145(c)(4) cross-referencing § 217.134(f)(2): HFX = 8% because the exposure and collateral are in different currencies and Northgate is using standard supervisory haircuts (not own-estimates). The protection amount must be adjusted downward for both the maturity mismatch and the 8% currency mismatch haircut before applying the partial coverage formula. Northgate's proposal does not mention these mismatch adjustments — this is a deficiency in its proposed calculation.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a mezzanine tranche in a commercial mortgage-backed securitization. The securitization pool consists entirely of wholesale commercial real estate loans with no retail or equity exposures. The institution's risk management team has calculated all of the following for the underlying pool: the exposure at default of each individual loan, the loss given default for each obligor, the probability of default for each obligor, and the expected credit losses for the pool as a whole. The institution can maintain and update these calculations on an ongoing basis. The tranche the institution holds has a current face amount of $25 million. The total securitization pool has an unpaid principal balance of $500 million. Subordinated tranches below the institution's tranche total $75 million. The institution has determined that KIRB for the pool equals 0.09 (9%), the credit enhancement level L equals 0.15 (15%), and the tranche thickness T equals 0.05 (5%). The institution's tranche percentage (TP) is 100% (it holds the entire tranche). One of the underlying exposures in the pool is itself a securitization exposure — specifically, a $10 million B-piece interest in a separate CMBS transaction. For purposes of computing the amount of underlying exposures (UE) in the SFA calculation, the institution must determine how to classify and measure this embedded securitization exposure. Separately, the institution's compliance team is evaluating whether the simplified supervisory formula approach would be available as a fallback if the primary approach cannot be applied. Explain: (1) how the $10 million embedded securitization exposure should be measured and included in the UE parameter, citing the definitional standard that governs what qualifies as a 'securitization exposure' for this purpose; (2) whether the institution qualifies to use the primary risk-weighting approach for this tranche, and if so, compute the SFA risk-based capital requirement and the resulting risk-weighted asset amount; and (3) under what conditions the simplified supervisory formula approach would be available as a fallback, and what data currency requirement applies to the underlying exposure data.
required_facts: The $10 million embedded B-piece is included in UE as a 'securitization exposure' (not as a wholesale EAD), with its classification governed by the definition in § 217.142(e), as cross-referenced by § 217.143(e)(1).
UE = $500 million (= $490M wholesale EAD + $10M securitization exposure amount).
The institution qualifies for the SFA because it can calculate all § 217.143(e) parameters on an ongoing basis, satisfying § 217.143(a).
Because KIRB (0.09) is less than or equal to L (0.15), the applicable SFA branch is § 217.143(c)(2), and the capital requirement equals UE × TP × max(F·T, S[L+T] − S[L]).
Risk-weighted assets for the tranche = SFA risk-based capital requirement × 12.5.
SSFA is available as a fallback only if the institution does not qualify for SFA; since SFA applies here, SSFA is not available for this exposure.

If SSFA were applicable, § 217.144(a) requires that underlying exposure data be no more than 91 calendar days old when the contracts require monthly or quarterly payments; otherwise a 1,250 percent risk weight must be assigned.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.143(e)(1) defines UE and cross-references § 217.142(e) for the definition of 'securitization exposure' as applied to underlying exposures that are themselves securitization exposures; § 217.142(a)(2)-(3) establishes the hierarchy under which SFA is the primary approach and SSFA is the fallback; § 217.144(a) governs SSFA eligibility and data currency requirements.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — UE parameter and embedded securitization exposure: Under § 217.143(e)(1), UE equals the EAD of wholesale and retail underlying exposures plus the amount of any underlying exposures that are securitization exposures (as defined in § 217.142(e)) plus the adjusted carrying value of equity exposures. The $10 million B-piece is an underlying exposure that is itself a securitization exposure. Its classification as a 'securitization exposure' is governed by the definition in § 217.142(e). Therefore, the $10 million is included in UE at its face/carrying amount under the securitization exposure prong of the UE formula, not the wholesale EAD prong. The remaining $490 million of wholesale loans are included at EAD. UE = $490M + $10M = $500M. Step 2 — SFA eligibility and capital requirement: Under § 217.142(a)(2), the institution must apply the SFA if it qualifies under § 217.143(a). § 217.143(a) requires the institution to be able to calculate each SFA parameter in § 217.143(e) on an ongoing basis. The facts state the institution can do so. Therefore, SFA applies. With KIRB = 0.09, L = 0.15, L + T = 0.20: since KIRB (0.09) < L (0.15), the exposure falls in the case described in § 217.143(c)(2). The SFA risk-based capital requirement = UE × TP × max(F·T, S[L+T] − S[L]). With TP = 1.0 and UE = $500M, the formula yields a capital requirement driven by the supervisory formula S[·] values (the exact numeric result requires the supervisory formula in § 217.143(d), but the applicable branch is § 217.143(c)(2) because KIRB ≤ L). Risk-weighted assets = SFA capital requirement × 12.5. Step 3 — SSFA fallback: Under § 217.142(a)(3), SSFA is available only if the exposure does not qualify for SFA. Since the institution qualifies for SFA here, SSFA is not available as a fallback in this scenario. However, if SFA were unavailable (e.g., the institution could not calculate KIRB on an ongoing basis), § 217.144(a) would permit SSFA provided the institution has accurate data for the five SSFA parameters. § 217.144(a) further requires that if the underlying exposure contracts require monthly or quarterly payments, the parameter data must be no more than 91 calendar days old; otherwise a 1,250 percent risk weight is mandatory.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has entered into a credit default swap (CDS) with an eligible double default guarantor to hedge a wholesale corporate loan exposure (non-sovereign) with an exposure at default (EAD) of $80 million. The protection amount under the CDS is $60 million. The institution wishes to apply double default treatment to the protected portion of the exposure. As part of calculating the adjusted protection amount, the institution must account for a currency mismatch: the CDS is denominated in euros while the hedged loan is denominated in US dollars. The institution does not currently qualify for own-estimates haircuts based on a ten-business-day holding period, and it revalues the CDS once every 30 business days rather than daily. Determine (1) the appropriate foreign exchange haircut percentage the institution must apply to the protection amount, (2) whether and how that haircut must be adjusted given the revaluation frequency, and (3) how the institution should split the exposure into protected and unprotected portions after applying the adjusted protection amount, including the EAD assigned to each portion.
required_facts: Because the protection amount ($60M) is less than the EAD ($80M), the institution must apply partial coverage treatment, splitting the exposure into a protected portion and an unprotected portion.

The base foreign exchange haircut (HFX) is 8% because the institution does not qualify for own-estimates of FX volatility under the collateral haircut approach, simple VaR methodology, or internal models methodology.

Because the institution revalues the CDS every 30 business days rather than at least every 10 business days, the 8% HFX must be scaled upward using the square-root-of-time formula: adjusted HFX = 8% × sqrt(30/10) ≈ 13.86%.
The adjusted protection amount is approximately $51.68M (i.e., $60M × (1 − 0.1386)).
The protected portion is assigned EAD equal to the adjusted protection amount (~$51.68M) and is risk-weighted using the double default capital formula.
The unprotected portion is assigned EAD equal to the original EAD minus the adjusted protection amount (~$80M − $51.68M = $28.32M) and is risk-weighted under the standard wholesale risk-weight rules.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.135(c) governs partial coverage double default treatment and directs to § 217.134(d)/(e)/(f) for mismatch adjustments; § 217.134(f)(2) sets the base FX haircut at 8% and conditions own-estimates eligibility on qualifying for § 217.132(b)(2)(iii); § 217.134(f)(3) requires upward adjustment via the square-root-of-time formula in § 217.132(b)(2)(iii)(A)(2) when revaluation is less frequent than every ten business days.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Confirm double default treatment eligibility under § 217.135(a): the exposure is a wholesale non-sovereign exposure hedged by an eligible CDS from an eligible double default guarantor, so the criteria are met. Step 2 — Identify partial coverage: protection amount P = $60M < EAD = $80M, so § 217.135(c) applies, requiring the institution to split into a protected exposure (EAD = P) and an unprotected exposure (EAD = original EAD − P). Step 3 — Apply mismatch adjustments per § 217.135(d), which directs to § 217.134(f) for currency mismatch. Step 4 — Under § 217.134(f)(2), the base HFX is 8% unless the institution qualifies for own-estimates of FX volatility. Own-estimates eligibility requires qualifying for § 217.132(b)(2)(iii) (own-estimates haircuts), § 217.132(b)(3) (simple VaR), or § 217.132(d) (internal models). The institution does not qualify for any of these, so HFX = 8%. Step 5 — Under § 217.134(f)(3), because the institution revalues the CDS less frequently than every ten business days (it revalues every 30 business days), it must scale HFX upward using the square-root-of-time formula in § 217.132(b)(2)(iii)(A)(2): adjusted HFX = 8% × sqrt(30/10) = 8% × sqrt(3) ≈ 8% × 1.7321 ≈ 13.86%. Step 6 — Compute adjusted protection amount: P_adjusted = $60M × (1 − 0.1386) ≈ $60M × 0.8614 ≈ $51.68M. Step 7 — Split the exposure: protected portion EAD = $51.68M (risk-weighted under § 217.135(e) double default formula); unprotected portion EAD = $80M − $51.68M = $28.32M (risk-weighted under § 217.131).

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a securitization exposure in the form of an OTC interest rate swap that references the cash flows from a pool of residential mortgage loans held in a special purpose entity. The swap is not a credit derivative and is not cleared through a central counterparty. The institution has determined that the exposure does not constitute a gain-on-sale or a credit-enhancing interest-only strip, and the exposure does not qualify for the supervisory formula approach. The institution has chosen not to apply the simplified supervisory formula approach. To determine the exposure amount for risk-weighting purposes, the institution must calculate the exposure at default (EAD) for this OTC derivative contract. The institution and its counterparty have executed a qualifying master netting agreement covering this swap. The current replacement cost of the swap is $4.2 million in the institution's favor. The potential future exposure add-on, calculated using the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk, is $1.1 million. No eligible financial collateral has been posted by the counterparty. What is the exposure amount of this securitization exposure that the institution must use as the basis for its risk-based capital requirement, and what risk weight must be applied to it given the hierarchy of approaches available to the institution?
required_facts: The exposure amount of an OTC derivative securitization exposure (other than a credit derivative) equals the EAD calculated under the counterparty credit risk rules, not the notional or carrying value
Because a qualifying master netting agreement is in place, the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) must be used to calculate EAD under § 217.132(c)

The institution has exhausted the higher-priority approaches in the hierarchy (gain-on-sale/CEIO deduction does not apply; supervisory formula approach does not qualify; simplified supervisory formula approach not elected)
The applicable risk weight under the residual step of the hierarchy is 1,250 percent
The risk-weighted asset amount for this exposure = $7.42M × 12.5 = $92.75 million

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.142(e)(3) directs that the exposure amount of a securitization exposure that is an OTC derivative contract (other than a credit derivative) equals the EAD calculated under § 217.132; § 217.132(c) then provides the standardized approach (SA-CCR) formula for EAD of OTC derivative contracts subject to a qualifying master netting agreement, yielding EAD = replacement cost + potential future exposure add-on.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the exposure type: The securitization exposure is an OTC derivative contract (interest rate swap) that is not a credit derivative and is not a cleared transaction. Step 2 — Navigate the exposure amount rule: Under § 217.142(e)(3), the exposure amount for a securitization exposure that is an OTC derivative contract (other than a credit derivative) or cleared transaction (other than a credit derivative) is the EAD calculated under § 217.132 or § 217.133. Because this is an OTC (non-cleared) derivative, § 217.132 applies. Step 3 — Apply § 217.132(c): For an OTC derivative contract subject to a qualifying master netting agreement, the institution must use the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) in § 217.132(c) to calculate EAD. Under SA-CCR, EAD = alpha × (RC + PFE), where alpha = 1.4, RC is the replacement cost, and PFE is the potential future exposure add-on. With no eligible collateral, RC = $4.2 million and PFE = $1.1 million, so EAD = 1.4 × ($4.2M + $1.1M) = 1.4 × $5.3M = $7.42 million. Step 4 — Determine the risk weight: Because the exposure does not require deduction or a 1,250% risk weight under the gain-on-sale/CEIO rule, does not qualify for the supervisory formula approach, and the institution has chosen not to apply the simplified supervisory formula approach, the institution must apply a 1,250% risk weight to the exposure under the residual rule in the hierarchy of approaches.

scenario_parameters.exposure_type: OTC interest rate swap referencing securitization cash flows

question_text: Maple Re Holdings, a supervised insurance organization subject to the Building Block Approach, has identified an inventory company called Maple Conduit LLC. Maple Conduit LLC was established solely to transfer catastrophe risk from three affiliated insurers within the supervised insurance organization to unaffiliated reinsurers in the capital markets — it enters into no other transactions. Maple Conduit LLC is not a depository institution and is not subject to any regulatory capital framework. The supervised insurance organization's compliance team is considering whether to elect not to treat Maple Conduit LLC as a material financial entity. If that election is made, describe the specific adjustment that must be added to the company capital requirement of any building block parent whose building block contains a member that transacts with Maple Conduit LLC, and identify the conditions under which that adjustment is required.
required_facts: Maple Conduit LLC qualifies for the material financial entity election under § 217.605(c)(2) because it engages solely in transactions that transfer risk from affiliated insurers to unaffiliated third parties.
The election must be included with the first financial statements submitted to the Board after Maple Conduit LLC is included in the supervised insurance organization's inventory.
A second condition for the election is that the supervised insurance organization must be able to calculate the adjustment for investments in own capital instruments (the § 217.607(b)(4) adjustment).

Once the election is made, § 217.607(b)(3) requires an additive adjustment to the company capital requirement of each building block parent whose building block contains a member that transacts with Maple Conduit LLC.

The adjustment equals the difference between the building block parent's company capital requirement and that requirement recalculated to include the risks of Maple Conduit LLC (excluding internal credit risks) allocated to the building block parent based on its transactions with members of that building block.
The total allocation of Maple Conduit LLC's risks across all building block parents must capture all material risks and avoid double counting.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.607(b)(3) governs the capital adjustment for risks of certain intermediary entities and is triggered only when an election has been made under § 217.605(c) not to treat a company as a material financial entity; the conditions for that election are defined in § 217.605(c)(2), which requires the company to engage solely in risk-transfer or asset-investment transactions and the organization to be able to calculate the § 217.607(b)(4) adjustment.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the election mechanism: § 217.605(c)(1) permits a supervised insurance organization to elect not to treat an inventory company as a material financial entity, provided the conditions in § 217.605(c)(2) are satisfied. Step 2 — Check eligibility of Maple Conduit LLC: Under § 217.605(c)(2)(i)(A), the company must engage in transactions consisting solely of transferring risk from one or more affiliates to one or more third parties. Maple Conduit LLC transfers catastrophe risk from affiliated insurers to unaffiliated reinsurers and enters into no other transactions — this satisfies the condition. Additionally, § 217.605(c)(2)(ii) requires the organization to be able to calculate the adjustment required in § 217.607(b)(4) (investments in own capital instruments). Step 3 — Consequence of the election: Once the election is made under § 217.605(c), § 217.607(b)(3) is triggered. That paragraph requires the supervised insurance organization to add to the company capital requirement of any building block parent whose building block contains a member that transacts with Maple Conduit LLC (and for which Maple Conduit LLC engages in one or more transactions described in § 217.605(c)(2) with a third party) the difference between: (i) the building block parent's company capital requirement; and (ii) the building block parent's company capital requirement recalculated taking into account the risks of Maple Conduit LLC (excluding internal credit risks under § 217.607(b)(1)), allocated to the building block parent, reflecting the transactions Maple Conduit LLC engages in with members of that building block parent's building block. The total allocation across all building block parents must capture all material risks and avoid double counting.
