question_text: A Board-regulated institution that is not an advanced approaches institution holds a portfolio of equity derivative contracts referencing publicly traded common stock of non-financial corporations. The institution has not elected to treat any of these contracts as covered positions under the market risk subpart. The total adjusted carrying value of the on-balance sheet components of these equity derivative contracts is $85 million, and the effective notional principal amount of the off-balance sheet components (calculated as the hypothetical on-balance sheet equivalent) is $40 million, with no net unrealized gains excluded from regulatory capital components. The institution has not made an AOCI opt-out election. None of the contracts are subject to a qualifying master netting agreement, and none are cleared transactions. The institution is also calculating its standardized total risk-weighted assets for general credit risk purposes and must determine which exposures are excluded from that general credit risk calculation. Explain how the institution must treat these equity derivative contracts for risk-based capital purposes: specifically, (1) which risk-weighting framework applies to the equity exposure component, (2) what the adjusted carrying value of the combined equity exposure is for that framework, and (3) whether the counterparty credit risk of these contracts must also be separately capitalized, and if so, under which exposure measurement methodology.
required_facts: The equity derivative contracts must be treated as equity exposures and risk-weighted under the Simple Risk-Weight Approach (SRWA) in § 217.52, because the institution is not treating them as covered positions and they are not exposures to an investment fund.
No AOCI opt-out adjustment applies to the on-balance sheet component because the institution has not made an AOCI opt-out election.

State that a non-advanced-approaches institution would use CEM unless it elected SA-CCR, but because the contracts are risk-weighted under SRWA, § 217.34(e)(3) allows the institution to choose not to hold CCR capital for them.

Equity OTC derivative contracts are not excluded from the general credit risk mechanics calculation; only equity exposures other than equity OTC derivative contracts are carved out from that calculation.

Because the contracts are not treated as covered positions under the market risk subpart, no separate counterparty credit risk charge is required under the covered-position pathway; the CCR charge arises instead through the general credit risk framework using CEM exposure amounts.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.34(e) directs equity derivative treatment to §§ 217.51–217.53; § 217.51(b) defines adjusted carrying value using the § 217.2 definition of 'separate account' (cross-subpart); § 217.31(a)(1)(v) carves out equity exposures (other than equity OTC derivatives) from the general credit risk mechanics, confirming equity derivatives remain in § 217.31 scope for counterparty credit risk while the equity exposure component goes to § 217.51–217.53.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.34(e)(1): Because the institution is not treating the equity derivative contracts as covered positions under subpart F, it must treat each contract as an equity exposure and compute a risk-weighted asset amount under §§ 217.51 through 217.53. Step 2 — § 217.34(e)(2): In addition, because the contracts are NOT treated as covered positions under subpart F, the institution does NOT separately calculate a counterparty credit risk capital requirement under § 217.34 for these contracts (paragraph (e)(2) only requires the additional CCR charge when the contract IS a covered position). Step 3 — § 217.34(e)(3): The institution is not using SRWA for these contracts (that option only allows omitting CCR if SRWA is used), so this paragraph is not directly triggered, but confirms the SRWA election option exists. Step 4 — § 217.51(a)(1): Since the equity exposures are not exposures to an investment fund, the institution must use the Simple Risk-Weight Approach (SRWA) under § 217.52. Step 5 — § 217.51(b): The adjusted carrying value of the equity exposure equals: (b)(1) the on-balance sheet carrying value of $85 million (no AOCI opt-out election was made, so no unrealized gain adjustment under (b)(2) applies), plus (b)(3) the off-balance sheet component = effective notional principal amount of $40 million minus the on-balance sheet adjusted carrying value already counted — but (b)(3) defines the off-balance sheet component as the effective notional principal amount of the exposure equivalent to a hypothetical on-balance sheet position, minus the adjusted carrying value of the on-balance sheet component. Here the $40 million is already stated as the net off-balance sheet equivalent, so total adjusted carrying value = $85M + $40M = $125 million. Step 6 — § 217.51(a)(2) cross-references § 217.2 definition of 'separate account' to confirm these are not separate account investments (they are plain equity derivatives), so no separate account look-through applies. Step 7 — § 217.31(a)(1)(v): The general credit risk mechanics exclude equity exposures other than equity OTC derivative contracts from the § 217.31 calculation. Because these ARE equity OTC derivative contracts, they are NOT excluded by (a)(1)(v) — meaning the counterparty credit risk component of equity OTC derivatives remains subject to § 217.31 general credit risk treatment (i.e., the CCR exposure amount calculated under § 217.34(b) CEM is included in the § 217.31 risk-weighted asset calculation). Conclusion: (1) Equity exposure component → SRWA under § 217.52; (2) Adjusted carrying value = $125 million; (3) Counterparty credit risk must be separately capitalized under § 217.34(b) CEM (since the institution is not an advanced approaches institution and has not elected SA-CCR), and that CCR exposure feeds into the § 217.31 general credit risk RWA calculation.

scenario_parameters.reference_asset_type: publicly traded common stock of non-financial corporations

question_text: A Board-regulated institution operates a trading book that includes a portfolio of investment-grade corporate bond positions for which its internal VaR model does not fully capture specific risk. The institution also holds, on its balance sheet, a portfolio of equity securities classified as available-for-sale (AFS). The institution has elected to opt out of recognizing accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) in its regulatory capital components. For the most recent quarter, the institution's backtesting results show 7 exceptions over the preceding 250 business days. The institution's VaR-based measure for the prior business day was $18 million, and the average daily VaR-based measure over the preceding 60 business days was $14 million. The specific risk add-on for the corporate bond portfolio, calculated using the standardized measurement method, is $9 million. The AFS equity portfolio has a carrying value of $50 million, which includes $4 million of net unrealized gains that are excluded from the institution's regulatory capital components due to the AOCI opt-out election. The institution seeks to determine: (1) its total standardized measure for market risk, incorporating the correct multiplication factor given its backtesting exceptions; and (2) the adjusted carrying value it must use when computing risk-weighted asset amounts for the AFS equity portfolio under the equity exposures framework.
required_facts: 7 backtesting exceptions correspond to a multiplication factor of 3.65 per Table 1 to § 217.204
VaR-based capital requirement = max($18M, $14M × 3.65) = max($18M, $51.1M) = $51.1M

Specific risk add-ons for the corporate bond portfolio must be calculated in accordance with the standardized measurement method under § 217.210 because the VaR model does not capture all material aspects of specific risk
Total standardized measure for market risk = $51.1M (VaR-based) + $9M (specific risk add-on) = $60.1M (assuming no other components)
The AOCI opt-out election triggers the adjusted carrying value rule for AFS equity exposures under the equity exposures framework
Adjusted carrying value of the AFS equity portfolio = $50M carrying value − $4M net unrealized gains excluded from regulatory capital = $46M

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.204 defines the standardized measure for market risk and directs the institution to calculate specific risk add-ons in accordance with § 217.210; § 217.210 governs the standardized measurement method for specific risk; § 217.204(b) and Table 1 set the multiplication factor based on backtesting exceptions; § 217.51(b)(2) governs adjusted carrying value for AFS equity exposures where an AOCI opt-out election has been made under § 217.22(b)(2).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.204(b) backtesting: The institution has 7 exceptions. Per Table 1 to § 217.204, 7 exceptions correspond to a multiplication factor of 3.65. Step 2 — § 217.204(a)(2)(i) VaR-based capital requirement: Greater of (A) prior day VaR = $18M, or (B) 60-day average VaR × multiplication factor = $14M × 3.65 = $51.1M. The VaR-based capital requirement = $51.1M. Step 3 — § 217.204(a)(2)(iii) specific risk add-ons: The institution must calculate specific risk add-ons for portfolios where VaR does not capture all material aspects of specific risk, calculated in accordance with § 217.210. The specific risk add-on for the corporate bond portfolio = $9M (given, computed under § 217.210). Step 4 — Total standardized measure for market risk (§ 217.204(a)(2)): Assuming no stressed VaR, incremental risk, comprehensive risk, or de minimis components are provided, the total = VaR-based capital requirement + specific risk add-on = $51.1M + $9M = $60.1M. Step 5 — Adjusted carrying value for AFS equity (§ 217.51(b)(2)): For an on-balance sheet equity exposure classified as AFS where the institution has made an AOCI opt-out election under § 217.22(b)(2), the adjusted carrying value = carrying value less any net unrealized gains excluded from regulatory capital = $50M − $4M = $46M. The cross-subpart link is § 217.51(b)(2) referencing § 217.22(b)(2) for the AOCI opt-out condition.

question_text:
Northgate Savings Bank is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has completed its parallel run and received the required notification from its primary federal regulator. The bank is currently preparing its quarterly public disclosures and is evaluating whether it must include supplementary leverage ratio disclosures in addition to its standard capital structure tables.

Separately, the bank's structured finance team is reviewing a synthetic securitization it entered into last quarter. In that transaction, the bank used a guarantee from a corporate counterparty to hedge $850 million of underlying commercial loan exposures. The guarantee was issued by an investment-grade non-bank financial company and covers first-loss risk on the portfolio. The bank's credit risk team notes that the guarantee does not satisfy one specific operational requirement that would otherwise be needed for it to qualify as an eligible guarantee under the applicable definitions — specifically, the guarantee lacks an unconditional and irrevocable obligation clause. The bank is trying to determine whether it can still recognize the credit risk transfer for regulatory capital purposes under the synthetic securitization framework, given that the synthetic securitization rules contain a carve-out for exactly this type of deficiency.

For the $850 million in underlying commercial loan exposures that cannot be excluded from risk-weighted asset calculations (assuming the credit risk transfer is not recognized), the bank applies the standardized approach. Each exposure is a funded term loan to a corporate obligor with no eligible financial collateral and no eligible guarantor. The applicable risk weight for these corporate exposures under the standardized approach is 100%.

Determine: (1) whether Northgate must include supplementary leverage ratio disclosures in its public reporting, (2) whether the synthetic securitization's credit risk transfer can be recognized for regulatory capital purposes despite the guarantee's missing clause, and (3) if the credit risk transfer is not recognized, what is the total risk-weighted asset contribution from the $850 million portfolio under the standardized approach.
required_facts: Northgate, as an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution subject to supplementary leverage ratio disclosure under § 217.172(d), must include Table 13 supplementary leverage ratio disclosures in its public reporting (subject to the consolidated subsidiary exception).

The synthetic securitization operational criteria in § 217.141(b)(1)(ii) explicitly permit a guarantee that satisfies all requirements of an eligible guarantee except paragraph (3) of the definition in § 217.2.
The missing unconditional/irrevocable feature does not match paragraph (3); paragraph (3) concerns coverage of contractual payments.
Because the carve-out is only for paragraph (3), a guarantee lacking the unconditional/irrevocable requirement would not qualify on that carve-out.
If credit risk transfer were not recognized, § 217.141(b) requires the bank to hold risk-based capital against the $850 million underlying exposures as if unsecuritized.

Under the standardized approach mechanics, each $850 million corporate term loan exposure is multiplied by the 100% risk weight, yielding total risk-weighted assets of $850 million for that portfolio.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.173 governs disclosure obligations for advanced approaches institutions including supplementary leverage ratio disclosure; § 217.141(b)(1)(ii) sets operational criteria for synthetic securitizations and explicitly carves out paragraph (3) of the eligible guarantee definition; § 217.2 defines 'eligible guarantee' including the unconditional/irrevocable clause in paragraph (3); § 217.31 provides the mechanics for calculating risk-weighted assets under the standardized approach when credit risk transfer is not recognized.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.173(a)(2): An advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that is required to publicly disclose its supplementary leverage ratio pursuant to § 217.172(d) must make the disclosures required under Table 13 to § 217.173, unless it is a consolidated subsidiary of a qualifying parent subject to the same requirements. Northgate is an advanced approaches institution that has completed parallel run, so it must assess whether § 217.172(d) requires supplementary leverage ratio disclosure; assuming it does (as is standard for advanced approaches institutions post-parallel run), Northgate must include Table 13 supplementary leverage ratio disclosures unless the subsidiary exception applies. Step 2 — § 217.141(b)(1)(ii): For synthetic securitizations, the credit risk mitigant may be a guarantee that meets all requirements of an eligible guarantee in § 217.2 *except for paragraph (3) of the definition*. The missing clause (unconditional and irrevocable obligation) corresponds to paragraph (3) of the eligible guarantee definition in § 217.2. Because § 217.141(b)(1)(ii) explicitly carves out paragraph (3), the guarantee can still qualify as a credit risk mitigant for synthetic securitization purposes despite lacking that clause. Therefore, the credit risk transfer CAN be recognized. Step 3 — Hypothetical: If the credit risk transfer were not recognized, § 217.141(b) requires the bank to hold risk-based capital against the underlying exposures as if they had not been synthetically securitized. Under § 217.31(a)(1) and (a)(2), the bank must determine the exposure amount of each on-balance sheet exposure and multiply by the applicable risk weight. For $850 million in 100%-risk-weighted corporate term loans with no collateral or guarantor offsets, risk-weighted assets = $850 million × 100% = $850 million. Under § 217.31(b), total risk-weighted assets for general credit risk equals the sum of these amounts, so the portfolio contributes $850 million to total RWA.

scenario_parameters.credit_risk_mitigant: guarantee from investment-grade non-bank financial company
scenario_parameters.missing_guarantee_clause: unconditional and irrevocable obligation (eligible guarantee definition paragraph 3)

question_text: A Board-regulated institution operates as a market risk institution and maintains an internal VaR-based model approved for market risk capital purposes. The institution holds a portfolio of asset-backed securities (ABS) tranches that it classifies as covered positions. For this ABS portfolio, the institution's risk management team has determined that the VaR-based measure does not fully capture all material aspects of specific risk — in particular, it does not adequately model idiosyncratic spread movements for the mezzanine tranches. The portfolio includes: (1) $180 million notional in mezzanine ABS tranches that are not modeled under the institution's correlation trading framework, and (2) $45 million notional in a program-wide credit enhancement provided to an asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) program, structured as an off-balance sheet securitization exposure that is also not modeled under the correlation trading framework. The institution cannot apply the simplified supervisory formula approach (SSFA) to the ABCP credit enhancement and chooses not to apply the gross-up approach. The institution's internal models group has confirmed that neither of these positions qualifies as a correlation trading position. For the ABCP credit enhancement, the institution must determine the applicable credit conversion factor (CCF) and the resulting exposure amount before assigning a risk weight. The institution is not subject to the advanced approaches framework for purposes of the securitization risk-weighting rules in this analysis. Determine: (a) the method the institution must use to calculate the specific risk add-on for both the mezzanine ABS tranches and the ABCP credit enhancement, (b) the exposure amount of the ABCP credit enhancement for risk-weighting purposes, and (c) the risk weight that must be assigned to the ABCP credit enhancement given that neither the SSFA nor the gross-up approach is applied.
required_facts: The institution must use the standardized measurement method under § 217.210 to calculate the specific risk add-on for both the mezzanine ABS tranches and the ABCP credit enhancement, because these securitization positions are not modeled under the correlation trading / § 217.209 framework.
Neither position qualifies as a correlation trading position under the § 217.2 definition, so both remain securitization positions for purposes of the specific risk add-on calculation.
Do not treat the ABCP program-wide credit enhancement as an eligible ABCP liquidity facility unless the source facts establish that classification.
Use the source-supported exposure amount rule for the actual exposure type rather than 45 million × 50%.

Because the institution cannot or chooses not to apply the SSFA or the gross-up approach to the ABCP credit enhancement, it must assign a risk weight to that exposure under the fallback rule, which directs to a 1,250% risk weight.
Recompute RWA using the source-supported exposure amount.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.207(c) mandates the standardized measurement method (§ 217.210) for securitization positions not modeled under § 217.209; § 217.210(a) references the definition of 'correlation trading position' in § 217.2 to confirm these positions are treated as securitization positions; § 217.210 then directs the institution to calculate the specific risk add-on for securitization positions, and for the ABCP exposure the CCF and risk weight are governed by § 217.42, specifically § 217.42(a)(3) directing to § 217.44 when SSFA and gross-up are unavailable.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.207(c)(2): Because the mezzanine ABS tranches and the ABCP credit enhancement are securitization positions that are NOT modeled under § 217.209, the institution MUST calculate a specific risk add-on for them using the standardized measurement method described in § 217.210. Step 2 — § 217.210(a): The institution calculates the total specific risk add-on under § 217.210. The section also clarifies (via cross-reference to the definition of 'correlation trading position' in § 217.2) that positions qualifying as debt or equity but for the correlation trading position definition are treated as debt or equity — but here these are securitization positions, so they remain securitization positions for § 217.210 purposes. Step 3 — § 217.2 (definition of 'correlation trading position'): Confirms that neither the mezzanine ABS tranches nor the ABCP credit enhancement qualifies as a correlation trading position, so they are treated as securitization positions throughout. Step 4 — § 217.42(c)(3)(ii) and (iii): For the ABCP credit enhancement (an eligible ABCP liquidity facility / off-balance sheet securitization exposure to an ABCP program), the CCF depends on whether SSFA applies. Since SSFA does NOT apply, the CCF is 50%, yielding an exposure amount of $45M × 50% = $22.5 million. Step 5 — § 217.42(a)(3): Because the ABCP credit enhancement does not require deduction under § 217.42(a)(1) and the institution cannot or chooses not to apply SSFA or the gross-up approach, the institution must assign a risk weight under § 217.44 (the 1,250% risk weight for securitization exposures where no approved approach is available).

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has entered into a synthetic securitization in which it uses a credit derivative to hedge a pool of corporate loan exposures. The credit derivative references an eligible guarantee from a third-party guarantor. The institution's legal counsel has confirmed enforceability of the credit risk mitigant in all relevant jurisdictions, and the securitization contains no provisions that would allow termination of credit protection due to credit quality deterioration of the underlying exposures. However, the guarantee does not satisfy the requirement that the guarantor must make payment to the institution within a specified period after a credit event is declared — a condition that appears in the definition of the relevant instrument type used in the synthetic securitization. Separately, the institution holds a $45 million equity exposure to a registered investment fund. The fund's prospectus permits investments in corporate equities (300 percent risk weight), sovereign debt (0 percent risk weight), and residential mortgage-backed securities (50 percent risk weight), with investment limits of 60 percent, 30 percent, and 40 percent respectively (totaling 130 percent). The institution does not use the full look-through approach for this fund exposure, and the exposure does not qualify as a community development equity exposure. The institution's adjusted carrying value for the fund exposure is $45 million. Using the alternative modified look-through approach, determine: (1) whether the synthetic securitization credit risk mitigant qualifies for recognition under the applicable operational criteria, and (2) the risk-weighted asset amount for the $45 million equity exposure to the investment fund.
required_facts: State that 217.41(b)(1)(iii) waives only eligible-guarantee paragraph (3), not the timely-payment requirement in paragraph (7).
State that the mitigant does not qualify because the unwaived timely-payment requirement remains applicable.
Equity exposures to investment funds are risk-weighted under § 217.53, as directed by § 217.52(a).

Under the alternative modified look-through approach in § 217.53(d), because the fund's investment limits sum to 130 percent (exceeding 100 percent), the institution must allocate to the highest risk-weight exposure type first: 60 percent to corporate equities (300% risk weight) and 40 percent to RMBS (50% risk weight), exhausting the 100 percent total.
RWA for the corporate equity allocation: $45M × 60% × 300% = $81 million.
RWA for the RMBS allocation: $45M × 40% × 50% = $9 million.
Total risk-weighted asset amount for the $45 million investment fund equity exposure = $90 million.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.41(b)(1)(iii) conditions for synthetic securitization credit derivatives cross-reference the definition of 'eligible credit derivative' and 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2 (Subpart A); separately, § 217.52(a) routes investment fund equity exposures to § 217.53, and § 217.53(d) governs the alternative modified look-through approach with investment limit cap logic.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.41(b)(1)(iii): For a synthetic securitization using a credit derivative, the credit risk mitigant qualifies only if it meets all criteria in the definition of 'eligible credit derivative' in § 217.2, except for the criteria in paragraph (3) of the definition of 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2. This requires navigating to § 217.2 (Subpart A) to look up both definitions. Step 2 — § 217.2 definitions: The definition of 'eligible credit derivative' in § 217.2 incorporates by reference the criteria of 'eligible guarantee,' except paragraph (3). Paragraph (3) of 'eligible guarantee' typically requires that the guarantor make payment within a specified period after a credit event. Since § 217.41(b)(1)(iii) explicitly carves out paragraph (3) of 'eligible guarantee' from the requirements for a credit derivative used in synthetic securitization, the failure to satisfy that payment-timing condition does NOT disqualify the credit derivative. Therefore, the credit risk mitigant qualifies for recognition, provided all other conditions in § 217.41(b) are met (legal opinion obtained per § 217.41(b)(3), no prohibited provisions per § 217.41(b)(2), eligible clean-up calls per § 217.41(b)(4)) — all of which are stated as satisfied in the scenario. Conclusion for Part 1: The synthetic securitization credit risk mitigant qualifies. Step 3 — § 217.52(a): Total risk-weighted assets for equity exposures to investment funds are determined under § 217.53. Step 4 — § 217.53(d) alternative modified look-through approach: The institution assigns the $45 million adjusted carrying value pro rata based on investment limits. The fund's investment limits sum to 130 percent (exceeds 100 percent), so the institution must assume the fund invests to the maximum in the highest risk-weight exposure type first, then next highest, until 100 percent is reached. Risk weights: corporate equities = 300% (limit 60%), RMBS = 50% (limit 40%), sovereign = 0% (limit 30%). Ordered by risk weight descending: (1) corporate equities 300%, limit 60% → allocate 60% of $45M = $27M at 300%; (2) RMBS 50%, limit 40% → allocate 40% of $45M = $18M at 50%; total allocated = 100%, stop. Sovereign (0%) is not reached. RWA = ($27M × 300%) + ($18M × 50%) = $81M + $9M = $90M. Minimum risk weight floor of 20% does not bind here since all assigned weights exceed 20%.

scenario_parameters.disqualifying_condition_present: payment-timing requirement (paragraph 3 of eligible guarantee definition)

question_text:
First National Bancorp is a top-tier U.S. bank holding company that is not a consolidated subsidiary of another bank holding company. It has been identified as a global systemically important BHC (G-SIB) under the Board's framework. The institution has been operating under the advanced approaches framework for several years and, as of last quarter, received formal notification from the Board that it has successfully completed the parallel run process and is approved to exit parallel run. First National Bancorp does not have a parent bank holding company or savings and loan holding company that is itself subject to advanced approaches disclosure requirements, and it is not a subsidiary of a non-U.S. banking organization.

First National Bancorp's compliance team is now evaluating its public disclosure obligations going forward. Specifically, the team wants to know: (1) whether the institution is now required to make quarterly public disclosures of its total and tier 1 risk-based capital ratios and their components as calculated under the advanced approaches framework; (2) whether the institution must also disclose its supplementary leverage ratio and its components on a quarterly basis; and (3) what the threshold criterion is that makes the institution subject to the advanced approaches capital calculation framework in the first place, given its G-SIB designation.

For each of the three questions, state the applicable requirement and the basis for it.
required_facts: First National Bancorp is required to publicly disclose each quarter its total and tier 1 risk-based capital ratios and their components (CET1 capital, additional tier 1 capital, tier 2 capital, total qualifying capital, and total risk-weighted assets) as calculated under the advanced approaches framework, because it has completed the parallel run process and received Board notification to exit parallel run.

The quarterly supplementary leverage ratio disclosure requirement (tier 1 capital and total leverage exposure as calculated under subpart B) applies to First National Bancorp as an advanced approaches institution, and this requirement applies regardless of whether the institution has completed the parallel run process.

The threshold criterion making First National Bancorp subject to the advanced approaches capital framework is its identification as a global systemically important BHC (G-SIB), which is one of the applicability conditions for top-tier U.S. bank holding companies under the advanced approaches subpart.

Because First National Bancorp is an advanced approaches institution making disclosures under the advanced approaches disclosure regime, it is carved out of the standard Subpart D disclosure requirements that apply to non-advanced-approaches institutions with $50 billion or more in total consolidated assets.

First National Bancorp must comply with the full quarterly advanced approaches disclosure requirements (rather than the subsidiary exemption) because it is not a consolidated subsidiary of a bank holding company, savings and loan holding company, or depository institution that is itself subject to these disclosure requirements, and it is not a subsidiary of a non-U.S. banking organization subject to comparable home-jurisdiction disclosure requirements.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a variable annuity separate account with a carrying value of $180 million. The institution has entered into a contract with a third-party insurer under which the insurer is obligated to pay the institution an amount equal to the shortfall between the fair value and cost basis of the separate account if the institution surrenders the policy. The carrying value of the separate account is split as follows: $40 million is attributable to the protection provided by the insurer's contract, and the remaining $140 million represents the institution's residual equity interest in the underlying portfolio. The institution is a top-tier depository institution holding company that, as of June 30 of the prior calendar year, held 28 percent of its total consolidated assets (calculated under GAAP) in insurance underwriting companies (excluding assets associated with insurance underwriting for credit risk). Determine: (1) how the institution must classify and treat the $40 million and $140 million portions of the separate account for risk-weighting purposes; and (2) whether the institution is subject to the overall capital adequacy framework applicable to Board-regulated institutions significantly engaged in insurance activities, and on what basis.
required_facts: The contract described qualifies as 'stable value protection' because the insurer is obligated to pay the shortfall between fair value and cost basis of the separate account upon policy surrender.
The institution must confirm the instrument is a 'separate account' as defined in § 217.2 before applying the equity exposure treatment in § 217.51(a)(2).

The $40 million portion attributable to the stable value protection must be treated as a credit exposure to the third-party insurer (the protection provider), not as an equity exposure to an investment fund.
The remaining $140 million must be treated as an equity exposure to an investment fund and risk-weighted using the look-through approaches.
The institution holds 28% of total consolidated GAAP assets in insurance underwriting companies (excluding credit-risk insurance assets), which exceeds the 25% threshold.

Because the 25% threshold is exceeded, the institution is subject to the overall insurance capital adequacy framework in Subpart J, which establishes building-block available capital and capital requirement aggregation across diverse capital frameworks.

The institution's 28% insurance asset concentration then triggers applicability under § 217.601(b)(2) (Subpart J), which the reader must locate by following the cross-reference to 'subpart J of this part' embedded in the definitions and applicability provisions.

Step 4 — Determine insurance capital framework applicability: The institution holds 28% of total consolidated GAAP assets in insurance underwriting companies (excluding credit-risk insurance assets), which exceeds the 25% threshold in § 217.601(b)(2) (Subpart J). Therefore, the institution is subject to the building-block insurance capital adequacy framework established in Subpart J.

scenario_parameters.protection_trigger: shortfall between fair value and cost basis upon policy surrender

question_text: A Board-regulated institution is an advanced approaches institution that has completed its parallel run and received the requisite notification from its primary federal supervisor. In preparing its regulatory capital calculation, the institution's finance team identifies the following items on its balance sheet: (1) mortgage servicing assets (MSAs) with a carrying value of $1.8 billion; (2) deferred tax assets (DTAs) arising from temporary differences that could not be realized through net operating loss carrybacks, with a carrying value of $2.1 billion; and (3) significant investments in the capital of unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock, with a carrying value of $3.4 billion. The institution's common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital elements, before any adjustments or deductions, sum to $38 billion, and its total risk-weighted assets under the advanced approaches equal $310 billion. The institution also has eligible credit reserves of $900 million and an expected credit loss estimate of $1.35 billion. The institution's risk and capital team must determine: (a) which of the three asset categories listed above are subject to deduction from CET1 versus a risk-weight treatment, and under what threshold conditions; (b) what the applicable risk weight is for any amounts that escape deduction; and (c) whether the institution's expected credit loss position requires an additional CET1 deduction, and if so, how much. Provide a complete analysis of the CET1 deduction and risk-weighting treatment for each item, including the aggregate threshold that governs items (1), (2), and (3) collectively, and state the institution's resulting CET1 capital after all required adjustments.
required_facts: MSAs, DTAs from temporary differences not realizable via NOL carrybacks, and significant investments in unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock are each subject to an individual 10% CET1 threshold deduction and a collective 15% CET1 aggregate threshold deduction under the regulatory capital deduction framework.
Amounts of those three items that fall below the applicable thresholds are not deducted from CET1 but instead receive a 250% risk weight for purposes of risk-weighted asset calculation.

Because the institution is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has completed the parallel run and received the required supervisory notification, it must deduct from CET1 the amount by which its expected credit loss ($1.35 billion) exceeds its eligible credit reserves ($900 million), resulting in a $450 million CET1 deduction.
Use the §217.22(d)(2)(ii) formula: aggregate threshold about $5.34B and deduction about $1.96B (assuming $37.55B base and $7.3B threshold items).
No individual item exceeds its own 10% CET1 threshold (~$3.755 billion), so no item-level deduction is triggered independently; only the aggregate 15% threshold is breached.

The definition of 'advanced approaches Board-regulated institution' is a prerequisite for applying the ECL-excess deduction rule, linking the capital components section to the definitions section and then to the advanced approaches risk-weighting mechanics.
Resulting CET1 is about $35.59B, not $35.883B, assuming no other adjustments.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.20(b) defines CET1 capital as CET1 elements minus deductions in § 217.22; § 217.22(d) sets the threshold deduction rules for MSAs, DTAs from temporary differences, and significant investments in unconsolidated financial institutions, referencing the definition of 'advanced approaches Board-regulated institution' in § 217.2; § 217.131(e)(3)(vi) specifies the 250% risk weight for amounts of those items that are not deducted under § 217.22(d).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.20(b): CET1 capital equals the sum of CET1 elements minus regulatory adjustments and deductions in § 217.22. This directs the reader to § 217.22 for the deduction mechanics.

Step 2 — § 217.22(d): The threshold deduction framework applies to three categories: MSAs, DTAs arising from temporary differences that the institution could not realize through net operating loss carrybacks, and significant investments in the capital of unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock. Each individual item is subject to a 10% CET1 threshold: any amount of a single item exceeding 10% of CET1 (computed after all other deductions except these three) must be deducted. Additionally, the aggregate of all three items is subject to a 15% CET1 threshold: any combined amount exceeding 15% of CET1 must also be deducted. Amounts below these thresholds are not deducted but instead receive a 250% risk weight (cross-reference to § 217.131).

Step 3 — § 217.2: The definition of 'advanced approaches Board-regulated institution' is needed to confirm that § 217.22(a)(6) applies — i.e., the deduction for expected credit loss (ECL) exceeding eligible credit reserves applies only to an advanced approaches institution that has completed the parallel run and received Board notification per § 217.121(d). The institution in the scenario meets this definition.

Step 4 — § 217.22(a)(6): Because the institution is an advanced approaches institution that has completed parallel run, it must deduct from CET1 the amount by which ECL ($1.35 billion) exceeds eligible credit reserves ($900 million). Deduction = $1.35B − $0.90B = $0.45 billion.

Step 5 — § 217.22(d) threshold computation (illustrative): Assume CET1 after all other deductions (excluding the three threshold items and the ECL deduction) is approximately $38B − $0.45B = $37.55B. 10% threshold per item = $3.755B. 15% aggregate threshold = $5.633B.
  - MSAs: $1.8B < $3.755B → no individual deduction.
  - DTAs (temp diff): $2.1B < $3.755B → no individual deduction.
  - Significant investments: $3.4B < $3.755B → no individual deduction.
  - Aggregate: $1.8B + $2.1B + $3.4B = $7.3B > $5.633B → excess = $7.3B − $5.633B = $1.667B must be deducted from CET1 (allocated pro-rata across the three items).
  - Remaining amounts not deducted = $7.3B − $1.667B = $5.633B → these receive a 250% risk weight per § 217.131(e)(3)(vi).

Step 6 — § 217.131(e)(3)(vi): Confirms that the risk-weighted asset amount for MSAs, DTAs from temporary timing differences that could not be realized through NOL carrybacks, and significant investments in the capital of unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock that are not deducted pursuant to § 217.22(d) equals the amount not subject to deduction multiplied by 250%.

Step 7 — Final CET1: $38B (elements) − $0.45B (ECL deduction) − $1.667B (aggregate threshold deduction) = approximately $35.883B.

question_text: First National Bancorp is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that holds a portfolio of wholesale exposures partially hedged with eligible credit derivatives. One of those exposures is a $50 million term loan to a corporate obligor denominated in euros, while the credit derivative protecting it is denominated in US dollars. The bank's risk management team has determined that the institution qualifies to use its own internal estimates of foreign exchange volatility (based on a ten-business-day holding period and daily marking-to-market) rather than the flat 8% haircut prescribed for currency mismatches. The team is now preparing the quarterly capital adequacy report and needs to confirm the minimum capital ratios the institution must satisfy. Specifically: (1) Does the institution's qualification to use internal FX volatility estimates depend on its eligibility for any particular collateral or counterparty credit risk methodology under the repo-style and OTC derivatives framework, and if so, which one(s)? (2) What are the minimum common equity tier 1 capital ratio, tier 1 capital ratio, total capital ratio, and supplementary leverage ratio that this advanced approaches institution must maintain? (3) If the institution's tier 1 capital is $9.6 billion and its total leverage exposure (calculated as the sum of on-balance sheet assets and off-balance sheet exposures net of applicable deductions) is $240 billion, does it satisfy the supplementary leverage ratio requirement?
required_facts: A Board-regulated institution may use internal FX volatility estimates (instead of the 8% flat haircut) for currency mismatches under the credit derivative hedging framework if it qualifies for the own-estimates haircuts in the collateral haircut approach, the simple VaR methodology, or the internal models methodology for repo-style transactions and OTC derivatives

The own-estimates haircut qualification referenced for this purpose is found in the counterparty credit risk framework governing repo-style transactions, eligible margin loans, and OTC derivative contracts

As an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution, the minimum CET1 capital ratio is 4.5%, the minimum tier 1 capital ratio is 6%, the minimum total capital ratio is 8%, and the minimum leverage ratio is 4%
An advanced approaches Board-regulated institution must also maintain a supplementary leverage ratio of at least 3%
The supplementary leverage ratio equals tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure: $9.6B / $240B = 4.0%
4.0% exceeds the 3% minimum supplementary leverage ratio requirement, so the institution satisfies that requirement

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.134(f)(2) governs the currency mismatch haircut for credit derivatives and states that a bank may use internal FX volatility estimates if it qualifies for the own-estimates haircuts in § 217.132(b)(2)(iii), the simple VaR methodology in § 217.132(b)(3), or the internal models methodology in § 217.132(d). § 217.132(b)(2)(iii) is the collateral haircut approach own-estimates provision within the repo-style/OTC derivatives counterparty credit risk framework. The chain then continues: once the institution is confirmed as an advanced approaches institution (a prerequisite for using these methodologies), § 217.10(a)(1)(v) and § 217.10(c) specify the supplementary leverage ratio requirement of 3% applicable to advanced approaches institutions.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.134(f): The bank has a currency mismatch between the euro-denominated hedged exposure and the USD-denominated credit derivative. Under § 217.134(f)(1), the bank must apply a haircut (HFX) to the effective notional amount of the credit risk mitigant. Step 2 — § 217.134(f)(2): The default HFX is 8%, but the bank may use its own internal estimates of FX volatility if it qualifies for: (i) the own-estimates haircuts in § 217.132(b)(2)(iii); (ii) the simple VaR methodology in § 217.132(b)(3); or (iii) the internal models methodology in § 217.132(d). This cross-reference leads to § 217.132. Step 3 — § 217.132(b)(2)(iii): This provision describes the collateral haircut approach under which a Board-regulated institution may use its own internal estimates of haircuts (including FX haircuts) for repo-style transactions and eligible margin loans, subject to supervisory standards. Qualifying for this provision (or the simple VaR or internal models methodology) is the gateway to using internal FX volatility estimates under § 217.134(f)(2). Step 4 — Institution category: The institution is identified as an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution, which is the category that has access to internal models methodologies under § 217.132(d) and the own-estimates haircut approach under § 217.132(b)(2)(iii). Step 5 — § 217.10(a)(1): Cross-subpart navigation to Subpart B. For an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution, the minimum capital ratios are: CET1 = 4.5%, Tier 1 = 6%, Total capital = 8%, Leverage ratio = 4%, and Supplementary leverage ratio = 3% (per § 217.10(a)(1)(v)). Step 6 — § 217.10(c): The supplementary leverage ratio is tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure. With $9.6 billion tier 1 capital and $240 billion total leverage exposure: SLR = 9.6 / 240 = 4.0%, which exceeds the 3% minimum. The institution satisfies the supplementary leverage ratio requirement.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution operates as a clearing member client and holds a portfolio of interest rate swap positions that have been centrally cleared through a qualifying central counterparty (QCCP). The institution has posted $50 million in initial margin to the clearing member, held in a segregated account at a third-party custodian that is structured to be bankruptcy remote from both the clearing member and other clearing member clients. The institution has also posted $12 million in variation margin directly to the QCCP, which is not held in a bankruptcy-remote arrangement. Separately, the institution's market risk model does not fully capture specific risk for a subset of its cleared interest rate swap positions, and the institution has identified that certain of these swaps qualify as correlation trading positions under the applicable regulatory definition — specifically, positions that would otherwise be classified as debt positions but for the fact that they meet the correlation trading position criteria. For the swaps that are derivatives with linear payoffs and are not correlation trading positions, the institution assigns specific risk-weighting factors to the fair value of the effective notional amount. The institution's compliance team must determine: (1) what risk weight applies to the cleared transactions with the QCCP given the collateral arrangement described, and (2) how the correlation trading positions that would otherwise be debt positions should be treated when calculating the specific risk add-on for the market risk capital requirement. Provide a complete analysis of both determinations, including the applicable risk weight percentage and the correct classification of the correlation trading positions for specific risk purposes.
required_facts: Correlation trading positions that would otherwise qualify as debt positions must be treated as debt positions for purposes of the specific risk add-on calculation under the standardized measurement method, per the reclassification rule that requires cross-referencing the definition of 'correlation trading position' in the definitions section of the regulation.

The applicable risk weight for cleared transactions with a QCCP where the posted collateral is held by a custodian in a bankruptcy-remote arrangement (protecting against joint default or concurrent insolvency of the clearing member and other clients) and the institution has conducted sufficient legal review is 2 percent.
If the bankruptcy-remote and legal review conditions are not satisfied, the applicable risk weight for cleared transactions with a QCCP rises to 4 percent.

The $50 million initial margin held at a third-party custodian in a bankruptcy-remote arrangement qualifies for the 2% risk weight, assuming the institution has completed the required legal review and documentation.

The $12 million variation margin posted directly to the QCCP without a bankruptcy-remote arrangement is included in the trade exposure amount and is not excluded from capital requirements under the custodian collateral carve-out.

The reclassification of correlation trading positions as debt or equity positions for specific risk purposes applies notwithstanding any other definition or requirement in Subpart F, and is triggered specifically by positions meeting paragraph (2) of the correlation trading position definition.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.210(a) specific risk add-on rules, which references the definition of 'correlation trading position' in §217.2 (Subpart A), then separately the cleared transaction risk weight determination requires §217.35 (Subpart D) which governs clearing member client risk weights based on collateral bankruptcy-remoteness conditions.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — §217.210(a) general requirement: The institution must calculate a specific risk add-on for debt and equity positions where its VaR-based measure does not capture all material aspects of specific risk. The final sentence of §217.210(a) states that a position that would have qualified as a debt position or equity position but for the fact that it qualifies as a correlation trading position under paragraph (2) of the definition of 'correlation trading position' in §217.2 shall be considered a debt position or equity position, respectively, for purposes of §217.210. Step 2 — §217.2 definition of 'correlation trading position': The answerer must look up the definition in Subpart A to confirm that paragraph (2) of that definition covers positions that would otherwise be debt or equity positions. This cross-subpart reference (Subpart F → Subpart A) is essential to confirm the reclassification rule. Step 3 — Applying the reclassification: The correlation trading positions that would otherwise be debt positions must be treated as debt positions for specific risk add-on purposes under §217.210, not as correlation trading positions. Step 4 — §217.35(b)(3) cleared transaction risk weights (Subpart D): For the cleared transaction risk weight question, the institution is a clearing member client transacting with a QCCP. Under §217.35(b)(3)(i)(A), a 2% risk weight applies if collateral posted is subject to an arrangement preventing losses due to joint default or concurrent insolvency of the clearing member and other clients, AND the institution has conducted sufficient legal review. Under §217.35(b)(3)(i)(B), a 4% risk weight applies if those conditions are not met. Step 5 — Applying to the facts: The $50 million initial margin is held at a third-party custodian in a bankruptcy-remote arrangement — this satisfies the condition for the 2% risk weight, provided the institution has conducted the required legal review. The $12 million variation margin posted directly to the QCCP without bankruptcy-remote protection does not qualify for the collateral exclusion under §217.35(b)(4)(i) (which only excludes custodian-held bankruptcy-remote collateral), so it is included in the trade exposure amount. The collateral arrangement for the initial margin meets the §217.35(b)(3)(i)(A) standard, so the applicable risk weight for the cleared transactions is 2%.

question_text:
A Board-regulated institution is the originator of a synthetic securitization. It has entered into a credit default swap with a highly rated corporate guarantor to hedge a pool of commercial real estate loans with varying maturities — the shortest tranche matures in 18 months and the longest in 7 years. The credit default swap does not cover the full notional amount of the underlying pool; the uncovered portion remains on the institution's books. The institution wants to recognize the risk-mitigating effect of the credit default swap for risk-based capital purposes and apply the collateral haircut approach to determine the net exposure amount for the hedged portion.

The credit default swap is denominated in U.S. dollars, and the underlying loans are also dollar-denominated. The institution uses standard supervisory haircuts rather than internal estimates. The guarantor is not a sovereign, central bank, or public sector entity.

For the hedged portion of the pool, the institution needs to determine: (1) whether the credit default swap qualifies as an eligible credit risk mitigant for the synthetic securitization, including what criteria the instrument must satisfy and which criterion is explicitly waived in this context; (2) what residual maturity the institution must use when calculating any maturity mismatch adjustment for the hedged exposures; and (3) under the collateral haircut approach, how the net exposure amount is computed, including the role of currency mismatch haircuts given the facts presented.
required_facts: The credit default swap qualifies as an eligible credit risk mitigant for the synthetic securitization only if it meets all criteria of the eligible credit derivative definition in § 217.2, except for the criterion in paragraph (3) of the eligible guarantee definition — that paragraph (3) criterion is explicitly waived for synthetic securitization purposes.

The institution must satisfy the operational criteria for synthetic securitizations (including transfer of credit risk and other conditions) before it may recognize the credit default swap for risk-based capital purposes.

Because the hedged pool contains exposures with different residual maturities, the institution must use the longest residual maturity — 7 years — as the residual maturity of all hedged exposures when computing any maturity mismatch adjustment.
Because both the credit default swap and the underlying loans are denominated in U.S. dollars, there is no currency mismatch, and the currency mismatch haircut term (Efx × Hfx) equals zero.

The institution must apply a risk weight to the uncovered (unhedged) portion of the pool based on the applicable risk weight for those exposures under Subpart D, without benefit of the credit risk mitigant.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.45(a)(1) conditions recognition of the credit risk mitigant on satisfying § 217.41 operational criteria; § 217.41(b)(1)(iii) specifies the eligible credit derivative criteria from § 217.2 but waives the criterion in paragraph (3) of the eligible guarantee definition in § 217.2; § 217.45(b) governs maturity mismatch and mandates use of the longest residual maturity; § 217.45(a)(1) then permits recognition under § 217.37, whose paragraph (c) governs the collateral haircut approach including the currency mismatch haircut rule in § 217.37(c)(4)(iv).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.45(a)(1): An originating Board-regulated institution that has obtained a credit risk mitigant to hedge a synthetic securitization may recognize it under § 217.37, but only if the securitization satisfies the operational criteria in § 217.41.

Step 2 — § 217.41(b)(1)(iii): For synthetic securitizations, the credit risk mitigant (here, a credit default swap) must meet all criteria of the 'eligible credit derivative' definition in § 217.2, EXCEPT for the criterion in paragraph (3) of the 'eligible guarantee' definition in § 217.2. This is the explicit waiver the institution must identify.

Step 3 — § 217.2 (definitions): The 'eligible credit derivative' definition incorporates by reference the 'eligible guarantee' definition's criteria, with paragraph (3) of the eligible guarantee definition (typically the direct, unconditional, irrevocable, and on-demand payment requirement) being the one waived in the synthetic securitization context per § 217.41(b)(1)(iii).

Step 4 — § 217.45(b): Because the credit default swap covers multiple hedged exposures with different residual maturities (18 months through 7 years), the institution must use the LONGEST residual maturity — 7 years — as the residual maturity of ALL hedged exposures when computing any maturity mismatch adjustment under § 217.36(d), (e), and (f).

Step 5 — § 217.37(c): Having satisfied § 217.41 and § 217.45, the institution may apply the collateral haircut approach. The net exposure amount equals max{0, [(ΣE − ΣC) + Σ(Es × Hs) + Σ(Efx × Hfx)]}. Because both the credit default swap and the underlying loans are denominated in U.S. dollars, there is no currency mismatch, so the Hfx (currency mismatch haircut) term is zero and does not affect the calculation.

question_text: A supervised insurance organization is seeking to include in its building block available capital a newly issued subordinated debt instrument from one of its inventory companies. The instrument was issued and paid-in on March 1, 2024, with an original maturity of seven years, no guarantee from the building block parent or any affiliate, and no security interest. The instrument's terms permit the building block parent to call it after five years, but also include a provision allowing early redemption if the instrument receives a rating downgrade below investment grade (a 'rating event'). The instrument does not contain any dividend step-up or other feature creating a redemption incentive beyond the rating event clause. The top-tier depository institution holding company has not yet sought Board approval to exercise any call option. The supervised insurance organization has not previously obtained Board approval to include this specific instrument in its building block available capital, and the instrument was not a capital element for the issuer prior to May 19, 2010. The organization's compliance team is evaluating whether this instrument qualifies as a qualifying capital instrument for building block available capital purposes, and specifically whether the rating event call provision disqualifies it. Additionally, the team wants to confirm what general eligibility criteria apply to the instrument's terms regarding dividend and distribution payments — specifically whether the building block parent must retain full discretion to cancel distributions without triggering a default or payment-in-kind obligation. Analyze whether the instrument qualifies, identifying any conditions that must be satisfied and any criteria that could disqualify it.
required_facts: The rating event early call provision is not among the enumerated permitted early call triggers under the qualifying capital instrument criteria (which allow early calls only for regulatory events precluding capital inclusion, tax events, or Investment Company Act registration), so the provision facially violates the call option eligibility criterion.

The safe harbor that would excuse a rating event call provision applies only to instruments that were company capital elements issued prior to January 1, 2014; because this instrument was issued on March 1, 2024, the safe harbor is unavailable and the rating event provision disqualifies the instrument.
Replace this with the actual incorporated criteria from §217.20(d)(1)(vi) through (ix) and (xi); do not state a distribution-cancellation-discretion requirement as part of that cross-reference.

Because the instrument was not a capital element for the issuer prior to May 19, 2010, and is not shown to be equivalent to a previously Board-approved instrument, the supervised insurance organization must obtain Board prior approval before including the instrument in building block available capital.

The Board retains reservation of authority to exclude capital elements that do not meet loss-absorption criteria or that present safety and soundness concerns, reinforcing the prior-approval requirement for novel instruments.
The instrument fails to qualify as a qualifying capital instrument in its current form primarily due to the rating event call provision combined with the post-2014 issuance date.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.608(a)(1) qualifying capital instrument criteria, which cross-references §217.20(d)(1)(vi)–(ix) and (xi) for additional eligibility criteria; §217.20(d)(1)(vi) requires the Board-regulated institution (here, building block parent) to retain full discretion to cancel distributions without triggering default or payment-in-kind; §217.608(f) provides a safe harbor for rating-event call provisions only for instruments that were company capital elements issued prior to January 1, 2014; §217.1(f) governs the Board's reservation of authority over capital elements and is implicated by the Board prior-approval requirement under §217.608(g) for instruments not previously approved and not equivalent to a previously approved element.

A rating event is NOT among the enumerated permitted early call triggers under §217.608(a)(1)(v). The rating event call provision therefore disqualifies the instrument under §217.608(a)(1)(v). Step 4 — §217.608(a)(1)(vii): Even if the rating event issue were resolved, the instrument must also meet the criteria in §217.20(d)(1)(vi) through (ix) and (xi), with 'Board-regulated institution' replaced by 'building block parent.' §217.20(d)(1)(vi) requires that the building block parent retain full discretion at all times to cancel distributions on the instrument without triggering an event of default, a requirement to make a payment-in-kind, or any other restriction.
