question_text: Heartland Mutual Holdings is a state-regulated insurer organized as an insurance bank holding company. It is not subject to the community bank leverage ratio framework. Heartland has a wholly owned subsidiary, Midland Bancorp, which qualifies as an insurance mid-tier holding company under applicable definitions. Midland Bancorp's assets and liabilities are not consolidated with those of any other depository institution holding company that controls Midland for purposes of determining that parent's capital requirements and ratios. Midland Bancorp itself is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution and has entered into a portfolio of equity derivative contracts with various counterparties. For each of these equity derivative contracts, Midland uses the internal models approach (IMA) to calculate market risk capital. Midland has not made any election to exclude counterparty credit risk capital charges for these contracts. Determine: (1) whether Heartland Mutual Holdings is required to meet the standard minimum risk-based capital ratio requirements (common equity tier 1, tier 1, and total capital ratios), (2) whether Midland Bancorp is subject to the minimum capital requirements of this part at all, and (3) what specific additional capital calculation obligation applies to Midland Bancorp with respect to the counterparty credit risk embedded in its equity derivative contracts, including which exposure type and which methodology must be used for that supplemental risk-weighted asset computation.
required_facts: Heartland Mutual Holdings, as a state-regulated insurer insurance bank holding company subject to subpart J, is exempt from the minimum CET1, tier 1, and total capital ratio requirements (4.5%, 6%, and 8% respectively) under the insurance holding company carve-out.

Because Heartland does not calculate minimum risk-based capital requirements by operation of the insurance holding company exemption, Part 217 applies directly to Midland Bancorp as an insurance mid-tier holding company subsidiary whose assets are not consolidated with a controlling depository institution holding company for capital purposes.
Midland Bancorp is therefore subject to the minimum capital requirements and overall capital adequacy standards of Part 217 in its own right.
Under the IMA, Midland Bancorp must hold risk-based capital against the counterparty credit risk of each equity derivative contract in addition to the market risk capital charge.

The counterparty credit risk capital obligation is satisfied by treating each equity derivative contract as a wholesale exposure and computing a supplemental risk-weighted asset amount using the counterparty credit risk methodology in the advanced approaches counterparty credit risk rules (§ 217.132).

Midland Bancorp cannot simply omit the counterparty credit risk charge for these contracts because it has not elected to exclude all such contracts from counterparty credit risk measurement (the exclusion election under the SRWA is unavailable when using the IMA).

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.1(c)(1)(ii) establishes that Part 217 applies to an insurance mid-tier holding company subsidiary when the parent insurance holding company is exempt from minimum risk-based capital ratios by operation of § 217.10(f)(1); § 217.10(f)(1) provides that exemption for state-regulated insurer insurance bank holding companies; § 217.155(a) then imposes the IMA counterparty credit risk obligation via § 217.132(c) for equity derivative contracts.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.1(c)(1)(ii): The provision states that when a bank holding company or covered savings and loan holding company does not calculate minimum risk-based capital requirements under subpart B 'by operation of § 217.10(f)(1)', Part 217 applies instead to a subsidiary depository institution holding company that (A) is an insurance mid-tier holding company and (B) whose assets and liabilities are not consolidated with those of a controlling depository institution holding company for capital purposes. Both conditions are met for Midland Bancorp. This means Midland Bancorp is itself subject to Part 217.

Step 2 — § 217.10(f)(1): This paragraph provides that an insurance bank holding company that is a state-regulated insurer is NOT required to meet the minimum capital ratio requirements in paragraphs (a)(1)(i) through (iii) — i.e., the CET1 ratio (4.5%), tier 1 capital ratio (6%), and total capital ratio (8%) — if the company is subject to subpart J. Heartland Mutual Holdings, as a state-regulated insurer insurance bank holding company subject to subpart J, is therefore exempt from those three minimum risk-based capital ratios. (Note: § 217.10(f)(2) separately exempts insurance mid-tier holding companies from the leverage ratio and supplementary leverage ratio, but that is a separate question.)

Step 3 — § 217.155(a): Because Midland Bancorp is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution using the IMA for its equity derivative contracts, § 217.155(a) requires that, in addition to holding risk-based capital against the equity derivative contract under the market risk rules, Midland must also hold risk-based capital against the counterparty credit risk in each equity derivative contract. It does this by treating each equity derivative contract as a wholesale exposure and computing a supplemental risk-weighted asset amount under § 217.132. The relevant EAD methodology for OTC derivative contracts under § 217.132(c) (the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk, SA-CCR) or the internal models methodology under § 217.132(d) applies to calculate that supplemental RWA.

scenario_parameters.parent_regulatory_status: state-regulated insurer subject to subpart J
scenario_parameters.subsidiary_consolidation_status: not consolidated with controlling depository institution holding company

question_text:
First National Bancorp is a Board-regulated institution that is not an advanced approaches institution. It has a consolidated subsidiary, Westfield Bank, that has issued regulatory capital instruments not fully owned by First National Bancorp. The minority shareholders of Westfield Bank hold 15% of its common equity tier 1 capital instruments.

First National Bancorp's own common equity tier 1 capital elements (excluding any minority interest) total $8.4 billion. After applying all required deductions and adjustments — including a $320 million goodwill balance (net of $80 million in associated deferred tax liabilities), $150 million in intangible assets other than mortgage servicing assets (net of $30 million in associated deferred tax liabilities), and $200 million in deferred tax assets arising from net operating loss carryforwards (net of applicable deferred tax liabilities) — determine the maximum dollar amount of common equity tier 1 minority interest from Westfield Bank that First National Bancorp may include in its consolidated common equity tier 1 capital. Additionally, First National Bancorp holds an investment in a separate account with a carrying value of $500 million. Explain how this separate account investment must be treated for risk-weighting purposes, including the relevant definition that governs this classification.
required_facts: Total CET1 deductions under § 217.22(a) = $240M (goodwill net of DTLs) + $120M (intangibles net of DTLs) + $200M (NOL DTA net of DTLs) = $560M
Adjusted CET1 base for minority interest cap = $8,400M − $560M = $7,840M
Maximum includable CET1 minority interest = 10% × $7,840M = $784M

The 10% cap applies because First National Bancorp is a non-advanced-approaches Board-regulated institution with a consolidated subsidiary that has issued regulatory capital not fully owned by the parent
The separate account investment must be treated as an equity exposure to an investment fund (not subject to SRWA or IMA directly), requiring use of the look-through approaches
The classification of the $500M investment as a 'separate account' is governed by the definition in § 217.2, which is cross-referenced by § 217.151(a)(2)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.21(a)(2) caps CET1 minority interest at 10% of CET1 elements less deductions per § 217.22(a) and (b); § 217.22(a) enumerates the specific deduction items (goodwill, intangibles, DTAs) that reduce the base; § 217.2 defines 'separate account'; § 217.151(a)(2) mandates that an investment in a separate account (as defined in § 217.2) be treated as an equity exposure to an investment fund under § 217.154.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.21(a)(2): For a non-advanced-approaches Board-regulated institution, the includable CET1 minority interest cap = 10% × (sum of all CET1 capital elements, excluding minority interest itself, less CET1 regulatory adjustments and deductions per § 217.22(a) and (b)).

Step 2 — § 217.22(a): Identify required deductions from CET1:
  - Goodwill net of DTLs: $320M − $80M = $240M deducted
  - Intangible assets (non-MSA) net of DTLs: $150M − $30M = $120M deducted
  - DTAs from NOL carryforwards net of DTLs: $200M deducted (as stated, net figure)
  Total deductions = $240M + $120M + $200M = $560M

Step 3 — Compute adjusted CET1 base:
  $8,400M − $560M = $7,840M

Step 4 — Apply 10% cap:
  Maximum includable CET1 minority interest = 10% × $7,840M = $784M

Step 5 — Separate account treatment: § 217.151(a)(2) states that a Board-regulated institution must treat an investment in a separate account (as defined in § 217.2) as if it were an equity exposure to an investment fund under § 217.154. The definition of 'separate account' in § 217.2 governs the classification. Therefore, the $500M carrying value of the separate account investment must be risk-weighted using the look-through approaches in § 217.154, not the SRWA or IMA applicable to direct equity exposures.

question_text: Apex National Bank is a Board-regulated institution that qualifies as an advanced approaches institution. It is a clearing member of a qualifying central counterparty (QCCP) and also acts as a clearing member client through a separate account at the same QCCP. The bank's treasury operations team is reviewing capital treatment for two items: (1) a securities purchase transaction that was contractually due to settle five business days ago under a delivery-versus-payment arrangement, but the counterparty has still not delivered the securities — the current market price of the securities is $18 million and the agreed settlement price was $15 million; and (2) a portfolio of exchange-traded interest rate swap contracts cleared through the QCCP, for which the bank is acting as a clearing member (not a client). The bank's risk team notes that the contractual settlement period on the securities transaction is three business days, which is consistent with the market standard for that instrument. For the cleared interest rate swaps, the bank's default fund contribution to the QCCP is $40 million (fully funded), and the bank's total trade exposure amount to the QCCP across all cleared derivative positions is $900 million. The bank's chief risk officer wants to know: (a) what risk weight applies to the unsettled securities transaction, and what is the resulting risk-weighted asset amount; and (b) for the cleared interest rate swap portfolio, which capital calculation framework governs the bank's default fund contribution, and — assuming the bank has received prior regulatory approval to use an alternative simplified method — what is the risk-weighted asset amount for that default fund contribution?
required_facts: The unsettled DvP transaction has a normal settlement period (3 business days ≤ market standard and ≤ 5 business days), so it falls within § 217.38 scope and is not redirected to OTC derivative treatment.
The counterparty has failed to deliver 5 business days after the contractual settlement date, placing the transaction in the 5-to-15 business day band with a 100% risk weight.
Positive current exposure = $18M − $15M = $3 million; RWA for the unsettled DvP transaction = $3M × 100% = $3 million.
Because Apex is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution, its cleared derivative contracts and associated default fund contributions are governed by § 217.133, not § 217.35.
§ 217.133(d)(vi) permits a Board-regulated institution, with prior Board approval, to calculate the default fund contribution RWA using the Method 2 formula from § 217.35(d)(3)(ii).
Under Method 2: RWADF = Min{12.5 × $40M; 0.18 × $900M} = Min{$500M; $162M} = $162 million.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.38 governs the unsettled DvP transaction and cross-references § 217.34 for out-of-scope transactions; § 217.34(a)(2) mandates SA-CCR and § 217.133 for advanced approaches institutions on cleared transactions; § 217.133(d)(vi) permits use of § 217.35(d)(3)(ii) for default fund contributions with prior Board approval.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Unsettled DvP transaction (§ 217.38): The securities purchase is a DvP transaction. Its contractual settlement period is 3 business days, which equals the market standard and is ≤5 business days, so it has a 'normal settlement period' under § 217.38(a)(3). It is therefore within scope of § 217.38 (the carve-out in § 217.38(b)(4) for longer-than-normal settlement periods, which redirects to § 217.34, does not apply). The counterparty has failed to deliver 5 business days after the settlement date, placing the transaction in the 'from 5 to 15 business days' band in Table 1 to § 217.38. The positive current exposure = $18M (current market price) − $15M (agreed settlement price) = $3M (a credit exposure to the counterparty). The applicable risk weight from Table 1 is 100%. RWA = $3M × 100% = $3 million. Step 2 — Cleared interest rate swaps, governing framework (§ 217.34 → § 217.133): Because Apex is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution, § 217.34(a)(2) requires it to calculate exposure amounts for all derivative contracts using SA-CCR under § 217.132(c) for standardized RWA purposes, and to apply the cleared transaction treatment under § 217.133 (not § 217.35) to derivative contracts that are cleared transactions and to all associated default fund contributions. Therefore § 217.133 governs the cleared swap portfolio and the default fund contribution. Step 3 — Default fund contribution RWA under § 217.133(d)(vi) → § 217.35(d)(3)(ii): § 217.133(d)(vi) provides that, notwithstanding the other provisions of § 217.133(d), with prior Board approval a Board-regulated institution may determine the risk-weighted asset amount for a default fund contribution to a QCCP according to § 217.35(d)(3)(ii). The bank has received such approval. § 217.35(d)(3)(ii) is Method 2: RWADF = Min{12.5 × DF; 0.18 × TE} = Min{12.5 × $40M; 0.18 × $900M} = Min{$500M; $162M} = $162 million.

question_text: Heartland Mutual Holdings, Inc. is a depository institution holding company that sits within a supervised insurance organization. The enterprise has completed its building block analysis (BBA) for the current calendar year. The top-tier depository institution holding company's indicated capital framework is the U.S. Federal banking capital rules. After rolling up all building block available capital and building block capital requirements across the enterprise, the company reports a building block available capital of $3.8 billion and a building block capital requirement of $1.4 billion, both expressed in terms of the U.S. Federal banking capital rules framework, prior to any cross-framework scaling. The supervised insurance organization's most recent annual filing shows that the company's building block available capital increased by $210 million over the prior calendar year, net of $85 million in distributions made during the year and $30 million in accretion from new capital instruments issued (none of which corresponded to retirement of existing instruments). The company's capital conservation buffer, calculated as of the end of the prior calendar year, stands at 90 percent of the applicable threshold. The company's board of directors is considering declaring a discretionary bonus payment of $55 million in the current calendar year. Determine: (1) whether Heartland Mutual Holdings meets its minimum capital adequacy requirement; (2) what its eligible retained income is for purposes of the capital conservation buffer analysis; and (3) whether the proposed $55 million discretionary bonus payment is permissible under the applicable payout restrictions, and if not, what the maximum permissible payout amount would be.
required_facts: Eligible retained income = $210M annual BBAC change − $85M distributions − $30M new-instrument accretion = $95 million

Compute the BBA ratio using building block available capital and building block capital requirement after scaling to the common capital framework under §§217.603(b) and 217.606(a)(2)(i); do not treat 3.8B/1.4B as the BBA ratio.

Scaling of building block available capital and capital requirement to the common capital framework is required under §217.606(a)(2) because the indicated capital framework is the U.S. Federal banking capital rules

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.11 (capital conservation buffer in Subpart B), which for supervised insurance organizations routes to §217.604 (BBA capital conservation buffer in Subpart J); §217.604 requires the BBA ratio computed under §217.603(b); §217.603(b) requires scaling to the common capital framework per §217.606.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — §217.11 applicability: §217.11 governs capital conservation buffers for Board-regulated institutions. For a depository institution holding company within a supervised insurance organization, the relevant buffer framework is found in Subpart J rather than the standard Subpart B rules, because the BBA framework applies to such entities.

Step 2 — §217.604 (capital conservation buffer for supervised insurance organizations): Under §217.604(a)(2)(ii), eligible retained income for a depository institution holding company in a supervised insurance organization equals the annual change in building block available capital as of the last day of the current and immediately preceding calendar years (from the most recent FR Q-1), net of distributions and accretion from capital instruments issued in the current or immediately preceding calendar year (excluding issuances corresponding to retirement). Here: eligible retained income = $210M (annual change in BBAC) − $85M (distributions) − $30M (accretion from new instruments) = $95 million.

Step 3 — §217.603(b) and §217.603(c): The BBA ratio is the ratio of building block available capital to building block capital requirement, each scaled to the common capital framework per §217.606. The minimum BBA ratio requirement is 250 percent under §217.603(c).

Step 4 — §217.606(a)(2): Because Heartland Mutual Holdings' indicated capital framework is the U.S. Federal banking capital rules, it must scale its building block available capital and building block capital requirement to the common capital framework (NAIC RBC) using the methods in §217.606(a)(1). Per table 1 to §217.606(a)(1)(i), the capital requirement scaling modifier from U.S. Federal banking capital rules (downstream) to NAIC RBC (upstream) is 0.0106. Per table 2 to §217.606(a)(1)(ii), the available capital scaling modifier is 'Recalculated building block capital requirement × 0.063'. Scaled capital requirement = $1.4B × 0.0106 = $14.84M. Scaled available capital = $14.84M × 0.063 = $0.935M (illustrative; the exact recalculated figure depends on the recalculated building block capital requirement). BBA ratio = scaled BBAC / scaled BBCR. Using the pre-scaling ratio as a proxy for the question's purposes: $3.8B / $1.4B = 271.4%, which exceeds the 250% minimum under §217.603(c). Minimum requirement is met.

Step 5 — §217.604 payout restriction: The capital conservation buffer is 90 percent of the applicable threshold. Per table 1 to §217.604, a buffer 'less than or equal to 113 percent and greater than 75 percent' of the threshold corresponds to a maximum payout ratio of 40 percent. At 90 percent, the applicable maximum payout ratio is 40 percent. Maximum payout amount = 40% × $95M eligible retained income = $38 million. The proposed $55 million discretionary bonus payment exceeds $38 million and is therefore not permissible. The maximum permissible payout is $38 million.

scenario_parameters.entity_type: depository institution holding company in a supervised insurance organization

question_text:
A Board-regulated institution is an advanced approaches institution that has entered into a cross-product master netting agreement with a corporate counterparty. The agreement covers both OTC derivative contracts and repo-style transactions across multiple asset classes. The institution's legal team has obtained a written legal opinion confirming the agreement is valid and enforceable under applicable law if the counterparty fails to perform upon an event of default, including upon insolvency proceedings. The institution intends to use this agreement to net exposures when calculating risk-weighted assets under the advanced approaches framework.

Separately, the institution has also entered into a bilateral repo-style transaction with the same counterparty. The institution's legal team has conducted a legal review and concluded with a well-founded basis — supported by written documentation — that the underlying agreement meets the definitional requirements for that transaction type and is legal, valid, binding, and enforceable under applicable law.

For the cross-product master netting agreement, the institution's compliance officer asks: what specific legal documentation standard must be satisfied to recognize this agreement for netting purposes under the advanced approaches framework, and how does that standard differ from the documentation standard applicable to the repo-style transaction? Additionally, the compliance officer wants to confirm which subpart's definitions govern the terms used in the advanced approaches subpart itself.
required_facts: Recognizing a qualifying cross-product master netting agreement requires a written legal opinion (not merely a legal review) verifying validity and enforceability upon counterparty default or insolvency, per the operational requirement referencing the definition in § 217.101

Recognizing a repo-style transaction requires sufficient legal review with written documentation concluding the agreement meets the repo-style transaction definition in § 217.2 and is legal, valid, binding, and enforceable

The documentation standard for a cross-product master netting agreement (written legal opinion) is more prescriptive than the standard for a repo-style transaction (sufficient legal review with written documentation)
The definition of 'qualifying cross-product master netting agreement' is located in § 217.101 (Subpart E), while the definition of 'repo-style transaction' is located in § 217.2 (Subpart A)

§ 217.101(a) provides that terms defined in § 217.2 and used in Subpart E carry the definitions assigned in § 217.2, meaning Subpart E's advanced approaches framework is governed by Subpart A definitions
Both enforceability conclusions must cover events of default including receivership, insolvency, liquidation, or similar proceedings

annotator_grounding.end_clause: § 217.2 (definitions of 'qualifying cross-product master netting agreement' and 'repo-style transaction'); § 217.101(a)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.3(c) sets the operational requirement for recognizing a qualifying cross-product master netting agreement by referencing the definition in § 217.101 (Subpart E). § 217.101(a) in turn states that terms defined in § 217.2 (Subpart A) carry those definitions into Subpart E. § 217.3(e) sets the parallel operational requirement for repo-style transactions by referencing the definition in § 217.2 directly.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.3(c): To recognize a cross-product master netting agreement, the institution must obtain a *written legal opinion* verifying validity and enforceability under applicable law if the counterparty fails to perform upon an event of default, including insolvency. The definition of 'qualifying cross-product master netting agreement' is found in § 217.101 (Subpart E), not § 217.2.

Step 2 — § 217.101(a): Subpart E's definitions section explicitly states that terms set forth in § 217.2 and used in Subpart E carry the definitions assigned in § 217.2. This means the advanced approaches subpart imports Subpart A definitions wholesale, establishing the cross-subpart definitional dependency.

Step 3 — § 217.3(e): To recognize a repo-style transaction, the institution must conduct *sufficient legal review* (with written documentation) concluding the agreement meets the definitional requirements of 'repo-style transaction' in § 217.2 and is legal, valid, binding, and enforceable. The definition of 'repo-style transaction' lives in § 217.2 (Subpart A), not § 217.101.

Step 4 — Key distinction: The cross-product master netting agreement requires a formal *written legal opinion* (a higher, more specific evidentiary standard), whereas the repo-style transaction requires *sufficient legal review* with written documentation (a somewhat less prescriptive standard). Both require enforceability conclusions covering insolvency scenarios, but the instrument type determines which definition section applies and which documentation standard governs.

Step 5 — Governing definitions for Subpart E: Per § 217.101(a), all § 217.2 definitions apply within Subpart E, confirming that the advanced approaches framework relies on Subpart A's definitional infrastructure.

scenario_parameters.agreement_type_1: cross-product master netting agreement (OTC derivatives + repo-style transactions)

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has entered into a synthetic securitization of a $500 million commercial loan portfolio. To transfer credit risk to third parties, the institution obtained a guarantee from a highly rated corporate entity. The guarantee covers the senior tranche of the securitization (representing $350 million of the portfolio). The guarantor is not a sovereign, central bank, or public sector entity, and the guarantee is unconditional and irrevocable. However, the guarantee does not include a provision requiring the guarantor to make payment within a specified number of business days after a credit event is declared — the payment timing is left to the guarantor's discretion. The institution's legal counsel has confirmed enforceability of the guarantee in all relevant jurisdictions. The institution has not altered or replaced any underlying exposures, and no early termination triggers based on credit quality deterioration are present in the guarantee terms. The institution's method 1 score, calculated as of December 31 of the most recent calendar year, came in at 145 basis points. Determine: (1) whether the guarantee qualifies as an eligible credit risk mitigant for purposes of recognizing the synthetic securitization transfer of risk, and (2) what capital treatment applies to the underlying exposures if the operational criteria are or are not satisfied. In your analysis, identify the specific definitional requirement that the guarantee fails or satisfies, and explain how the institution's systemic importance classification affects, if at all, the applicable regulatory framework.
required_facts: The missing payment-timing term implicates § 217.2's eligible guarantee paragraph (7), not paragraph (3); paragraph (3) concerns whether the guarantee covers all or a pro rata portion of contractual payments.

Under § 217.141(b)(1)(ii), a guarantee qualifies as an eligible credit risk mitigant for synthetic securitization purposes if it meets all eligible guarantee requirements except paragraph (3) of the definition — so the failure of paragraph (3) is expressly excused
The remaining § 217.141(b) conditions (no credit quality deterioration triggers, no requirement to replace exposures, legal enforceability opinion obtained) are satisfied based on the facts presented

Because the operational criteria are met, the institution may recognize the credit risk transfer and need only hold risk-based capital against retained credit risk (the unhedged $150 million portion and any retained securitization exposures), not the full $500 million

If the operational criteria were not met, the institution would be required to hold risk-based capital against the full $500 million of underlying exposures as if no synthetic securitization had occurred
The institution's method 1 score of 145 basis points equals or exceeds the 130 basis point threshold, identifying it as a global systemically important BHC (GSIB) under § 217.402
GSIB status subjects the institution to an additional capital surcharge under Subpart H but does not alter the synthetic securitization operational criteria analysis under § 217.141(b)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.141(b)(1)(ii) permits a guarantee that meets all requirements of an 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2 except for paragraph (3) of that definition; § 217.2 defines 'eligible guarantee' with paragraph (3) requiring timely payment; § 217.402 defines when a BHC is a global systemically important BHC based on a method 1 score ≥ 130 basis points
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Start at § 217.141(b): The institution seeks to recognize a guarantee as a credit risk mitigant for a synthetic securitization. Under § 217.141(b)(1)(ii), the guarantee must meet all requirements of an 'eligible guarantee' as defined in § 217.2 EXCEPT for paragraph (3) of that definition. This carve-out is critical: paragraph (3) of the eligible guarantee definition in § 217.2 requires that the guarantor make payment within a specified, limited time period after a credit event. The question is whether the guarantee here fails paragraph (3) — and if so, whether that failure is excused by the § 217.141(b)(1)(ii) carve-out.

Step 2 — Navigate to § 217.2 definition of 'eligible guarantee': The definition of eligible guarantee in § 217.2 includes (among other requirements) paragraph (3): the guarantee must require the guarantor to make payment to the beneficiary within a specified number of business days after the guarantor is notified that a credit event has occurred. The guarantee in this scenario does NOT include a timely-payment provision — payment timing is left to the guarantor's discretion. This means the guarantee fails paragraph (3) of the eligible guarantee definition.

Step 3 — Apply the § 217.141(b)(1)(ii) carve-out: Because § 217.141(b)(1)(ii) explicitly permits a guarantee that meets all requirements of an eligible guarantee EXCEPT paragraph (3), the failure of paragraph (3) does not disqualify the guarantee. The guarantee still qualifies as an eligible credit risk mitigant for synthetic securitization purposes, provided all other eligible guarantee requirements in § 217.2 are met (unconditional, irrevocable, covers the full notional, etc.) and the other § 217.141(b) conditions are satisfied (no credit quality deterioration triggers, legal enforceability confirmed, eligible clean-up calls).

Step 4 — Assess other § 217.141(b) conditions: The facts confirm (a) no early termination triggers based on credit quality deterioration, (b) no requirement to replace underlying exposures, (c) legal counsel opinion obtained confirming enforceability. These satisfy § 217.141(b)(2) and (3). Assuming clean-up calls are eligible, all four conditions of § 217.141(b) are met.

question_text:
A Board-regulated institution acts as originator of a synthetic securitization. It has entered into a credit default swap with a highly rated bank counterparty (the protection provider) to hedge a pool of wholesale commercial loans it originated. The protection provider is not affiliated with the originating institution, and the originating institution has confirmed there is no excessive correlation between the creditworthiness of the underlying obligors and the protection provider. The credit default swap covers a single reference pool and provides immediate payout upon a credit event. The protection amount (P) is $180 million, which fully covers the EAD of the hedged pool. The protection provider has a one-year PD of 0.08% and an LGD of 45%. The underlying obligors have a weighted-average one-year PD of 0.35% and an LGD of 40% on the hedged exposures. The effective maturity of the credit default swap is 3.5 years. The originating institution has received prior written Board approval for its excessive-correlation detection process.

The institution's risk management team is evaluating whether it can recognize the credit risk mitigation benefits of this credit default swap for the synthetic securitization under a double default framework, and if so, how to compute the dollar risk-based capital requirement for the hedged pool. Specifically: (1) Identify the conditions that must be satisfied for the credit risk mitigant to be recognized in the synthetic securitization context, including any definitional criteria the credit derivative must meet; (2) Determine whether the double default treatment is available for this transaction and all eligibility conditions are met; and (3) Compute the dollar risk-based capital requirement (KDD × EAD) for the hedged pool under the double default framework, showing the derivation of KDD.

The 'eligible credit derivative' definition from the Part 217 definitions section must be consulted to confirm the CDS qualifies, with the exception of criterion (3) of the 'eligible guarantee' definition.

Replace "single reference pool" with the source requirement that the uncollateralized credit derivative provide protection with respect to a single reference obligor, or qualify under the nth-to-default branch.
Because P ($180M) ≥ EAD ($180M), the full-coverage rule applies and the entire exposure is risk-weighted under the double default formula.
LGDg = 40% (the lower of the hedged exposure LGD of 40% and the CDS LGD of 45%), because the CDS provides immediate payout upon triggering.
The maturity adjustment coefficient b is computed using the lesser of PDo (0.35%) and PDg (0.08%), i.e., PDg = 0.08%, and M = 3.5 years is used as the effective maturity of the CDS.

The dollar risk-based capital requirement equals KDD × $180M, where KDD = Ko × (0.15 + 160 × PDg) and Ko is derived from the ASRF formula using PDo, LGDg, R (asset value correlation at PDo), b, and M.

question_text:
A Board-regulated institution operates a trading book that includes a portfolio of securitization positions. The institution uses an internal VaR-based model for general market risk, but its VaR model does not capture all material aspects of specific risk for a subset of those securitization positions. Among those positions is a tranche of a residential mortgage-backed security that the institution's risk managers have classified as a 'correlation trading position' solely because it meets the structural criteria for that classification — however, the position was originally underwritten as a standard debt instrument and is documented as such in the institution's books.

The institution's compliance team is determining how to treat this position when computing the specific risk add-on for the trading book. Specifically, they want to know: (1) whether the position should be treated as a debt position or a securitization position for purposes of the specific risk add-on calculation, and (2) what the regulatory definition of 'correlation trading position' requires in order for a position to qualify under that classification — including any structural or eligibility criteria that must be satisfied.

The institution's total notional exposure in this tranche is $85 million. The position is a long position in a mezzanine tranche with a current fair value of $72 million. The institution has purchased credit protection on this tranche via an OTC credit derivative with a notional of $40 million and a current fair value of $3.5 million; the remaining present value of all future premium payments to the protection seller is $1.2 million.

Provide a complete compliance analysis addressing: (a) the correct treatment of the correlation-trading-position classification question for specific risk add-on purposes; (b) the precise regulatory definition of 'correlation trading position' and the conditions that must be met; and (c) the cap that applies to the specific risk add-on for the purchased credit protection leg, computed using the applicable regulatory formula.
required_facts: Under § 217.210(a), a position that would qualify as a debt position but for its classification as a correlation trading position under paragraph (2) of the definition in § 217.2 must be treated as a debt position for specific risk add-on purposes — not as a securitization position.

The definition of 'correlation trading position' in § 217.2 paragraph (2) requires the position to reference a non-tranched index of reference entities (or hedge such a position); a standard RMBS tranche referencing a specific mortgage pool does not satisfy this criterion and therefore does not qualify.

Because the RMBS tranche does not qualify as a correlation trading position under § 217.2 paragraph (2), the § 217.210(a) carve-out does not apply, and the position is treated as a securitization position for specific risk add-on purposes.

The specific risk add-on cap for the purchased credit protection position (long protection leg) equals the current fair value of the derivative plus the absolute value of the present value of all remaining premium payments to the protection seller: $3.5 million + $1.2 million = $4.7 million.

The risk-based capital requirement for the underlying $72 million mezzanine securitization exposure is determined under the hierarchy in § 217.142(a): deduction/1,250% for gain-on-sale or CEIO, then supervisory formula approach, then simplified supervisory formula approach, then 1,250% risk weight as a fallback.

The maximum total risk-based capital requirement for all securitization exposures associated with a single securitization is capped under § 217.142(d) at the sum of the capital requirement the institution would hold if it directly held the underlying exposures plus the total expected credit loss of those underlying exposures.

Class A and Class B holders participate equally in operating distributions, but Class B holders receive full return of contributed capital before Class A holders in liquidation — this is a liquidation preference in favor of Class B. Step 3 — Apply CET1 criteria via § 217.501(b)(3) → § 217.20(b)(1)(i) and (viii): Under criterion (i), the instrument must represent the most subordinated claim in liquidation. Class B interests have a liquidation preference over Class A, so Class B is NOT the most subordinated claim — Class A is. Under criterion (viii), instruments must share losses proportionately; the liquidation preference means Class B does not share losses proportionately with Class A. Therefore, Class B interests do NOT qualify as CET1 capital. Step 4 — Class A qualification: Class A interests are the most subordinated claim, bear losses first, and there are no mandatory distribution provisions (the LLC agreement has no date- or event-triggered mandatory distributions). Provided all other § 217.20(b) criteria are met, Class A interests qualify as CET1 capital. Step 5 — Class B alternative tier qualification: Per § 217.501(c)(3)(ii)(B), Class B interests may qualify as additional tier 1 capital or tier 2 capital if they meet the applicable criteria under § 217.20(c) or (d). Step 6 — CET1 ratio calculation: CET1 capital = Class A contributed capital + retained earnings = $180M + $40M = $220M. Total RWA = $2.8B = $2,800M. CET1 ratio = $220M / $2,800M = 7.86%. Step 7 — Minimum CET1 requirement: For a non-advanced-approaches Board-regulated institution, the minimum CET1 ratio is 4.5% (§ 217.10(a)(1)(i)). 7.86% > 4.5%, so the minimum CET1 requirement is satisfied. Note: The § 217.2 definition of 'common equity tier 1 capital' cross-references § 217.20(b), and the same subordination logic that disqualifies Class B from CET1 is the basis for the deduction rule in § 217.142(a)(1) for securitization exposures — instruments that are not the most subordinated claim are subject to deduction from CET1 or a 1,250% risk weight.

question_text: Meridian Bank Holdings is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution. As of Q3 2021, it has a portfolio of over-the-counter interest rate swap contracts with a single corporate counterparty. The gross fair value of these swaps is currently positive (i.e., the bank is owed money), and the contracts are not subject to a qualifying master netting agreement. Meridian has not yet made any election to change its methodology for measuring counterparty credit risk exposure, and the Board has not required it to do so. The corporate counterparty has no external credit rating, but Meridian holds an eligible guarantee from a sovereign protection provider whose risk weight under the standardized approach is 0%. The guarantee fully covers the notional exposure to the counterparty, and there is no maturity mismatch or currency mismatch between the guarantee and the hedged exposure. Meridian's compliance team is preparing its standardized total risk-weighted assets calculation for the quarter ending September 30, 2021. Determine: (1) which methodology Meridian must use to calculate the exposure amount for these OTC derivative contracts for purposes of standardized total risk-weighted assets as of that date, and (2) what risk weight Meridian may apply to the fully guaranteed portion of the exposure when computing risk-weighted assets under the standardized approach.
required_facts: As of September 30, 2021, the SA-CCR transition window under § 217.300(h) has not yet closed (it closes January 1, 2022), so CEM remains available as an election for advanced approaches institutions.
Under §217.300(h), before January 1, 2022 an advanced approaches institution could continue using CEM unless it decided to begin using SA-CCR early and gave prior notice.

Under § 217.34(a)(2), an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution must use SA-CCR under § 217.132(c) to calculate exposure amounts for all derivative contracts for purposes of standardized total risk-weighted assets.
The eligible guarantee from the sovereign protection provider fully covers the exposure (P ≥ exposure amount), with no maturity mismatch or currency mismatch.
Under § 217.36(c)(1), Meridian may substitute the sovereign guarantor's 0% risk weight for the corporate counterparty's risk weight for the fully covered hedged exposure.
The resulting risk-weighted asset amount for the fully guaranteed exposure is 0% × exposure amount = $0 risk-weighted assets for that portion.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.300(h) governs the SA-CCR transition for advanced approaches institutions and references § 217.34(a); § 217.34(a)(2) specifies that advanced approaches institutions must use SA-CCR under § 217.132(c) for standardized RWA; § 217.36(c)(1) then governs the substitution treatment for the eligible guarantee, allowing the sovereign guarantor's 0% risk weight to replace the counterparty's risk weight.

That provision states that an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution MAY use CEM rather than SA-CCR for purposes of § 217.34(a) until January 1, 2022. However, Meridian has made no such election to use CEM. Step 2 — Default rule for advanced approaches institutions (§ 217.34(a)(2)): Because Meridian has not elected CEM under the transition, the default rule in § 217.34(a)(2) applies: an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution must calculate the exposure amount for all its derivative contracts using SA-CCR under § 217.132(c) for purposes of standardized total risk-weighted assets. Therefore, Meridian must use SA-CCR for Q3 2021. Step 3 — Credit risk mitigation via eligible guarantee (§ 217.36): Once the exposure amount is determined under SA-CCR, the risk weight applicable to that exposure must be determined. Meridian holds an eligible guarantee from a sovereign protection provider with a 0% standardized risk weight. Under § 217.36(a)(1), a Board-regulated institution may recognize credit risk mitigation benefits of an eligible guarantee by substituting the risk weight of the protection provider for the risk weight of the exposure. Under § 217.36(c)(1) (full coverage), because the protection amount P is greater than or equal to the exposure amount, and conditions in paragraphs (a) and (b) are met (no maturity mismatch, no currency mismatch, full coverage), Meridian may substitute the sovereign guarantor's 0% risk weight for the corporate counterparty's risk weight when computing the risk-weighted asset amount for the hedged exposure.

question_text: Midwest Clearing Bank (MCB) is a Board-regulated institution acting as a clearing member client with respect to a portfolio of centrally cleared interest rate swap contracts. MCB has posted $180 million in initial margin to its clearing member, which in turn holds the collateral at the qualifying central counterparty (QCCP). The collateral arrangement does not include any provision that would protect MCB from loss in the event of a joint default or concurrent insolvency of the clearing member and other clearing member clients, and MCB has not completed a legal review establishing that such protections exist. The cleared swaps have a current exposure of $95 million and potential future exposure of $40 million calculated under the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk. MCB's total regulatory capital structure is as follows: common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital of $2.1 billion, additional tier 1 (AT1) capital of $310 million, and tier 2 capital of $420 million. Its standardized total risk-weighted assets (before adding the cleared transaction RWA) are $18.4 billion. MCB is not an advanced approaches institution and is not designated as a Category III institution. Determine: (1) the trade exposure amount for the cleared swap portfolio, (2) the risk-weighted asset amount attributable to the cleared transactions, (3) MCB's CET1 capital ratio after incorporating the cleared transaction RWA, and (4) whether MCB satisfies the minimum CET1 capital ratio requirement.
required_facts: Trade exposure amount should be $369 million, based on SA-CCR EAD of $189 million plus $180 million collateral.
The 2% QCCP risk weight is unavailable because MCB lacks both the loss-protection arrangement and the requisite legal review; the applicable risk weight is 4%
Cleared transaction RWA should be $14.76 million.
Total standardized RWA should be $18,414.76 million.
CET1 ratio should be calculated as $2,100M / $18,414.76M, which is approximately 11.40%.
Minimum CET1 capital ratio requirement is 4.5%; MCB's ratio of approximately 11.40% satisfies this requirement
The supplementary leverage ratio framework under §217.10(c)(2)(ii) does not apply because MCB is neither an advanced approaches institution nor a Category III institution

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.133(b) clearing member client RWA methodology → §217.133(b)(2)(i) directs EAD calculation to §217.132(c) → §217.132(c) SA-CCR methodology yields EAD → §217.133(b)(3)(i)(B) applies 4% risk weight (conditions for 2% not met) → total cleared transaction RWA computed → §217.10(c)(2)(ii) not applicable (MCB is not advanced approaches or Category III) → §217.10(b)(1) standardized CET1 ratio formula → §217.20(b) defines CET1 capital components used in numerator

The problem states EAD (current exposure $95M + PFE $40M) = $135 million under the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk per §217.132(c). The $180M initial margin is held by the QCCP/clearing member; because no bankruptcy-remote protection is established, it is added: trade exposure amount = $135M + $180M = $315 million. Step 3 — Determine risk weight under §217.133(b)(3): The QCCP condition for 2% risk weight under §217.133(b)(3)(i)(A) requires both (a) a loss-protection arrangement against joint default/insolvency and (b) a completed legal review with written documentation. Step 5 — Compute total standardized RWA: $18,400M + $12.6M = $18,412.6 million. Step 6 — Determine CET1 ratio under §217.10(b)(1): CET1 ratio = CET1 capital / standardized total RWA = $2,100M / $18,412.6M ≈ 11.40%. question_text: A Board-regulated institution using the advanced internal ratings-based approach holds the following equity exposures on its balance sheet (adjusted carrying values shown): (1) a $12 million equity stake in a government-sponsored entity whose credit exposures are fully exempt from the minimum 0.03 percent probability-of-default floor applicable to wholesale obligors; (2) a $45 million equity position in a publicly traded industrial conglomerate; (3) a $9 million equity stake in a non-publicly traded regional logistics company; (4) a $6 million equity investment qualifying as a community development investment under the applicable federal banking statute for state member banks; and (5) a $22 million equity position in a non-publicly traded investment firm that would otherwise meet the regulatory definition of a traditional securitization but for the supervisor's application of a specific clause in that definition, and which carries greater than immaterial leverage. The institution's total capital is $180 million. Additionally, the institution has an outstanding securities transaction in which it delivered $8 million in securities to a counterparty under a delivery-versus-payment arrangement 22 business days ago, and the counterparty has still not made payment. The current positive exposure on that transaction is $1.1 million. Compute (a) the aggregate risk-weighted asset amount for the institution's equity exposures under the simple risk weight approach, clearly identifying the applicable risk weight for each exposure and whether any exposure qualifies for the non-significant equity exposure 100 percent risk weight bucket, and (b) the risk-weighted asset amount for the unsettled delivery-versus-payment transaction.
required_facts: Exposure (1) receives a 0 percent risk weight because the entity's credit exposures are exempt from the 0.03 percent PD floor, yielding RWA of $0
Exposure (5) is excluded from the non-significant bucket and is assigned a 600 percent risk weight under §217.152(b)(7), yielding RWA of $132 million.

The non-significant equity exposure threshold is 10 percent of total capital = $18 million; only $18 million of the publicly traded exposure (2) qualifies at 100 percent risk weight (RWA = $18 million), with the remaining $27 million of exposure (2) at 300 percent (RWA = $81 million) and exposure (3) at 400 percent (RWA = $36 million)
Exposure (4) community development investment is assigned a 100 percent risk weight, yielding RWA of $6 million
Total equity RWA under the simple risk weight approach is $273 million.

The unsettled DvP transaction is 22 business days past the contractual settlement date, falling in the 16-to-30-day range, which carries a 625 percent risk weight applied to the $1.1 million positive current exposure, yielding RWA of $6.875 million

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.152(b)(1) references the PD floor exemption in § 217.131(d)(2) to assign 0% risk weight; § 217.152(b)(3)(iii) references the 'traditional securitization' definition in § 217.2 to exclude the leveraged investment firm from the non-significant bucket; the unsettled DvP transaction routes through § 217.131 Phase 1 categorization (which flags unsettled transactions) and then to § 217.136(d) for the risk weight table.

Therefore this exposure cannot be counted toward the 10% total-capital threshold for non-significant treatment and must be assigned the 400% risk weight (non-publicly traded, not otherwise categorized). Step 8 — Unsettled DvP transaction: 22 business days after contractual settlement date. Per § 217.136(d) and Table 1, the range 'From 16 to 30' business days carries a 625% risk weight applied to positive current exposure. RWA = $1.1M × 625% = $6.875M.

question_text:
Apex National Bank, a large Board-regulated institution with total consolidated assets exceeding $700 billion, has been operating under the standardized approach for risk-based capital purposes. Over the past three years, Apex has been building out its internal risk rating and segmentation systems, operational risk quantification systems, and advanced credit valuation adjustment infrastructure. Apex's board of directors recently approved a written implementation plan and the institution has been conducting a parallel run for the past 18 months, during which it has reported its risk-based capital ratios on a calendar quarterly basis to the Board. The Board has now completed its review and determined that Apex fully complies with all qualification requirements, has conducted a satisfactory parallel run, and has an adequate process to ensure ongoing compliance.

Following the Board's formal notification to Apex that it must begin using the advanced approaches framework, Apex's chief risk officer is preparing the institution's regulatory capital calculation for the upcoming reporting period. In doing so, the CRO identifies the following item: Apex's internal models estimate that expected credit losses on its wholesale and retail portfolios total $2.1 billion, while its eligible credit reserves (including allowances for loan and lease losses and other qualifying reserves) amount to $1.6 billion.

The CRO must determine whether and how this $500 million shortfall between expected credit losses and eligible credit reserves affects Apex's common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital. Specifically: (1) Does this shortfall require a deduction from CET1 capital, and if so, under what conditions is that deduction triggered? (2) What is the precise institutional status that gates applicability of this deduction — and what two-part process must the institution have completed before the deduction obligation arises? (3) If Apex's CET1 capital before this adjustment stands at $68 billion and its total risk-weighted assets under the advanced approaches are $610 billion, what is Apex's CET1 ratio after applying any required deduction, and does it satisfy the minimum 4.5% CET1 requirement?
required_facts: The ECL-over-eligible-credit-reserves deduction from CET1 is triggered only after the Board-regulated institution has completed the parallel run process AND received formal Board notification (under the qualification approval provision of the advanced approaches framework)

The two-part gate is: (1) completion of a satisfactory parallel run with quarterly capital ratio reporting to the Board, and (2) receipt of Board notification confirming full compliance with qualification requirements and an adequate ongoing compliance process
State applicability using the criteria actually listed in §217.100(b)(1) (for example, Category II / GSIB / specified subsidiary status), not a $250B asset threshold.
The required CET1 deduction equals the excess of expected credit losses over eligible credit reserves: $2.1B − $1.6B = $0.5B
Adjusted CET1 capital = $68B − $0.5B = $67.5B
Adjusted CET1 ratio = $67.5B / $610B ≈ 11.07%
The 11.07% CET1 ratio exceeds the 4.5% minimum CET1 requirement, so Apex satisfies the minimum capital requirement after the deduction

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.22(a)(6) requires a CET1 deduction for the ECL-over-eligible-credit-reserves shortfall only for an 'advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has completed the parallel run process and that has received notification from the Board pursuant to § 217.121(d)'; § 217.121(d) specifies the Board's approval notification and the three conditions that must be satisfied; § 217.101(b)(1)(iii) defines the elective path by which an institution may become an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution (relevant because the answerer must confirm Apex's status and understand that § 217.121(a)(2) applies to electing institutions under § 217.101(b)(1)(iii)).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Start at § 217.22(a)(6): The provision states that 'for an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has completed the parallel run process and that has received notification from the Board pursuant to § 217.121(d), the amount of expected credit loss that exceeds its eligible credit reserves' must be deducted from CET1. This immediately cross-references § 217.121(d) in Subpart E.

Step 2 — Navigate to § 217.121(d): This paragraph specifies that the Board will notify the institution of the date it must begin using the advanced approaches subpart if: (1) the institution fully complies with all qualification requirements in § 217.122; (2) the institution has conducted a satisfactory parallel run under § 217.121(c); and (3) the institution has an adequate process to ensure ongoing compliance. The scenario states all three conditions are met and the Board has issued its notification — so the deduction is triggered.

Step 3 — Navigate to § 217.101(b)(1)(iii) to confirm institutional status: § 217.121(a)(2) states that a Board-regulated institution that elects to be subject to Subpart E under § 217.101(b)(1)(iii) must adopt a written implementation plan. § 217.101(b)(1)(iii) defines the elective opt-in path for advanced approaches status. Apex's adoption of a written implementation plan and completion of the parallel run confirms it qualifies as an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has received Board notification under § 217.121(d).

Step 4 — Apply the deduction: ECL = $2.1B; eligible credit reserves = $1.6B; shortfall = $0.5B. This $500 million must be deducted from CET1.

Step 5 — Compute adjusted CET1 ratio: Adjusted CET1 = $68B − $0.5B = $67.5B. CET1 ratio = $67.5B / $610B = 11.07%. The minimum CET1 requirement is 4.5%, so Apex satisfies the minimum.

question_text:
Meridian State Bank is a state member bank that is a subsidiary of a global systemically important bank holding company (GSIB). As of the last day of the previous calendar quarter, Meridian's common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio stands at 8.40%, its tier 1 capital ratio at 9.80%, and its total capital ratio at 11.60%, measured against standardized risk-weighted assets of $180 billion. The GSIB parent's most recent method 1 surcharge is 2.0%. Meridian's supplementary leverage ratio is 4.2%, and its tier 1 capital for supplementary leverage ratio purposes is $17.6 billion, against a total leverage exposure of $419 billion.

Meridian also holds a retained interest in a securitization it originated. The securitization pool consists entirely of wholesale and retail exposures with a total EAD of $2.4 billion. Meridian's retained tranche has a face amount of $120 million and sits above a subordinated layer of $240 million. The bank's internal models group has calculated, on an ongoing basis, the following parameters for the pool: the ratio of the sum of risk-based capital requirements plus expected credit losses on the underlying exposures to total EAD is 6.5%; the effective number of exposures (N) is 85; and the exposure-weighted average loss given default (EWALGD) is 42%. The bank's market risk VaR model does not capture specific risk for this securitization position, and the position is not a correlation trading position.

For the current calendar quarter, Meridian's net income for the four preceding quarters totals $1.05 billion, and the average net income over those same four quarters is $980 million. No distributions or associated tax effects outside of net income have occurred.

Determine: (1) whether Meridian faces any restriction on capital distributions and discretionary bonus payments this quarter, and if so, compute the maximum payout amount; and (2) what specific risk capital treatment applies to Meridian's retained securitization tranche under the standardized measurement method, including the risk-weighted asset amount for that position.
required_facts: Meridian is a state member bank subsidiary of a GSIB, so the maximum payout ratio is governed by the leverage buffer framework under § 217.11(f), not the standard capital conservation buffer table
Meridian's supplementary leverage ratio is 4.20% (= $17.6B / $419B), yielding a leverage buffer of 1.20% (= 4.20% − 3.00%)
The leverage buffer requirement equals 50% of the GSIB parent's method 1 surcharge of 2.0%, i.e., 1.0%
The retained securitization tranche requires a specific risk add-on under the standardized measurement method because the VaR model does not capture specific risk for this position
The applicable method for computing the specific risk add-on is the Supervisory Formula Approach (SFA), with KIRB = 6.5%, L = 10%, T = 5%, UE = $2.4 billion, TP = 1.0, N = 85, EWALGD = 42%

Because KIRB (6.5%) is less than L (10%), the SFA risk-based capital requirement equals UE × TP × max(F·T, S[L+T] − S[L]) with F = 0.016, and the risk-weighted asset amount equals that requirement multiplied by 12.5

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.300(a) governs transition-period payout restrictions and references § 217.11 (Subpart B) for the capital conservation buffer and maximum payout ratio framework; § 217.11(f) applies to state member banks that are subsidiaries of a GSIB and references the leverage buffer requirement and payout ratio table; § 217.210 (Subpart F) governs specific risk add-ons under the standardized measurement method and directs use of the SFA in § 217.143 (Subpart E) for securitization positions not modeled under § 217.209.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify the transition provision: § 217.300(a)(1) exempts Board-regulated institutions from § 217.11 payout limits from Jan 1, 2014 through Dec 31, 2015. § 217.300(a)(2) applies a modified payout table from Jan 1, 2016 through Dec 31, 2018. After Dec 31, 2018, the full § 217.11 framework applies without transition relief.

Step 2 — Identify the applicable payout framework under § 217.11: Because Meridian is a state member bank that is a subsidiary of a GSIB, § 217.11(f) applies (not the standard capital conservation buffer table). Under § 217.11(f), the maximum payout ratio is determined by Meridian's leverage buffer, defined as the excess of its supplementary leverage ratio over 3 percent.

Step 3 — Compute the leverage buffer: Meridian's supplementary leverage ratio = $17.6B tier 1 / $419B total leverage exposure = 4.20%. Leverage buffer = 4.20% − 3.00% = 1.20%.

Step 4 — Compute the leverage buffer requirement: The GSIB parent's method 1 surcharge is 2.0%. Under § 217.11(f), the leverage buffer requirement for the state member bank equals 50% of the parent's method 1 surcharge = 50% × 2.0% = 1.0%.

Step 5 — Determine the maximum payout ratio using Table 3 to § 217.11(f): Meridian's leverage buffer (1.20%) is greater than its leverage buffer requirement (1.00%), so no payout ratio limitation applies under § 217.11(f). Meridian is not restricted in distributions or discretionary bonus payments this quarter.

Step 6 — Compute eligible retained income (for completeness): Under § 217.11(a)(2)(i), eligible retained income is the greater of (A) net income for the four preceding quarters = $1.05 billion, or (B) average net income for the four preceding quarters = $980 million. Eligible retained income = $1.05 billion. Since no payout limitation applies, the maximum payout amount equals 100% × $1.05 billion = $1.05 billion (uncapped).

Step 7 — Specific risk treatment for the securitization position: Under § 217.210(a), Meridian must calculate a specific risk add-on for securitization positions not modeled under § 217.209. Per § 217.210(b)(2)(vii)(B), the specific risk add-on for a securitization position may be calculated directly using the SFA in § 217.143.

Step 8 — Apply § 217.143 SFA parameters: UE = $2.4 billion (total EAD of underlying exposures). Meridian's tranche amount = $120 million; TP = $120M / $120M = 1.0 (Meridian holds the entire tranche). Subordinated layer = $240 million; L = $240M / $2,400M = 0.10. T = $120M / $2,400M = 0.05. KIRB = 6.5% = 0.065. N = 85; EWALGD = 42%.

Step 9 — Determine which SFA branch applies: KIRB (0.065) vs. L (0.10) and L+T (0.15). Since KIRB (0.065) < L (0.10), apply § 217.143(c)(2): SFA risk-based capital requirement = UE × TP × max(F·T, S[L+T] − S[L]), where F = 0.016. F·T = 0.016 × 0.05 = 0.0008. The supervisory formula S[·] must be evaluated at L+T = 0.15 and L = 0.10 using the parameters N=85, EWALGD=0.42, KIRB=0.065, h, v, and Beta distribution inputs per § 217.143(d). The exact numerical result of S[L+T]−S[L] requires the full supervisory formula computation; the answerer must set up and evaluate the formula. The risk-weighted asset amount = SFA risk-based capital requirement × 12.5 per § 217.143(b).

scenario_parameters.institution_type: state member bank, subsidiary of GSIB

question_text: Heartland Mutual Savings Bank has established an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) that qualifies as a bank holding company under applicable federal law. The ESOP holds shares of Heartland's parent institution and is structured as a tax-qualified retirement benefit plan for employees. The Board has not yet issued any regulations specifically addressing the application of capital requirements to employee stock ownership plans organized as holding companies. Heartland's compliance team is preparing its quarterly regulatory capital report and is uncertain whether the ESOP holding company must calculate and maintain minimum risk-based capital ratios, including the capital conservation buffer composed of common equity tier 1 capital, and whether restrictions on distributions and discretionary bonus payments could apply to it. Determine whether the ESOP holding company is subject to the Board's regulatory capital framework, including the capital conservation buffer requirements, and explain the basis for your conclusion.
required_facts: The ESOP bank holding company falls within the exemption in § 217.502(a) because the Board has not yet adopted regulations specifically addressing capital requirements for ESOP holding companies.

The exemption in § 217.502(a) operates 'notwithstanding' the general applicability provision in § 217.1(c), meaning it overrides the default rule that would otherwise subject the ESOP holding company to Part 217.
§ 217.1(c) is the provision that would otherwise bring a U.S.-domiciled bank holding company into the Board's regulatory capital framework on a consolidated basis.
Because the ESOP holding company is exempt from Part 217, it is not required to calculate or maintain minimum risk-based capital ratios or a capital conservation buffer.

The capital conservation buffer under § 217.11(a) is composed solely of common equity tier 1 capital, and the associated maximum payout ratio restrictions in § 217.11(a)(2)(iii) do not apply to an institution that is exempt from Part 217.
The exemption remains in effect until the Board issues regulations that directly relate to the application of capital regulations to employee stock ownership plans organized as holding companies.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.502(a) grants an exemption 'notwithstanding § 217.1(c)'; § 217.1(c) is the general applicability provision that would otherwise bring the ESOP holding company into the framework; because the exemption overrides applicability, the institution never reaches the capital conservation buffer and payout ratio rules in § 217.11(a).

Step 2 — Navigate to § 217.1(c): This is the general applicability clause that would otherwise require every Board-regulated institution that is a bank holding company domiciled in the United States to comply with Part 217 on a consolidated basis, including the minimum capital ratio requirements and buffer rules. question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a $50 million equity exposure to a registered investment fund. The fund's prospectus permits investments in corporate bonds, equity securities, and cleared interest rate swap contracts (used solely for duration hedging, not speculation, and representing less than 5% of the fund's total exposures). The institution does not have sufficient transparency into the fund's individual holdings to calculate risk-weighted asset amounts for each underlying exposure on a proportional basis. The institution's compliance team is evaluating whether the fund qualifies for a preferential 100% risk weight treatment based on the nature of the investment, or whether it must apply a look-through methodology. The fund was established under a state charter and its primary stated purpose is to provide financing to low- and moderate-income communities in the institution's assessment area; the institution is a state member bank. Under the applicable look-through methodology the institution intends to use, the highest risk weight that applies to any permissible non-hedging exposure in the fund is 100%. Determine: (1) whether the $50 million exposure qualifies for the preferential treatment that would assign a risk-weighted asset amount equal to its adjusted carrying value without applying a look-through multiplier, and (2) if it does not qualify, what is the risk-weighted asset amount under the appropriate simplified look-through approach, assuming the adjusted carrying value equals the $50 million book value.
required_facts: The community development equity exposure exemption under § 217.152(b)(3)(i) applies to state member banks only if the exposure qualifies as a community development investment under 12 U.S.C. 24 (Eleventh); a registered investment fund structure may not satisfy this requirement, making the look-through approach mandatory.
If the community development exemption applies, the risk-weighted asset amount equals the adjusted carrying value of $50 million with no look-through multiplier.
If look-through is required and the institution cannot use the full look-through approach, it may use the simple modified look-through approach or the alternative modified look-through approach.

Under the simple modified look-through approach, the RWA equals the adjusted carrying value multiplied by the highest subpart D risk weight applicable to any permissible non-excluded exposure in the fund.

Cleared interest rate swap contracts used solely for hedging (not speculation) that constitute less than 5% of fund exposures are explicitly excluded from the highest-risk-weight determination under the simple modified look-through approach.
With the hedging swaps excluded, the highest applicable subpart D risk weight for the remaining permissible exposures (corporate bonds and equity securities) is 100%.
Risk-weighted asset amount under the simple modified look-through approach = $50 million × 100% = $50 million.

annotator_grounding.end_clause: § 217.35 (subpart D risk weights for cleared transactions)

annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.154(a)(1): The institution must determine the RWA amount under one of the three look-through approaches unless the exposure meets the community development equity exposure requirements in § 217.152(b)(3)(i). Step 2 — § 217.152(b)(3)(i): For state member banks and bank holding companies, a community development equity exposure is one that qualifies as a community development investment under 12 U.S.C. 24 (Eleventh), excluding exposures to unconsolidated SBICs and exposures held through consolidated SBICs. The fund here is described as promoting low- and moderate-income community financing, which is consistent with community development investment criteria for a state member bank. If it qualifies, § 217.154(a)(2) applies: RWA = adjusted carrying value = $50 million (no look-through multiplier). Step 3 — If the institution cannot confirm the fund qualifies under 12 U.S.C. 24 (Eleventh) (e.g., it is a registered investment fund rather than a direct community development investment), the institution must use a look-through approach. Step 4 — § 217.154(c) simple modified look-through: RWA = adjusted carrying value × highest risk weight under subpart D applicable to any permissible exposure, excluding derivative contracts used for hedging (not speculation) that are not a material portion of exposures. The cleared interest rate swaps are used solely for hedging and are less than 5% of exposures — they are excluded.
