question_text: Apex State Bank is a state member bank and a wholly-owned subsidiary of a global systemically important bank holding company (GSIB). The GSIB parent's most recently calculated Method 1 surcharge is 2.5 percent. Apex State Bank reports the following capital figures as of the last day of the previous calendar quarter: tier 1 capital of $18 billion, total capital of $22 billion, and common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital of $16 billion. Its standardized total risk-weighted assets are $200 billion, and its average total consolidated assets are $240 billion. Its total leverage exposure for supplementary leverage ratio purposes is $300 billion. Apex State Bank also maintains a large portfolio of repo-style transactions that are included in its internal models-based market risk capital framework. For the repo-style transactions included in that market risk framework, the bank uses the collateral haircut approach to recognize collateral benefits for counterparty credit risk purposes. The bank's compliance team is assessing whether Apex State Bank may make discretionary bonus payments this quarter. As part of that assessment, determine: (1) whether Apex State Bank meets all applicable minimum capital ratio requirements, (2) what leverage buffer the bank holds and whether it satisfies the leverage buffer requirement applicable to it as a GSIB subsidiary, and (3) what maximum payout ratio applies to the bank's distributions and discretionary bonus payments this quarter. Additionally, confirm whether the bank's use of the collateral haircut approach for its repo-style transactions included in the market risk VaR-based measure is a permissible methodology under the counterparty credit risk rules.
required_facts: Apex State Bank's supplementary leverage ratio is 18/300 = 6.0%, which satisfies the 3.0% minimum supplementary leverage ratio requirement applicable to advanced approaches or Category III Board-regulated institutions under the minimum capital rules
The leverage buffer requirement for Apex State Bank as a GSIB subsidiary equals the lesser of 1.0% or 50% of the GSIB parent's Method 1 surcharge (50% × 2.5% = 1.25%), which is 1.0%
Apex State Bank's leverage buffer equals its supplementary leverage ratio minus 3.0%, i.e., 6.0% − 3.0% = 3.0%

Because the leverage buffer of 3.0% exceeds the leverage buffer requirement of 1.0%, no maximum payout ratio limitation applies to Apex State Bank's distributions and discretionary bonus payments this quarter

The collateral haircut approach is a permissible methodology for recognizing collateral benefits on repo-style transactions included in the VaR-based measure under the market risk framework, as explicitly authorized under the counterparty credit risk collateral recognition rules

The VaR-based measure must be calculated using a one-tail 99.0% confidence level and a holding period equivalent to a 10-business-day movement in underlying risk factors, based on a historical observation period of at least one year

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.11(f) governs payout restrictions for state member bank subsidiaries of GSIBs, which requires computing the leverage buffer requirement under § 217.11(a)(2)(v) and comparing it to the leverage buffer under § 217.11(f)(3). The leverage buffer requirement references the Method 1 surcharge. The minimum capital ratios needed to assess compliance are set in § 217.10. The supplementary leverage ratio calculation under § 217.10(c) is needed because Apex is a Category III or advanced approaches institution. The repo-style transaction collateral methodology question chains from § 217.132(c) (which governs permissible EAD methodologies for OTC derivatives and repo-style transactions) and § 217.132(a)(1) (which explicitly permits the collateral haircut approach for repo-style transactions included in the VaR-based measure under subpart F), with the VaR-based measure itself defined in § 217.205(b).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Minimum capital ratios (§ 217.10(a)): Apex must meet CET1 ≥ 4.5%, Tier 1 ≥ 6%, Total Capital ≥ 8%, Leverage ≥ 4%, and supplementary leverage ratio ≥ 3% (as a Category III or advanced approaches institution). Compute: CET1 ratio = 16/200 = 8.0% ≥ 4.5% ✓; Tier 1 ratio = 18/200 = 9.0% ≥ 6.0% ✓; Total capital ratio = 22/200 = 11.0% ≥ 8.0% ✓; Leverage ratio = 18/240 = 7.5% ≥ 4.0% ✓; Supplementary leverage ratio = 18/300 = 6.0% ≥ 3.0% ✓. All minimums met. Step 2 — Leverage buffer requirement for GSIB subsidiary (§ 217.11(a)(2)(v)(B)): The leverage buffer requirement = lesser of 1.0% or 50% × 2.5% = lesser of 1.0% or 1.25% = 1.0%. Step 3 — Leverage buffer held (§ 217.11(f)(3)(ii)): Leverage buffer = supplementary leverage ratio − 3% = 6.0% − 3.0% = 3.0%. Step 4 — Maximum payout ratio (§ 217.11(f)(1) and Table 3 to § 217.11(f)): Leverage buffer of 3.0% is greater than the leverage buffer requirement of 1.0%, so no payout ratio limitation applies. Step 5 — Permissibility of collateral haircut approach for repo-style transactions in VaR-based measure (§ 217.132(a)(1)(i) and § 217.205(b)): § 217.132(a)(1) explicitly permits the collateral haircut approach to recognize collateral benefits for repo-style transactions included in the VaR-based measure under subpart F. § 217.205(b) sets the quantitative requirements for the VaR-based measure (one-tail 99% confidence, 10-business-day holding period, at least one year of historical data). The use of the collateral haircut approach is permissible provided the VaR-based measure meets the § 217.205(b) requirements.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution's trading desk holds a position in a collateralized debt obligation (CDO) tranche. The underlying reference portfolio of the CDO consists entirely of single-name corporate credit default swaps, each referencing a different investment-grade company for which an active two-way market exists. The institution's risk managers are debating whether this CDO tranche qualifies as a correlation trading position for internal models purposes. Separately, the institution also holds a direct equity stake in a foreign private company that is not publicly traded and is not domiciled in the United States; the foreign jurisdiction supervises and regulates that company in a manner comparable to how the United States regulates investment companies registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940. The institution's treasury team needs to determine the adjusted carrying value of this equity stake for risk-weighted asset calculation purposes. The on-balance sheet carrying value of the equity stake is $18 million, and the institution has written an unfunded, unconditional commitment to invest an additional $7 million in the same entity. Determine: (1) whether the CDO tranche qualifies as a correlation trading position, and (2) the adjusted carrying value of the equity exposure to the foreign private company that must be used when computing risk-weighted assets under the equity exposure framework.
required_facts: The CDO tranche does not qualify as a correlation trading position because its underlying exposures reference multiple different companies, not a single company or a commonly traded index based on single-company exposures.

The equity stake in the foreign private company is not excluded from covered position treatment because the foreign entity is supervised and regulated similarly to a registered investment company under the Investment Company Act of 1940, satisfying the exception for non-US non-publicly-traded equity positions.
The on-balance sheet component of the adjusted carrying value is $18 million (the institution's carrying value of the exposure).
The unfunded unconditional commitment of $7 million contributes an off-balance sheet component equal to its full notional amount of $7 million.
The total adjusted carrying value of the equity exposure is $25 million ($18 million on-balance sheet + $7 million off-balance sheet).

The definition of 'correlation trading position' in Subpart F incorporates general definitions from the Part 217 master definitions section, and the adjusted carrying value methodology for equity exposures is governed by the equity exposure introduction and measurement rules in Subpart E.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.202 defines 'correlation trading position' and 'covered position' (including the exclusion for non-publicly-traded equity of non-US entities supervised like registered investment companies), which cross-references § 217.2 for the definition of 'separate account' and related terms, which in turn leads to § 217.151 for the adjusted carrying value methodology applicable to equity exposures.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.202 'correlation trading position': The CDO tranche is a securitization position. Under the definition in § 217.202, a correlation trading position includes a securitization position where all or substantially all of the value of the underlying exposures is based on the credit quality of a single company for which a two-way market exists, OR on commonly traded indices based on such exposures. Here the underlying portfolio consists of multiple single-name CDS (not a single company and not a commonly traded index), so the CDO tranche does NOT qualify as a correlation trading position. It also does not qualify under the hedge prong (paragraph (2) of the definition). Step 2 — § 217.202 'covered position' exclusion for non-publicly-traded equity: The equity stake in the foreign private company is not publicly traded. Under § 217.202 paragraph (3)(vii) of the 'covered position' definition, a non-publicly-traded equity position is excluded from covered positions (and thus from market risk capital treatment) UNLESS it is a derivative referencing a publicly traded equity OR a position in an entity not domiciled in the United States that is supervised and regulated in a manner similar to entities described in paragraph (3)(vi) — i.e., similar to registered investment companies under the Investment Company Act. The foreign company meets this exception, so the equity stake IS a covered position and must be treated under the equity exposure framework. Step 3 — § 217.202 cross-reference to § 217.2: § 217.202(a) states that terms used in Subpart F that are defined in § 217.2 carry those definitions. The term 'separate account' is defined in § 217.2 and is relevant to how equity exposures to investment funds are treated. Step 4 — § 217.151(b) adjusted carrying value: Under § 217.151(b), the adjusted carrying value of an equity exposure is: (1) for the on-balance sheet component, the carrying value = $18 million; (2) for the off-balance sheet component (the unfunded unconditional commitment), the effective notional principal amount equals the notional amount of the commitment = $7 million (per § 217.151(b)(3)), minus the on-balance sheet adjusted carrying value attributable to that component (zero, since the commitment is unfunded). Total adjusted carrying value = $18 million + $7 million = $25 million.

scenario_parameters.CDO_underlying: multiple single-name corporate CDS (different investment-grade companies)
scenario_parameters.foreign_entity_supervision: comparable to US Investment Company Act registered investment company

question_text:
Apex National Bank is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has completed its parallel run and received Board notification. It operates a correlation trading desk and uses an internal model to measure the price risk of its correlation trading portfolio. The bank calculates its comprehensive risk measure weekly. For the most recent week, the bank's internal model produces a comprehensive risk measure of $180 million. The average of the comprehensive risk measures over the prior 12 weeks is $210 million. The bank has not yet held the required one-year track record needed to qualify for the alternative floor treatment. Separately, the bank's total specific risk add-on for its modeled correlation trading positions, calculated under the standardized measurement method, is $95 million.

The bank's CET1 capital is $9.8 billion, its additional tier 1 capital is $1.2 billion, and its tier 2 capital is $1.5 billion. Its total risk-weighted assets under the standardized approach are $98 billion. The bank is not a global systemically important BHC and is not subject to the GSIB surcharge. Its capital conservation buffer, measured as of the last day of the previous calendar quarter, stands at 1.9% above the minimum CET1 requirement. The bank's board of directors is considering paying $320 million in discretionary bonuses to senior traders this quarter. The bank's net income for the four preceding calendar quarters totals $850 million (net of distributions and associated tax effects), and the average net income over those same four quarters is $780 million.

Determine: (1) the bank's comprehensive risk capital requirement, including the required surcharge component; (2) whether the bank's capital conservation buffer position restricts its ability to make the proposed $320 million discretionary bonus payment this quarter, and if so, what the maximum permissible payout amount is; and (3) whether the bank is required to publicly disclose its supplementary leverage ratio, and if so, whether it must include the standardized market risk-weighted assets and advanced market risk-weighted assets in its public disclosures.
required_facts: The comprehensive risk capital requirement surcharge equals the total specific risk add-on of $95 million multiplied by 8.0 percent, yielding $7.6 million, because the bank has not satisfied the one-year track record needed for the alternative floor treatment under the comprehensive risk measurement rules.

The comprehensive risk capital requirement is the greater of the 12-week average comprehensive risk measure (approximately $217.6 million including surcharge) and the most recent weekly measure (approximately $187.6 million including surcharge), resulting in a capital requirement of approximately $217.6 million.
Replace this with: under Table 1, a 1.9% buffer is not in the no-limit tier; it falls below the >2.5% threshold and therefore does not support a no-limitation conclusion.
Keep eligible retained income at $850 million, but do not say the maximum payout amount is $850 million with no restriction; the payout cap must follow the applicable §217.11 ratio.

As an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has completed the parallel run, the bank must publicly disclose standardized market risk-weighted assets and advanced market risk-weighted assets under the capital adequacy disclosure table, including separate line items for the standardized approach for specific risk and the internal models approach for specific risk.
The bank must disclose its supplementary leverage ratio publicly if required under the supplementary leverage ratio disclosure rules, unless it qualifies for the consolidated subsidiary exemption.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.173 disclosure requirements for advanced approaches institutions trigger review of capital buffer restrictions under § 217.11, which governs maximum payout ratios based on the capital conservation buffer; the comprehensive risk capital requirement under § 217.209(d) depends on the surcharge formula in § 217.210; and the disclosure of market risk-weighted assets under Table 3 to § 217.173 requires understanding of what § 217.210 produces as a specific risk add-on feeding into § 217.209.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 (§ 217.209(d) — comprehensive risk capital requirement): The bank has not met the one-year track record requirement, so it cannot use the alternative floor under § 217.209(a)(2)(ii). It must use § 217.209(a)(2)(i), which sets the comprehensive risk measure as the sum of: (A) the modeled measure of all price risk, and (B) a surcharge equal to the total specific risk add-on for modeled correlation trading positions as calculated under § 217.210, multiplied by 8.0%. Surcharge = $95 million × 8.0% = $7.6 million. Weekly comprehensive risk measure (with surcharge) = $180M + $7.6M = $187.6 million. The comprehensive risk capital requirement under § 217.209(d) is the greater of: (1) the average of the comprehensive risk measures over the previous 12 weeks, or (2) the most recent comprehensive risk measure. The 12-week average must also incorporate the surcharge: $210M + $7.6M = $217.6M (assuming the surcharge is consistent; alternatively the question intends the $210M and $180M as the full measures pre-surcharge, so the surcharge is added to each). The capital requirement = greater of $217.6M and $187.6M = $217.6 million. Step 2 (§ 217.11(a) — capital conservation buffer and maximum payout): The bank's capital conservation buffer is 1.9% above the minimum CET1 requirement. Under Table 1 to § 217.11(a)(4)(iv), a buffer greater than 1.25% but less than or equal to 1.875% of RWA triggers a 60% maximum payout ratio; a buffer greater than 0.625% but less than or equal to 1.25% triggers 40%; a buffer greater than 0% but less than or equal to 0.625% triggers 20%; a buffer of 0% triggers 0%. At 1.9%, the buffer exceeds 1.875% (the top threshold below the full 2.5% buffer), so no payout restriction applies — wait: the full conservation buffer is 2.5%, so the bank is 0.6% below the full buffer (2.5% - 1.9% = 0.6% shortfall). The buffer is in the range greater than 0.625% × (2.5%/2.5%) = 0.625% and less than or equal to 1.25% of the full buffer... Re-reading: the table uses the buffer amount itself. The bank's buffer = 1.9%. The thresholds in Table 1 to § 217.11(a)(4)(iv) are: >1.875%: no restriction; >1.25% and ≤1.875%: 60%; >0.625% and ≤1.25%: 40%; >0% and ≤0.625%: 20%; =0%: 0%. Since 1.9% > 1.875%, no payout ratio limitation applies. Eligible retained income = greater of $850M and $780M = $850M. Maximum payout amount = $850M × no restriction = unlimited (up to full eligible retained income). The $320M bonus is less than $850M, so it is permissible. Step 3 (§ 217.173(a)(2) and Table 3): As an advanced approaches institution that has completed parallel run, the bank must make disclosures under Tables 1–12 to § 217.173. Table 3 requires disclosure of standardized market risk-weighted assets and advanced market risk-weighted assets as calculated under subpart F, including the standardized approach for specific risk and the internal models approach for specific risk. The bank must also disclose its supplementary leverage ratio under § 217.173(a)(2) if required under § 217.172(d), unless it is a consolidated subsidiary of a qualifying parent subject to the same requirements.

question_text: Heartland Community Bank is a Board-regulated institution with total consolidated assets of $4.2 billion as of the most recent calendar quarter-end. It has elected to use the community bank leverage ratio framework and currently reports a leverage ratio of 8.6 percent. The bank holds a portfolio of publicly traded equity securities classified as available-for-sale (AFS) with a carrying value of $38 million. Due to rising interest rates, these AFS equity securities have accumulated net unrealized losses of $4.2 million, which are reflected in the carrying value. The bank made an AOCI opt-out election when it first became subject to the regulatory capital rules. It has no off-balance sheet securitization exposures, no trading assets or liabilities, and off-balance sheet exposures totaling 18 percent of total consolidated assets. The bank is not an advanced approaches institution. During the current quarter, the bank's leverage ratio declined from 9.4 percent to 8.6 percent due to loan growth. Determine: (1) whether the bank remains eligible to use the community bank leverage ratio framework and, if not, what transition relief is available; (2) if the bank must transition to standard risk-based capital reporting, what adjusted carrying value it must assign to the AFS equity securities portfolio for purposes of calculating risk-weighted assets under the equity exposure rules.
required_facts: Heartland's leverage ratio of 8.6 percent is below the 9 percent threshold required to remain a qualifying community banking organization under the CBLR framework

Because the leverage ratio is above 8 percent, the bank is entitled to a grace period lasting through the last day of the second consecutive calendar quarter following the quarter in which it ceased to qualify
During the grace period the bank continues to be treated as a qualifying community banking organization and must continue calculating and reporting its leverage ratio
At grace period expiration the bank must comply with standard minimum capital requirements and report all required capital measures
The bank's AOCI opt-out election triggers the special adjusted carrying value rule for AFS equity exposures under the equity exposure risk-weighting rules

The adjusted carrying value formula subtracts net unrealized gains (not losses) from carrying value; because the AFS equity portfolio has net unrealized losses of $4.2 million (no unrealized gains), the adjusted carrying value equals the full carrying value of $38 million

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.12 CBLR eligibility and grace period rules → § 217.22(b)(2) AOCI opt-out election treatment → § 217.51(b)(2) adjusted carrying value for AFS equity exposures where AOCI opt-out was elected
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.12(a)(2)(i): A qualifying community banking organization must have a leverage ratio greater than 9 percent. Heartland reports 8.6 percent, which is below the 9 percent threshold. Therefore, the bank no longer satisfies the criterion to be a qualifying community banking organization. Step 2 — § 217.12(c)(6): Notwithstanding the general grace period provisions in § 217.12(c)(1)–(4), a Board-regulated institution that has a leverage ratio of 8 percent or less does not have a grace period. However, Heartland's leverage ratio is 8.6 percent, which is above 8 percent, so § 217.12(c)(6) does not eliminate the grace period. Step 3 — § 217.12(c)(1)–(2): Because the bank no longer satisfies the qualifying criteria (leverage ratio fell below 9 percent) but its ratio is above 8 percent, it enters a grace period. The grace period begins at the end of the calendar quarter in which it ceases to satisfy the qualifying criteria and ends on the last day of the second consecutive calendar quarter following the beginning of the grace period. During the grace period, the bank continues to be treated as a qualifying community banking organization and must continue calculating and reporting its leverage ratio. Step 4 — § 217.12(c)(1): At the end of the grace period, the bank must comply with the minimum capital requirements under § 217.10(a)(1) and report the required capital measures. Step 5 — § 217.22(b)(2) AOCI opt-out election: When the bank transitions to standard risk-based capital reporting, it must apply the AOCI opt-out election it previously made. Under § 217.22(b)(2), a Board-regulated institution that has made an AOCI opt-out election excludes from regulatory capital components net unrealized gains and losses on AFS debt and equity securities. Step 6 — § 217.51(b)(2): For purposes of calculating risk-weighted assets for equity exposures, the adjusted carrying value of an on-balance sheet equity exposure that is classified as available-for-sale where the Board-regulated institution has made an AOCI opt-out election under § 217.22(b)(2) equals the carrying value of the exposure less any net unrealized gains on the exposure that are reflected in such carrying value but excluded from the Board-regulated institution's regulatory capital components. Here, the AFS equity securities have net unrealized losses (not gains) of $4.2 million. Because there are no net unrealized gains to subtract, the adjusted carrying value equals the full carrying value of $38 million. (If the unrealized position were a gain, it would be subtracted; losses are not added back under this formula.)

question_text: Apex State Member Bank is a large Board-regulated institution with average total consolidated assets of $220 billion over the four most recent quarters as reported on its Call Reports. Apex has been identified as an advanced approaches institution and submitted a written implementation plan to the Board three years ago. The Board has been evaluating Apex's parallel run performance for the past 18 months. As of the current quarter, the Board has not yet issued a notification to Apex approving the use of advanced approaches for purposes of calculating its minimum risk-based capital ratios. Apex's compliance team is preparing its quarterly public disclosures and is debating two positions: (1) whether Apex is subject to the quarterly public disclosure requirements applicable to large Board-regulated institutions, and (2) whether Apex's minimum risk-based capital ratios for the current quarter must be determined under the standardized, generally applicable framework rather than the advanced approaches framework. Apex is not a consolidated subsidiary of another bank holding company or depository institution that already makes the relevant public disclosures, and it is not a subsidiary of a non-U.S. banking organization subject to comparable home-jurisdiction disclosure requirements. Evaluate both positions and identify the applicable capital adequacy framework governing Apex's minimum risk-based capital ratios during this period.
required_facts: Apex qualifies as a large Board-regulated institution subject to quarterly public disclosure requirements because its average total consolidated assets ($220 billion) exceed the $50 billion threshold.

Because Apex is an advanced approaches institution that has not received Board approval to exit parallel run under the qualification process approval provision, it is subject to the §§217.62 and 217.63 disclosure requirements rather than being exempt under the §217.172 advanced approaches disclosure regime.

The absence of Board notification approving Apex's use of advanced approaches means Apex remains in parallel run status, and the parallel run provision explicitly states that minimum risk-based capital ratios during this period are determined under the generally applicable subpart D framework.

Subpart D's applicability provision establishes that it sets forth methodologies for determining risk-weighted assets for purposes of the generally applicable risk-based capital requirements for all Board-regulated institutions.
Apex's minimum risk-based capital ratios for the current quarter must be determined under the standardized, generally applicable capital framework (Subpart D), not the advanced approaches framework.
Apex's none of the subsidiary/non-U.S. organization exemptions apply, so no disclosure carve-out is available to it under §217.61.

annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Start at §217.62: The disclosure requirements of §217.62 apply to a 'Board-regulated institution described in §217.61.' To determine whether Apex is subject to these requirements, the reader must follow the cross-reference to §217.61.

Step 2 — §217.61 (Purpose and scope): This section establishes that its disclosure requirements apply to Board-regulated institutions with total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more (Apex qualifies at $220 billion). Critically, §217.61 contains a carve-out: an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution making public disclosures pursuant to §217.172 is excluded. However, §217.61 also states that 'An advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has not received approval from the Board to exit parallel run pursuant to §217.121(d) is subject to the disclosure requirements described in §§217.62 and 217.63.' Because Apex has not received Board approval under §217.121(d), it falls squarely within this clause and IS subject to §§217.62–217.63 disclosures. Position (1) is confirmed: Apex must make quarterly public disclosures.

Step 3 — §217.121(d) (Qualification process — approval to exit parallel run): The cross-reference in §217.61 points to §217.121(d), which defines the conditions under which the Board notifies an institution that it must begin using the advanced approaches subpart. Since the Board has not issued such notification, Apex remains in parallel run status under §217.121(c).

Step 4 — §217.121(c) (Parallel run): This paragraph states that 'During this period, the Board-regulated institution's minimum risk-based capital ratios are determined as set forth in subpart D of this part.' This is the operative cross-subpart reference directing the reader from Subpart E (Advanced Approaches) back to Subpart D.

Step 5 — §217.30(a) (Subpart D Applicability): Subpart D, specifically §217.30(a), establishes that 'This subpart sets forth methodologies for determining risk-weighted assets for purposes of the generally applicable risk-based capital requirements for all Board-regulated institutions.' Therefore, Apex's minimum risk-based capital ratios during the parallel run period are governed by the standardized, generally applicable framework in Subpart D. Position (2) is confirmed.

question_text: Meridian Financial Group is a large bank holding company that has been identified as a global systemically important BHC. Its compliance team is reviewing capital requirements for the current year. Meridian holds a portfolio of equity derivative contracts written on publicly traded equities of non-financial corporations. Specifically, Meridian has provided equity total return swaps referencing a basket of investment-grade equities, with a total notional value of $2.4 billion and a current fair value (to Meridian as protection seller) of negative $85 million. These contracts are not treated as covered positions under the market risk subpart and are not subject to a qualifying master netting agreement. Meridian also holds a 12% ownership stake in a separately managed insurance separate account with a carrying value of $340 million; the separate account is not publicly traded and Meridian has not made an AOCI opt-out election. Meridian's method 1 score (calculated under the GSIB scoring framework) is 385 basis points, and its method 2 score is 680 basis points. Determine: (1) how Meridian must treat the equity derivative contracts for risk-weighted asset purposes, including which exposure measurement methodology applies and what the adjusted carrying value of the off-balance-sheet component is; (2) how Meridian must treat its investment in the separate account for risk-weighted asset purposes; and (3) what GSIB surcharge Meridian must apply for the current year.
required_facts: The equity total return swaps must be treated as equity exposures under §§ 217.51–217.53 (not under the counterparty credit risk CEM/SA-CCR framework alone) because they are equity derivative contracts not treated as covered positions under the market risk subpart.

The adjusted carrying value of the off-balance-sheet component of the equity derivatives is $2.4 billion (effective notional of $2.4 billion minus $0 on-balance-sheet asset component, since fair value to Meridian is negative).

Meridian's investment in the insurance separate account must be treated as an equity exposure to an investment fund, subject to the look-through approaches, because a 'separate account' as defined in the Part 217 definitions is treated as an investment fund for equity exposure purposes.
The adjusted carrying value of the separate account investment equals its carrying value of $340 million (no AOCI opt-out election was made, so no unrealized gain adjustment applies).
The method 1 surcharge corresponding to a method 1 score of 385 basis points (in the 330–429 range) is 2.0%.
The method 2 surcharge corresponding to a method 2 score of 680 basis points (in the 630–729 range) is 3.5%.
Meridian's applicable GSIB surcharge is 3.5%, being the greater of the method 1 surcharge (2.0%) and the method 2 surcharge (3.5%).

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.34(e) directs equity derivative treatment to §§ 217.51–217.53; § 217.51(a)(2) directs separate account treatment and references the definition of 'separate account' in § 217.2; § 217.51 adjusted carrying value rules feed into the SRWA under § 217.52; separately, Meridian's GSIB scores must be evaluated under § 217.403 to determine the applicable surcharge.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.34(e)(1): Because the equity total return swaps are equity derivative contracts and are NOT treated as covered positions under subpart F, Meridian must treat them as equity exposures and compute risk-weighted asset amounts under §§ 217.51 through 217.53. This is the cross-subpart pivot from Subpart D (§ 217.34) to Subpart D's equity exposure section (§ 217.51). Step 2 — § 217.51(b)(3): For the off-balance-sheet component of an equity exposure that is not an equity commitment, the adjusted carrying value equals the effective notional principal amount (the delta-equivalent size that would produce the same fair value change as a hypothetical on-balance-sheet position) minus the adjusted carrying value of any on-balance-sheet component. Since the current fair value is negative $85 million (Meridian owes), the on-balance-sheet carrying value of the asset component is $0 (fair value is negative, so no asset is recorded). The effective notional principal amount for a total return swap referencing $2.4 billion notional must be computed as the delta-equivalent amount; for a linear equity derivative (total return swap), the delta is 1.0, so the effective notional equals $2.4 billion. Adjusted carrying value of the off-balance-sheet component = $2.4 billion − $0 = $2.4 billion. Step 3 — § 217.51(a)(2): Meridian's investment in the insurance separate account must be treated as if it were an equity exposure to an investment fund, directing the institution to use the look-through approaches in § 217.53. Step 4 — § 217.51(a)(2) cross-references 'separate account' as defined in § 217.2 (Subpart A definitions). The § 217.2 definition of 'separate account' confirms this is a separately maintained account held by an insurance company where the assets are insulated from the general account — Meridian's 12% stake with $340 million carrying value qualifies. Since Meridian has not made an AOCI opt-out election, § 217.51(b)(1) applies: the adjusted carrying value of the on-balance-sheet component equals the carrying value of $340 million. Step 5 — § 217.403(a): Meridian must calculate its GSIB surcharge as the greater of the method 1 surcharge and the method 2 surcharge. Step 6 — § 217.403(b) and Table 1: Method 1 score of 385 basis points falls in the 330–429 range → method 1 surcharge = 2.0%. Step 7 — § 217.403(c) and Table 2: Method 2 score of 680 basis points falls in the 630–729 range → method 2 surcharge = 3.5%. Step 8 — § 217.403(a): GSIB surcharge = greater of 2.0% and 3.5% = 3.5%.

question_text: A large Board-regulated institution operates a trading desk that holds a portfolio of positions including corporate bonds, equity derivatives, foreign exchange forwards, and a tranche of a residential mortgage-backed securitization. The institution's risk management team is preparing its market risk capital calculations and needs to classify each position correctly before applying the appropriate capital treatment. One of the positions is a credit derivative that the institution has recognized as a guarantee for purposes of calculating risk-weighted asset amounts under the standardized approach. A second position is a foreign exchange forward with no restrictive covenants on tradability and a two-way market available. A third position is a non-publicly-traded equity stake in a domestic operating company (not an investment company registered with the SEC). A fourth position is a corporate bond held on the trading book with the intent of short-term resale, free of restrictive covenants. The institution's chief risk officer asks the compliance team to determine which of these four positions qualify as covered positions subject to market risk capital requirements, and which must be excluded. Provide a complete classification analysis for each of the four positions, citing the applicable definitional criteria.
required_facts: The credit derivative recognized as a guarantee for standardized approach RWA purposes is excluded from the definition of 'covered position' and is NOT subject to market risk capital requirements.
The foreign exchange forward qualifies as a covered position because foreign exchange positions are included regardless of whether they are classified as trading assets or liabilities.

The non-publicly-traded equity stake in a domestic operating company (not an SEC-registered investment company) is excluded from the covered position definition and is NOT subject to market risk capital requirements.
The corporate bond held with short-term resale intent and free of restrictive covenants qualifies as a covered position because it is a trading position free of tradability restrictions.

The covered position definition contains specific carve-outs that must each be checked independently; a position that otherwise meets the general trading asset criteria may still be excluded if it falls within one of the enumerated exceptions.

Foreign exchange positions are covered positions by category, without requiring a separate trading intent analysis, as long as they are not structural foreign currency positions excluded with prior supervisory approval.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.1(c)(4) establishes that market risk Board-regulated institutions must use Subpart F methodologies; navigating to Subpart F requires applying the 'covered position' definition in § 217.202(b), which contains multiple exclusion carve-outs that must each be checked against the four described positions.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.1(c)(4)(i): A market risk Board-regulated institution must use Subpart F (in addition to Subpart D) to calculate standardized total risk-weighted assets, meaning Subpart F definitions govern which positions are in scope. Step 2 — Navigate to § 217.202(b) definition of 'covered position': A covered position is (1) a trading asset or trading liability that (i) is a trading position or hedges another covered position AND (ii) is free of restrictive covenants or hedgeable in a two-way market; OR (2) a foreign exchange or commodity position regardless of trading book classification. Step 3 — Apply exclusions in § 217.202(b) covered position paragraph (3): (iv) excludes any credit derivative recognized as a guarantee for RWA calculation under Subpart D or E; (vi) excludes any non-publicly-traded equity position that is not a derivative referencing a publicly traded equity and not a registered investment company. Step 4 — Classify each position: Position 1 (credit derivative recognized as guarantee under standardized approach) → excluded under paragraph (3)(iv) of the covered position definition; NOT a covered position. Position 2 (FX forward, no restrictive covenants, two-way market available) → qualifies under paragraph (2) of the covered position definition as a foreign exchange position regardless of trading book status; IS a covered position. Position 3 (non-publicly-traded equity in domestic operating company, not an SEC-registered investment company) → excluded under paragraph (3)(vi); NOT a covered position. Position 4 (corporate bond, trading intent, no restrictive covenants) → qualifies under paragraph (1): it is a trading asset meeting conditions (i) trading position and (ii) free of restrictive covenants; IS a covered position.

scenario_parameters.position_2: foreign exchange forward, no restrictive covenants, two-way market available

question_text: A Board-regulated institution has entered into a synthetic securitization in which it uses a credit derivative to transfer credit risk on a $500 million portfolio of commercial loans to a third party. The credit derivative documentation includes a provision that allows the protection seller to terminate the arrangement if the weighted-average credit quality of the underlying loan pool deteriorates below a specified threshold. The institution's legal counsel has provided a well-reasoned opinion confirming enforceability of the credit derivative in all relevant jurisdictions, and any clean-up calls associated with the transaction qualify as eligible clean-up calls. The institution holds a $75 million equity interest in an investment fund. The fund's prospectus permits investments in corporate bonds, residential mortgage-backed securities, and equity securities of publicly traded companies. The institution cannot obtain the fund's underlying portfolio holdings and therefore cannot calculate risk-weighted asset amounts for its proportional ownership share of each exposure held by the fund. The highest risk weight that applies to any exposure the fund is permitted to hold under its prospectus is 600 percent. Determine: (1) whether the institution may recognize the credit derivative for risk-based capital purposes in connection with the synthetic securitization, and explain the capital consequence if it cannot; and (2) what risk-weighted asset amount the institution must assign to its equity exposure to the investment fund, and which look-through method applies given the institution's inability to obtain underlying holdings data.
required_facts: The credit derivative contains a termination provision triggered by deterioration in the credit quality of the underlying exposures, which disqualifies it under the operational criteria for synthetic securitizations.

Because the credit derivative fails the operational criteria, the institution must hold risk-based capital against the $500 million commercial loan portfolio as if it had not been synthetically securitized, receiving no capital relief.
The definition of 'eligible credit derivative' in § 217.2 is the cross-reference that governs whether the credit derivative qualifies as a credit risk mitigant for synthetic securitization purposes.
For the investment fund equity exposure, the institution must use a look-through approach under the equity exposure framework introduced in § 217.151.
Because the institution cannot calculate risk-weighted asset amounts for its proportional ownership share of each fund holding, the full look-through approach is unavailable.
The simple modified look-through approach applies: risk-weighted asset amount = $75 million adjusted carrying value × 600% highest permissible risk weight = $450 million.

The 600 percent risk weight is the highest risk weight under subpart D applicable to any exposure the fund is permitted to hold under its prospectus, as required by the simple modified look-through approach.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.41(b) sets operational criteria for synthetic securitizations and cross-references the definition of 'eligible credit derivative' in § 217.2; § 217.2 defines 'eligible credit derivative' and cross-references 'eligible guarantee' criteria; § 217.151 introduces the equity exposure framework and directs use of § 217.154 for investment fund exposures; § 217.154(c) provides the simple modified look-through approach applicable when the institution cannot perform a full look-through.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Synthetic securitization eligibility (§ 217.41(b)): The institution seeks to use a credit derivative as a credit risk mitigant. Under § 217.41(b)(1)(iii), the credit derivative must meet all criteria in the definition of 'eligible credit derivative' in § 217.2, except for the criteria in paragraph (3) of the definition of 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2. Step 2 — Definition of 'eligible credit derivative' (§ 217.2): The definition of 'eligible credit derivative' in § 217.2 requires, among other things, that the credit protection not include provisions that allow termination due to deterioration in the credit quality of the underlying exposures. Step 3 — Disqualifying provision (§ 217.41(b)(2)(i)): § 217.41(b)(2)(i) independently prohibits provisions that 'allow for the termination of the credit protection due to deterioration in the credit quality of the underlying exposures.' The credit derivative here contains exactly such a provision (termination triggered by pool credit quality deterioration). Therefore, the credit derivative fails the operational criteria of § 217.41(b). Step 4 — Capital consequence of failure (§ 217.41(b)): Because the institution fails to meet the conditions, it must hold risk-based capital against the underlying exposures as if they had not been synthetically securitized — i.e., the $500 million commercial loan portfolio is treated as unsecuritized for risk-weighting purposes, and the institution receives no capital relief from the credit derivative. Step 5 — Investment fund equity exposure (§ 217.151): § 217.151(a)(1) directs that a Board-regulated institution must use the look-through approaches in § 217.154 to calculate risk-weighted asset amounts for equity exposures to investment funds. Step 6 — Full look-through unavailable (§ 217.154(b)): The full look-through approach under § 217.154(b) requires the institution to be able to calculate a risk-weighted asset amount for its proportional ownership share of each exposure held by the fund. Because the institution cannot obtain underlying holdings data, the full look-through approach is unavailable. Step 7 — Simple modified look-through approach (§ 217.154(c)): Under the simple modified look-through approach, the risk-weighted asset amount equals the adjusted carrying value of the equity exposure multiplied by the highest risk weight assigned under subpart D that applies to any exposure the fund is permitted to hold under its prospectus. The highest permissible risk weight is 600 percent. Risk-weighted asset amount = $75 million × 600% = $450 million.

question_text: Midland State Bancorp is a Board-regulated institution classified as a Category III bank holding company. It is also an advanced approaches institution that has completed the parallel run process and received the required Board notification. The institution is evaluating a synthetic securitization in which it intends to use a guarantee as the credit risk mitigant to hedge a pool of commercial loan exposures. The guarantee in question satisfies all standard conditions for recognition as an eligible guarantee under the applicable definitions — except that it does not satisfy condition (3) of that definition. Midland's compliance team wants to know: (1) whether the synthetic securitization credit risk mitigant can still be recognized for risk-based capital purposes under the operational criteria for synthetic securitizations, and (2) what the consequence is if the mitigant cannot be recognized. Separately, Midland's leverage ratio calculation team is computing the institution's supplementary leverage ratio. Tier 1 capital is $18.4 billion. On-balance sheet assets averaged $310 billion over the reporting quarter. Off-balance sheet exposures averaged $42 billion over the last day of each of the most recent three months. Goodwill net of associated deferred tax liabilities is $2.1 billion, and the institution has $0.9 billion of intangible assets other than mortgage servicing assets, net of associated deferred tax liabilities. No other items require deduction from tier 1 capital for leverage purposes. Compute the supplementary leverage ratio and determine whether it meets the applicable minimum threshold.
required_facts: Category III Board-regulated institutions are subject to a supplementary leverage ratio minimum of 3 percent
Total leverage exposure = mean on-balance sheet assets ($310B) + mean off-balance sheet exposures ($42B) − § 217.22(a) deductions (goodwill $2.1B + intangibles $0.9B = $3.0B) = $349.0B
Supplementary leverage ratio = $18.4B / $349.0B ≈ 5.27%, which exceeds the 3% minimum
The definition of 'eligible guarantee' (including its numbered conditions) is found in the Part 217 definitions section

A guarantee that meets all eligible guarantee requirements except condition (3) of that definition is expressly permitted as a qualifying credit risk mitigant for a synthetic securitization under the operational criteria

Therefore, Midland's guarantee CAN be recognized for risk-based capital purposes, and the institution must hold risk-based capital only against any credit risk it retains in connection with the synthetic securitization
If the operational criteria for synthetic securitization were not met, the institution would hold risk-based capital against the underlying exposures as if they had not been synthetically securitized

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.10(c) defines the supplementary leverage ratio and references § 217.22(a),(c),(d) for deductions from tier 1 capital in the leverage exposure denominator; § 217.22(a) lists the specific CET1 deduction items (goodwill, intangibles, etc.) that reduce the denominator; § 217.2 defines 'eligible guarantee' (including its numbered conditions); § 217.141(b)(1)(ii)–(iii) permits a guarantee or credit derivative that meets all eligible guarantee/eligible credit derivative requirements except condition (3) to qualify as a credit risk mitigant for synthetic securitization recognition.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Supplementary leverage ratio applicability: Under § 217.10(a)(1)(v), a Category III Board-regulated institution must maintain a supplementary leverage ratio of at least 3 percent. Under § 217.10(c)(1), the supplementary leverage ratio equals tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure. Step 2 — Total leverage exposure denominator: Per § 217.10(c)(1)(i)–(ii), total leverage exposure is the mean of on-balance sheet assets ($310B) plus the mean of off-balance sheet exposures ($42B), minus applicable deductions under § 217.22(a),(c),(d). Step 3 — Identify § 217.22(a) deductions: § 217.22(a)(1) requires deduction of goodwill net of associated DTLs ($2.1B) and § 217.22(a)(2) requires deduction of intangible assets other than MSAs net of associated DTLs ($0.9B). Total deductions = $3.0B. Step 4 — Compute total leverage exposure: $310B + $42B − $3.0B = $349.0B. Step 5 — Compute supplementary leverage ratio: $18.4B / $349.0B = 5.27%. This exceeds the 3% minimum, so the requirement is met. Step 6 — Synthetic securitization recognition: Under § 217.141(b)(1)(ii), a guarantee qualifies as a credit risk mitigant for a synthetic securitization if it meets all requirements of an eligible guarantee except for condition (3) of that definition. The definition of 'eligible guarantee' is found in § 217.2. Because Midland's guarantee satisfies all conditions except condition (3), it expressly qualifies under § 217.141(b)(1)(ii), and the credit risk mitigant CAN be recognized. If the mitigant failed to meet the § 217.141(b) conditions entirely, the institution would be required to hold risk-based capital against the underlying exposures as if they had not been synthetically securitized.

question_text: Heartland Bancorp is a large domestic bank holding company that recently crossed the threshold to become an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution. It is not a consolidated subsidiary of any other bank holding company or foreign banking organization. As of December 31 of the current year, Heartland has completed its systemic risk scoring exercise and its method 1 score came in at 142 basis points. Heartland's common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital is $38 billion, its additional tier 1 capital is $5 billion, and its tier 2 capital is $8 billion. Its standardized total risk-weighted assets are $480 billion. Heartland's capital conservation buffer, measured as of the last day of the previous calendar quarter, stands at 1.8% above the minimum CET1 requirement. Heartland also has aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities equal to $52 billion, representing 11% of its quarter-end total assets as reported on its most recent FR Y-9C. Heartland's board of directors is considering declaring a discretionary cash dividend of $900 million in the current calendar quarter. Determine: (1) whether Heartland qualifies as a global systemically important BHC and what timing obligations apply to its surcharge calculation; (2) what GSIB surcharge Heartland must use when determining its maximum payout ratio, and when that surcharge becomes effective for payout ratio purposes; and (3) whether Heartland is subject to market risk capital requirements, and what that means for its overall regulatory capital framework.
required_facts: Heartland qualifies as a global systemically important BHC because its method 1 score of 142 basis points equals or exceeds the 130 basis point identification threshold.

Heartland must calculate its GSIB surcharge by December 31 of the year it is identified as a global systemically important BHC, and that surcharge applies to the maximum payout ratio determination beginning January 1 of the year immediately following the full calendar year after identification.

The GSIB surcharge is incorporated into the maximum payout ratio framework under Table 1 to § 217.11, and because Heartland is subject to 12 CFR 225.8 as an advanced approaches BHC, its maximum payout ratio is determined under the GSIB-adjusted buffer stack rather than the standard conservation buffer table.

With a capital conservation buffer of 1.8% above the minimum CET1 requirement, Heartland's buffer position relative to the combined requirement (conservation buffer plus GSIB surcharge) determines whether the $900 million dividend is permissible or restricted.

Heartland is subject to Subpart F market risk capital requirements because its aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities equal 11% of quarter-end total assets, satisfying the 10%-or-more threshold, and also exceed $1 billion.

Subpart F requires Heartland to calculate a standardized measure for market risk and, if applicable, an advanced measure for market risk, and to comply with public disclosure requirements under the market risk framework.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.402 identifies Heartland as a GSIB (score ≥ 130 bps) and conditions the calculation obligation on § 217.400(b)(2); § 217.400(b)(2) specifies the surcharge calculation deadline and ties the surcharge to the maximum payout ratio under Table 1 to § 217.11; § 217.11 governs the capital conservation buffer and maximum payout ratio framework; the trading asset threshold in § 217.201(b)(1) triggers Subpart F market risk requirements.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — GSIB identification (§ 217.402): Heartland's method 1 score is 142 basis points, which equals or exceeds the 130 basis point threshold. Therefore Heartland qualifies as a global systemically important BHC. § 217.402 also states that the annual calculation obligation is subject to § 217.400(b)(2), so the answerer must follow that cross-reference.

Step 2 — Applicability and timing (§ 217.400(b)): Under § 217.400(b)(1), the subpart applies because Heartland (i) is an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution, (ii) is not a consolidated subsidiary of a bank holding company, and (iii) is not a consolidated subsidiary of a foreign banking organization — all three conditions are satisfied. Under § 217.400(b)(2)(i), because Heartland became an advanced approaches institution in the current year, it must determine whether it qualifies as a GSIB by December 31 of the immediately following year (though here it has already scored above 130 bps in the current year). Under § 217.400(b)(2)(ii), Heartland must calculate its GSIB surcharge under § 217.403 by December 31 of the year it is identified as a GSIB, and must use that surcharge for purposes of determining its maximum payout ratio under Table 1 to § 217.11 beginning on January 1 of the year immediately following the full calendar year after identification.

Step 3 — Maximum payout ratio and capital conservation buffer (§ 217.11): The GSIB surcharge feeds into the maximum payout ratio determination under § 217.11. For a Board-regulated institution subject to 12 CFR 225.8 (which applies to advanced approaches BHCs), the maximum payout ratio is determined under § 217.11(c)(1)(ii), which incorporates the GSIB surcharge into the buffer stack. With a capital conservation buffer of 1.8% above the minimum CET1 requirement, the answerer must assess where Heartland falls in the payout ratio table relative to the combined buffer requirement (2.5% conservation buffer + GSIB surcharge). The $900 million dividend must be evaluated against the maximum payout amount (eligible retained income × maximum payout ratio).

Step 4 — Market risk applicability (§ 217.201(b)(1)): Heartland's aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities are $52 billion, representing 11% of quarter-end total assets. Under § 217.201(b)(1)(i), the market risk subpart applies to any Board-regulated institution with trading assets and liabilities equal to 10% or more of quarter-end total assets, or under (b)(1)(ii), $1 billion or more. Heartland satisfies both prongs (11% ≥ 10%, and $52 billion ≥ $1 billion). Therefore Subpart F market risk capital requirements apply to Heartland, meaning it must calculate a standardized measure for market risk (and potentially an advanced measure) and comply with associated public disclosure requirements, layering additional capital obligations on top of the Subpart B and Subpart H requirements.

question_text: Meridian Bank Holdings, an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution, maintains a portfolio of equity derivative contracts referencing publicly traded equities. The institution uses the Internal Models Approach (IMA) for market risk capital purposes on these positions. For calendar year 2020, Meridian's compliance team is evaluating whether it must also hold risk-based capital against the counterparty credit risk embedded in these equity derivative contracts, and if so, how to compute the relevant exposure amount. The institution has not yet transitioned to SA-CCR and is considering whether it may still use the Current Exposure Method (CEM) for the relevant exposure calculation during this period. Meridian's netting agreements with its counterparties qualify as master netting agreements under applicable standards. Assume the institution's total notional exposure across these equity derivative contracts is $2.4 billion, and the current replacement cost across all netting sets is $180 million. Determine: (1) whether Meridian must hold capital against counterparty credit risk for these equity derivative contracts given its use of IMA for market risk, (2) which methodology Meridian must use to compute the exposure at default (EAD) for these contracts for counterparty credit risk purposes, and (3) whether Meridian may use CEM rather than SA-CCR for this EAD calculation during calendar year 2020.
required_facts: Under IMA, Meridian must hold risk-based capital against counterparty credit risk in its equity derivative contracts by treating them as wholesale exposures and computing a supplemental RWA amount under § 217.132
The option to forgo counterparty credit risk capital for equity derivatives (§ 217.155(b)) is available only under SRWA, not IMA, so Meridian cannot elect out

EAD for OTC derivative contracts subject to a qualifying master netting agreement must be computed using the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk in § 217.132(c) (SA-CCR), absent Board approval for the internal models methodology
The transition provision in § 217.300(h) permits an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution to use CEM rather than SA-CCR for purposes of § 217.132(c) until January 1, 2022
Calendar year 2020 falls within the CEM-permissible transition window, so Meridian may use CEM for the § 217.132(c) EAD calculation during 2020
If Meridian elects to begin using SA-CCR before January 1, 2022, it must provide prior notice to the Board and may not subsequently revert to CEM

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.300(h) governs the SA-CCR transition and explicitly references § 217.132(c) as the provision for which CEM may be substituted until January 1, 2022. § 217.155(a) requires that under IMA, a Board-regulated institution must treat equity derivative contracts as wholesale exposures and compute a supplemental risk-weighted asset amount under § 217.132. § 217.132(c) is the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) methodology for computing EAD for OTC derivative contracts.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.155(a): Because Meridian uses the IMA for market risk on its equity derivative contracts, it must ALSO hold risk-based capital against the counterparty credit risk in those contracts by treating each equity derivative contract as a wholesale exposure and computing a supplemental risk-weighted asset amount under § 217.132. This is mandatory under IMA; the option to exclude counterparty credit risk capital (available only under SRWA per § 217.155(b)) does not apply here. Step 2 — § 217.132(c): The supplemental RWA computation for OTC derivative contracts (including equity derivatives treated as wholesale exposures under § 217.155(a)) must use the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk set forth in § 217.132(c) — i.e., SA-CCR — to calculate EAD, unless the institution has Board approval to use the internal models methodology in § 217.132(d). The qualifying master netting agreement means the netting set-level SA-CCR calculation applies. Step 3 — § 217.300(h): The transition provision in § 217.300(h) explicitly permits an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution to use CEM rather than SA-CCR for purposes of § 217.132(c) until January 1, 2022. Since calendar year 2020 falls within this window, Meridian may elect to use CEM instead of SA-CCR for computing EAD under § 217.132(c), including for the equity derivative counterparty credit risk calculation required by § 217.155(a). The institution must provide prior notice to the Board if it decides to begin using SA-CCR before January 1, 2022, and once it begins using SA-CCR it may not revert to CEM.

question_text: First National Bancorp is a U.S. bank holding company that qualifies as an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution and is also subject to the supplementary leverage ratio disclosure requirement. During the first quarter of 2020, the institution held $18 billion in U.S. Treasury securities and $6 billion in funds on deposit at a Federal Reserve Bank on its balance sheet. The institution opted in to exclude these items from its on-balance sheet assets when computing its total leverage exposure, having notified its regulator before the applicable deadline. In the same quarter, the institution also acted as an originator in a traditional securitization: it transferred a pool of commercial loans with an aggregate carrying value of $2.4 billion to a securitization SPE. The transferred loans are no longer reported on the institution's consolidated balance sheet under GAAP, credit risk has been fully transferred to third-party investors, and no early amortization provisions or revolving credit features are present. The institution retained a subordinated tranche with a carrying value of $120 million and a senior tranche with a carrying value of $80 million. The institution does not qualify for the supervisory formula approach on the retained senior tranche, and it has not elected to apply the simplified supervisory formula approach to that tranche. For the retained subordinated tranche, the institution has determined it constitutes an after-tax gain-on-sale. Determine: (1) how the institution must treat the excluded Treasury securities and Federal Reserve deposits in its required public leverage disclosures for that quarter, and (2) what risk-based capital treatment applies to each of the two retained securitization tranches.

The traditional securitization satisfies all operational criteria under § 217.141(a) — off-balance sheet under GAAP, full credit risk transfer, no revolving features, no early amortization — so the $2.4 billion transferred pool is excluded from risk-weighted assets.

The risk-weighted asset amount for the senior tranche equals $80 million × 1,250% = $1 billion.

question_text: A supervised insurance organization is calculating the building block capital requirement for one of its building block parents, Holdco A. As part of this calculation, the compliance team needs to determine whether Holdco A or any member of its building block holds an investment in Holdco A's own capital instruments. The organization has identified a separate account asset within the building block that references a fund whose underlying portfolio includes a position in Holdco A's Tier 1 capital instruments. The fund's total net asset value is $200 million, and the net long position in Holdco A's own capital instruments within that fund — calculated without applying any separate-account carve-out — amounts to $8 million. The organization is also evaluating whether the SSFA may be used to assign a specific risk-weighting factor to a securitization position held by a Board-regulated institution affiliate. That affiliate has data on the underlying exposures that is 95 calendar days old; the contracts governing those exposures require quarterly payments. The weighted-average total capital requirement of the underlying exposures, calculated using the standardized approach, is 6.4%, and the position is not a resecuritization. The attachment point is 9% and the detachment point is 14%. Determine: (1) whether the separate account asset associated with the fund must be treated as an indirect exposure to Holdco A's own capital instruments for purposes of the building block capital requirement deduction, and (2) whether the Board-regulated institution affiliate may use the SSFA for the securitization position, and if so, identify the supervisory calibration parameter p that applies.
required_facts: The net long position in Holdco A's own capital instruments within the fund is $8M / $200M = 4% of fund value, which is below the 5% threshold in § 217.607(b)(4)(ii)

Because the fund's net long position is less than 5% of fund value, the separate account asset is NOT treated as an indirect exposure and no deduction to the building block capital requirement is required on that basis

The Board-regulated institution affiliate's data is 95 calendar days old; because the underlying contracts require quarterly payments, the data must be no more than 91 calendar days old to use the SSFA
Because the data exceeds the 91-day freshness limit, the affiliate may NOT use the SSFA and must assign a specific risk-weighting factor of 100% to the securitization position
Had the data been timely, the supervisory calibration parameter p would equal 0.5 because the position is a securitization position that is not a resecuritization position

The SSFA eligibility question requires navigating to § 217.211(b), which imposes a 91-calendar-day data freshness requirement for quarterly-payment contracts, and § 217.211(b)(5) specifies p = 0.5 for non-resecuritization positions.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.607(b)(4)(ii): The supervised insurance organization must determine the net long position in Holdco A's own capital instruments using the method in § 217.22(h). The separate account asset is NOT treated as an indirect exposure UNLESS the net long position of the underlying fund (calculated under § 217.22(h) without the carve-out) equals or exceeds 5% of the fund's value. Here, $8M / $200M = 4%, which is below the 5% threshold. Therefore, the separate account asset is NOT regarded as an indirect exposure, and no deduction is required on account of that fund position. Step 2 — § 217.1(f): Confirm the Board-regulated institution affiliate is within scope of Part 217 (state member bank, bank holding company, or covered SLHC domiciled in the US). The scenario stipulates it is a Board-regulated institution, so Part 217 applies. Step 3 — § 217.211(a): To use the SSFA, the data used to assign the parameters must be no more than 91 calendar days old when the underlying contracts require quarterly payments. The affiliate's data is 95 calendar days old, which exceeds the 91-day limit. Therefore, the affiliate may NOT use the SSFA for this position and must instead assign a specific risk-weighting factor of 100% to the position. Step 4 — § 217.211(b)(5): Had the data been timely, p = 0.5 would apply because the position is not a resecuritization position.

question_text: A state member bank that is not a subsidiary of any depository institution holding company has total consolidated assets of $320 billion, cross-jurisdictional activity of $85 billion, and on-balance sheet foreign exposure of $55 billion. The bank holds a portfolio of on-balance sheet loans totaling $180 billion, unfunded loan commitments of $40 billion (each with an original maturity greater than one year), and a portfolio of OTC interest rate swap contracts with a gross notional of $25 billion. None of these exposures are cleared transactions, default fund contributions, securitization exposures, or equity exposures. The bank uses the standardized approach for credit risk. Describe the process the bank must follow to determine its total risk-weighted assets for general credit risk, and identify which of its exposure types are subject to that process versus those that are carved out.
required_facts: The bank qualifies as a Category II Board-regulated institution because it has total consolidated assets of $320 billion (exceeding $100 billion) and cross-jurisdictional activity of $85 billion (exceeding $75 billion), based on the definitions in § 217.2
Under § 217.31(a)(1), the bank must determine the exposure amount for each on-balance sheet exposure, OTC derivative contract, and off-balance sheet commitment unless a carve-out applies
The $180 billion on-balance sheet loan portfolio is in scope for general credit risk RWA calculation under § 217.31 — no carve-out applies
The $40 billion unfunded loan commitments are off-balance sheet commitments and are in scope under § 217.31(a)(1) — no carve-out applies

The $25 billion OTC interest rate swaps are in scope under § 217.31(a)(1) because they are not cleared transactions, not default fund contributions, not securitization exposures, and not equity exposures
Under § 217.31(a)(2), each in-scope exposure amount must be multiplied by the risk weight appropriate to the exposure type, counterparty, eligible guarantor, or financial collateral
Total risk-weighted assets for general credit risk equals the sum of all risk-weighted asset amounts calculated under § 217.31, per § 217.31(b)

annotator_grounding.end_clause: § 217.31 (mechanics for calculating risk-weighted assets for general credit risk)

With $85 billion in cross-jurisdictional activity, the bank does not meet the $75 billion threshold that would make it Category II solely on that basis (Category II requires $75 billion or more in cross-jurisdictional activity AND $100 billion or more in total assets for a non-subsidiary state member bank — actually the $85 billion cross-jurisdictional activity exceeds $75 billion, so this bank is Category II). Step 2 — Having established the institution's category, the standardized approach under Subpart D applies. Step 3 — Under § 217.31(a)(1), the bank must determine the exposure amount of each on-balance sheet exposure, each OTC derivative contract, and each off-balance sheet commitment, trade and transaction-related contingency, guarantee, repo-style transaction, financial standby letter of credit, forward agreement, or other similar transaction — UNLESS the exposure falls into one of the five carve-outs: (i) unsettled transactions, (ii) cleared transactions, (iii) default fund contributions, (iv) securitization exposures, or (v) equity exposures (other than equity OTC derivative contracts). Step 4 — Apply carve-out analysis: The $180 billion loan portfolio is on-balance sheet and not carved out → in scope. The $40 billion unfunded commitments are off-balance sheet commitments → in scope. The $25 billion OTC interest rate swaps are OTC derivative contracts and are not cleared transactions → in scope. Step 5 — Under § 217.31(a)(2), multiply each exposure amount by the appropriate risk weight based on exposure type, counterparty, eligible guarantor, or financial collateral. Step 6 — Under § 217.31(b), total risk-weighted assets for general credit risk equals the sum of all risk-weighted asset amounts calculated under § 217.31.

question_text:
A Board-regulated institution operates as a market risk institution and maintains an internal VaR-based model for its trading book. The institution holds a mixed portfolio that includes corporate bond positions, equity positions, and a set of structured credit positions. For its corporate bond and equity portfolios, the institution's compliance team has determined that the VaR-based measure does not fully capture all material aspects of specific risk — in particular, it fails to adequately reflect idiosyncratic default risk and credit migration risk for those portfolios. The institution has not elected to compute an incremental risk measure for these portfolios. Separately, the institution holds a tranche of a residential mortgage-backed security (RMBS) that was originated and structured by a third party; this securitization position is not modeled under the institution's correlation trading framework.

For the corporate bond and equity portfolios where VaR-based specific risk is insufficient, the institution must calculate a specific risk add-on using the standardized measurement method. Under that method, the institution encounters a structured credit position that would ordinarily qualify as a debt position but for the fact that it meets the definition of a 'correlation trading position' — specifically, it is an nth-to-default credit derivative that is not a correlation trading position eligible for internal model treatment. The institution's risk team asks: for purposes of applying the standardized specific risk add-on calculation to this structured credit position, should it be treated as a debt position or as a securitization position? Additionally, the institution holds a sold credit protection position (a single-name CDS referencing an investment-grade corporate obligor) with a notional amount of $50 million and a current fair value of negative $2 million (i.e., the institution owes $2 million mark-to-market). What is the maximum specific risk add-on that can be attributed to this sold protection position under the standardized method? Finally, for the RMBS securitization tranche that is not internally modeled, identify the applicable treatment and the regulatory framework that governs how the institution must classify that exposure when computing its total risk-weighted assets under the advanced approaches — specifically, whether it falls into the wholesale, retail, securitization, or equity exposure category.
required_facts: Because the VaR-based measure does not capture all material aspects of specific risk for the corporate bond and equity portfolios, the institution must calculate a specific risk add-on using the standardized measurement method (not an internal model add-on).

A position that qualifies as a correlation trading position solely under the second prong of that definition in § 217.2 is treated as a debt position (not a securitization position) for purposes of the standardized specific risk add-on calculation under § 217.210.
The specific risk add-on for the sold credit protection CDS position is capped at the notional amount of the contract, which is $50 million — the negative fair value does not reduce this cap.
The RMBS securitization tranche that is not modeled under the correlation trading framework must have its specific risk add-on calculated under the standardized measurement method.
Under Phase 1 categorization for advanced approaches RWA, the RMBS tranche is classified as a securitization exposure — not a wholesale, retail, or equity exposure.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.207(c) directs unmodeled specific risk to the standardized method in § 217.210; § 217.210(a) references the definition of 'correlation trading position' in § 217.2 to resolve the debt-vs-securitization classification question; § 217.210(a)(1) caps the sold credit protection add-on at notional; § 217.210 also directs that unmodeled securitization positions use the standardized method, and § 217.131(b) governs Phase 1 categorization of exposures — including securitization exposures — for total wholesale and retail RWA calculation under the advanced approaches.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.207(c)(1): Because the VaR-based measure does not capture all material aspects of specific risk for the corporate bond and equity portfolios, the institution must calculate a specific risk add-on under the standardized measurement method described in § 217.210. Step 2 — § 217.207(c)(2): Because the RMBS securitization tranche is not modeled under § 217.209, the institution must also calculate a specific risk add-on for it under § 217.210. Step 3 — § 217.210(a) (first paragraph, last sentence): A position that would qualify as a debt or equity position but for the fact that it qualifies as a correlation trading position under paragraph (2) of the definition of 'correlation trading position' in § 217.2 shall be treated as a debt or equity position, respectively, for purposes of § 217.210. Therefore the nth-to-default credit derivative that meets the correlation trading position definition only under paragraph (2) of that definition is treated as a debt position for standardized specific risk add-on purposes. Step 4 — § 217.210(a)(1): The specific risk add-on for a sold credit protection position is capped at the notional amount of the credit derivative contract. The notional is $50 million, so the maximum specific risk add-on is $50 million regardless of fair value. Step 5 — § 217.131(b) (Phase 1 categorization): When computing total wholesale and retail risk-weighted assets under the advanced approaches, the institution must categorize each exposure. The RMBS tranche is a securitization exposure and must be identified as such in Phase 1 — it does not fall into the wholesale, retail, or equity exposure categories.
