question_text: A mid-sized Board-regulated institution holds a portfolio of equity derivative contracts on publicly traded common stock. The institution's aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities equal $1.2 billion, representing 8 percent of its quarter-end total assets. The institution does not qualify as an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution. For a subset of these equity derivative contracts, the institution has elected to treat them as covered positions subject to the market risk capital framework rather than as equity exposures under the general credit risk rules. For the remaining equity derivative contracts not designated as covered positions, the institution applies the Simple Risk-Weight Approach. The institution asks its compliance team to determine: (1) whether the market risk capital framework applies to this institution at all, and if so, on what basis; (2) what counterparty credit risk capital treatment applies to the equity derivative contracts that are designated as covered positions; and (3) whether the institution may omit a counterparty credit risk capital charge for the equity derivative contracts that are not designated as covered positions and are subject to the Simple Risk-Weight Approach, assuming it applies that election consistently across all such contracts.
required_facts: Subpart F (market risk framework) applies to this institution because its aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities equal $1.2 billion, meeting the $1 billion or more threshold, even though the 10-percent-of-total-assets threshold is not met (8% < 10%).

For equity derivative contracts designated as covered positions under subpart F, the institution must calculate a counterparty credit risk capital requirement under the derivative contracts section in addition to the market risk capital charge.

For equity derivative contracts not designated as covered positions that are risk-weighted under the Simple Risk-Weight Approach, the institution may elect to hold no risk-based capital against counterparty credit risk, provided the election is applied consistently to all such contracts.
The institution is not an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution, which is relevant to the methodology available for calculating exposure amounts under the derivative contracts rules.

The cross-reference to 'covered position under subpart F' in the equity derivative counterparty credit risk rule requires first confirming that subpart F is applicable to the institution before the covered-position designation is permissible.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.34(e) governs counterparty credit risk for equity derivatives and references 'subpart F of this part' to determine whether a contract is a covered position; resolving that reference requires reading § 217.201(b) to determine whether the market risk framework (subpart F) even applies to this institution.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Start at § 217.34(e)(1): a Board-regulated institution must treat an equity derivative as an equity exposure under §§ 217.51–217.53 unless the institution is treating the contract as a covered position under subpart F of this part. Step 2 — The phrase 'subpart F of this part' is the cross-reference trigger. Navigate to § 217.201(b) (subpart F) to determine applicability. Step 3 — § 217.201(b)(1) states subpart F applies to any Board-regulated institution with aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities equal to (i) 10 percent or more of quarter-end total assets, OR (ii) $1 billion or more. Step 4 — Apply to the scenario: trading assets/liabilities = $1.2 billion ≥ $1 billion threshold → subpart F applies on the dollar-amount prong, even though the 10-percent prong is not met (8% < 10%). Step 5 — Because subpart F applies, the institution may designate equity derivative contracts as covered positions. Step 6 — Return to § 217.34(e)(2): for contracts designated as covered positions under subpart F, the institution must also calculate a counterparty credit risk capital requirement under § 217.34. Step 7 — § 217.34(e)(3): if the institution uses the Simple Risk-Weight Approach (SRWA) for equity derivative contracts NOT designated as covered positions, it may choose not to hold risk-based capital against counterparty credit risk for those contracts, provided it does so consistently for all such contracts.

question_text:
A Board-regulated institution originates a $200 million commercial loan portfolio and structures a transaction in which it transfers credit risk on the portfolio to a special purpose entity. The SPE issues two tranches of notes to third-party investors: a senior tranche absorbing losses only after the junior tranche is exhausted, and a junior tranche that absorbs first losses up to $30 million. The institution retains no interest in the junior tranche but does retain the senior tranche. The institution argues that because it has transferred credit risk to third parties and the exposures are no longer on its consolidated balance sheet under GAAP, it should be able to exclude the underlying $200 million portfolio from its risk-weighted asset calculation entirely, treating the retained senior tranche as a simple guaranteed exposure eligible for substitution treatment using the risk weight of the SPE as protection provider.

Separately, the institution's compliance team notes that the SPE qualifies as a 'securitization SPE' under applicable definitions, and that the transaction involves a credit risk mitigant in the form of a guarantee from a highly rated third-party bank (risk weight: 20%) covering the senior tranche on a full basis, with no maturity mismatch, no currency mismatch, and no restructuring event carve-out in the guarantee documentation.

Determine: (1) whether the institution may apply simple substitution treatment to the retained senior tranche or whether a different capital framework governs that exposure; (2) what operational conditions, if any, must be satisfied before the institution can exclude the underlying $200 million portfolio from its risk-weighted assets; and (3) assuming those conditions are satisfied and the guarantee on the senior tranche is recognized, what risk weight applies to the senior tranche and what adjustments, if any, are required to the effective notional amount of the guarantee.
required_facts: The two-tranche structure constitutes a tranching of credit risk with at least two levels of seniority, making the retained senior tranche a securitization exposure subject to the securitization framework rather than simple substitution treatment under the guarantee/credit derivative substitution rules.

The institution may not apply substitution treatment directly to the senior tranche as if it were a plain guaranteed exposure; the securitization operational criteria must first be satisfied before the underlying portfolio can be excluded from risk-weighted assets.

To exclude the $200 million portfolio, the institution must satisfy all operational conditions for traditional securitizations, including: off-balance-sheet treatment under GAAP, transfer of credit risk to third parties, eligible clean-up calls only, and absence of revolving exposures with early amortization provisions.

Failure to meet any operational condition requires the institution to hold risk-based capital against the full $200 million underlying portfolio as if unsecuritized, and to deduct any after-tax gain-on-sale from common equity tier 1 capital.

The third-party bank guarantee on the senior tranche must qualify as an eligible guarantee under the applicable definitions, meeting criteria including being written, unconditional, irrevocable, and legally enforceable.

Assuming the operational criteria are satisfied and the guarantee is eligible, the applicable risk weight for the senior tranche is 20% (the risk weight of the guarantor bank), with no adjustment to the effective notional amount because there is no maturity mismatch, no currency mismatch, and no restructuring event carve-out.

annotator_grounding.end_clause: § 217.35 (context for cleared transaction carve-outs, referenced via subpart D scope)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.36(a)(3) directs tranched-risk exposures to §§ 217.41–217.45 (securitization framework); § 217.41 sets operational criteria for traditional securitizations and references the definition of 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2; § 217.2 defines 'eligible guarantee' with specific criteria; once the senior tranche qualifies as a securitization exposure governed by §§ 217.41–217.45, the substitution treatment of § 217.36 does not apply to it directly, but if the institution satisfies § 217.41 operational criteria and the guarantee meets § 217.2 eligibility, the risk weight of the guarantor (20%) may be applied under subpart D to the retained securitization exposure, with no notional adjustments needed given no maturity mismatch, currency mismatch, or restructuring carve-out.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.36(a)(3): The transaction involves two tranches with at least two different levels of seniority (senior and junior), constituting a tranching of credit risk. § 217.36(a)(3) explicitly states that exposures with tranched credit risk 'generally are securitization exposures subject to §§ 217.41 through 217.45.' Therefore, the institution cannot apply the simple substitution treatment of § 217.36 to the retained senior tranche; it is a securitization exposure governed by the securitization framework.

Step 2 — § 217.41(a): To exclude the underlying $200 million portfolio from risk-weighted assets, the institution must satisfy all four operational criteria for traditional securitizations: (1) the exposures are not reported on the consolidated balance sheet under GAAP; (2) credit risk associated with the underlying exposures has been transferred to one or more third parties; (3) any clean-up calls are eligible clean-up calls; and (4) the securitization does not include revolving exposures with an early amortization provision. The institution states conditions (1) and (2) are met; conditions (3) and (4) must also be confirmed. If any condition fails, the institution must hold capital against the full $200 million as if unsecuritized and deduct any after-tax gain-on-sale from CET1.

Step 3 — § 217.41(b)(1)(ii) cross-reference to § 217.2 definition of 'eligible guarantee': For synthetic securitizations the credit risk mitigant must meet the 'eligible guarantee' definition in § 217.2 (except criterion (3) of that definition). For the traditional securitization scenario here, the retained senior tranche is a securitization exposure; the third-party bank guarantee covering it must qualify as an 'eligible guarantee' under § 217.2 to receive substitution treatment under subpart D's securitization rules.

Step 4 — § 217.2 'eligible guarantee' definition: The guarantee must be written, unconditional, irrevocable, cover all amounts owed, legally enforceable, and meet other criteria enumerated in § 217.2. The scenario states the guarantee is full coverage with no carve-outs described as disqualifying; assuming it meets all § 217.2 criteria, it is an eligible guarantee.

Step 5 — Risk weight and notional adjustments: The guarantor bank has a 20% risk weight under subpart D. Under the substitution approach applicable to securitization exposures (incorporating § 217.36(c)(1) principles as applied through the securitization subpart), the institution substitutes the 20% risk weight of the guarantor for the risk weight otherwise applicable to the senior tranche. No maturity mismatch adjustment is needed (no mismatch stated). No currency mismatch adjustment is needed (no currency difference stated). No restructuring event adjustment is needed (no restructuring carve-out in the guarantee). Therefore, the effective notional amount of the guarantee equals its face amount with no reduction, and the senior tranche is risk-weighted at 20%.

question_text: Heartland Bancorp, a Board-regulated institution with $320 billion in total consolidated assets, has been operating under the standardized approach for risk-based capital. Over the past two years, Heartland has invested heavily in the common stock of several unconsolidated financial institutions. As of the current quarter-end, Heartland reports the following: common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital of $28 billion (before any threshold deductions), total capital of $35 billion, and standardized total risk-weighted assets of $280 billion. Heartland holds $4.2 billion in significant investments in the capital of unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock. These investments have not been deducted from CET1 capital because Heartland's compliance team determined they fall below the applicable deduction threshold. Separately, Heartland has been working toward qualifying for the advanced approaches framework. It adopted a written implementation plan 18 months ago, has been conducting its parallel run for the past five consecutive calendar quarters, and recently received formal notification from the Board that it may begin using the advanced approaches for purposes of its risk-based capital ratios. Heartland's chief risk officer now asks: (1) What risk weight must Heartland assign to the $4.2 billion in significant common-stock investments in unconsolidated financial institutions that were not deducted from CET1 capital, and (2) now that Heartland has received Board notification to use the advanced approaches, what additional CET1 deduction — if any — must Heartland recognize that it was not required to take during the parallel run period?
required_facts: Significant investments in the capital of unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock that are not deducted from CET1 capital pursuant to the threshold deduction rules must be assigned a 250 percent risk weight under the SRWA.

The threshold deduction rule requires deduction of significant common-stock investments in unconsolidated financial institutions only to the extent they exceed 10 percent of CET1 capital; the $4.2 billion holding exceeds the $2.8 billion threshold (10% × $28B), so $1.4 billion must be deducted from CET1 and only the remaining $2.8 billion receives the 250% risk weight.

The 250% risk weight cross-references the CET1 deduction provision in the regulatory capital adjustments section (Subpart C), meaning the two rules operate in tandem: amounts above the threshold are deducted; amounts at or below the threshold are risk-weighted at 250%.

The deduction of expected credit loss in excess of eligible credit reserves is required only for advanced approaches institutions that have both completed a satisfactory parallel run and received formal Board notification to begin using the advanced approaches framework.
A satisfactory parallel run requires no less than four consecutive calendar quarters of compliance with the qualification requirements; Heartland's five-quarter parallel run meets this minimum.

Upon receiving Board notification under the qualification process approval provision, Heartland must begin recognizing the expected-credit-loss deduction from CET1 that was not required during the parallel run period.

During the parallel run, minimum risk-based capital ratios are determined under the standardized approach (Subpart D), not the advanced approaches; the advanced approaches capital floor and ECL deduction obligations activate only after the Board's formal notification.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.52(b)(4) assigns 250% risk weight to significant investments in unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock that are NOT deducted under § 217.22(d)(2); § 217.22(d)(2) governs the threshold deduction rules for such investments; § 217.22(a)(6) requires deduction of expected credit loss exceeding eligible credit reserves only for advanced approaches institutions that have completed the parallel run AND received Board notification under § 217.121(d).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Risk weight for non-deducted significant investments: Navigate to the SRWA equity risk-weight schedule. § 217.52(b)(4) states that significant investments in the capital of unconsolidated financial institutions in the form of common stock that are NOT deducted from capital pursuant to § 217.22(d)(2) must be assigned a 250 percent risk weight. Because Heartland's compliance team confirmed these $4.2 billion in investments were not deducted (they fell below the § 217.22(d)(2) threshold), the correct risk weight is 250%, producing risk-weighted assets of $10.5 billion for this portfolio. Step 2 — Cross-reference to § 217.22(d)(2): The cross-reference in § 217.52(b)(4) directs the reader to § 217.22(d)(2) in Subpart C to confirm the deduction threshold mechanics. Under § 217.22(d)(2), significant investments in common stock of unconsolidated financial institutions are subject to a threshold deduction only to the extent they exceed 10% of CET1 (after certain adjustments). Heartland's $4.2 billion is below 10% of $28 billion CET1 ($2.8 billion threshold), so the excess above the threshold ($4.2B − $2.8B = $1.4 billion) would actually need to be deducted, and the remaining $2.8 billion receives the 250% risk weight. (The question tests whether the answerer catches that the compliance team's blanket 'no deduction' conclusion was partially incorrect — the $1.4 billion excess must be deducted.) Step 3 — Advanced approaches notification and § 217.22(a)(6): § 217.22(a)(6) requires an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution that has completed the parallel run AND received Board notification pursuant to § 217.121(d) to deduct from CET1 the amount by which expected credit loss exceeds eligible credit reserves. During the parallel run, this deduction was not required. Now that Heartland has received the § 217.121(d) notification, it must begin taking this deduction. § 217.121(d) specifies the Board will notify the institution of the date it must begin using the advanced approaches after confirming: full compliance with qualification requirements in § 217.122, a satisfactory parallel run of at least four consecutive calendar quarters, and an adequate ongoing compliance process. Heartland's five-quarter parallel run satisfies the minimum four-quarter requirement. Upon receiving that notification, the § 217.22(a)(6) deduction becomes mandatory.

question_text: First National Bancorp is a Board-regulated institution that qualifies as a Category III institution under the federal banking agencies' tailoring rules. It has completed the parallel run process and received the required notification from its primary federal regulator. As of the most recent quarter-end, First National Bancorp publicly discloses its supplementary leverage ratio as required for institutions of its category. The institution's treasury desk maintains a large portfolio of repo-style transactions with a diverse set of counterparties. For one significant netting set, the institution's risk management team has developed an internal models methodology to calculate exposure at default (EAD), which the Board has approved in writing. This internal model is also used to generate a VaR-based measure that the institution incorporates into its market risk capital framework for covered positions. The institution's market risk team asserts that the VaR-based measure fully captures all material aspects of specific risk for its portfolio of debt positions associated with these repo-style counterparties. A compliance officer is reviewing whether: (1) the institution's quarterly public disclosures must include a supplementary leverage ratio table, and if so, under what conditions that obligation can be waived; (2) the internal models methodology for EAD on the repo-style netting set satisfies the applicable regulatory standard, given that the Board's written approval was obtained; and (3) if the VaR-based measure does indeed capture all material aspects of specific risk for the debt portfolio, what is the consequence for the institution's specific risk add-on calculation for those positions? Provide a complete compliance analysis addressing all three questions.
required_facts: A Category III Board-regulated institution required to publicly disclose its supplementary leverage ratio must make the disclosures required under Table 13 to § 217.173, as directed by § 217.63(d) cross-referencing § 217.173(a)(2).

The Table 13 supplementary leverage ratio disclosure obligation under § 217.173(a)(2) is waived only if the institution is a consolidated subsidiary of a bank holding company, savings and loan holding company, or depository institution already subject to these disclosure requirements, or a subsidiary of a non-U.S. banking organization subject to comparable public disclosure requirements in its home jurisdiction.

Use of the internal models methodology under § 217.132(d) to calculate EAD for a repo-style netting set requires prior written approval of the Board; because such approval was obtained, the institution satisfies the regulatory prerequisite.

If the Board-regulated institution's VaR-based measure captures all material aspects of specific risk for a portfolio of debt positions, the institution has no specific risk add-on for that portfolio under § 217.207(b)(2).

The chain of cross-references runs from the Subpart D disclosure section (§ 217.63(d)) to the Subpart E advanced approaches disclosure section (§ 217.173(a)(2)), then to the Subpart E counterparty credit risk methodology (§ 217.132(d)), and finally to the Subpart F specific risk provision (§ 217.207(b)(2)).

annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Supplementary leverage ratio disclosure (§ 217.63(d) → § 217.173(a)(2)): § 217.63(d) states that a Category III Board-regulated institution required to publicly disclose its supplementary leverage ratio pursuant to § 217.172(d) is subject to the supplementary leverage ratio disclosure requirement at § 217.173(a)(2). Navigating to § 217.173(a)(2), the rule requires an advanced approaches Board-regulated institution and a Category III Board-regulated institution that is required to publicly disclose its supplementary leverage ratio pursuant to § 217.172(d) to make the disclosures required under Table 13 to § 217.173, UNLESS the institution is a consolidated subsidiary of a bank holding company, savings and loan holding company, or depository institution that is itself subject to these disclosure requirements, or a subsidiary of a non-U.S. banking organization subject to comparable public disclosure requirements in its home jurisdiction. The same written-approval requirement applies to repo-style netting sets under § 217.132(a)(3). Therefore, if the VaR-based measure fully captures all material aspects of specific risk for the debt portfolio, First National Bancorp has no specific risk add-on for that portfolio.

question_text: Heartland State Bank, a state member bank supervised by the Federal Reserve, holds the following assets on its balance sheet as of the most recent reporting date: (1) $180 million in U.S. Treasury securities; (2) $95 million in loans fully insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation; (3) $60 million in direct loans to the government of Brazil, which is an OECD member country but has no Country Risk Classification (CRC) assigned to it; (4) $40 million in loans to a foreign bank headquartered in Germany (an OECD member with no CRC); (5) $25 million in loans to a foreign bank headquartered in Vietnam, whose home country carries a CRC of 3; (6) $15 million in preferred stock issued by Fannie Mae, a government-sponsored enterprise (GSE); and (7) $30 million in commercial real estate loans secured by income-producing properties in the United States, where the loan-to-value ratio is 85 percent. Heartland State Bank uses the standardized approach to calculate its risk-weighted assets. Determine the appropriate risk weight for each of the seven asset categories listed above, and compute the total standardized risk-weighted assets (RWA) attributable to these holdings. Assume no other adjustments or deductions apply to these specific assets.
required_facts: Heartland State Bank is a state member bank and therefore a Board-regulated institution subject to 12 CFR Part 217, required to use Subpart D methodologies for standardized risk-weighted assets

U.S. Treasury securities and FDIC-insured loans each receive a 0% risk weight as exposures to or unconditionally guaranteed by the U.S. government or its agencies, resulting in $0 RWA for the combined $275 million
Brazil is an OECD member sovereign with no CRC, and therefore receives a 0% risk weight under the sovereign exposure rules, resulting in $0 RWA on the $60 million sovereign loan
The German foreign bank exposure receives a 20% risk weight because Germany is an OECD member with no CRC, resulting in $8 million RWA on the $40 million exposure

The Vietnamese foreign bank exposure receives a 100% risk weight because Vietnam's home country CRC is 3, per the foreign bank risk-weight table, resulting in $25 million RWA on the $25 million exposure
Preferred stock issued by a GSE (Fannie Mae) receives a 100% risk weight, resulting in $15 million RWA on the $15 million holding
Total standardized RWA for the seven asset categories equals $78 million ($0 + $0 + $0 + $8M + $25M + $15M + $30M)

Step 2 — §217.2: Resolve key definitions needed to classify each asset. 'Board-regulated institution' confirms applicability. 'GSE' is defined to include Fannie Mae. 'Sovereign exposure' and 'foreign bank' definitions govern how to classify the Brazil sovereign loan and the foreign bank loans. These definitions gate which rows of the risk-weight tables in §217.32 apply.

Step 3 — §217.32 risk weight assignments:
  (a)(1)(i)(A): U.S. Treasury securities → 0% risk weight. $180M × 0% = $0 RWA.
  (a)(1)(i)(B): FDIC-insured loans are unconditionally guaranteed by the U.S. government → 0% risk weight. $95M × 0% = $0 RWA.
  (a)(5): Brazil is an OECD member sovereign with no CRC → per §217.32(a)(5), assign 0% risk weight. $60M × 0% = $0 RWA.
  (d)(2)(ii): German foreign bank, home country is OECD member with no CRC → 20% risk weight. $40M × 20% = $8M RWA.
  (d)(2)(i) + Table 2: Vietnamese foreign bank, home country CRC of 3 → 100% risk weight per Table 2. $25M × 100% = $25M RWA.
  (c)(2): Preferred stock issued by a GSE (Fannie Mae) → 100% risk weight. $15M × 100% = $15M RWA.
  (l)(2) or (l)(5): Commercial real estate loans at 85% LTV — high-volatility commercial real estate (HVCRE) rules may apply; if not HVCRE, standard CRE at 100% risk weight under §217.32(l)(2) or the catch-all 100% under §217.32(l)(5). $30M × 100% = $30M RWA.

Total standardized RWA = $0 + $0 + $0 + $8M + $25M + $15M + $30M = $78 million.

question_text:
First National Bancorp (FNB) is a Board-regulated institution that is not an advanced approaches institution. FNB has a wholly-owned consolidated subsidiary, Midwest Community Bank (MCB), which has issued $180 million of common equity tier 1 capital instruments to third-party investors (i.e., not owned by FNB). MCB is adequately capitalized and its capital instruments qualify as regulatory capital under applicable standards.

At the consolidated level, FNB reports the following capital figures (before including any minority interest from MCB):
- Common equity tier 1 capital elements (excluding minority interest): $2,100 million
- Common equity tier 1 regulatory adjustments and deductions (under applicable deduction rules): $95 million
- Additional tier 1 capital elements: $310 million
- Tier 2 capital elements: $220 million
- Standardized total risk-weighted assets: $18,500 million

Of the $180 million in MCB common equity tier 1 capital held by third parties, FNB's compliance team is attempting to determine how much, if any, may be included in FNB's consolidated common equity tier 1 capital.

Separately, FNB's board of directors is considering declaring a discretionary cash dividend for the current calendar quarter. FNB's capital conservation buffer, calculated as of the last day of the previous calendar quarter, stood at 1.875% of risk-weighted assets. FNB is not subject to any leverage-based capital plan requirements and is not a state member bank subsidiary of a global systemically important bank holding company.

Determine: (1) the maximum amount of MCB's minority interest that FNB may include in its consolidated common equity tier 1 capital, and (2) whether FNB faces any restriction on its discretionary dividend payment, and if so, what maximum payout ratio applies.
required_facts: The applicable minority interest rule for a non-advanced-approaches Board-regulated institution is the 10% cap under § 217.21(a)(2), not the advanced approaches formula in § 217.21(b).
The CET1 minority interest cap = 10% × ($2,100M − $95M) = 10% × $2,005M = $200.5 million.
Because MCB's third-party CET1 of $180 million is less than the $200.5 million cap, FNB may include the full $180 million in consolidated CET1 capital.
FNB's capital conservation buffer of 1.875% is below the 2.5% minimum required buffer, triggering payout restrictions under the capital conservation buffer framework.

A capital conservation buffer of 1.875% falls in the bracket greater than 1.25% and up to 1.875% of risk-weighted assets (i.e., greater than 50% and up to 75% of the 2.5% requirement), which corresponds to a maximum payout ratio of 40% of eligible retained income.
FNB may not pay discretionary dividends exceeding 40% of eligible retained income in the current calendar quarter unless the Board permits the payment upon request.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.20(b)(4) includes common equity tier 1 minority interest subject to limitations in § 217.21; § 217.21(a)(2) sets the 10% cap formula for non-advanced-approaches institutions and references § 217.22(a) and (b) for deductions; § 217.21(b) (advanced approaches path, not applicable here) references § 217.11 for distribution restrictions; the dividend restriction question independently requires § 217.11(a) capital conservation buffer payout table.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify the minority interest inclusion rule: § 217.20(b)(4) states that common equity tier 1 minority interest is includable in CET1 capital, subject to the limitations in § 217.21.

Step 2 — Apply § 217.21(a)(1): FNB is not an advanced approaches institution, so paragraph (a) applies. MCB has issued regulatory capital not owned by FNB, so the minority interest limitation is triggered.

Step 3 — Apply § 217.21(a)(2) formula: The maximum includable CET1 minority interest = 10% × (sum of all CET1 capital elements of FNB, excluding the minority interest itself, less CET1 regulatory adjustments and deductions under § 217.22(a) and (b)).
  = 10% × ($2,100M − $95M)
  = 10% × $2,005M
  = $200.5 million

Step 4 — Compare cap to actual minority interest: MCB's third-party CET1 = $180 million. Since $180M < $200.5M cap, FNB may include the full $180 million in its consolidated CET1 capital.

Step 5 — Dividend restriction analysis: § 217.11(a) governs the capital conservation buffer. FNB's capital conservation buffer is 1.875% as of the prior quarter-end. The minimum required capital conservation buffer is 2.5%. Since 1.875% < 2.5%, FNB is within the buffer range that triggers payout restrictions.

Step 6 — Determine the applicable bracket from Table 1 to § 217.11(a)(4)(iv): The capital conservation buffer of 1.875% falls in the range greater than 1.25% and less than or equal to 1.875% (i.e., greater than 50% and up to 75% of the 2.5% buffer requirement). This corresponds to a maximum payout ratio of 40% of eligible retained income.

Conclusion: (1) FNB may include up to $200.5M of CET1 minority interest; since MCB's actual third-party CET1 is $180M, the full $180M is includable. (2) FNB's capital conservation buffer of 1.875% triggers distribution restrictions; the maximum payout ratio for discretionary dividends is 40% of eligible retained income.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution that qualifies as an advanced approaches institution maintains a trading book that includes a portfolio of correlation trading positions. The institution uses an internal model approved by the Board to measure comprehensive risk for this portfolio. Over the most recent 12-week period, the institution's weekly comprehensive risk measures (in millions) were as follows: Week 1: $210M, Week 2: $195M, Week 3: $220M, Week 4: $205M, Week 5: $230M, Week 6: $215M, Week 7: $225M, Week 8: $200M, Week 9: $240M, Week 10: $218M, Week 11: $235M, Week 12: $228M. The most recent (Week 12) comprehensive risk measure is $228M. Separately, the institution's total specific risk add-on for the same correlation trading positions, calculated under the standardized measurement method, is $180M. The institution has been using the internal model for comprehensive risk for 18 months and has demonstrated model effectiveness through ongoing validation and benchmarking. The Board has approved the institution to use the alternative calculation method for the comprehensive risk capital requirement. In addition, the institution is a Board-regulated institution that is not subject to the GSIB surcharge and is not a state member bank subsidiary of a global systemically important BHC. As of the last day of the previous calendar quarter, the institution's common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital conservation buffer stood at 1.8 percent. The institution is currently in calendar year 2019 (i.e., the transition period under the capital buffer rules has fully phased in). The institution's board of directors is considering declaring a discretionary cash dividend of $95M and paying discretionary bonuses totaling $30M this quarter. The institution's eligible retained income for the current quarter is $200M. Determine: (1) the institution's comprehensive risk capital requirement, and (2) whether the proposed distributions and discretionary bonus payments are permissible without restriction under the capital conservation framework, and if not, the maximum permissible payout amount.
required_facts: The 12-week average of comprehensive risk measures is $2,621M / 12 = $218.42M, and the most recent measure is $228M; the comprehensive risk capital requirement is max($218.42M, $228M) = $228M

Under the Board-approved alternative method, the comprehensive risk measure equals the greater of the modeled all-price-risk measure ($228M) and the specific risk add-on ($180M) multiplied by 8.0% ($14.4M), yielding $228M

The transition period payout restrictions under § 217.300(a)(2) applied only through December 31, 2018; in calendar year 2019 the full capital conservation buffer framework under § 217.11 applies without transitional modification
With a 1.8% capital conservation buffer and no applicable countercyclical buffer, the maximum payout ratio is 40%, not 60%.
Maximum payout amount = $200M × 40% = $80M.
The proposed $125M payout exceeds the $80M maximum payout amount, so it is not fully permissible; aggregate distributions and discretionary bonus payments may not exceed $80M this quarter.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.300(a) governs transition rules for the capital conservation buffer and references § 217.11 for the payout restriction framework; § 217.11 defines eligible retained income, maximum payout ratio, and maximum payout amount; § 217.11 also cross-references the specific risk add-on calculation, which for correlation trading positions flows through § 217.210 (standardized measurement method) and § 217.209 (comprehensive risk), the latter specifying the comprehensive risk capital requirement formula including the alternative calculation method.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Comprehensive risk capital requirement (§ 217.209(d)): The institution has Board approval to use the alternative method under § 217.209(a)(2)(ii) (approved, >1 year of use, demonstrated effectiveness). Under § 217.209(a)(2)(ii), the comprehensive risk measure is the GREATER of: (A) the modeled measure of all price risk, or (B) the total specific risk add-on for modeled correlation trading positions as calculated under § 217.210 multiplied by 8.0 percent. The specific risk add-on under § 217.210 is $180M; 8.0% × $180M = $14.4M. The modeled measure (most recent week) is $228M. However, the comprehensive risk capital requirement under § 217.209(d) is the GREATER of: (1) the average of the comprehensive risk measures over the previous 12 weeks, or (2) the most recent comprehensive risk measure. Average = ($210+$195+$220+$205+$230+$215+$225+$200+$240+$218+$235+$228M) / 12 = $2,621M / 12 = $218.42M. Most recent = $228M. So the comprehensive risk capital requirement = max($218.42M, $228M) = $228M. Under the alternative method, the comprehensive risk measure itself = max(modeled all-price-risk measure, specific risk add-on × 8%) = max($228M, $14.4M) = $228M. The comprehensive risk capital requirement = $228M. Step 2 — Capital conservation buffer payout restrictions (§ 217.300(a) → § 217.11): Since the institution is in calendar year 2019, the transition period under § 217.300(a)(2) (which covered 2016–2018) has expired. The full § 217.11 capital conservation buffer rules apply. Under § 217.11(a)(2)(iii), for a Board-regulated institution not subject to 12 CFR 225.8 or 238.170 and not a state member bank subsidiary of a GSIB, the maximum payout ratio is determined by the capital conservation buffer as of the last day of the previous calendar quarter. The institution's CET1 capital conservation buffer = 1.8%. No GSIB surcharge applies; no countercyclical buffer is specified (assume 0% for simplicity). Under Table 1 to § 217.11(a)(4)(iv), a capital conservation buffer greater than 1.25% but less than or equal to 1.875% (i.e., in the range >62.5% but ≤100% of the 2.5% requirement) corresponds to a maximum payout ratio of 60%. Maximum payout amount = eligible retained income × maximum payout ratio = $200M × 60% = $120M. Proposed payout = $95M (dividend) + $30M (bonuses) = $125M. Since $125M > $120M, the proposed distributions are NOT fully permissible. The maximum permissible payout amount is $120M.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution enters into a foreign exchange forward contract with a corporate counterparty. The contract has a contractual settlement period of 12 business days, which exceeds the market standard of 2 business days for such instruments. The institution has delivered USD 50 million to the counterparty but has not yet received the agreed EUR equivalent. It is now 8 business days after the counterparty's delivery was due, and the current fair value of the EUR deliverables owed to the institution is USD 51.2 million. The institution's aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities equal USD 1.3 billion, and its quarter-end total assets are USD 18 billion. Determine: (1) whether the unsettled-transactions framework applies to this contract and, if not, how it should be treated instead; (2) the correct risk-weighted asset amount for this position; and (3) whether the institution is subject to any additional market risk capital requirements beyond the standard credit-risk framework, and on what basis.
required_facts: The contractual settlement period of 12 business days exceeds the market standard of 2 business days, so the transaction does not have a 'normal settlement period' as defined in the unsettled-transactions rule.

Because the contractual settlement period is longer than the normal settlement period, the transaction is excluded from the unsettled-transactions framework and must be treated as an OTC derivative contract under the derivative contracts rule.
The risk-weighted asset amount is calculated using the OTC derivative contract exposure methodology (CEM or SA-CCR), not the 1,250 percent risk weight or the non-DvP/non-PvP escalation table.
The institution's aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities of USD 1.3 billion meet or exceed the $1 billion threshold, triggering applicability of the Subpart F market risk capital framework.
The institution is therefore subject to both Subpart D credit-risk capital requirements (for the derivative exposure) and Subpart F market risk capital requirements (due to trading book size).

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.38(b)(4) excludes transactions with contractual settlement periods longer than the normal settlement period and redirects them to § 217.34 as OTC derivative contracts; § 217.34 governs derivative contract exposure amounts; separately, the institution's trading book size triggers applicability under § 217.201(b)(1)(ii) of Subpart F market risk requirements.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.38(a)(3): A 'normal settlement period' requires the contractual settlement period to be ≤ the market standard AND ≤ 5 business days. The market standard for FX forwards is 2 business days; the contractual settlement period here is 12 business days. Therefore 12 > 2, so the transaction does NOT have a normal settlement period.

Step 2 — § 217.38(b)(4): Transactions with a contractual settlement period longer than the normal settlement period are explicitly excluded from § 217.38 and are instead 'treated as OTC derivative contracts as provided in § 217.34.' The unsettled-transactions framework does not apply.

Step 3 — § 217.34: The institution must calculate an exposure amount for this OTC derivative contract. If it is not an advanced approaches institution, it uses CEM under § 217.34(b) (or SA-CCR if elected). The risk-weighted asset amount is determined by multiplying the exposure amount by the applicable counterparty risk weight under Subpart D — NOT by the 1,250% risk weight table in § 217.38 or the non-DvP/non-PvP rules in § 217.38(e)(3).

Step 4 — § 217.201(b)(1)(ii): The institution's aggregate trading assets and trading liabilities are USD 1.3 billion, which meets the threshold of '$1 billion or more.' Therefore Subpart F market risk capital requirements apply to this institution, imposing an additional layer of capital requirements beyond the Subpart D credit-risk framework.

question_text: Heartland Mutual Holdings, Inc. is a bank holding company domiciled in the United States. Its primary operating subsidiary is a state-chartered insurance company that is regulated as a state-regulated insurer under applicable state insurance law. Heartland Mutual Holdings qualifies as an insurance bank holding company under the Board's capital rules and is subject to the Board's consolidated capital framework. The holding company has not elected to be treated under any alternative capital framework for insurance holding companies. Heartland Mutual Holdings reports the following consolidated capital figures: common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital of $3.2 billion, additional tier 1 (AT1) capital of $0.4 billion, and tier 2 capital of $0.6 billion. Its standardized total risk-weighted assets are $28 billion, and its average total consolidated assets are $35 billion. A compliance officer at the holding company is preparing the quarterly capital adequacy report and must determine: (1) whether Heartland Mutual Holdings is required to maintain the standard minimum CET1, tier 1, and total capital ratio requirements that apply to Board-regulated institutions generally; (2) whether it is required to maintain a leverage ratio; and (3) what condition, if any, must be satisfied for the exemption from the risk-based minimum capital ratios to apply. Provide a complete analysis of the holding company's minimum capital ratio obligations.
required_facts: An insurance bank holding company that is a state-regulated insurer is exempt from the minimum CET1, tier 1, and total capital ratio requirements only if it is subject to Subpart J of Part 217

Because Heartland Mutual Holdings has not elected the alternative framework under Subpart J, the gating condition for the risk-based ratio exemption is not satisfied, and the standard minimums (4.5% CET1, 6% tier 1, 8% total capital) apply
Heartland Mutual Holdings' CET1 ratio is 3.2/28 = approximately 11.43%, which exceeds the 4.5% minimum
Heartland Mutual Holdings' tier 1 capital ratio is 3.6/28 = approximately 12.86%, which exceeds the 6% minimum
Heartland Mutual Holdings' total capital ratio is 4.2/28 = 15.0%, which exceeds the 8% minimum
An insurance bank holding company is unconditionally exempt from the leverage ratio and supplementary leverage ratio requirements, regardless of Subpart J applicability

The exemption from risk-based minimum capital ratios under the insurance holding company provision requires both (a) status as a state-regulated insurer and (b) being subject to Subpart J — both conditions must be met

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.1(c)(1)(ii) establishes that Part 217 applies to mid-tier holding companies of insurance depository institution holding companies when the parent does not calculate minimum risk-based capital requirements under Subpart B by operation of § 217.10(f)(1); § 217.10(f)(1) then provides the substantive exemption — an insurance bank holding company that is a state-regulated insurer is not required to meet the minimum CET1, tier 1, and total capital ratio requirements if it is subject to Subpart J; § 217.10(f)(2) separately exempts insurance holding companies from the leverage ratio and supplementary leverage ratio requirements.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify the entity type: Heartland Mutual Holdings is an insurance bank holding company (a bank holding company whose primary subsidiary is a state-regulated insurer). Step 2 — Navigate to § 217.1(c)(1)(ii): This provision notes that the applicability of Part 217 to mid-tier holding companies turns on whether the parent 'does not calculate minimum risk-based capital requirements under subpart B of this part by operation of § 217.10(f)(1).' This cross-reference directs the reader to Subpart B. Step 3 — Navigate to § 217.10(f)(1): This paragraph states that an insurance bank holding company that is a state-regulated insurer is NOT required to meet the minimum capital ratio requirements in § 217.10(a)(1)(i) through (iii) — i.e., the 4.5% CET1 ratio, 6% tier 1 ratio, and 8% total capital ratio — IF the company is subject to Subpart J of Part 217. Step 4 — Identify the gating condition: The exemption from risk-based minimum ratios applies only if Heartland Mutual Holdings is subject to Subpart J (the alternative capital framework for insurance holding companies). The scenario states the holding company has not elected any alternative framework, so the gating condition for the § 217.10(f)(1) exemption is not met, and the standard risk-based minimums apply. Step 5 — Navigate to § 217.10(f)(2): Separately, an insurance bank holding company is not required to meet the leverage ratio (§ 217.10(a)(1)(iv)) or supplementary leverage ratio (§ 217.10(a)(1)(v)) requirements. This exemption is unconditional — it does not require Subpart J applicability. Step 6 — Compute ratios for completeness: CET1 ratio = 3.2/28 = 11.43%; Tier 1 ratio = 3.6/28 = 12.86%; Total capital ratio = 4.2/28 = 15.0%; Leverage ratio = 3.6/35 = 10.29%. Since the Subpart J condition is not met, the risk-based minimums (4.5%, 6%, 8%) apply and are all satisfied. The leverage ratio requirement does not apply regardless.

question_text: A Board-regulated institution is the originating party in a synthetic securitization of a $500 million commercial loan portfolio. To hedge its retained exposure, the institution has obtained a guarantee from a highly rated corporate entity. The guarantee covers the full notional amount of the retained tranche and was issued in writing, is unconditional, and is legally enforceable. However, the guarantee does not include a provision requiring the guarantor to make payment within a specified number of business days after the obligor fails to pay — instead, it permits the guarantor up to 90 days to evaluate and respond to a payment demand. The institution's compliance team is assessing whether this guarantee qualifies as a credit risk mitigant that can be recognized for risk-based capital purposes in connection with the synthetic securitization. Separately, the institution's risk team notes that the underlying loan portfolio includes several revolving credit facilities where borrowers may vary drawn amounts within agreed limits, and the securitization structure contains an early amortization provision triggered if the portfolio's excess spread falls below 1.0% for two consecutive months. Determine whether the institution may recognize the guarantee as a credit risk mitigant for the synthetic securitization, and identify any structural features of the securitization that independently affect the institution's ability to exclude the underlying exposures from its risk-weighted asset calculation.
required_facts: Recognition of the guarantee as a credit risk mitigant under § 217.45(a)(1) is conditioned on the synthetic securitization satisfying the operational criteria in § 217.41.

The guarantee must meet all criteria of the 'eligible guarantee' definition in § 217.2 (except criterion (3)) to satisfy § 217.41(b)(1)(ii); the 90-day response window likely fails the prompt-payment requirement in that definition, disqualifying the guarantee.

Because the guarantee does not qualify as an eligible guarantee under § 217.2, the condition in § 217.41(b)(1)(ii) is not met, and the institution cannot recognize the guarantee as a credit risk mitigant for risk-based capital purposes.

The securitization structure independently fails the operational criteria under § 217.41(a)(4) because it simultaneously includes revolving exposures with variable drawn amounts and an early amortization provision.

Failure to meet the § 217.41(a)(4) conditions means the institution must hold risk-based capital against the underlying exposures as if they had not been securitized and must deduct any after-tax gain-on-sale from common equity tier 1 capital.

The 'eligible guarantee' definition in § 217.2 also has cross-subpart relevance to the counterparty credit risk framework in § 217.132, including the standardized approach for OTC derivatives and repo-style transactions.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.45(a)(1) conditions credit risk mitigant recognition on satisfying operational criteria in § 217.41; § 217.41(b)(1)(ii) requires the guarantee to meet the definition of 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2 (except criterion (3)); § 217.2 defines 'eligible guarantee' with a prompt-payment criterion; § 217.41(a)(4) bars exclusion of transferred exposures from RWA if the securitization contains revolving exposures with variable drawn amounts AND an early amortization provision; § 217.132(c)(8) is reached via the definition of 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2 which cross-references haircut methodology for collateral recognition context.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — § 217.45(a)(1): An originating Board-regulated institution that has obtained a credit risk mitigant to hedge its exposure to a synthetic securitization may recognize the mitigant only if the securitization satisfies the operational criteria in § 217.41.

Step 2 — § 217.41(b): For synthetic securitizations, the institution may recognize a credit risk mitigant only if each condition in § 217.41(b) is satisfied. Condition (b)(1)(ii) requires that a guarantee meet all criteria in the definition of 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2, EXCEPT for criterion (3) of that definition.

Step 3 — § 217.2 definition of 'eligible guarantee': The definition lists several criteria. Criterion (2) requires that the guarantee be 'written, unconditional, and legally enforceable.' Criterion (4) (or the prompt-payment criterion, depending on enumeration) requires that upon default or non-payment by the obligor, the guarantor will pay the Board-regulated institution promptly. The 90-day evaluation window in the scenario's guarantee likely fails the prompt-payment requirement embedded in the eligible guarantee definition, meaning the guarantee does NOT qualify as an eligible guarantee under § 217.2 (even setting aside the excepted criterion (3)).

Step 4 — § 217.41(b)(1)(ii) consequence: Because the guarantee fails to meet the eligible guarantee definition criteria (other than the excepted criterion (3)), the condition in § 217.41(b)(1)(ii) is not satisfied. Therefore, the institution cannot recognize the guarantee as a credit risk mitigant for the synthetic securitization under § 217.45(a)(1).

Step 5 — § 217.41(a)(4): Separately, for the question of whether the underlying exposures can be excluded from RWA (relevant to the traditional securitization operational criteria, and informative for the synthetic securitization analysis), § 217.41(a)(4) provides that the securitization must not include underlying exposures where borrowers may vary drawn amounts within an agreed limit under a line of credit AND contain an early amortization provision. The scenario's structure includes both revolving credit facilities with variable drawn amounts AND an early amortization provision triggered by excess spread falling below 1.0%. This dual condition under § 217.41(a)(4)(i) and (ii) means the institution cannot exclude the transferred exposures from its RWA calculation, and must deduct any after-tax gain-on-sale from CET1.

Step 6 — § 217.132(c)(8): The definition of 'eligible guarantee' in § 217.2 is also relevant to the collateral haircut and counterparty credit risk framework under § 217.132, specifically paragraph (c)(8), which addresses the treatment of guarantees in the context of the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR). This cross-subpart link confirms that the eligible guarantee definition in § 217.2 has operative consequences not only in Subpart D but also in Subpart E's counterparty credit risk calculations.

scenario_parameters.guarantee_defect: 90-day evaluation window before payment (fails prompt-payment criterion)
scenario_parameters.structural_defect_1: revolving credit facilities with variable drawn amounts in underlying pool
scenario_parameters.structural_defect_2: early amortization provision triggered at excess spread < 1.0% for 2 consecutive months

question_text: A Board-regulated institution is a clearing member client that has entered into an interest rate swap with a central counterparty (CCP) through a clearing member. The institution posts initial margin of $8 million and variation margin of $2 million to the clearing member, who holds these funds in a segregated omnibus account established under applicable CFTC regulations. The CCP is currently recognized as a qualifying central counterparty (QCCP), but the institution's compliance team has just identified that the CCP failed to satisfy one of the three core QCCP eligibility requirements two months ago and has not yet remedied the deficiency. The institution wants to continue treating the CCP as a QCCP for risk-weighting purposes while it monitors the situation. Separately, the institution is also evaluating whether it can apply the collateral haircut approach to recognize the credit risk mitigation benefits of the posted collateral for this cleared transaction. The collateral consists entirely of U.S. Treasury securities (zero percent risk-weight sovereign) with a current fair value of $9.5 million, and the exposure amount of the derivative contract (before collateral recognition) is $10.2 million. Assuming the institution uses standard supervisory haircuts and there is no currency mismatch, determine: (1) whether the institution may continue to treat the CCP as a QCCP at this point in time, and for how long it may do so going forward if the deficiency remains unremedied; and (2) the net exposure amount under the collateral haircut approach for this transaction, identifying which transaction types are eligible for that approach and confirming whether this cleared derivative qualifies.
required_facts: Under the QCCP grace period rule, a Board-regulated institution may continue to treat a non-compliant CCP as a QCCP for up to three months following the determination of the deficiency; since only two months have elapsed, continued QCCP treatment is still permissible.

If the CCP does not remedy the deficiency within three months of the initial determination, the institution must cease treating it as a QCCP and may not resume QCCP treatment until the CCP has satisfied the eligibility requirements continuously for three months.

The omnibus account established under 17 CFR parts 190 and 300 expressly satisfies the collateral segregation operational requirement for cleared transactions, supporting recognition of the exposure as a cleared transaction.
State that §217.37(c) covers collateralized OTC derivative contracts, not cleared transactions; do not say the cleared swap itself qualifies as a collateralized derivative contract.
Do not plug the posted $9.5M Treasury collateral into ΣC; under the source text, posted collateral belongs in the Es term, and §217.37(c) is not the right cleared-transaction formula in any event.

With no currency mismatch (Hfx = 0) and applying the appropriate standard supervisory haircut to the U.S. Treasury collateral, the net exposure amount is greater than zero, meaning the collateral does not fully offset the exposure after haircuts.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.3(f) for QCCP grace period rules (which references the QCCP definition in §217.2), then §217.3(a) for cleared transaction operational requirements (also referencing §217.2 definition of 'cleared transaction'), and finally §217.37(c) in Subpart D for the collateral haircut approach eligibility and exposure amount formula applicable to collateralized derivative contracts.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — §217.3(f): The institution identified that the CCP failed to satisfy one or more of the QCCP requirements (paragraphs (2)(i)–(2)(iii) of the QCCP definition in §217.2) two months ago. Under §217.3(f), a Board-regulated institution may continue to treat a CCP as a QCCP for up to three months following the determination of non-compliance. Since only two months have elapsed, the institution may still treat the CCP as a QCCP. However, if the deficiency is not remedied within three months of the initial determination, the institution must stop treating the CCP as a QCCP. It has approximately one month remaining in the grace period. Step 2 — §217.3(a) + §217.2 definition of 'cleared transaction': The omnibus account established under 17 CFR parts 190 and 300 satisfies the collateral segregation requirement of §217.3(a)(2), which is one of the operational requirements for recognizing an exposure as a cleared transaction under the definition in §217.2. This confirms the transaction can be treated as a cleared transaction. Step 3 — §217.37(c)(1) in Subpart D: The collateral haircut approach is available for eligible margin loans, repo-style transactions, collateralized derivative contracts, and single-product netting sets of such transactions. A cleared interest rate swap is a collateralized derivative contract, so it qualifies. Step 4 — §217.37(c)(2) exposure amount formula: Exposure = max{0, [(ΣE − ΣC) + Σ(Es × Hs) + Σ(Efx × Hfx)]}. ΣE = exposure amount of the OTC derivative = $10.2 million. ΣC = fair value of collateral (U.S. Treasuries) = $9.5 million. For U.S. Treasury securities (sovereign, zero risk weight, assume residual maturity drives haircut — standard supervisory haircut for sovereign securities with maturity ≤1 year is 0.5%; for 1–5 years is 2%; assume a representative haircut of 2% for intermediate maturity). Es × Hs = $9.5M × 0.02 = $0.19M (collateral haircut applied to net collateral position). No currency mismatch so Hfx = 0. Net exposure = max{0, [($10.2M − $9.5M) + $0.19M]} = max{0, $0.70M + $0.19M} = $0.89 million. (Note: exact haircut depends on maturity of the Treasury securities; the answer must demonstrate the formula structure and identify the applicable haircut from the standard supervisory haircut table in §217.37(c)(3).)

scenario_parameters.collateral_type: U.S. Treasury securities (zero percent risk-weight sovereign)
scenario_parameters.collateral_account_type: segregated omnibus account under 17 CFR parts 190 and 300
scenario_parameters.ccp_status: QCCP deficiency identified 2 months ago, not yet remedied

question_text: A Board-regulated institution holds a $50 million investment in a separate account offered through a variable annuity product. The institution has also entered into a stable value protection contract on that same separate account, under which it is the purchaser of the protection. The carrying value of the investment is $50 million, of which $8 million is attributable to the stable value protection feature. The remaining $42 million represents the institution's direct equity exposure to the underlying fund assets. The institution is not an advanced approaches institution and has not elected to use the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk for its OTC derivative contracts. The stable value protection contract is structured as an OTC derivative. Determine: (1) how the $8 million portion attributable to the stable value protection must be treated for risk-weighting purposes, including what methodology applies to measure the exposure amount of the derivative; and (2) how the $42 million remaining portion must be treated, including which look-through or risk-weight approach applies and why the separate account classification is the operative trigger.
required_facts: The investment qualifies as a 'separate account' as defined in § 217.2, which triggers treatment as an equity exposure to an investment fund under § 217.51(a)(2).

The $8 million portion attributable to the stable value protection must be treated as an exposure to the protection provider (not as a fund equity exposure), because the institution is the purchaser of stable value protection under § 217.51(a)(3)(ii).
The $8 million exposure to the protection provider is characterized as an equity derivative, with adjusted carrying value determined under § 217.51(b)(1) and (b)(3).

Because the institution is not an advanced approaches institution and has not elected SA-CCR, the exposure amount for the OTC equity derivative must be calculated using the current exposure methodology (CEM) under § 217.34(b), not SA-CCR.
§ 217.133 (cleared transactions, Subpart E) is not applicable here because the institution has not made the SA-CCR election under § 217.34(a)(1)(ii) that would trigger its application.
The remaining $42 million is an equity exposure to an investment fund and must be risk-weighted using the look-through approaches in § 217.53, not the Simple Risk-Weight Approach (SRWA) in § 217.52.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.51(a)(2) requires treating a 'separate account' investment as an equity exposure to an investment fund; 'separate account' is defined in § 217.2 (Subpart A); § 217.51(a)(3)(ii) splits the carrying value — the stable value protection portion is treated as an equity derivative exposure to the protection provider, with adjusted carrying value per § 217.51(b)(1) and (b)(3); § 217.51(a)(3)(iii) directs that the institution providing stable value protection treats it as an equity derivative, but here the institution is the purchaser, so the $8M is an exposure to the provider; the derivative exposure amount for a non-advanced-approaches institution not electing SA-CCR is calculated under § 217.34(b) (CEM); § 217.34(a)(1)(ii) notes that if SA-CCR is elected, § 217.133 applies to cleared transactions — but since no election is made, CEM under § 217.34(b) governs; the $42M remainder is an equity exposure to an investment fund under § 217.51(a)(1) and must use the look-through approaches in § 217.53.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — § 217.51(a)(2): The investment is in a 'separate account' (as defined in § 217.2), so the entire investment must initially be treated as if it were an equity exposure to an investment fund. Step 2 — § 217.2 (Subpart A): Locate the definition of 'separate account' to confirm the product qualifies, establishing the cross-subpart link from Subpart D to Subpart A. Step 3 — § 217.51(a)(3)(ii): Because the institution purchased stable value protection on the separate account, the carrying value is bifurcated: the $8M attributable to the stable value protection is treated as an exposure to the protection provider (not as an equity exposure to the fund), and the remaining $42M continues as an equity exposure to an investment fund. Step 4 — The $8M exposure to the protection provider is characterized as an equity derivative. Its adjusted carrying value is determined under § 217.51(b)(1) and (b)(3). The exposure amount for this OTC derivative contract must be calculated using the current exposure methodology (CEM) under § 217.34(b), because the institution is not an advanced approaches institution and has not elected SA-CCR under § 217.34(a)(1)(ii). Step 5 — § 217.34(a)(1)(ii) cross-references § 217.133 (Subpart E) for cleared transactions only when SA-CCR is elected; since no election was made, § 217.133 is not triggered and CEM applies. Step 6 — The $42M remainder is an equity exposure to an investment fund and must be risk-weighted using the look-through approaches in § 217.53, not the SRWA in § 217.52, per § 217.51(a)(1).

question_text: Heartland Mutual Bancshares is a bank holding company organized as a limited liability company (LLC) under state law. It has issued two classes of membership interests: Class M interests and Class N interests. Under the LLC agreement, both Class M and Class N holders share equally in operating distributions and bear losses proportionate to their capital contributions. However, upon liquidation, Class N holders are entitled to receive the full return of their contributed capital before any distributions are made to Class M holders. The holding company has total assets of $4.2 billion and is subject to the Board's regulatory capital framework. A compliance officer is evaluating whether either class of membership interests qualifies as common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital. As part of that analysis, the officer must also determine the correct risk-weighting treatment for the holding company's $180 million portfolio of on-balance sheet commercial loans, none of which are cleared transactions, securitization exposures, or equity exposures. Specifically: (1) Which class or classes of membership interests, if any, qualify as CET1 capital, and why does the other class fail to qualify? (2) What is the risk-weighted asset amount for the commercial loan portfolio, assuming a 100% risk weight applies to each exposure, and what is the general mechanics framework the institution must follow to arrive at that figure?
required_facts: Class N membership interests do not qualify as CET1 capital because they hold a liquidation preference over Class M interests, meaning they are not the most subordinated claim and do not share losses proportionately with Class M (failing the subordination and loss-sharing criteria for CET1 eligibility).

Class M membership interests qualify as CET1 capital (provided all other applicable CET1 criteria are satisfied) because they are the most subordinated claim in liquidation and bear losses proportionate to capital contributions.
Class N interests may potentially qualify as additional tier 1 capital or tier 2 capital if they satisfy the applicable criteria for those tiers.
The institution must determine the exposure amount of each on-balance sheet commercial loan and multiply it by the applicable risk weight to compute risk-weighted assets for general credit risk.
Risk-weighted assets for the $180 million commercial loan portfolio = $180 million × 100% = $180 million.
Total risk-weighted assets for general credit risk equals the sum of all individual risk-weighted asset amounts calculated under the general risk-weighting mechanics framework.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: § 217.501 governs CET1 eligibility for non-stock holding companies and cross-references § 217.20(b) criteria (defined in § 217.2 via the Additional tier 1 capital and CET1 definitions) and directs the institution to apply risk-weighting mechanics under § 217.31 for general credit risk exposures.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Applicability of § 217.501: Heartland Mutual Bancshares is organized as an LLC (a non-stock legal entity) and is subject to Part 217, so § 217.501 applies. Step 2 — CET1 criteria for non-stock companies (§ 217.501(c)(3)): The scenario mirrors the 'Senior and junior classes' example in § 217.501(c)(3). Class N interests have a liquidation preference over Class M interests, meaning Class N is not the most subordinated claim and does not share losses proportionately — failing criteria (i) and (viii) of § 217.20(b)(1). Therefore Class N does NOT qualify as CET1. Class M interests are the most subordinated claim and bear losses first; provided all other § 217.20(b) criteria are met, Class M qualifies as CET1. Step 3 — Definition cross-reference via § 217.2: The term 'Board-regulated institution' is defined in § 217.2, confirming Heartland Mutual Bancshares falls within the scope of Part 217's capital and risk-weighting rules. Step 4 — Risk-weighting mechanics under § 217.31: For the $180 million commercial loan portfolio, the institution must follow § 217.31(a)(1) to determine the exposure amount of each on-balance sheet exposure, then under § 217.31(a)(2) multiply each exposure amount by the applicable risk weight (100% for standard commercial loans). Risk-weighted assets = $180M × 100% = $180 million. Total RWA for general credit risk under § 217.31(b) equals the sum of all such risk-weighted amounts = $180 million.

question_text: Heartland Mutual Insurance Holding Company is an insurance bank holding company that is a state-regulated insurer. As of January 1, 2023, it was not subject to the Board's capital framework. On February 15, 2025, Heartland's board of directors is considering declaring a discretionary cash dividend of $85 million and awarding $12 million in discretionary bonus payments to senior executives. Heartland's net income for the four preceding calendar quarters totals $310 million, and the average net income over those same four quarters is $295 million. Heartland's common equity tier 1 capital ratio, calculated as of December 31, 2024, stands at 7.2%, against standardized total risk-weighted assets of $4.8 billion. Heartland also maintains a portfolio of OTC interest rate swap contracts with a single counterparty, for which it uses the standardized approach to calculate exposure-at-default; the portfolio is subject to a qualifying master netting agreement. Determine: (1) whether Heartland is currently subject to restrictions on distributions and discretionary bonus payments, and if so, what maximum payout amount applies; and (2) what methodology Heartland must use to calculate exposure-at-default for its OTC derivative portfolio, and whether any alternative methodology is available with prior regulatory approval.
required_facts: Heartland qualifies for the §217.306(a) BBA transition exemption because it is an insurance bank holding company that was not subject to Part 217 on January 1, 2023
The §217.306 exemption remains in effect on February 15, 2025 because that date precedes the March 31, 2026 expiration in §217.306(b)
Heartland is NOT subject to distribution or discretionary bonus payment restrictions under §217.11 during the exemption period; no maximum payout amount limitation applies
Eligible retained income, if the §217.11 framework were applicable, would be $310 million (the greater of trailing four-quarter net income of $310M and average net income of $295M)

State that §217.11(a)(3)(i) defines the capital conservation buffer as the lowest of the CET1, Tier 1, and Total capital excesses over their minimums; the provided facts do not establish that full buffer from CET1 alone.
For OTC derivative contracts subject to a qualifying master netting agreement, Heartland must use the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) under §217.132(c) to calculate EAD
Heartland may use the internal models methodology under §217.132(d) as an alternative for its OTC derivative EAD calculation only with prior written approval of the Board

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Start at §217.306 BBA transition relief (exempts qualifying insurance holding companies from §217.11 distribution restrictions until March 31, 2026), then trace §217.11 to understand the capital conservation buffer payout restriction framework, then §217.10 for minimum capital ratio requirements that underpin the buffer calculation, then §217.132(c) for the mandatory EAD methodology for OTC derivatives subject to a qualifying master netting agreement.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — §217.306(a): Heartland is an insurance bank holding company that was not subject to Part 217 on January 1, 2023. §217.306(a) provides that, notwithstanding any other provision of Part 217, such an institution is not subject to any restrictions on distributions or discretionary bonus payments under §217.11. Step 2 — §217.306(b): This exemption ceases to be effective after March 31, 2026. Since the proposed action date is February 15, 2025, which is before March 31, 2026, the exemption is still in force. Therefore Heartland is NOT subject to the §217.11 capital conservation buffer payout restrictions, and no maximum payout amount calculation is required for the dividend or bonus payments. Step 3 — §217.11 (intermediate, for completeness): Had the exemption not applied, §217.11(a)(2)(i) defines eligible retained income as the greater of (A) net income for the four preceding quarters net of distributions = $310M, or (B) average net income = $295M, so eligible retained income = $310M. The maximum payout amount would equal eligible retained income multiplied by the applicable maximum payout ratio, determined by the capital conservation buffer as of December 31, 2024. Step 4 — §217.10(a)(1)(i): The minimum CET1 ratio is 4.5%. Heartland's CET1 ratio of 7.2% exceeds this minimum. The capital conservation buffer = 7.2% − 4.5% = 2.7%, which exceeds the 2.5% minimum conservation buffer threshold, meaning no payout restriction would apply even absent the §217.306 exemption. Step 5 — §217.132(c): For OTC derivative contracts subject to a qualifying master netting agreement, a Board-regulated institution must use the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) methodology in §217.132(c) to calculate EAD, or, with prior written approval of the Board, the internal models methodology in §217.132(d). No other methodology is permissible for this exposure type.

scenario_parameters.otc_portfolio: interest rate swaps subject to qualifying master netting agreement

question_text: Heartland Mutual Holdings, Inc. is a top-tier depository institution holding company that owns and operates several insurance underwriting subsidiaries. As of June 30 of the prior calendar year, approximately 31 percent of Heartland's total consolidated assets (calculated under GAAP) were held in insurance underwriting companies unrelated to credit risk. Heartland files financial statements under GAAP (not exclusively under Statutory Accounting Principles), is subject to a state insurance capital requirement, and has no subsidiary depository institution holding company that files exclusively under SAP. Heartland's common equity tier 1 capital is $3.8 billion, its tier 1 capital is $4.2 billion, and its total capital is $5.1 billion. Its standardized total risk-weighted assets are $38 billion. Heartland is not subject to the Federal Reserve's stress testing requirements and is not a global systemically important bank holding company. Its capital conservation buffer, calculated as of the last day of the previous calendar quarter, stands at 1.9 percent. Heartland's board of directors is considering declaring a discretionary cash dividend of $180 million and paying discretionary bonuses totaling $40 million to senior executives this quarter. Heartland's eligible retained income for the current quarter is $310 million. Determine: (1) whether Heartland is subject to the specialized capital framework applicable to institutions significantly engaged in insurance activities, and (2) whether Heartland's proposed distributions and discretionary bonus payments are permissible under its capital conservation buffer constraints, including the applicable maximum payout ratio and maximum payout amount.

Heartland's capital conservation buffer of 1.9% falls in the range greater than 1.875% and less than or equal to 2.5%, yielding a maximum payout ratio of 60%
Maximum payout amount = $310 million eligible retained income × 60% = $186 million
Proposed aggregate distributions and discretionary bonus payments total $220 million ($180M dividend + $40M bonuses)
$220 million exceeds the $186 million maximum payout amount, so the proposed payments are not permissible as structured
Heartland must reduce total distributions and discretionary bonus payments to no more than $186 million in the current calendar quarter

Total capital ratio = 5.1/38 = 13.42%; minimum total = 8.0%; total capital buffer = 5.42%. Capital conservation buffer = lowest = 5.05% (tier 1 buffer).
